Fay’s acts to take over Mann Drug 


By Michael Friedman 

HIGH POINT, N.C.—Fay's 
Drug Company has moved to 
strengthen its thrust into the 
Southeast by signing a letter of 
intent to purchase the 28-unit 
Mann ng Company of North 
Carolina for an undisclosed 
amount of cash. 


The acquisition, which still 
awaits approval by Fay’s board 
of directors and Mann's stock- 
holders, would more than dou- 
ble Fay’s holdings in the Car- 
olinas. 

The chain currently operates 
25 stores in South Carolina and 
one in North Carolina, as well as 


75 outlets in New York State and 
one in Pennsylvania. 

The Mann takeover would 
also be Fay’s fourth chain ac- 
quisition since August 1978, ina 
period which saw the chain 
grow from 51 outlets to its cur- 
rent roster of 102.

Eckerd will celebrate 
1,000th-store opening 


NEW YORK—Eckerd will become the 
second chain to reach the 1,009 store 
mark this November, chairman and 
president Stewart Turley told a group of 
stock analysts here at a meeting of the 
New York Society of Security Analysts 
(NYSSA). 

The Clearwater, Fla.-based chain will 
herald its 1,000th store milestone with a 
heavily promoted “1001 Drug Store Cel- 
ebration” slated to begin mid-November. 

The promotion will be chainwide, 
since there will be no specific 1,000th 
store. Each of the chain's 13 divisions will 
be opening one or two new stores during 
November, and construction plans indi- 
cate that at least 1,000 units will be open 
by then, possibly as many as 1,010. 

The promotion will include a chain- 
wide consumer prize contest featuring 
six winners for each store. Store man- 
agers will conduct their own drawings 
and the results will be delivered to head- 
quarters. The six store-level winners be- 
come eligible for five grand prizes. 


The first grand prize is a choice be- 
tween 1001 items from any Eckerd store 
or $20,000. Second prize is matching 
his and her Chevy Vega automobiles, 
and third prize is a Datsun B-210. Fourth 
prize is a Boston Whaler boat (with 
motor and trailer), while the fifth prize is a 
Sony Betamax Video Recorder and 
Color TV set. 

The festivities also include cash prize 
incentives for employees. Through a 
mystery shopper system, 40 to 50 em- 
ployees vill be chosen as eligible to win 
up to £1001 per division. 

The contest will be advertised through 
television and newspaper spots which 
will break Nov. 15. Ad drop-ins will sup- 
plement daily advertisement on subse- 
quent days until the grand openings. 

The first chain to clear the 1,000 store 
mark was Revco, which achieved this 
milestone in early 1978. Today, the 
Twinsburg, Ohio, chain operates 1,180 
units, the greatest number of stores in

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


17 


As they face the coming decade, 
drug wholesalers must be ready to 
avail themselves of the numerous 
challenges and opportunities that lie 
ahead, and to confront the problems 
that will undoubtedly accompany 
them into the 1980's. 

To get a glimpse of the future, one 
must take a good\ long look at the 
present, particulanly the events of 
the past year: 

@ The Louis Zahn Drug Co. con- 
verted to a fully automated ware- 
housing system, with the installa- 
tion of 12 SI ITEMatic picking 
machines. 

e After 134 years in drug wholesal- 
ing, the Henry B. Gilpin Co. is 
forced to liquidate all its distribution 
holdings, effectively pulling out of 
the business. — 

@ Bergen Brunswig entered the 
Sunbelt market with the purchase of 
two former Gilpin houses, and a 


DRUG ST@RE NEWS 


third opened in Houston. 

@ The Alco Standard Corp., a dis- 
tribution-manufacturing-resources 
conglomerate, strengthens its hold- 
ings in drug distribution by acquir- 
ing the Geer Drug Co., and Gilpin’s 
Baltimore house. 

e Fifty-year-old Southwestern 
Drug Co. is acquired by another 
conglomerate, Gulf United Corp., 
which previously had no properties 
in drug distribution. 

@ America’s largest drug whole- 
saler, McKesson Drug Co.. puts all 
Skaggs’ Arizona drug stores on-line 


with its Econoscript in-pharmacy 
computers. 

@ The National Wholesale Drug- 
gists’ Association establishes an 
order “Clearinghouse” for vendors 
and wholesalers. 

@ Gilman Bros. drug wholesalers 
acquires a Providence, R.I., jobber, 
Dexter Co., committing in a big way 
to service merchandising. 

® LAD Co. purchases Allied Dis- 
tributors, a supplier of sundry mer- 
chandise, enabling the drug whole- 
saler to beef up its offerings to drug 
stores. 


@ Joseph L. Garde, president of 
Spectro Industries and the NWDA, 
testifies before an F.D.A. hearing to 
provide the wholesaler’s viewpoint 
on patient labeling. 

® McKesson Drug Co. sheots past 
the $1 billion mark in volume for the 
second year in a row. 

Clearly, the past 12 months or so 
have been nothing short of dramatic 
for wholesale druggists. Equally ap- 
parent is the realization that the 
spoils of drug wholesaling go to 
those who run the most efficient 
shops, cultivate the strongest retail 
customers, provide the best, most 
needed services, offer the most com- 
plete merchandise packages, and 
keep a tight grip on warehousing 
and delivery costs. 

In the words of one industry mem- 
ber, it’s “a survival of the fittest” en- 
vironment. And it’s not likely to be 
anything less in the years to come. 


n an effort to trim 

costs and main- 

tain profits, most 

wholesalers have 
attempted to streamline 
warehouse operations, 
and cut back on person- 
nel. But while 58% of 
those wholesalers polled 
said they pared down 
staffs, 89% claimed the 
cost of labor has in- 
creased.

Drug Store News, in an effort to 
bring the wholesaler picture into 
focus, polled members of the indus- 
try nationwide to learn about their 
customer and merchandise mix, the 
services they offer, their methods of 
warehousing and delivery, the na- 
ture of their businesses in general. 

Survey indications 

From the responses Drug Store 
News gathered, it was determined 
that the average wholesaler services 
630 retail customers, via 410 daily 
orders out of two warehouses, with 
an average size of 55,000 sq. ft. His 
customer base is increasing, accord- 
ing to 69% of the respondents, which 
could be attributed to greater chain 
business. An upswing of chain cus- 
tomers was reported by 52% of the 
respondents, and 34% see small 
chains and independents as their 
chief market in the future. A 1% to 
10% jump in chain business was re- 
ported by nearly half the respon- 
dents. 

“It seems to me that wholesalers 
already have a good degree of chain 
accommodations,” says Charles 
Trefrey, executive vp of the Wash- 
ington-based Drug Wholesalers As- 
sociation. “In some instances, it’s 
fill-in. But even there wholesalers 
can provide substantial service, 
with precise deliveries that mini- 
mize labor.” 

As for overall business growth, 
which the majority of respondents 
reported, there might well be a con- 
nection with the stepped-up use of 
wholesalers by vendors, as a less ex- 
pensive means of distributing prod- 
uct. 

“As the cost of manufacturer calls 
on retailers increases, vendors are 
going to wholesalers in increasing 
numbers,” says Jack Fenstermaker, 
a consultant to drug wholesalers and 
manufacturers based in San Fran- 
cisco. 

The poll also revealed that whole- 
salers are supplying a greater num- 
ber of services to retailers than they 
did in the past. Electronic order en- 


Rh 


try is provided by 82% of the respon- 
dents. In-pharmacy computers are 
offered by 59%. Inventory manage- 
ment is offered by 56%. Eighty-five 
per cent have co-op ad programs, 
and 79% will make emergency deliv- 
eries. Service merchandising is sup- 
plied by 49%, and 49% have volun- 
tary groups. 

Though wholesalers apparently 
no longer see themselves as just a 
source of product, a major whole- 
saler complaint is that retailers ex- 
press little interest in their rosters 
of management and operations-re- 
lated services. 

Expanding merchandise mix 

“Wholesalers have to do a better 
job of selling these services,” says 
Fenstermaker. “I see a tendency to- 
ward more services, and I look for 


more in the future.” 

Merchandise mix has definitely 
expanded among wholesalers and, 
as evidenced by the LAD Co.’s ac- 
quisition of a sundries house, drug 
distributors are putting more em- 
phasis on the front-end of the phar- 
macy to get on board a trend toward 
one-source supplying. Nearly 83% 
of those questioned claimed they 
had expanded their mix in the last 
five years. New lines mentioned by 
respondents included cosmetics, 
gift items, appliances, convalescent 
aids, housewares, and food. As a 
matter of fact, some 33% said they 
broadened their mixes to include 
groceries. 

“McKesson and LAD present in- 
teresting developments in merchan- 
dise,” says Fenstermaker, “in that 
they’re trying to reach their custom- 
ers with greater lines.” 

Wholesalers are also trying to re- 
ach their customers through 
stronger link-ups like affiliated 
groups. The days when retailers 
cherry-picked suppliers have got to 
be over, most wholesalers believe, in 
order for the retailer and supplier to 
survive. 

Importance of affiliated groups 

Not surprisingly, when asked if 
they believed affiliated groups were 
important for the future of drug 
wholesaling, 79% answered yes. But 
only 49% said they had a voluntary 
program (a wholesaler-originated 
affiliated group of retailers). 

The ages-old problem with setting 
up a voluntary is getting indepen- 
dent retailers to relinquish some of 
that independence. 

“IT see more voluntaries coming,” 
says Fenstermaker. “It’s a slow 
change in philosophy for the retailer. 
Tying into order entry, for example, 
is like surrendering some of his free- 
dom.” 

But Charles Trefrey of DWA ad- 
vises: “Affiliated groups seem to be 
successful in certain markets. But 
they’re not a panacea for every 
wholesaler in every market.” 

In some markets, cooperative 
groups (in which retailers band to- 
gether for the purpose of group ad- 
vertising and buying power, choos- 
ing one or more wholesalers for 
supply) are more effective than the 
voluntaries.

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


based co-op with 60-plus members 
in the Metropolitan N.Y. Area, is 
just such an example. Using whole- 
saler Ketchum Distributors for 
pharmaceutical and OTC merchan- 
dise, the group buys sundry and 
promotional items on a direct basis, 
and provides its members with ad- 
vertising and merchandising exper- 
tise. 

“There is a greater need than ever 
to find viable solutions to the chang- 
ing buying habits and competition 
confronting the independent drug 
store owner,” says Sy Schwartz, ex- 
ecutive director of Tabard. “With 
the threat of chain drug stores, and 
tightening profit margins, there are 
more demands on the independent 
than ever before.” 

Changes are coming rapidly for 
wholesalers in the area of warehous- 
ing and distribution. As wholesaler 
profit margins decrease, cutbacks in 
operational costs become more and 
more imperative. But with those 
shrinking margins have come bal- 
looning labor costs in the ware- 
house. 

Poll responses indicated that 65% 
of the wholesalers surveyed operate 
manual warehouses, 35% sport 
semiautomated warehousing opera- 
tions (using conveyors, gravity 
feeds), and 5% have fully automated 
systems (using computerized pick- 
ing, or mechanical picking). 

Warehouse personnel numbers 
(which average 45 per warehouse ac- 
cording to the poll), have been de- 
creased by 58% of the respondents 
in the last five years. But 89% stated 
that the cost of warehouse labor has 
increased, on an average of 40% per 
wholesaler operation in that same 
time period. 


The blessings of automation have 
evidently not come to most whole- 
salers. 

“Automation is very appropriate 
for wholesalers of a certain size,” 
explains Fenstermaker. “But it’s 
probably out of the reach of other 
smaller wholesalers.” 

According to Charles Trefrey, la- 
bor costs may come down in the fu- 
ture, solving the problem of high- 
cost warehousing. 

“Labor is only a problem in certain 
markets,” he says, “where the 
unions can be difficult. But in 
Dallas, and markets like it, the 
problem is reversed. Dallas is a full- 
employment market, and whole- 
salers have a very difficult time find- 
ing people.” 

Obviously, the state of wholesal- 
ing in general is changing. The gi- 
ants of the industry—like McKessgn 
and Bergen Brunswig—continue to 
grow, and continue to take advan- 
tage of the opportunities made avail- 
able by both vendors and retailers. 

Says Joseph L. Garde, president 
of Spectro; “We’re delivering prod- 
ucts a lot more efficiently than ever 
before. And we’re delivering. . . at 
a very reasonable cost.” 

Unfortunately, as the great and 
powerful in drug wholesaling be- 
come even more great and powerful, 
the small, regional one-house whole- 
saler is crushed beneath the weight 
of spiraling costs, weak customers, 
stiff competition, and decreasing 
margins. 

Recently, several major corpora- 
tions have jumped into drug whole- 
saling from a base of other related or 
unrelated businesses. These com- 
panies see a potential in drug dis- 
tribution through the type of financ- 


ing they can provide, and are build- 
ing empires on the acquisition of 
small, entrepreneurial drug houses. 

The Alco Standard Corp. is per- 
haps the prime example of this 
trend. A nearly $2 billion company 
with holdings in manufacturing, dis- 
tribution, and resources, Alco en- 
tered drug distribution with the 
acquisition of Philadelphia-based 
The Drug House in 1977, following 
with the 1978 purchase of Chat- 
tanooga, Tenn.-based Duff Bros. 
Earlier this year, the conglomerate 
completed a deal to acquire Geer 
Drug Co. of Charleston, S.C., and 
most recently purchased the Bal- 
timore Metroplex facility owned by 
the Henry B. Gilpin Co. 

The pattern is very apparent. Alco 
buys drug houses that are usually 
family-owned, and pumps in the nec- 
essary finances and support ser- 
vices to make them hum. 

“We foresee a drug distribution 
system that will be one of the lead- 
ers in the country,” said Ed Patrone, 
Alco’s head of distribution services, 
at the time of the Geer agreement in 
principle. “We have no timetable per 
se, but it is our definite intention to 
create a national distribution sys- 
tem.” 

In light of Alco’s efforts, not to 
mention those of the established 
super powers in drug distribution, it 
appears that the future might be 
shakey for the small wholesaler. 

“There is a lot of outside money 
looking at wholesale drug distribu- 
tion as a very advantageous busi- 
ness to be in,” says Charles Trefrey. 
“What this means for the future I 
don’t know... . . But the little entre- 
preneurial houses are still coming 
into existence.”

While independent drug store op- 
erators all across the country value 
the wholesaler for the broad mer- 
chandise mix he can supply, they 
find that they need more than prod- 
uct to survive against the growing 
power of the chains. 

On the one hand, they require a 
price structure that allows them to 
stay in the discount ball park; on the 
other hand, they seek help in 
planogramming, promotion and ad- 
vertising. Nor is a merchandise se- 
lection of any good unless it arrives 
on time, in the proper quantities, 
and does so consistently. 

Arnold Albert of Albert’s Drug 
Stores in Orlando, Fla., has a great 
deal of chain competition in his trad- 
ing area, not the least of which is 
represented by the Jack Eckerd 
Corp. “But the product mix I get 
from McKesson keeps me current 
and competitive in the market,” says 
Albert. who operates three outlets 
with a food service unit in each. 

“I think the mix I| receive is a good 
one,’ says Kenneth Rogers, proprie- 
tor of — Pharmacy in Attica, 
Kan. “I can buy goods for less money 
if { buy direct from the manufac- 
turer, but since I’ve switched over to 
McPike Inc.. I’ve gotten all the sun- 
dries I need and much better inven- 
tory control.” 

Pricing under attack 

Independent pharmacists, how- 
ever, are somewhat more critical of 
the prices wholesalers charge for 
this merchandise. 

“Although I’m getting the right 


merchandise, I’m paying too much 
for it,” says George Griffon, general 
manager of Griffon’s Pharmacy in 
Baton Rouge, La. “Lately, prices 
seem to go up on a daily basis. ” 

“In some instances, the pricing is 
good,’ says Diane Croteau of 
Robillard’s Pharmacy, in Gardner, 
Mass. “Usually, we make out well 
when there’s a deal run by the com- 
pany. But in day-to-day business, we 
cant compete with discounters and 
chain drug stores. We buy some- 
times at the price they sell for.” 

“I see things sold for less than I 
bought them for,” says a spokesman 
for Edison Pharmacy, in Edison, 
N.J. “One example would be baby 
formula. I’ve seen it on sale for 


$1.09, when I bought it from a 
wholesaler for $1.20.” 

Independent operators seem to 
accept this disadvantage, realizing 
that larger chains can beat most 
wholesalers at the volume-buying 
game. Many, however, believe that 
wholesalers might obtain better 
deals for them if they concentrated 
their efforts more in that direction. 

“The wholesaler is no longer price- 
conscious,” says Laurence J. Brown, 
president and general manager of 
Low Cost Drugs in Walla Walla, 
Wash. “He’s supposedly providing 
us with goods at a lower cost, but in 
some cases the wholesale price is not 
that low. He may buy an item for a 
dollar, and that’s his cost, but if he 
worked on it, he might get it for 80¢, 
and lower our acquisition costs.” 

srown, who operates six stores 
under six different logos, says that 
the wholesaler has become more !ike 
a distributor than a source of price- 
discounted merchandise. 

For their part, wholesalers say 
that they have indeed been trying Lo 
cut the retailer's Thev ve de- 
veloped order-entry systems, which 
save them time and iabor expenses 
and transiate. in the tong run, into 
savings for the drug store operator. 

“Sure. order-entry is good,’ says 
Brown. “It’s good for the wholesaler. 
It saves him money, which he’s sup- 
posedly passing along to us. But in 
the store, someone has to take the 
time to do the ordering, so we’re 
earning whatever discount we’re 
getting.”

“Order-entry devices have saved 
1% to 2% of our overhead because of 
the time we used to spend in pric- 
ing,” says Tom Lewis, manager of 
Jay-Scott Drug in Burbank, Calif., 
“but it hasn’t helped in the phar- 
macy. On the contrary, it causes ex- 
tra work. 

“A pharmacist comes in at 10 a.m., 
and he orders a quantity of a drug 
because he’s out of it. A second phar- 
macist comes in at noon and orders it 
again, and the work is repeated by 
the third pharmacist, who starts 
work at 6 p.m. So the order is tri- 
pled. To avoid this, the first pharma- 
cist must write down the items he 
ordered, and that takes time.” 

Darrel Davis of Davis Drug, in 
Kent, Wash., also finds fault with 
order-entry. “McKesson offers me a 
tone-dial phone system with which 
to place orders, but I don’t use it. I 
prefer to deal directly over the 
phone with an order taker, a person 
who can tell me right then and there 
whether the item is in stock and 
what my previous orders were.” 

Other pharmacists resent being 
“coerced” into using computer sys- 
tems. 

“I have a small store,” says Ken- 
neth Rogers. “I pretty much know 
what I’m doing already, without the 
aid of a computer. But if I don’t use 
the service, I’m docked on discounts 
because I’m costing the wholesaler 
money. I understand his position, 
too, but I just don’t like to be forced 
into anything.” 

Joel Hoffman, who owns and runs 
the Holly Hills Pharmacy in Los An- 
geles, on the other hand, is quite 
pleased with the order-entry system 
supplied to him by Bergen 
Brunswig. 

“Bergen Brunswig’s Ultra-Phase 
program has a lot to offer,” he says. 
“Through their system, we get more 
turns out of our stock and also main- 
tain tighter inventory control. With 
cost-plus, there is no worry that we 
will overstock on deals.” 

Arnold Albert does not subscribe 
to Bergen Brunswig’s services, but 
he admires the wholesaler’s space 
management program, whereby in- 
store departments are remerchan- 
dised or updated on a weekly basis. 
Albert feels that the physical pre- 
sence of a wholesaler’s representa- 
tive in his store can be more of a boon 
than some form of detached mer- 
chandising help. 

Promotional servicing 

“T think that these programs give 
me an edge against my competi- 
tion,” says Wheeler. “But I would 
take advantage of even more promo- 
tional and merchandising help if it 
were available.” 

“A planogram service? I’d more 
than welcome it,” says E. Nelson, 
who operates Rehoboth Pharmacy 
in Rehoboth Beach, Del., as well as 
the Milford Pharmacy in nearby 
Milford. 

“We are not exactly blessed with 
one of the more progressive whole- 
salers,” he says. “They’ve only made 
small attempts at promotional help,

in special-shipment ordering by sub-

be, says Tom Lewis.

pendent stores,” he says. “For-

But computers have slowed the pro-

ment.”

to see at the wholesaler level? 

“I would prefer to deal with only 
one wholesaler,” says Sid Seltoff of 
Philadelphia's Bell-Edge Pharmacy. 
“It would be much easier to write a 
single check, but I can’t take a 
chance on them being out of the 
products I need. I have to have a 
back-up.” 

“Dealing with one wholesaler 
would be a lot less confusing, but I 
find that I need a primary source as- 
well as a short-end wholesaler for 
back-up merchandise,” says Dave 
Glowney of Kilbourne Drugs in 
Flint, Mich. 

“We use three wholesalers to get a 
better variety of products,” says 
Ram. “We would rather use one, but 
we haven’t found a wholesaler we 
can depend on for all our merchan- 
dise needs.” 

Don McCosh would also like to see 
wholesalers offer something in the 
way of new-store planning. “Six 
years ago, we relocated a 2,500-sq.- 
ft. store to an 11,000-sq.-ft. location. 
We did it the hard way. We were 
working in the dark, frankly. The 
independent needs help in assessing 
the location, finding sources of fi- 
nancing, store design, establishing a 
mix and shelf layout.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


‘WHOLESALERS TUNE ADVERTISING 
TO A WIDE VARIETY OF see 


Flexibility is the key note in the 
more successful advertising pro- 
grams that wholesalers have or- 
chestrated among independent 
pharmacists. Those plans that in- 
clude options for the small operator 
as well as the large one attract the 
greatest followings. 

Northwestern Drug Company of 
Auburn, Wash., is a good example. 
Northwestern offers independents a 
relatively inexpensive weekly news- 
paper ad, as well as a more am- 
bitious eight-page tabloid. 

“The weekly ad is for the small 
independent who can’t cost-justify 
using the circular,” explains adver- 
tising manager Jack Blunk. “We’ve 
got a couple of hundred stores in- 
volved in the weekly program, as 
opposed to 60 to 75 that use the cir- 
cular each time it comes out.” 

Of course, says Blunk, there is 
some overlap in that estimate, since 
some stores take advantage of both 
options for maximum coverage. 
“The independent pharmacist can 
employ any combination of ads and 
the circulars—there’s a different set 
of incentives for each formula,” he 
adds. 

While volume is usually the crite- 
rion in determining this formula, 
other factors also come into play. 

“Some shopping centers impose 
restrictions on what drug stores can 
sell,” Blunk points out. “If there’s a 
food store in the center, the drug 
retailer may be prohibited from pro- 
moting food.” Since food has been 
featured in Northwestern’s tabloid 
circulars for a number of years now, 
a member pharmacist who operates 
in a shopping center can opt for the 
weekly ad, which concentrates on 
H&BA items. 

Davis & Calvert Inc., the Bal- 
timore-based full-liner formed in the 
merger of wholesalers F. A. Davis 
and Calvert Drug, offers options 
within options. 

On the one hand, Davis & Calvert 
supplies independents with a per- 
sonalized, eight-page tabloid, which 
can either be mailed out to custom- 
ers or be delivered door-to-door. 
Mailing is by far the more expensive 
alternative, at 15¢ per circular; for 
only 9¢ each, the tabloid is hand- 
delivered. 

Both fees include the cost of the 
tabloid itself, as well as that of a 
merchandising kit, which contains 
in-store signs, window banners and 
shelf-talkers. 


“For our smaller stores, however, 
we have a different plan,” says Wil- 
liam Weiner, vp and general man- 
ager. “It’s an in-store promotion, 
which includes a two-page handbill 
and window signs. The handbill fea- 
tures H&BA items, and it’s good for 
two or three weeks.” 

The circular, by contrast, features 
a full line of drug store merchan- 
dise—convenience foods, dispos- 
ables, seasonal sundries, household 
items and toys. 

“Our largest stores will combine 
the two programs,” adds Weiner. 
“Since the tabloid comes out 10 times 
a year, they’ll use the handbill in be- 
tween circular promotions.” 

Davis & Calvert currently boasts 
some 65 independent pharmacy 
owners on the tabloid program, 
which originated with Calvert Drug 
under the “Astro” advertising ban- 
ner. The handbill approach is taken 
by about 35 drug retailers, who may 
also take advantage of one or two of 
the circulars in the course of a year. 

Tabloid circulars a best bet 

In most cases, where the indepen- 
dent can afford it, wholesalers rec- 
ommend tabloid circulars for max- 
imum use of the advertising dollar. 

“Tt all comes down to money, when 
you re dealing with independent 
store owners,” says Bob Madden, vp 
and general sales manager for 
Strother Drug Company, headquar- 
tered in Lynchburg, Va. Strothers 
supplies approximately 130 retailers 
with advertising, from three divi- 
sional offices in the Southeast. 


“The independent,” maintains 
Madden, “is limited as to what he 
can spend on promotions. The circu- 
lar gives him more punch for his 
money because he can zero in on his 
trading area.” 

Other advertising media, says 
Madden, provide a broader, some- 
what more diluted approach, which 
may be more effective for chains. 

Experimentation with broadcast 

In some instances, however, 
wholesaler ad programs are experi- 
menting with broadcast media, 
though different reasons are given 
for it. 

“Some items seem to sell better 
when they’re on radio or TV,” says 
Bill Albright, vp of Albers Drug 
Co., in Knoxville, Tenn. “We’ve got 
some TV spots ready, which we 
haven’t run with yet but hope to use 
soon.” 

“We've gone to radio advertising,” 
says Weiner. “Sometimes we’ve got 
more money on hand through co-op 
deals than it’s possible to put into a 
tabloid, so we supplement our print 
material with some radio.” 

The goal in all these advertising 
efforts is to endow member-inde- 
pendents with a promotional iden- 
tity. 

“Our customers’ customers are 
now used to looking for sales in their 
stores,” says Jim Daly, assistant 
manager of James W. Daly Inc. The 
firm supplies some 125 independents 
with various kinds of franchised 
print advertising through its two di- 
visional offices in Massachusetts.

A CHORD 


KNOXVILLE—Despite the 
mounting onslaught of the major 
chains, independent retail phar-

chain would.”

newspaper ad, featuring 15 to 20 


promoted items.

change from market to market, but 
the H&BA merchandise stays 
mainly the same.”

ad on a biweekly basis—after a 
start-up charge of $150—depends on 
how many people the ad will reach.

a case where the newspapers carry- 
ing the ad claim 50% or more of a 
“major” market (25,000 or more po- 
tential readers). The fee is less in the 
25% to 49% range, and still less in 
the 10% to 24% range.

supplies about 100 independents on 
its own. The remainder of the Drug- 


Centers is tied to other wholesale | 


houses, such as Johnson Drug, Duff 
Brothers and Durr-Fillauer Medi- 
cal, who are licensed to offer the ser- 
vice.

Albers also provides a point-of-pur-

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


WHOLESALERS BROADEN LINES 
TO PROVIDE COMPETITIVE EDGE 


The quest to become “all things to 
all independents’ is still very much 
on the minds of all major whole- 
salers, who say they alone can keep 
the independents afloat in the 
treacherous waters of major chain 
competition. 

Traditionally the independents’ 
major source of Rx, H&BA and OTC 
preparations has been wholesalers, 
who, for the past five years, have 
been shifting their emphasis from 
traditional drug store fare toward 
sundry and front-end merchandise. 

On the threshold of the 80's, 
wholesalers are in a position to pre- 
sent a broader competitive edge to 
retailers by offering a line of mer- 
chandise encompassing everything 
from blow dryers to grape jelly. 

Following the chain lead, whole- 
salers have hitched the independent 
retailers’ wagons to the convenience 
grocery star. 

“There is a strong movement in 
the retail area to one-stop shopping, 
or a combo,” says John Monkman, 
president, LAD Co. “And a combo is 
made up of broader inventories. 
Broader inventories give retailers 
more expertise.” 

“Food items, convenience items 
mostly,” says a wholesaling exec 
from the Southeast, “is a developing 
trend. Basically, we are supplving 
the retailer with food items on a pro- 
motional basis. But convenience 
food is one of the more dominant 
trends in wholesaling.” 

Subcontracting 

Some wholesalers, in an effort to 

further broaden the independents’ 


traffic pulling power, are looking 


into the possibility of working with 
food wholesalers on a subcontract- 


ing basis. Wholesalers in this type of 


arrangement, would act as referral 
agents for their clients and as such 
would collect a referral fee for ser- 
vices rendered. 

“Along with sundries and promo- 
tionals,” says Ken Eads, executive 
vp, Northwestern Drug Co., “food is 


important. It can account for 5% of 


total sales.” 

“Initially, thev [retailers] were not 
receptive to food,” savs R. P. 
Rogers Jr., executive vp, North 
Carolina Mutua! Wholesale Drug 
Co. “But when they see what it does 
[in terms of store traffic] they ask for 
more of it. 


“The biggest problem with inde- 
pendents is that they are unwilling 
to take items that are low margin, 
low profit. They want those histor- 
ical profits that grow with tradi- 
tional drug store merchandise.” 

Eads concurs: “Retailers have a 
tendency to stick with high profit 
items—Rx, cards. It’s a mistake.” 

“It's a healthy sign that they are 
now willing to experiment with vari- 
ous types of merchandise,” says 
Rogers.

“Wholesalers can play a big part in

of merchandising,” says a South-

have the expertise necessary, and 
the wholesaler can help them.” 

“Independents need ideas to be- 
come competitive,” says Rogers. 
“They are slow in accepting some 
advertising gimmicks and methods, 
but are finding that it does produce

The need to give independents 
more merchandising savvy, has en-

chain expertise. 

Wholesalers, including North 
Carolina Mutual, are beginning to 
run merchandising seminars for re- 
tailing clients. 

Most are taking a more active role 
In preparing promotional material 
for retailer use. Major wholesaler 
Bergen Brunswig has, within the 
past six months, offered Space Man- 
ager, a comprehensive planogram- 
ming service to its clients, while 
LAD is involved in a broad advertis-

tailers.

retailers, in which merchandising 
strategies, display and related pro- 
motional subjects are discussed. 
Rogers feels the seminars give the 
retailers a chance to acquire some 
techniques the chains use. 

“They need merchandising exper- 
tise,” savs Rogers, “and we are help- 
ing them. We are providing them, as 
diplomatically as possible, with 
some planograms.” 

Although not as intricate or com- 
plete as Bergen Brunswig’s plan, 
North Carolina provides its retailers 
with a guide for stocking their 
shelves. “We now have the capability 
of showing them the top 100 or 200 


items, so they can check to see if 


they have those items,” savs Rogers. 
“More and more are asking for these 


tvpes of guides.We feel we can help.” 


LAD CO.GROWS BY ACQUISITION 


Wholesalers are aggressively 
committing themselves to broaden- 
ing supply capabilities to the retail 
trade. 

LAD Co. is one of the frontrun- 
ners in one-source supply. 

A division of conglomerate Di- 
Giorgio, LAD has built a solid base 
from which it can supply such di- 
verse products as Breck Shampoo or 
an electronic hand-held calculator. 

With an inventory stock of 25,000 
items, LAD supplies its 50/50 chain 
independent clientele split with 
drugs, H&BA, general merchan- 
dise, giftware and food products. 

Most recently, LAD added an- 
other merchandise wrinkle with the 
acquisition of Allied Distributors, a 
supplier of sundry merchandise to 
retailers, which include chain and 
independent drug stores, mass mer- 


chandisers, and department stores. 

With the acquisition of Allied, 
LAD has gained the added mer- 
chandise capabilities in electronics 
and personal care appliances, as well 
as a broader range of retailers. 

“We feel that wholesalers should 
build a broader capability to retail 
trade,” says John G. Monkman, 
LAD president. “We embrace that 
philosophy by the fact that we carry

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


AUTOMATION: HIGH-TICKET HOPE 
OF LABOR-TROUBLED WHOLESALERS 


The rising costs of wholesale drug 
distribution are still swallowing 
ever-shrinking profit margins, as 
wholesaler execs endeavor to cut 
warehouse overheads and increase 
productivity. 

All fingers seem to point to labor 
as the chief bugaboo, with whole- 
salers noting that wages have gone 
up though quality personnel are 
hard to find. 

“Finding good labor is a real prob- 
lem,” says Stanley Okin, vp of Gra- 
nain Drug in Freeport, N.Y. “In this 
area, the minimum wage is $3 but 
you can hardly get good people at 
that price. If you pay more, you cut 
into your already slashed margins.” 

Automated warehousing, via ca- 
rousels and mechanical picking sys- 


form of picking is going to revolu- 
tionize the industry in three or four 
years,” says Joe Garde, Spectro 
president. 

Future of automation 

Unfortunately for most other 
drug wholesalers, it’ll probably take 
half a decade or more for the price- 
tags on such systems to come down 
to the point where the smaller, re- 
gional houses can cost-justify their 
use on the basis of volume. 

“Labor is a continual problem,” 
says Gerald Estorge, president and 
general manager of Estorge Drug 
Co. in Lafayette, La. “It’s a question 
of finding the right people, people 
who want to work. But we’d have to 
double what we’re doing now to au- 
tomate.” 


Some 58% of wholesalers have 
decreased warehouse personnel over 
the past five years.

tems like the SI ITE Matics, seemed 
to offer hope for labor-troubled 
wholesalers when the systems were 
pioneered at Philadelphia-based 
Spectro subsidiary West Whole- 
salers, and later at Louis Zahn Drug 
Co. in Melrose Park, IIl. 

According to Mel Zahn, president 
of Zahn Drug, his 12 automatic pick- 
ing units (purchased at a total price 
of $2 million) provide increased pro- 
ductivity, speedier order selection, 
more efficient use of warehouse 
space and greater customer service. 

Automation also cut Zahn’s ware- 
house labor force roughly in half, 
and still maintained a capacity of ap- 
proximately 1,600 orders filled per 
day. 

At West, the results of automation 
have been equally dramatic. “This 


Semi-Automation with a com- 
puter link-up is the remedy Estorge 
and other drug wholesalers are tak- 
ing to combat high-cost distribution 
blues. Using the computer to pro- 
duce efficient, sequenced picking 
documents, the wholesaler can pro- 
gram the movement of warehouse 
personnel. For a manual warehouse 
operating with conveyors, its the 
most effective order-filling process 
just short of mechanical picking. 

Presequenced picking 

Burt Olin, president of Chicago- 
headquartered Humiston-Keeling & 
Co., claims “you can’t live without 
presequenced picking today.” 

Olin’s computer prints out an 
order-filling document that tells the 
packer exactly where to go—aisle 
location, shelf location—and the 


number of units to pick. The picker 
simply serves a mechanical function. 

“This system affords us the flex- 
ibility to move our personnel 
around,” he says. “There are no spe- 
cialists, so if we’re short in one sec- 
tion, we simply move our people 
there accordingly.” 

To further streamline the system, 
Humiston-Keeling divided the 
warehouse merchandise into “A” and 
“B” categories, positioning the 
wholesaler’s 3,000 fastest movers 
closest to the conveyors. The ware- 
house itself is also divided into six 
picking stations, which provide for 
an equal workload per picker. 

“We've even got our people walk- 
ing in sequence when they’re filling 
an order,” says Olin. 

Staff reduction 

On the bottom line, Humiston- 
Keeling has reduced a warehouse 
staff of 24 to 14 order-fillers, a signif- 
icant savings without the benefit of 
automation. 

“All the picking machines and 
fancy systems are labor intensive,” 
he says. “You’ve got to put items in 
to get them out.” 

Humiston-Keeling once used ¢a- 
rousels in the warehouse, but wound 
up scrapping them. “They just 
didn’t match up with what we were 
doing,” says Olin. 

Cost-conscious wholesalers are 
also taking aim at expensive deliv- 
ery programs and trucking, to boost 
profits and trim expenses. 

Walsh-Lumpkin Drug Co., based 
in Texarkana, Tex., has cut the num- 
ber of deliveries to its average retail 
customers from three to two. The 
wholesaler has also experimented 
with a propane-fueled truck, 
hopes of rigging all its long-distance 
vehicles with the necessary equip- 
ment to operate on a cheaper fuel 
supply. 

“We’ve been running the test 
truck since last April,” says Daryl 
Crouch, president. “We’re paying 
40¢ per gallon for pr opane, and get- 
ting 10% less mileage.” 

Other wholesalers have also re- 
duced the size of their trucking 
fleets, and the number of weekly de- 
liveries to customers. But Okin of 
Granain, as well as other distribu- 
tors operating in highly competitive 
markets, claims he can’t cut back on 
service without losing business. 


ZAHN'S PICK: THE SI ITEMATIC 


Automated picking systems are 
still vogue topics of conversation 
among wholesale drug distributors, 
who have been buzzing about these 
labor-savers ever since West Whole- 
sale Drug Co. and manufacturer SI 
Handling Systems Inc. made his- 
tory in the late spring of 1977 with a 
seven-unit SI ITE Matic installation 
in the wholesaler’s Jenkintown, Pa., 
warehouse, a first for the industry. 

But recently, Louis Zahn Drug 
Co. of Melrose Park, Ill., stole 
West's thunder when it completed a 
two-part installation with SI on July 
1, pulling into operation a 12-unit 
system in the wholesaler’s 200,000- 
sq.-ft. warehouse. 


The machines are now picking

In the meantime, Zahn executives

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


WHOLESALERS SUPPLY THE AMMO FOE 


With his computer strapped to his 
hip, and merchandising expertise 
for ammunition, the drug whole- 
saler is coming to the rescue of inde- 
pendent retailers with an array of 
services designed to fend off drug 
chain onslaughts. 

Today’s wholesalers are equipped 
with the tools to help single-store 
druggists merchandise the front- 
end, keep track of inventory, man- 
age the pharmacy, update prices 
and, in general, wage the war for 
survival in a highly competitive in- 
dustry. Of course, the wholesaler 
stands to gain a certain amount of 
retailer fidelity and dependence in 
exchange for his services, though 
there are still many independents 
who don’t look at that as a fair trade. 

At Selby Drug, based in Eliz- 
abeth, N.J., Michael Rosenberg, the 
wholesaler’s secretary-treasurer, 
claims that he can save his indepen- 
dent retailer customers roughly 
$265 per month through a revolu- 
tionary price updating capability 
tied in to Selby’s sticker program. 
Drug chains, says Rosenberg, can 
garner $1,000 per month savings 
with the program. 

Price updating 

“There are 75 stores right now on 
our price-updating program at a 
basic monthly cost of $54 per store 
for price stickers,” he says. “Along 
with his daily delivery, the retailer 
gets price stickers designed to his 
pricing structure for each item or- 


dered. He also gets a print-out of all 
the updates that went into effect 
that day, with six new stickers per 
item so that he can reticket his mer- 
chandise.” 

Rosenberg says that a retailer 
need only order one item for the day 
to get that day’s price updates. 

“I’m paying one person to do noth- 
ing else but get update prices,” he 
says. “He uses vendor releases, the 
trade journals and he calls all 300 
vendors once a month to get their 
latest prices.” 

Already, Rosenberg notes, Selby’s 
computer has logged 360 price up- 
dates for the month of November, 
ready to release them via sticker 
print-outs on the days they are to go 
into effect. Selby customers, there- 
fore, can respond immediately to in- 
creased prices on all the merchan- 
dise the wholesaler carries. 

“When we say we offer same-day 
delivery, that doesn’t mean the fol- 
lowing morning,” Rosenberg says. 
“That means the customer calls in 
the morning and the order goes out 
in the afternoon.” 

Charting product movement 

Lincoln Drug of Lincoln, Neb., is 
also using its computer to chart 
product movement in customer 
stores. 

“We furnish movement reports 
based on what the customer buys 
from Lincoln,” says Bill Lutes, data 
processing manager for the whole- 
saler. “The reports are back-dated 13 


months, so if they bought an item 13 
months ago, it’s still on there.” 

In conjunction with the reports, 
Lincoln’s sticker program provides 
coded price stickers with date of 
purchase and number of items per 
sku. Thus, Lincoln retailers can 
weed out slow-moving items, and 
plan promotions around fast- 
movers. 

“Our salespeople act in an advis- 
ory capacity to help them use that 
information,” says Lutes, who notes 
that he’s got six customers paying 
the $85 monthly charge for the prod- 
uct movement program. 

Lutes claims the wholesaler 
hasn’t “pushed” on the program 
hard bacause retailers have resisted 
it somewhat. 

By way of its year-ago acquisition 
of Dexter Co., a Providence, R.I., 
jobber, Boston- based drug whole- 
saler Gilman Bros. is now offering 
drug store customers a service mer- 
chandising capability. 

Service merchandising 

“We’re very happy with the prog- 
ress Dexter has made,” says Kalman 
Shmueli, Gilman’s board chairman. 
“The integration of our customer 
bases is going on right now. It’s well 
under way in New England, and ona 
limited basis in the New York area.” 

Dexter jobs hard lines like electri- 
cal supplies, plus books, toys, peg- 
ged candy and seasonal items, in 
addition to certain franchised lines 
like Hartz-Mountain pet supplies. 


DECENTRALIZATION PROPELS McKESS 


SAN FRANCISCO—It is not un- 
usual for a 146-year-old company to 
suffer from hardening of the ar- 
teries. 

That diagnosis does not apply to 
same-age McKesson Drug Co. 
(name changed from McKesson and 
Robbins last July). However, it is no 
secret that McKesson’s performance 
has been sluggish during some peri- 
ods in the past. 

But no longer. 

In fiscal 1979 (ended March 31, 
1979), the wholesaling arm of $3.3 
billion Foremost McKesson ran the 
sales flag past $1 billion for the sec- 
ond consecutive year. 

McKesson’s new dynamism, start- 
ing with a major reorganization in 
October 1976, has spearheaded the 
continuum of change. The big 
change: From a functional organiza- 
tion, where each main element was 
centrally controlled, to a de- 
centralized, locally controlled opera- 
tion. 

“We pushed the decision-making 
down to where the action is,” says 
Kenneth L. Larson, senior vp and 
general manager of the wholesale 
drug division. 

Decentralization brought about 
the formation of three regions 
(Northern, Southern and Western) 
and 24 zones, with each zone’s gen- 
eral manager reporting to one of 
three regional general managers. 

Change also occurred in two other 
pivotal areas: distribution centers 
and retail services. 

Five years ago, McKesson oper- 
ated 95 distribution centers; today 
there are 66. In fiscal 1979, 15 dis- 
tribution centers will be consoli- 
dated into seven new distribution 
centers.

THE MAN BEHIND THE TURNAROUND 


SAN FRANCISCO—Food 
wholesaling history is repeating it- 
self in drug wholesaling—and who 
should know better than Roy B. 
Miner, a man whose career spans 
both? 

Miner, president of Foremost- 
McKesson Drug & Health Care 
Group (formerly McKesson & Rob- 
bins Drug), was president of food/ 
drug/discount retailer Cook-United, 
Cleveland, for eight years, and food 
wholesaler Scot Lad Foods, Chi- 
cago, for six. 

Miner says the drug industry is 
following food’s evolutionary prog- 
ress. “Twenty-five years ago, the 
voluntary food wholesaler was sell- 
ing the retailer 20¢ of every store 
sales dollar. Then the voluntary be- 
gan to add the other 80%—meat, 
produce, frozen food, dairy, ete. 


It was amazingly successful. 
Twenty-five years ago the food busi- 
ness was dominated by the chains; 
today the independents account for 


51%, the chains 49%. 

Miner believes that when the 
wholesaler builds his lines to be- 
come the primary vendor, the retail 
drug operator who uses order-entry 
will have more time to run his busi- 
ness, less time for myriad vendors. 

Miner says that as more stores go 
on order-entry, the economics of 
scale will make those devices more 
affordable for small stores. 

He sees a parallel in prescription 
terminals. “Today they are reason- 
ably high priced, and a drug store 
needs a good hundred prescriptions 
and up per day. But as more stores 
go on-line, there will be a diminution 
of costs. And in five or 10 years it wil! 
be impossible to operate a pharmacy 
without a terminal. Remember, 
pharmacy terminals are still in their 
infancy.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


GROWTH-MINDED ZAHN PUTS 


ACCENT ON SUPPORT PROGRAMS 


MELROSE PARK, I1].—Louis 
Zahn Drug Co. sales in 1979 will top 
$85 million, up 50% over the last 
three years. 

Some of that growth can be at- 
tributed to geographic expansion— 
Zahn is moving into southern Wis- 
consin, southern IIlinois and south- 
ern Michigan. 

Some of that growth, too, has 
come from Zahn’s hospital division, 
which has doubled its volume in the 
last two years as a result of a more 
aggressive marketing push, and 
from its business of supplying large 
chains. Zahn, for example, services 
Osco drug stores in its market area. 

Still another contributing factor 
to its recent sales growth has been 
the misfortune of other wholesalers, 
namely Lag Drug of Chicago and 
Mooney, Kiefer, Stewart, of Indi- 
anapolis. Zahn picked up many Lag 
customers after that wholesaler 
went bankrupt almost two years 
ago. And when Gilpin closed its In- 
dianapolis division last year, Zahn 
was quick to move into the central 
Indiana market. 

But it has been Zahn’ expanding 
array of support programs for inde- 
pendent drug stores and small 
chains that is the most striking as- 
pect of the wholesaler’s recent 
growth. 

These programs are not contribut- 
ing a significant share of Zahn’s vol- 
ume today (and they are not likely to 
even approach 50% in the future ei- 
ther), but they are important for 
what they indicate about Zahn’s fu- 
ture growth strategy. 

Zahn’s strategy 

That strategy is based on the 
premise that Zahn’s future pros- 
perity depends on the maintenance 
of a competitive, growing indepen- 
dent and small chain base. The sup- 
port programs Zahn Drug is ex- 
panding are designed to maintain 
this group’s competitiveness in the 
face of continued pressure from 
larger chains. 

“Today, we’ve taken on a complete 
retail posture,” says president Mel- 
vyn Zahn. That posture is a recogni- 
tion that wholesalers, if they are to 
survive, must become involved in re- 
tailing to the extent of helping their 
customers with services they need, 
but cannot economically provide 
themselves. 

Among the programs Zahn Drug 
has added recently to help retailers 
are: 

e@ A point-of-sale cash register pur- 


chase plan involving NCR's 7000 se- 
ries. 
@ A planogram service involving 
monthly photos of 12 H&BA depart- 
ments. 
e A private label vitamin line. 
@ New health-related departments. 
The first such department to be 
tested in stores is a 17-item section 
supplied by Futuro, a manufacturer 
of athletic knee pads, wrist sweat 
bands, socks and other similar prod- 
ucts. 

Testing optics 
@ Optical centers. Zahn has been 
testing several centers in stores, but 
the wholesaler has no immediate 
plans to begin actively marketing its 
optical center package. Results have 
been “encouraging,” Zahn says, but

@ Financing. Zahn, in conjunction 
with a local Chicago bank, has ar-

remodelings and also for estate plan- 
ning. 

Besides these new programs, 
Zahn has a variety of retailer pro- 
grams it has been offering for at 
least a year. They include: 

@ Six electronic services known as 
TIME (Techniques to Improve, 
Modernize and Enhance). The most 
widely used is Zahn’s electronic 


order-entry plan with item price 
stickers and shelf labels. Ninety per 
cent of the Chicago wholesaler’s

MELVYN ZAHN TALKS RETAILING 


Ask Melvyn Zahn about the fu- 
ture of drug wholesaling and he will 
talk to you about retailing. 

The confusion is intentional. 

“One of the biggest changes in our 
business over the past five or six 
years is that from a marketing 
standpoint we’ve gdne from the 
wholesaler to the retailer concept,” 
Zahn says. 

“It used to be that the wholesale 
drug salesman was concerned just 
with selling a product. Now he has 
to be concerned also with such ques- 
tions as, where is he [the retailer] 
going to put the product, will it sell 
through, is it right for him?” 

Simply put, the wholesaler who is 
going to survive must become a re- 


tailer, at least in the way he thinks— 
“or get out of the business.” 

“It’s a fundamental lesson, but it’s 
one that’s taken wholesalers 75 
years to learn,” Zahn says. 

“If you look at the drug whole- 
saler, he’s really a chain headquar- 
ters for independent customers. If 
we see any service which will help 


our customers—whether it be in the - 


financial area, or as a management 
consultant, merchandiser, computer 
expert or whatever—we’ll consider 
going into it.” 

This is not to say Zahn foresees a 
time when drug wholesalers, or, in 
particular, his company, will become 
primarily suppliers of support ser- 
vices. 


Support services are secondary 

“We look at our business as 
basically one of selling merchandise, 
and we won’t change that. Zahn 
thinks that the growing array of sup- 
port services must remain just that: 
supports forthe main task of helping 
retailers to sell more products. 

“We’re not going to lose money [on 
these supportive programs], but we 
aren’t—and shouldn’t be—making 
these major profit centers either.” 

The success of the partnership be- 
tween the wholesaler and the inde- 
pendent and small chain retailer 
depends on the growth of a “whole 
trust type of relationship.” He adds; 
“I don’t know if it’s quite there yet, 
but we’re getting closer.” 


DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


BERGEN BRUNSWIG COMMITTED 
TO CONTINUED SUNBELI GROWTH 


LOS ANGELES—It may still be 
the nation’s No. 2 drug wholesaler, 
but the Bergen Brunswig Corp. 
proved itself second to none in the 
area of vigorous expansion over the 
past year, with some major forays 
into the Sunbelt. 

Last spring, Bergen purchased 
Atlanta-based wholesaler John B. 
Daniel Co. and a distribution facility 
in Norfolk, Va., from the ailing 
Henry B. Gilpin Co. More recently, 
the wholesaler giant opened the 
doors on a new facility in Houston, 
giving Bergen 23 facilities across the 
nation and a third outpost in its new- 
est market, the Southeast. 

Based on initial successes in this 
territory, and Bergen’s overall ex- 
pansion commitments, Emil Mar- 
tini, board chairman and president, 
explained that Bergen would con- 
tinue to pursue Sunbelt growth. 

Bergen Brunswig’s nine-month 
sales for fiscal 1979 were $405 mil- 
lion, a 21.5% increase over the year- 
ago figure of $333 million. Net earn- 
ings for the same period, ended May 
31, were $5.2 million, a 44.6% in- 
crease over last year’s earnings of 
$3.6 million for the comparable pe- 
riod. Net-to-sales increased from 
1.1% for the first nine months last 
year, to 1.4% for the same period this 
year. 

For fiscal 1978, Bergen posted 
sales of $452.6 million for a 12.1% 
increase over 1977 sales of $403.6 
million. Aftertax earnings were $5.2 
million, a jump of 40.5% over the 
year-ago figure of $3.7 million. Net- 
to-sales increased to 1.2% from the 
1977 figure of 0.9%. 

Earnings per share reached a rec- 
ord high in 1978 of $1.17, a 38% in- 
crease over $0.85, the year-ago 
figure. 

Expenses as a per cent of sales 
were down in 1978 by 0.5%, from 
12.1% in 1977 to 11.4%. But gross 
margins also decreased to 14.15%, 
from 14.33% a year ago. 

Bergen attributes healthy earn- 
ings increases to its new or improved 
customer services, which had 
served to establish the wholesaler’s 
reputation as a drug distribution in- 
novator when they were introduced.

Specifically, Bergen’s data process-

Order-entry accounts, using 
Bergen’s Telephase and Ultraphase, 
represent more than 75% of the drug 
wholesaler’s customers. Ultraphase 
order-entry, employing hand-held 
devices with built-in wands, op-

keys in the desired quantity per sku, 
and transmits the order by tele-

In conjunction with this program,

which maintains the retailer's spe-

date, and management reports. 

As a supplement to Ultraphase, 
Bergen offers a touch-tone ordering 
system called Telephase. Orders can 
be keyed in through Telephase by 
using a touch-tone telephone from 
anywhere in the U.S. Telephase cus- 
tomers can also receive Bergen’s 
shelf labels, customized price stick- 
ers and management reports. 

As a result of electronic order en- 
try, the average Bergen account has 
increased in size 3.5 times, between 
1975 and 1978. According to Martini, 
those Bergen divisions with at least 
90% of sales coming by way of elec- 
tronic ordering have an operating 
expense level lower than 5%.

vices, Bergen offers retailers its 
Good Neighbor Pharmacy voluntary 
program. GNP provides indepen- 
dent retailers with merchandising 
expertise and guidance in-store, and 
the opportunity to take advantage of 
manufacturer co-op advertising dol- 
lars. 

Bergen also markets GNP to 15 
other drug wholesaler-franchisees, 
and reaches more than 3,200 retail- 
ers in 47 stations. 

Microphase, a microphotographic 
retrieval system, is a monthly sub- 
scription service provided by 
Bergen. It provides pharmacies 
with pricing information, drug in- 
teractions, news on products and 
merchandising. It also lists all prod- 
ucts offered by the wholesaler, and 


their product numbers. 


MARTINI: DISTRIBUTION WIZARD 


As he propels his Bergen 
Brunswig Corp. into a future of 
steady volume growth through in- 
creased computer services, the wiz- 
ard of drug distribution, Emil Mar- 
tini, reflects on the present and past 
for, direction. 

For example, on Bergen’s cam 
paign in the Sunbelt, Martini re- 
marks, “Atlanta and Norfolk, our 
first two entries in the Sunbelt, have 
shown good progress. We’re very 
gratified with the customer re- 
sponse we've gotten, and based on 
what we’ve said in the past, we’re 
going to expand.” 

Martini graduated from Purdue 
School of Pharmacy in 1952, where- 
upon he went to work for a small, 
Hackensack, N.J., drug wholesaler 
called the Bergen Drug Co. By 1956, 
when he was a few years shy of 30 
years old, Martini became president 
of Bergen and started plotting the 
course that has made his company 
the industry leader it is today. 


In 1969, he formed the perimeter 
of a national distribution network 
with the acquisition of Brunswig 
Drug Co., an old, full-line whole- 
saler based in Los Angeles. Soon 
after, corporate headquarters were 
moved to L.A., and Martini became 
chairman in 1970. 

But some rocky economic times 
led the wholesaler to regroup 
around strongholds, especially 
when Bergen reported a $1.8 million 
loss for 1972. The wholesaler cut 
back on distribution facilities, going 
from 30 houses to 20, and the cus- 
tomer base was trimmed from 8,000 
to 4,500 highly profitable opera- 
tions. 

In the years that followed, Mar- 
tini’s vision led him to realize that 
computerized services to retailers 
would be necessary to survive. Con- 
sequently, Phase, Telephase and U]I- 
traphase were developed to smooth 
out store-order hassles and increase 
efficiency through greater customer 


wholesaler communication. 

Shortly after these programs 
were initiated, Martini said: “For a 
whoiesaler today to operate without 
computer technology is to operate 
with an insurmountable handicap. 
Noncomputerized programs were 
okay when the wholesaler did 90% of 
his business with independent re- 
tailers. But today, chains are becom- 
ing much more important customers 
to the wholesaler. At the same time, 
aggressive independents are get- 
ting bigger. Thus, to improve his 
market share, the wholesaler must 
be more competitive on his pricing. 
And to be more competitive he must 
learn to operate at expense levels of 
5% to 8%... . Simply put, he cannot 
do it without the computer.” 

As Bergen’s sales volume closes in 
on one-half billion dollars, and prof- 
its make substantial yearly climbs, 
Martini has good cause to look back 
on his initial computer ventures and 
be pleased by his foresight.

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


SOUTHWESTERN SEEKS GROWTH 
DEEP IN THE HEART OF TEXAS 


DALLAS—Fifty-year-old South- 
western Drug made news recently 
when the il-division wholesaler 
completed a merger agreement with 
Jacksonville, Fla.-based Gulf 
United Corp., a holding company of 
insurance firms, broad-casting com- 
panies and others businesses unre- 
lated to drug distribution. 

On paper, the entire deal, consist- 
ing of a 150,000 share-for-share 
trade and cash buy-out is valued at 
$27.7 million. 

Significantly, the agreement 
serves to illustrate the recent 
trend—started by companies like 
the Aleo Standard Corp.—of large 
conglomerates seeking acquisitions 
in the wholesale drug industry. 

Why the sudden rush into drug 
wholesaling? Because acquisition- 
minded corporate executives see 
this segment of the health care in- 
dustry as a big volume producer— 
with the proper financial push—in 
the near future. 

“We think the outlook for this 
business in Texas and the Southwest 
is good,” says John Massey, Gulf 
United’s vp, finance. “It’s a good, 
stable business, as is our insurance 
business, with a bright long-term 
future.” 

Massey’s remarks echo those 
made by Alco Standard executives, 
upon their entry into drug distribu- 
tion. 

“IT would not be at all surprised if 
Southwestern made other drug 
wholesaling acquisitions somewhere 
down the road,” he says. 

F lat sales and profits 


Southwestern’s sales and profits 
have remained flat over the last sev- 
eral years, which is due, according 
to management, to “increased price 
competition in pharmaceutical prod- 
ucts throughout our marketing 
area.” 

Sales for fiscal 1979 were $105.5 
million, a 5.5% increase over the 
year-ago figure, $103.6 million. 
Earnings: increased 2%, from $1.8 
million in 1978 to $1.9 million in 1979. 
The company’s 1979 net-to-sales 
ratio was 1.8%, a slight increase over 
the 1978 figure, 1.7% 

Southwestern has experienced 
overall gross margin increases due, 
in part, to the wholesaler’s diver- 
sified and expanding merchandise 
mix. 

Sundry merchandise plays an im- 
portant part in the total offering to 
drug stores, and accounts for 19% to 
22% of Southwestern’s mix. In the

HOPPER: WE'RE GETTING SMARTER 


As the wholesale drug company 
he has managed for 11 years comes 
under the ownership of a large cor- 
poration with a diversity of inter- 
ests, Clifton C. Hopper, board chair- 
man and president of Southwestern 
Drug, views the future with unre- 
strained optimism. 

“We were looking ahead when we 
made the merger agreement with 
Gulf United,” Hopper says, “be- 
cause we want to be an important 
factor in this business.” 

Hopper feels Gulf United's strong 
financial prowess will insure South- 
western’s growth, and help the 
wholesaler become “a major factor” 
in drug wholesaling. 


‘The wholesaler is start- 
ing to recognize that he 
has to make a profit from 
every dollar, that we 
can’t continue discount- 
ing heavily’ 


Clifton C. Hopper 
Board chairman and president 
of Southwestern Drug 


A 40-year veteran of South- 
western Drug, having entered the 
business at 19, Hopper also believes 
that the wholesale drug community 
is sharpening up, taking a long, hard 


look at some of the problems of the 
past. 

“I think we’re getting smarter,” he 
says. “The wholesaler is starting to 
recognize that he has to make a prof- 
it from every dollar, that we can't 
continue discounting heavily.” 

For h.s own business, Hopper sees 

“continued careful growth into other 
marketplaces,” and the possibility of 
entering into other areas of distribu- 
tion. 

“We try to look at our business 
through the consumer's eyes,” he 
says, “as our interest in the sundries 
business indicates. I don’t think 
you'll hear that from a lot of other 
wholesalers.” 


DRUG STORE NEWS, October 29, 1979 


SPECTRO AFFIRMS COMMITTMENT 


TO TOTAL HE 


MARKET 


JENKINTOWN, Pa.—Spectro 
Industries, which maintains divi- 
sions in drug distribution, hospital 
equipment manufacturing and the 
development of convalescent aids, 
intensified its commitment to the 
total health care market earlier this 
year when the firms sold off the as- 
sets to the Kennedy Sewing Ma- 
chine Cos. 

On paper, Spectro received $4.8 
million in the sale, $1.1 million in 
cash and the balance payable by a 
long-term, secured-interest-bear- 
ing note. The sale also resulted in a 
one-time, non-recurring loss of $2.5 
milion for Spectro on discontinued 
operations, with a 70% goodwill 
write-off related to the purchase of 
Kennedy in 1971. 

Spectro intends to beef up cash 
flow as a result of the sale, and focus 
company energies on health care-re- 
lated businesses. 

For the first quarter of fiscal 1980, 
Spectro reported a 19% increase in 
sales, and a hefty 87% increase in 
earnings. Sales for the period to- 
taled $48.1 million, as compared to 
the year-ago figure of $40.4 million. 
Income was $711,000, vs. last year’s 
figure of $379,000. Per-share income 
was $0.23 over $0.19 for last year. 
And net-to-sales increased to 1.48% 
for the quarter as compared to 0.9% 
for the same period last year. 

Sales for 1979 reached a record 
$176 million for the year ended 
March 28, 1979, an increase of 19% 
over the 1978 figure of $148 million. 


Pre-tax income from continuing op- 
erations was $3.5 million for 1979, a 
40% increase over the year-ago fig- 
ure, $2.5 million. But due to a $2.5 
million loss from the discontinued 
Kennedy operation, net income for 
the fiscal year dropped 46.2%, from 
$1.3 million in 1978 to $700,000 in 
1979. 

The bulk of Spectro’s 1979 sales 
comes from its distribution division 
which posted a 16% increase from 
$143 million in 1978, to $165 million in 
1979. But the health products man- 
ufacturing division reported a 109% 
increase in sales from $4.8 million in 
1978, to $10.7 million in 1979, making 
its share of corporate sales 6.1%, as 
compared to 3.2% in 1978. 

Per-share earnings from continu- 
ing operations were $1.00 as com- 
pared to $0.67, the year-ago figure. 


ALTH CARE 


In the Health Care Products Man- 
ufacturing Group, Spectro operates 
Goodman Manufacturing Co., 
maker of hospital and leisure beds 
and related equipment, and Penn 
Chem Corp., manufacturer of am- 
bulatory patient care equipment. By 
amalgamating these two operations, 
Spectro was able to expand its cus- 
tomer base in 1979. 

Spectro also operates the Custom 
Pak Kit Co., which provides incom- 
ing hospital patients with admission 
kits, and Medical Eqiupment Un- 
limited, a chain of agencies which 
distributes the company’s product 
line of medical equipment. 

The distribution division includes 
Massachusetts Wholesale Drug, 
which has two divisions in Worces- 
ter and Springfield, District Whole- 
sale Drug in Landover, Md., Loewy 
Drug in Baltimore, and Spectro’s 
flagship house, West Wholesale 
Drug in Philadelphia. 

Distribution efficiency

oneering projects in distribution 
efficiency, with the installation of SI 
ITEMatic picking machines and 
White carousels.

brought on-line in 1977, giving West 
the capability of picking almost 
6,000 items per hour. The units pick 
over 5,000 skus, about 80% of the

GARDE: AN INDUSTRY STATESMAN 


Aside from being one of the key 
innovators in the wholesale drug in- 
dustry, Joseph L. Garde, president 
of Spectro Industries (and outgoing 
president of the NWDA), is also one 
of its leading statesmen and orators. 

Recently, Garde testified at a 
F.D.A. hearing on patient labeling, 
bringing the wholelsaler’s plight to 
the Government. 

“If 80% of all prescription drug 
products now being shipped to drug 
wholesalers were shipped with loose 
slips of patient labeling in the ship- 
ping containers, drug wholesalers 
alone could spend an estimated $10 
million in the first year capital in- 
vestments and $40 million to $80 mil- 
lion annually in additional patient 
labeling storage, handling, and cler- 


ical activities,” he said. 

But Garde did more than simply 
state the wholesaler’s case at that 
meeting. He got F.D.A. officials to 
agree to visit wholesale drug facili- 
ties, to learn more about that arm of 
the national health care body which 
they were trying to regulate. It was 
the fulfillment of one of Garde’s chief 
ambitions during his tenure as the 
NWDA president. 

“There’s only one way to get our 
message across,” the 50-year-old 
drug wholesaler said at the time he 
took office. “We have to make our 
voices heard as taxpaying voters. 
... You’ve got to bring your state 
representatives in, show them your 
operation, show them what you do, 
let them talk to your people. We’ve 


got to let them know that we have 
the best and most economical health 
care distribution system in the 
world.” 

Garde characterizes his one-year 
term as having three specific areas 
of emphasis: involvement in Govern- 
ment, research on the state of drug 
wholesaling, and increased contact 
with suppliers. 

“We probably visited with more 
vendors in the past year than at any 
other time in NWDA history,” he 
said, pointing out that good commu- 
nications with vendors are impor- 
tant to the entire scheme of drug 
wholesaling. 

“I think that things are going in a 
very positive direction,” he said of 
drug wholesaling, in general. 


BINDLEY WESTERN BANKROLLS ITS 
SINGLE -SOURCE SUPPLY THEORY 


INDIANAPOLIS—tThe 10-year- 
old Bindley Western Drug Co. con- 
tinues to grow at a rate of 22% to 
25%, generating a volume in excess 
of a quarter-hillion dollars this year, 
as the five-facility wholesaler con- 
tinues to bankroll on its unique the- 
ory and practice of drug distribu- 
tiou. 

Though drug chains traditionally 
use wholesalers for fill-ins and emer- 
gency delivery of pharmaceuticals, 
roughly 85% to 90% of Bindley West- 
ern’s volume comes from a client 
base of nearly 40 drug chain ac- 
counts. 


Bindley Western’s customer list 
reads like a veritable who's who in 
chain drug retailing, including 
Eckerd, Osco, Malone & Hyde 
(Super D, Sommers, and Petty) 
Cunningham, Hook, Haag and Ar- 
nold’s. 

There's no mystery to the method, 
says Jack Laughner, president. 

Single sources supply 

“The program we offer, designed 
by Bill Bindley, is based on a theory 
of single-source supply,” he says. 
“When drug chains buy direct, they 
have to contend with deliveries com- 
ing at all hours, by common carrier, 


and a variety of prices. We deliver 
with our own trucks, charge one 
price, and turnaround time is re- 
duced.” 

Bindley Western ships in full-case 
quantities to chain warehouses, 
where the Rx merchandise is dis- 
tributed through the retailer's own 
system. Consequently, breakage is 
greatly reduced, and deliveries are 
scheduled in such a way that chains 
can stand ready to receive merchan- 
dise when the wholesaler says the 
delivery is to arrive. Chains receive 
orders on a weekly basis, at the 
same time every week.

BILL BINDLEY: LINKED TO CHAINS 


Ten years ago, Bill Bindley envi- 
sioned a drug distribution business 
that was radically different from the 
one his family had operated since 
1865. 

“I could see the growth of the 
chains, their dominance, and 
thought that there had to be a way to 
put merchandise in their ware- 
houses that would give them some- 
what of a price advantage, and at the 
same time, give them a single major 
source for pharmaceuticals.” 

With his father’s blessing, he left 
the family-operated E. H. Bindley 
in Terre Haute, Ind., which services 


the independent market, and went 
off to found a distribution company 
of his own. 

A decade later, the 40-year-old 
Bindley has built a $250 million busi- 
ness based on his foresight. And 
though he still maintains the title of 
vice chairman at his father’s whole- 
sale drug business, he’s very much 
committed to servicing the chain 
drug industry. 

“We sell the products at an attrac- 
tive price, but somebody can always 
come up with a better price,” he 
says. “In setting up the program, we 
were looking at that aspect of inven- 


tory control.” 

Control comes in the form of Bind- 
ley Western’s precise delivery 
schedules. Deliveries are made ex- 
clusively on his trucks, at the same 
time each week. 

In addition, the wholesaler can aid 
in the management of a chain’s ware- 
house, showing distribution execu- 
tives exactly which items to stock, 
and how much footage to devote. 

Says one chain customer: “Bindley 
Western is attuned to the problems 
encountered by chains in that ware- 
house. They simply have the exper- 
tise.” 


OVEREXTENSION SPELLS DEMISE 


FOR THE HENRY B. GILPIN CO. 


WASHINGTON—For many ob- 
servers and insiders on the drug dis- 
tribution scene, 1979 will be remem- 
bered as the year the Henry B. 
Gilpin Co., a formidable and well- 
respected drug wholesaler for 
nearly a century and a half, came to 
a grinding halt. 

Unlike the sudden demise of Chi- 
cago-based wholesaler Lag Drug, 
which took place in 1976, Gilpin’s end 
was slow and painful, coming over a 
period of several months through a 
string of divestitures, which diluted 
its overall impact on the industry. 

But along with Lag, the Gilpin sit- 
uation serves as a warning to other 
drug distributors, a reminder that 
the industry has become highly vol- 
atile and that a certain degree of 
fiscal conservatism must be prac- 
ticed to survive. 

“I think the basic warning we get 
from these two incidents is to pay 
better attention to our businesses,” 
says one chief executive of a large 
wholesale drug operation. 

Where did the Gilpin train derail? 
And what factors, precisely, created 
the stormy economic climate that 
forced the wholesaler to sell off 
nearly all of its businesses? 

Analysts close to the Gilpin situa- 
tion claim the wholesaler overex- 
tended itself externally—with less 


‘ 
ome 


than favorable mergers and acquisi- 
tions—and internally, by developing 
an array of retailer services that 
sliced into margins. 
Where the problems began 
Gilpin’s troubles stern from the 
wholesaler’s ambitious efforts to 


grow, and to a rigorous five-year 
plan to effect that growth, which the 
company embarked upon at the 
start of the 1970’. 

At that time, James E. Allen, 
Gilpin’s president, was given the ad- 
ditional title of chairman of the 
board. Under his leadership, 
Gilpin’s management “decided to go 
into the distribution business in a 
very deliberate way, and in the 
health care products business in a 
very deliberate way. ... We also 
saw that size was important in order 


to be successful in this business. 


“We saw that we were doing about 
$32 million per year in sales,” Allen 
says. “And we appraised that the 
size we needed to be was a minimum 
of a $100 million company. We 
needed to get more financing, and 
be in the right geographical areas, 
which we found to be in the South for 
our field. So we put down a five-year 
plan to grow in those two areas, to 
expand by merger and acquisition, 
and to expand internally, by build- 
ing our business.” 

Gilpin’s $100 million goal would 
have made it the fourth or fifth larg- 
est wholesaler in the U.S. at that 
time, according to Allen, “and that, 
the size we thought we could go pub- 
lic with, a size the investment bank- 
ers called for.”

Gilpin’s stockhoiders’ investment toppled after 1975 


Fiscal year 


Just prior to its major expansion 
campaign, Gilpin operated facilities 
in Washington, Baltimore, Norfolk, 
Va., Dover, Del., Point of Purchase 
Service Merchandisers Inc. (head- 
quartered in Columbia, Md.), and 
Sentry Drug Centers, a 12-unit 
chain of franchised retail outlets. 
Then the acquisitions started com- 
ing, first a two-facility surgical sup- 
ply company, McKenna Surgical 
Supply Inc., and in mid-1972 the 
Ellis-Bagwell Drug Co., a Memphis 
wholesaler, which Gilpin purchased 
for $3.2 million. 

Gilpin was also delving into vari- 
ous data processing systems for its 
own operation, and as a service to 
retailers. A warehouse manage- 
ment system, called COMQUEST, 
was brought on-line, along with an 
inventory management system for 
customers, called Datarex. The 
wholesaler also operated a volun- 
tary program, called Care Drug, 


which it started in 1969. 

In 1974, Gilpin made another ma- 
jor acquisition in the form of the 
Mooney-Mueller,Ward Co., a 72- 
year-old wholesaler based in Indi- 
anapolis, and its subsidiary, Akron 
Surgical Supply. The Mooney pur- 
chase was to open the doors to the 
Midwest for Gilpin. Instead, the ail- 
ing wholesaler pinned Gilpin down, 
soaking up the parent company’s re- 
sources while producing little or no 
return. 

Gilpin endeavored to help 
Mooney’s management run the oper- 
ation, and improve productivity. But 
while trying to turn Mooney around, 
another Indianapolis drug house as 
old as Gilpin itself, Kiefer-Stewart 
Co., came to the Washington whole- 
saler’s attention, in 1975. 

“They [Kiefer] were not profit- 
able,” says Allen. “They had been 
losing money for five years, but they 
had a better operation than Mooney, 


which had also been losing money.” 

Management at Gilpin decided to 
merge the two acquisitions into one 
company, called Mooney- Kiefer- 
Stewart. 

On top of its troubles in drug dis- 
tribution, McKenna Surgical Supply 
also began to show signs of weaken- 
ing, despite Gilpin’s efforts to build 
volume from roughly $500,000 to $6 
million. Also, the stockmarket was 
not prevailing for the wholesaler, 
and retained earnings started to 
shrink. In 1976, they were down ap- 
proximately $300,000 from the year 
before. 

Gilpin has retained its corporate 
identity and will become a marketer 
of computer services and other sup- 
port features to drug wholesalers. 
The 63-year-old Allen, a member of 
the Gilpin team for 40 years, will 
continue as chairman of the board 
and president of the corporation, 
and is working “with fidelity and 
commitment” to make good Gilpin’s 
debts to creditors. 

Remaining corporate assets in- 
clude Gilpin’s data processing cen- 
ter, Point of Purchase Service Mer- 
chandisers, and the Medical House, 
an Arlington, Va., surgical supply 
company, all profitable operations. 
Other physical assets—buildings 
and property connected with 
Gilpin’s former businesses—are on 
the selling block.
