NWDA RESEARCHING THE FUTURE 
OF THE WHOLESALE INDUSTRY 


SCARSDALE, N.Y.—As it ap- 
proaches its 104th year, the National 
Wholesale Druggists’ Association is 
undoubtedly better equipped to sat- 
isfy the needs of its members than 
ever before. 

Indeed, the NWDA could be con- 
sidered the salvation for many 
smaller wholesaler-members, pro- 
viding them with the resources, 
computer know-how, operational 
and merchandising skills and Gov- 
ernmental representation necessary 
to make their businesses go. 

It has been a long, exciting, some- 
times harrowing year for the 
NWDA. Here are some of the high- 
lights of the last 12 months: 

@ At last year’s annual meeting, the 
NWDA announced a dues increase 
for all members, based on a sliding 
scale, which went into effect at the 
start of the association’s fiscal year 
on April 1. For many members it was 
the first dues hike in more than a 
decade. 

@ To give members greater educa- 
tion emphasis, the NWDA brought 
Henry R. Ziobro on board as direc- 
tor of education. 

@ As aresult of a terrorist bombing 


at Mobil’s Searsdale offices (the 


building is also headquarters for the 


NWDA), the association was forced - 


to move to a temporary location in 
Larchmont. The NWDA has since 
returned to its original home base. 
® Concern over product liability on 
the part of members behooved the 
NWDA to help create a captive in- 
surance corporation, domiciled in 
Bermuda. 

e After a year of successful opera- 
tion, the NWDA-sponsored Or- 
dernet Clearinghouse, a computer 


link-up between wholesalers and 
vendors for the purpose of ordering 
efficiency, has “met all expecta- 
tions.” 

An interview with Frazer 

To get a clear picture of the 
NWDAS present, and future status, 
Drug Store News interviewed W. W. 
(Nick) Fraser, the association’s di- 
rector of marketing and distribu- 
tion. It appears that the NWDA’s 
372 wholesaler-members, 242 asso- 
ciate (vendor) members, 66 non- 
manufacturing members and 31 in- 
ternational members have much to 
look forward to. 

Plan-O-Grams. Paralleling in- 
creasing wholesaler interest in this 
service to retailers, the NWDA 
marketing committee is taking steps 
to “help the retailer determine shelf 
space. 

The marketing committee has 
started gathering information from 
various vendors to calculate share- 
of-market, and NWDA wholesalers 


will soon be using that information 


in a viable plan-o-gram program for 
their retail customers. Videotapes 
and seminars will be the chief com- 
munications vehicles. 

Education. Throughout the 
course of the year, with the help of 
Ziobro, the NWDA has offered 
members educational seminars on 
professional selling skills. 

The NWDA will continue these 
and other educational seminars, and 
the association is working to create 
an educational videotape network. 

“We’re in the process of urging all 
our wholesaler-members to install 
playback equipment at their head- 
quarters for our educational cas- 
settes,” says Fraser. 


The future of wholesaling. Un- 
doubtedly the NWDA’s most am- 
bitious project is an intensive re- 
search study on the future of the 
industry, with focus on market con- 
ditions, services offered, the chang- 
ing product mix, the wholesaler’s 
customer base and the future of vol- 
untary groups. 

Working in conjunction with Man- 
agement Horizons Inc., an indepen- 
dent market research group based 
in Columbus, Ohio, the study is 
being prepared in three phases: (1) 
development of a format, (2) actual 
preparation of research, and (8) data 
playback to members, in the form of 
hard copy, seminars and videotapes. 

According to Fraser, the project 
may take two to three years to com- 
plete. : 

Government. Tr. NWDA will 
continue to take an active role in 
representing the wholesale drug in- 
dustry to those Federal bureaus and 
committees involved with the regu- 
lation of health care. 

Jack Fay, a pharmacist, and Ron 
Streck, a pharmacist-lawyer, con- 
tinue to operate the NWDA’s Wash- 
ington office. The two-man team 
monitors Washington activity and 
reports to members. 

Clearinghouse. The NWDA- 
sponsored communications vehicle 
for wholesaler and vendors, called 
Ordernet, has made significant ad- 
vances in membership over the past. 
year. There are now 60 wholesalers, 
representing 113 divisions, and 18 
manufacturers on the system. 

NWDA itself is in “very sound fi- 
nancial condition,” according to 
Fraser, and continues to take on new 
members.

Closed deals to add 
6 Drug Emporiums 


COLUMBUS, Ohio— The “organized 
chaos’ of the flourishing Drug Emporium 
here, with its orchestrated “urgency” of 
12 cash registers, customer-crammed, 
8-ft. aisles and cut-case, discounted 
merchandise, is spreading to six addi- 
tional outlets. 

“We're franchising four identical 
stores in Cincinnati, the first of which is 
already open and thriving,” said Gary 
Wilber, secretary of Drug Emporium. 

“We're opening a second store our- 
selves here in the Columbus suburb of 
Whitehall early next year. And we're fran- 
chising another store in Phoenix.” 

Striving to duplicate the $4 million vol- 
ume the Columbus Drug Emporium 
achieved by its second year, the Cincin- 
nati franchisees, Dale Obracay and 
Robert Michaels, are hewing to the basic 
pricing standards established here. 

“Under our franchise,” said Michaels, 
“we re working on a cost-plus basis, or 
the manufacturer's price plus 15% to 
20%, as in Columbus, holding to an 
overall gross margin of about 20%. 

“We don't run loss leaders,” Michael 
added. “We keep our prices on depend- 
able, day-by-day levels. Like the Colum- 
bus store, we estimate that 20 items in 
our Drug Emporium will cost the cus- 
tomer about a third less than the same 


purchases at any of our competiiors 
stores.” 

The first Drug Emporium was brought 
into being here two years ago by Philip 
Wilber, father of Gary and a former ex- 
ecutive with Gray and Lane, as a “low 
margin’ operation. 

“If | were back in the chain business 
and walked into a place like this,” he 
said, “I'd have a heart attack, shouting, 
‘Clear up this place.’ Anybody in the 
chain business would Say it's junky. But 
it's better than being well organized, with 
everything in its place.” 

With their Cincinnati Drug Emporium 
in the Springdale Mall, Obracay and 
Michaels struck it lucky on opening day, 
drawing 2,700 customers. 

“Because of our pricing,” said 
Obracay, “we attracted coverage from 
an ‘Inflation Fighter’ series on the news- 
cast of TV Ch. 9 in Cincinnati on our 
second day. Almost immediately, the 
phone started ringing and the store traf- 
fic count took off.” 

The Cincinnati offspring is roughly the 
same size as the Columbus parent— 
about 20,000 sq. ft., overall. In Colum- 
bus, about 14,000 sq. ft. is left for selling 
area. In Cincinnati, the selling area is 
Slightly larger, with wider, 10-ft. aisles,

INDIANAPOLIS—Peoples is moving 
to acquire Haag Drug and has reached 
an agreement in principle to purchase a 
majority interest in the Indianapolis 
chain. 

The 380-store, Alexandria, Va.-based 
Peoples organization is buying for an 
undisclosed amount of cash a 68% inter- 
est in Haag from a group of investors 
that, just three months ago, themselves 
purchased their Haag shares. 

At presstime, Peoples president and 
ceo Bud Fantle was unavailable for com- 
ment on the proposed acquisition. How- 
ever, if the deal is consummated, the 
Haag operation would represent a major 
extension of the Peoples chain, adding 
80 stores, $80 million in sales, about $1 
million in profits and four new states. 
Haag’s trading areas are contiguous to 
Peoples Midwestern markets. 

The 68% position that Peoples is 
seeking to purchase is now held by five 
investors in Indianapolis. Three of the 
investors are known: O. U. Mutz, presi- 
dent of the Mutz Corp. (air-conditioners); 
J. Fred Risk, former chairman of the In- 
diana National Bank, and Charles Lan- 
ham, president of Overhead Doors Inc. 

Although Haag is a public corporation, 


it is closely held by a limited number of 
shareholders. 

Currently, the most important share- 
holders are the investment group and 
certain members of management. 

All three investors have declined to 
comment on why they have sold their 
interest in Haag, after holding it only four 
months. 

In June 1979, the Mutz/Risk/Lanham 
investment group purchased about 
171,000 Haag shares (68% of the 
251,000 total outstanding) for roughly 
$3.1 million, or $18.75 a share. These 
shares had been owned by the Front- 
enac Company, a Chicago-based in- 
vestment banking firm which had helped 
members of Haag management to as- 
sume control of the company back in 
1971. 

At that time, several members of man- 
agement, including president Arnold 
Busse, vp merchandising Bill Eagleson, 
vp store operations George Tombs and 
assistant vp professional relations 
Henry Jones, formed HDC Inc. for the 
purpose of taking over Haag Drug Com- 
pany. The group got backing from Front- 
enac, which assumed a majority interest

smithKline’s Tagamet sales lead 
with a 29.7% share of Rx market 


EULESS, Tex.—Tagamet has 
captured first place among pre- 
scription drugs used for ulcer 
treatment. The SmithKline prod- 
uct’s command of nearly one 
quarter of the entire market may 
be attributed to brand switching 
at the expense of numerous 
other products. 

Prescription volume data 
gathered by pharmaceutical 
supplier Decision Data reveal! 
that the top three drugs in the 
category now control nearly half 
(47.5%) of the prescription mar- 
ket. 

SmithKiine, with a 29.7% 
share of Rx sales, is the market 
leader, followed by Robins, with 
29.2%; Roche, with 12.8%; and 
Merrell-National, with 9.2%. 

Prescription prices of all cate- 
gory products have increased 
over earlier levels. But, despite 
the price increases, retail mar- 
gins for the category have de- 
clined almost 5 points, from 
36.2% to 31.4% compared to 
year-ago levels. The per cent 
margin decline traces to a ma- 
jority of products among the top 
25 and in the “all other” group. 

The data also reveal a num- 
ber of additional characteristics 
that are somewhat unique to 
this product area. 

Price, refilis run high 

Average prescription prices 
are high for the category due to 
the product's use in mainte- 
nance therapy. For example,

Pay Less NW says no to buy-out 


BEAVERTON, Ore.—Pay 
Less Northwest has rejected an 
offer to be acquired by a corpo- 
ration formed by a venture capi- 
tal investment firm. The take- 
over provided for a cash pur- 
chase of all of Pay Less North- 
west's outstanding shares at 
$27.50 per share by the new 
corporation. 

The drug chain's present 
management was to have par- 
ticipated in the equity of the 
new corporation that was being 
formed by the investment firm of 
Kohlberg, Kravis, Roberts & Co. 
of New York. 

“It was a management deci- 
sion that led us to terminate dis- 
cussions of a buy-out,” says Ed 


Hart, president and chief execu- 
tive officer of the drug chain. 
“After studying the proposal 
more closely, we decided it was 
in the best interests of manage- 
ment and the stockholders to re- 
main as we are, an independent 
public corporation. There was 
no single issue that led to the 
rejection of the offer,” says Hart. 

The fact that the deal was 
turned down by the drug chains 
board of directors came as no 
surprise to a number of securi- 
ty analysts who follow the com- 
pany'’s stock. Most agree the 
spread between the market 
price before the announcement 
of the proposal, $18 a share on 
the New York Stock Exchange, 


and the final offer by the new 
investors—$27.50 per share 
was not great enough. More- 
over, the initial offer in Septem- 
ber was for only $26 a share, 
and the Kohlberg, Kravis, Rob- 
erts & Co. investor group, in re- 
action to criticism "rom Share- 
holders and analysts, boosted 
the offer by $1.50. Analysts in 
the financial community specu- 
late an offer of $30 per share 
would have been necessary to 
induce shareholders to accept 
the proposal. 
Offer too low? 

“There was institutional and 
large shareholder resistance 
because the price wasnt high 
enough,’ according to one West

world’s largest single industry 
trade show. Aithough the num-

Ffemain about the same, about 
1,820 manufacturers, there will

Retailers get ready 
for challenging year 


Drug retailers are entering the 
1980's with high levels of confi- 
dence, and with the sense that 
tremendous changes are going 
to be taking place in the way 
drug merchandise is sold to the 
consumer. 

However, drug retailers also 
realize that they will be faced 
with a number of difficult chal- 
lenges for which there are no 
easy answers. 

Specific expectations for this 
year are also positive, despite 
what many retailers see as an 
increasingly difficult economic 
climate. 

“We are looking forward to a 
good year,’ says Alex Grass, 
president and chairman of Rite 
Aid in Shiremanstown, Pa. “Our 
Stores should be able to pro- 
duce a growth rate similar to the 
one they generated this year.” 

Pay Less Northwest (Beaver- 
ton, Ore.) is shooting for an even 
better growth rate during 1980 
than last year, according to Ed 
Hart, president. “Our goal is a 
Sales increase of 12% to 15%,” 


- he says. 


Dave Hamilton, president of 
three-store Hamilton’s Drug in 
Pomona, Calif., is even more 


optimistic about 1980. “I think 
the biggest danger in 1980 is 
losing sales due to lack of inven- 
tory.” 

“With economic indicators 
pointing to a difficult year,” says 
Fred Canning, president of Wal- 
green, “it is well that our major 
expansion plans are directed to 
drug stores. . . . While no busi- 
ness is unaffected by an eco- 
nomic downturn, certainly the 
drug store is resistant to the 
tide. We are looking forward,” 
continues Canning, “to double- 
digit sales gains.” 

“Nineteen-hundred eighty will 
be a year of stiff competition for 
drug chains,” says Robert Bol- 
ger, president of the National 
Association of Chain Drug 
Stores, “both from within their 
own ranks and from the dis- 
count, supermarkets and box 
stores. But alert drug chains 
will, without a doubt, maintain 
and expand their markets dur- 
ing the 1980's.” 

Problems of 1980 

The problems that drug retail- 
ers face during 1980 are the 
same for all businessmen: Infla- 
tion and energy shortages.

Winter will apparently be 
working wonders for drug store 
sunglass business this year. 
The recent entry of winter sport 
lines into the market is helping 
retailers stretch the sunglass 
selling season—and thus 
stretch the profitability of this 
high-margined category. 

ith the edeaton of the 
longer selling season, drug 
store retailers stand to gain the 
maximum potential from a mer- 
chandise hoo ry which al- 
ready provides them with gross 
margins of 50% to 65% on aver- 
age. It will also help them boost 
sunglass sales from the $139 
million level achieved by chains 
in 1978 (a figure that was up 15% 
over the previous year's). 

The trends over the past sev- 
eral years have increasingly 
emphasized fashion in sunglass 
selling, and tha at-one-time 
summer category has steadily 
been becoming a year-round 
Category over the long term. 

“People need sunglasses as 
much to cut glare from the snow 
as from the sun,” said Martin 
Schecht, buyer at Illinois-based 
DeKoven Drug Co., which will 


testing The Bonneau Co.'s 
wife sport lines featuring 
styles with elastic bands and 
striped-colored frames. “Since 
we get plenty of snow here, 
there will be plenty of people 
needing sunglasses.” 

Foster Grant will be joining 
the winter sports lineup with its 
introduction in January of the 
“Sportables’” line, priced be- 
tween $8 to $10, and equipped 
with its own prepacked display. 
“The concept will undoubtedly 
expand the sunglass season,” 
says Richard Surrette, market- 
ing director at Foster Grant. 

“We want to capture the po- 
tential allowed by an expanded 
selling season in the northern 
tier of the United States with 
styles that appeal to consumers 
involved in sports activities.” 

Accessories important

in recent years in the Sunbelt

Stop & Shop 
names J. Gabbe 
director of PR. 


BOSTON—Jill S. Gabbe has 
been appointed director of pub- 
lic relations for The Stop & Shop 
Companies Inc., including the 
45-unit Medi Mart drug store 
chain. 

In her new position, Gabbe 
will be responsible for develop- 
ing public relations programs, 
overseeing media relations and 
directing external public rela- 
tions agencies for the diver- 
sified retailing concern. 

Gabbe joined Stop & Shop in 
1976 as a media relations as- 
sistant and was named man- 
ager of external affairs in 1978. 
She assumed the additional re- 
sponsibilities of acting director 
of public relations in May 1979. 

Gabbe has also worked as an 
editorial assistant for the Boston 
Herald American and served as 
editor of Mirror Newspapers, a 
chain of weekly community ie 
lications in southeastern Mas- 
sachusetts. 

In addition to the Medi Mart 
Outlets, Stop & Shop operates 
153 Stop & Shop supermarkets, 
83 Bradilees Department 
Stores, 48 Perkins Tobacco 
Shops, 26 Off the Rax women’s 
specialty shops and the Stop & 
Shop Manufacturing Company.

Antidepressant profits | increasing | 


EULESS, Tex.—Per cent 
margins for most retail anti- 
depressants have advanced 
over year-ago levels, reflecting 
pharmacies continuing practice 
of passing along cost increases, 
according to a survey by Deci- 
sion Data. 

Two companies control more 
than 50% of the market, the 
study said, with MSD controlling 
more than 36%, based on the 
performance of its Elavil and Tri- 
avil product lines. 

Pfizer/Roerig account for 
more than 12% on the strength 
of Sinequan and Navane. Ciba/ 
Geigy has more than 7% of the 
market. 

A breakdown of total scripts 
by brand, said Decision Data, 
shows Elavil at 20%, Triavil at 
17%, Sinequan 10.8% and Tof- 
ranil 7.5%. 


Decision Data estimated re- 
tail margins for antidepressants 
at 29.4%. That figure is below 
many prescription categories, 
but it represents nearly a four- 
point improvement over a pre- 
viously audited period. 

Eight products contributing to 
the gain in margin are: Elavil 
25mg, +4.7; Elavil 50mg, 
+ 5.2: Sinequan 25mg, +3.6; 
Sinequan 50mg, +6.6; generic 
amitriptyline 25mg, +25.3; 
Etrafon 2-25, +3.8; generic 
amitriptyline 50mg, + 32.0, and 
Navane 5mg, + 5.3. 

Besides the margin in- 

creases, these were other high- 
lights of the survey's findings: 
@ Quantity dispensed per aver- 
age antidepressant script has 
increased slightly, going from 62 
units per script to 63 units cur- 
rently. 


@ Generic scripts for amitrip- | 
tyline have made only minor § 
penetration into the market and § 
now account for more than 4%. 
What growth does exist may be § 
attributed to changes in price. @

amitriptyline 25mg went from 
0.095 in 1978 to 0.105 in 1979, § 
while the 50mg strength de-j 
clined from 0.175 to 0.131. 
@ Refills are playing a more sig- 
nificant role than in previous pe- 
riods. Currently, 60% of all 
antidepressant scripts are re- j 
fills, while during the previous 
period only 50% were refills. 
High per cent refill rates and siz- 
able quantities dispensed sug- 

gest maintenance therapy. 
@ The top 25 products account 

for 75.2% of the antidepressant 
Rx market, unchanged from last | 
period.

Prescription drug revenue continues to be the most important 
and fastest-growing segment of the independent pharmacy’s 
business, says the recently released 1979 Lilly Digest. During 
1978, Rx sales as a ratio to total sales expanded to 51.2% from 
50.4% the year before, as prescription sales experienced an 8.7% 
rate of growth, compared to 7% for all other classes of product in 
a community pharmacy. Moreover, the increase in the ratio of Rx 
volume to total sales has been increasing steadily over the past 
decade. For more analysis on the Lilly figures, see the CSA 
Magazine section starting on page 15. 


Fox-Vliet reorganizes 
its retailing structure 


Jewel, Pay Less NW 


vie for Pay Less 


CHICAGO—Jewel Cos. has filed suit in Cal- 
ifornia Superior Court charging Pay Less North- 
west Inc. with illegal interference with Jewels 
merger agreement with Pay Less Drug Stores of 
California, announced Weston Christopherson, 
Jewel president and chief executive officer. 

“We are going ahead with plans for the merger 
that was signed Nov. 9th, and we expect it to 
proceed,” he says. 

The suit stems from an announcement by Pay 
Less Northwest that it intends to make a tender 
offer of $22.50 a share for stock of Pay Less of 
California provided Pay Less of California aban- 
dons its plans to merge with Jewel. 

Jewel contends it entered into a “mutually 
binding” agreement with Pay Less of California 
whereby Pay Less shares would be exchanged 
at a rate of 0.652 for each share of Jewel com- 
mon stock. Based on the latest closing price of 
Jewel stock at presstime, $26.75 a share, Jewel 
common stock to be received by Pay Less of Cal- 
ifornia shareholders would be worth about 
$17.44 per share, making a $38.4 million trans- 
action. Assuming all 2.2 million outstanding 
shares of Pay Less of California were tendered, 
Pay Less Northwest would be offering $49.5 mil- 
lion for the same shares. 

lronically, both the firms seeking to purchase 
Pay Less of California, have recently been in- 
volved with other attempted mergers. Pay Less 
Northwest recently rejected an offer to be ac- 
quired by a corporation formed by a venture capi- 
tal investment firm. For its part, Jewel came very 
close to merging with Skaggs Drugs in June 
1978. 


_ LATE NEWS 


UNDER FEDERAL LAW, the Department of Health, Educa- 


Jewel has charged that Pay Less Northwest's 
condition that Pay Less of California abandon the 
Jewel offer cannot be legally met as Pay Less of 
California is bound to use its best efforts to com- 
plete the merger. Jewel called Pay Less North- 
west's actions “unlawful, malicious interference 
with Jewel's contractual rights.” 

So far, both Pay Less Northwest and Jewel 
each own about 12% to 13% of the outstanding 
shares of Pay Less of California. Pay Less North- 
west has bought 269,000 shares, or 12.2% of Pay 
Less of California stock. The purchases were 
made during the last two weeks of December on 
open market at prices ranging from $15.50 to 

17.25. 

On the other hand, Jewel has bought 297,000 
or 13.5% of Pay Less of California shares from 
the L. J. and Mary C. Skaggs Foundation for 
about $4.5 million in cash. Jewel also has the 
option to buy 421,486 shares of Pay Less of 
California owned by Mary Skaggs, widow of the 
drug chain's founder, if the merger with Jewel is 
not completed. Mary Skaggs would also receive 
for each of her shares, 0.652 of Jewel common. 
She has also entered a voting agreement with 
Jewel covering her block of shares which are 
being held in escrow. 

Jewel also says Pay Less of California inves- 
tors have been “seriously confused” about Pay

promotion, computer services,

operate their stores more effi- 
cientiy and effectively,” explains 
Bill Tauscher, chairman and 
chief executive officer. “As a 
wholesaler we have to provide 
the merchandise, advertising 
and computer services as- 
sistance that individual stores 
can't do on their own.” 

Named to head the advertis-

John Walz who has been pro-

and cooperative advertising

CALIFORNIA has passed a measure that, if adopted by the state 
board of pharmacy, would require all pharmacies to eliminate 
traditional price posters displaying prices of the 100 most com- 
monly prescribed drugs. In addition, the new ruling would mean 
that drug store consumers could obtain drug pricing information 
in-person or by telephone without having a prescription filled. 


THE ALCO STANDARD CORP., parent of four drug distribution 
firms in the South and Midwest, posted a revenues increase of 
24.4% on $1.925 billion for fiscal 1979. Net income increased 5.6%, 
to $50.4 million. The continued expansion of Alco’s health services 


group resulted in a 90% revenues growth through acquisition. 


Popularity of coupon promos vexes Rxmen 


DSNews Roundup 

x coupon promotion pro- 
grams are gaining in popularity 
as a method pharmaceutical 
manufacturers use to familiarize 
physicians and patients with 
their products. But the enthusi- 
asm for this type of prornotion 
ends at the pharmacist’s count- 
er. 

“Manufacturers fail to realize 
that the coupons entail the same 
costs as any third-party billing 
transaction,” says John Kogut, 
vp, director of pharmacy at Fay’s 
Drug, based in Liverpool, N.Y. 
“There are administrative costs 
of handling paperwork and addi- 
tional expenses due to delayed 


payment for products sold.” 

Most drug retailers feel that 
the nature of the pharmacist's re- 
lationship within the health com- 
munity leaves little choice but to 
accept the coupons despite their 
cost burden. 

“There is some social and ec- 
onomic coercion involved,” says 
the professional services direc- 
tor at one Southeastern drug 
chain. “Refusing the coupons is 
a good way to lose good custom- 
ers and create ill-will with physi- 
cians who have chosen to hand 
out these coupons.” 

How it works 

Rx coupon promotions pri- 

marily rely on the cooperation of 


the physician who is issued a 
coupon folder by either the man- 
ufacturer’s detail person or 
through a mailing house. The 
physician passes the coupon on 
to his patients along with their 
prescriptions. These are dis- 
pensed at the specified amount 
by the pharmacist who accepted 
ihe coupon in lieu of part of the 
cash payment. 

The pharmacist must then 
submit the coupon to the manu- 
facturer or middleman agency, 
handling it very much in the way 
he would handle any other third- 
party script. 

Drug retailers are then reim- 
bursed by the manufacturer 


through the middleman agency 
—such as complimentary Pre- 
scription Services or Pharma- 
scripts Inc.—for each coupon 
submitted. Some manufacturers 
handle their own claims. 
According to CPS estimates, 
an average drug retailer pro- 
cesses 80 of these coupons per 
month. However, some drug 
chains estimate that they aver- 
age as high as 300 per month. 
To compensate the costs in- 
volved, drug retailers suggest 
that a bookkeeping fee be 
tacked on their reimbursements, 
with most citing the NACDS 65¢ 
to 70¢ estimate of per-script cost

considering a plan to require

ated with the drug, and may or- 
der further labeling changes for 
the product, agency officials 
told Drug Store News.

has been under steady fire for 
over a year now as a result of a 
1973 World Health Organization 
Study indicating that high cho- 
lesterol patients who take the 
drug experience a 29% greater 
mortality rate than those who do 
not. 

But the latest flap over Atro- 
mid-S surfaced late last month 
on the heels of sharp criticism of 
Ayerst's efforts to promote the 
product to physicians. 

Although the four-page Atro- 
mid-S brochure developed by 
Ayerst last year contained a 


new boxed label warning written 
by F.D.A. as a result of the 
W.H.O. findings, officials at the 
drug agency nevertheless criti- 
cized the advertising as “mis-

over, for the second consecutive year, 
Rx sales accounted for more than 
half (51.2%) of total revenue for inde- 
pendent pharmacies.

In dollars per square foot, pre- 
scription sales generated $466.52 
per square foot in 1978 compared to 
$81.43 per square foot in sales of 
other products. These figures are 
based on an average square footage 
of 2,470. Prescription dollars per 
square foot rose 6.2% in 1978 from 
$439.27 in the previous year. 

The number of prescriptions dis- 
pensed in 1978 rose 1% over the aver- 
age number filled by a community 
pharmacy in 1977. According to the 
national survey, the average number 
of scripts dispensed per pharmacy on 
an annual basis rose to 26,918, up 
from 26,649 in the preceding year. 
The average prescription charge in- 
creased 47¢ to $6.57 from $6.10 in 
1977, a 7.7% increase. 

Ten years ago, the average pre- 
scription charge was $3.90. How- 
ever, in addition to inflation, rising 
Rx charges also stem from increas- 
ing dosages. In 1978, for example, 
the index for the average number of 
doses per prescription increased to 
138.6 with 1967 being the base year 
(= 100). 

The fact that prescription sales ac- 
count for more than half of a phar- 
macy's total sales “once again re- 
minds us of the strong impact the 
prescription department exerts on 
the financial picture of the average 
community pharmacy. The concept 
of the pharmacy as a primary health 
center is growing and is an integral 
part of the pharmacy’s economic fu- 
ture,” concludes the report. 

Higher sales 

In sales, 1978 marked the 29th con- 
secutive year pharmacies have 
posted higher sales. Volume was up 
an average 7% to $345,302 from 
$322,755 in 1977. The growth rate 
reversed a two-year trend to vard 
lower annual growth and was : bove 
the 6.2% average increase registered 
over the last decade. The 7% in- 
crease is significantly higher than 
the 4.2% sales rise reported in 1977. 
Over the last 10 years, on the aver- 
age, pharmacy sales have increased 
62% to $345,302 from $213,710. 

The cost of goods sold also rose 
7.5% in 1978 to $225,651 from 
$209,954 in 1977. As a percentage of 
sales, the cost of goods rose 0.2% to 
65.3% from 65.1% of sales in 1977. 
The result was an average gross mar- 
gin of 34.7% for the independent 
pharmacist, the lowest gross margin 
level since 1957. This was a major 
contributing factor to the drop in net 
profit. 


It now takes longer and the high- 
est percentage of sales volume in 
order to break even, according to the 
report. The average pharmacy’s 
breakeven point was 9.9 months and 
it took 82.7% of total sales. A decade 
earlier, one could realize a profit 
after 9.3 months or 77.7% of total 
sales. 

Due to rising costs, pharmacy 
managers tried to keep net profit be- 
fore taxes stable by reducing total 
expenditures. They attempted to re- 
duce one of the largest controllable 
portion of expenses, salaries and 
wages and miscellaneous costs. To a

Salaries of proprietors or man-

sales to 6.9% from 7% in 1977. How-

represented a slight increase in sal-

The average percentage of expen- 
diture on employee wages dropped 
slightly, as more efficient operations 
were run in an attempt to reduce 
total expenses. Wages dropped as a 
share of sales to 11.6% from 11.8% in 
1977. While wages as a percentage of 
sales was curbed, actual wages ex-

from $38,063 in 1977, a 4.9% in- 
crease. 

The net result was total expenses 
were successfully reduced by 0.1% 
share of sales to 31.4% compared to

1978.” 

The other major expense, rent, as 


a percentage of sales, dropped for 
the first time since 1962 to 2.4% of 
sales. Since 1962, it had remained 
unchanged at an average 2.5% share 
of sales. 

In 1978, although net profit before 
taxes rose 4% or $444 over the pre- 
vious year, as a per cent of sales, net 
profit slipped to 3.38% from 3.4% in 
1977. In dollars, net profit before 
taxes climbed to $11,467 in 1978 from 
$11,023 in 1977. 

Total income, as a shiare of sales for 
an average proprietor dropped 0.2% 
to 10.2% in 1978 from 10.4% of sales in 
1977. In dollars, income for the aver- 
age pharmacy attained a record high 
to $35,363 in 1978, up 5.1% from 
$33,645 in 1977. These figures are 
before taxes. 

Inventory investment in 1978 re- 
mained at 16.5% share of sales, un- 
changed from the previous year. In 
dollars, inventory at cost rose 5.1% 
to $56,942 from $53,382. The pre-

mained unchanged at 12% of sales, 
however, an additional $1,662 in in-

increased number and size of pre- 
scriptions filled. Inventory costs for 
other products remained the same at 
21.2% share of sales. In dollars, an 
additional $1,898 was needed to keep 
in stock of “other merchandise.” 

In 1978, the average number of 
hours an independent pharmacy was 
open was unchanged from 1977, 65 
hours per week.

Collapse of talks thwarts Fay’s 


By Michael Friedman 

LIVERPOOL, N.Y.—Fay’s 
Drug has met with a major set- 
back in its invasion of the South- 
east, having seen its merger 
talks with 28-store Mann Drug 
of High Point, N.C., cut short at 
the 11th hour. 

The acquisition of Mann, 
which would have more than 
doubled Fay’s holdings in the 
Carolinas, was slated to reach 
completion in March. 

“Our reasons for terminating 
negotiations are confidential, ” 
Fay’s chairman of the board 
Henry A. Panasci told Drug 
Store News. 

“The talks were terminated on 
very amicable terms,” said 
J. Henry Dowdy, president of 


the 56-year-old Mann operation. 
“Fay's is a fine organization. It's 
just that some things hadn't 
been resolved since the begin- 
ning.” 

Dowdy added that despite his 
chain’s near-acquisition by 
Fay’s, Mann Drug was not for 
sale. 

“This was an unusual situa- 
tion. We have always been 
friendly with the people at Fay’s, 
and we thought that both parties 
could benefit from a merger. 
But,” said Dowdy, “we are not 
looking to be acquired. Mann 
Drug will go on just as before.” 

Fay’s, on the other hand, 
must now be looking to other 
chains in the Southeast in order 
to continue the torrid rate of ex- 


pansion that management has 
oe in the last year anda 
half. 

Before August 1978, Liver- 
pool, N.Y.-based Fay’s operated 
just 51 drug stores, all in New 
York State except for a single 
unit in Pennsylvania. Then, 
Fay’s completed a merger with 
the seven-store, Charleston- 
based Berkeley Drug company 
of South Carolina and estab- 
lished its first outpost in the 
Sunbelt. 

The Northerner’s program ac- 
celerated with a takeover of 
Spartanburg, S.C.-based Craft 
Drug on Feb. 1, 1979. In addition 
to 14 retail outlets, Craft pro- 
vided Fay’s with a 21,000-sq.-ft. 
distribution center—since ex- 


panded by some 14,000 sa. ft. 
to serve as Southeastern opera- 
tions headquarters. 

Panasci called his chain’s 21 
outlets in South Carolina “a 
base from which to grow,” but 
his next major move came much 
closer to home. 

One year after the Berkeley 
transaction, Fay’s acquired Key 
Drug, a 20-store chain based in 
Rochester, N.Y. In doing so, the 
Liverpooler beefed up its repre- 
sentation in Rochester proper to 
17 outlets from four, and fortified 
its position in New York State 
against the encroachment of 
Rite Aid, Rhode Island-based 
Adams Drug and Consumer 
Value Stores, also quartered in

Walgreen takes Wisconsin 
with Rennebohm merger 


DEERFIELD, !!!—Walgreen Co.'s re- 
cent agreement to merge with Ren- 
nebohm Drug Stores Inc. of Madison, 
Wis., caps a year of feverish expansion 
activity in that state by the Deerfield- 
based chain. 

Assuming approval by Rennebohm's 
shareholders and a favorable review of 
the agreement by the Securities and Ex- 
change Commission, Walgreen expects 
to take over the Madison chain's 30 
stores by March 1. Included are 18 drug 
stores, three clinical pharmacies, seven 
freestanding restaurants, two health and 
beauty aid outlets and a card shop. The 
merger involves cash and an exchange 
of up to $8 million of Walgreen stock (a 
maximum of 244,667 shares) for Ren- 
nebohm shares. 

With the takeover, Walgreen will have 
more than doubled the number of drug 
stores it operates in Wisconsin in less 
than a year, increasing its count from 31 
to 65 units. Indications are that the next 
midwestern state slated for rapid Wal- 
green expansion is Minnesota, par- 
ticularly the big Minneapolis-St. Paul 
market, where the chain now has only 15 
stores.

DART DRUG has posted a 36% gain in net income for the nine 
months ended Oct. 31, 1979, as a result of improved margins, 
tightened expense controls and on-target sales promotion pro- 
grams. Earnings for the period amounted to $2.3 million or $1.31 
per share as opposed to $1.7 million or 92¢ per share a year ago. 
Sales improved 10.6% to $164 million from $148 million. 


Walgreen's recent blitz of Wisconsin is 
an example of the chain's strategy of 
concentrating expansion on filling in ex- 
isting markets. As of last May, Walgreen 
operated only 31 drug stores in the state, 
including only 19 in Milwaukee, the 
state's biggest market, and none in the 
second biggest market, Madison. 

Nine months and two acquisitions 
later, Walgreen has 65 Wisconsin stores, 
with three to four more scheduled for 
opening in the next six months, and the 
dominant chain position in both Mil- 
waukee and Madison. 

Acquisition favored 

Using a method increasingly favored 
by drug chains, Walgreen turned to ac- 
quisition as the best way to solidify its 
position in Wisconsin, a state which up 
to last May, had not attracted much at- 
tention from Walgreen management, 
notwithstanding its close proximity to 
Walgreen headquarters.

when Walgreen bought 16 Stein drug 
siores, 12 of them in the four-county Mil- 
waukee area. These, added to the 19

Pay ’n Save 
appeals to 
High Court 


WASHINGTON—Pay ’n Save 
has petitioned the U.S. Su- 
preme Court to reverse a 1979 
decision holding the chain le- 
gally responsible for the ac- 
curacy of manufacturer product 
claims contained in cooperative 
advertising. 

Unless that ruling is over- 
turned by the nation’s highest 
court, retail industry leaders in 
and out of the drug store field 
fear the decision will set a prec- 
edent discouraging retailers 
from accepting co-op ads in the 
future. 

Both the National Association 
of Chain Drug Stores and the 
broadly based American Retail 
Federation have joined with Pay 
'n Save in the Supreme Court 
appeal—an indication that the 
case remains a high priority 
concern among retailers across 
the country.

DRUG STORE NEWS, February 4, 1980 


ROCHE REIGNS IN TRANQUILIZERS 


Roche continues to dominate the 
tranquilizer market despite a per- 
sistent decline in the firm’s share of 
new and refill scripts compared to a 
year ago. 

As aresult, its aggregate share of 
the top 25 brands now comprises 
75% of the retail drug store tran- 
quilizer market compared to the 
82% share obtained during June of 
1978, according to Decision Data, 
Euless, Tex.-based supplier of phar- 
maceutical marketing research. 

A product-by-product comparison 
reveals that Valium 5mg’s share of 
scripts fell from 32% to 25% of the 
tranquilizer script market. Indeed, 
each of Roche’s products lost share 
in October 1979 compared to the 
year before. Yet, the firm dominates 
the class with the top four—Valium 
5mg, 10mg, and 2mg, and Librium 
10mg—representing over 41% of the 

class. 

Valium and similar drugs used in 
the treatment of anxiety are com- 
monly prescribed to relieve symp- 
toms of stress. Normally, these 
drugs produce a feeling of relaxation 
without inducing marked sleepi- 
ness, 

They are derived from ben- 
zodiazepine, a chemical whose ten- 
sion-reducing qualities were dis- 


covered by scientists at Roche’s U.S. 
laboratory in Nutley, N.J. While the 
precise working of the drug remains 
a mystery, it is known that about 20 
minutes after a Valium tablet is 
swallowed, the drug reaches tiny re- 
ceptors located in the brain’s emo- 
tion control centers, where it has a 
calming effect on the central ner- 
vous system. 

During the past few years, several 
new benzodiazepine-derivative 
tranquilizers have been launched by 
major manufacturers; notably 
Azene by New York-based Endo, 
Verstran by New Jersey-based 
Warner/Chilcott, and Ativan by 
Philadelphia-based Wyeth. Of these 
three brands, only Ativan lmg and 
2mg have penetrated the top 25 list 
of tranquilizers. 

However, even though the cate- 
gory is now more diverse, the 
monthly survey indicates that retail- 
ers’ per cent margin for the entire 
product class has increased from 
28.7% to 31.2%. This traces to an 
increase in the average retail price of 
a tranquilizer script which is already 
more than $3.00 greater than the 
overall average $6.50 paid by con- 
sumers for all types of scripts. 

Quantity dispensed, and therefore 
cost per unit, also plays a role in the 


class’ margin gain. Up 3%, quantity 
dispensed per script went from 58 to 
60 dosage units. Therefore higher 
consumer prices can’t be traced to a 
corresponding increase in quantity 
dispensed and must be attributed to 
continually rising cost of goods and 
wider margins. 

The importance of refills to this 
class of drugs is apparent when one 
considers that they now account for 
51% of all tranquilizer scripts, ad- 
vancing from 45% a year ago. 

The current situation with Valium 
is a problem for Roche in that the 
product line makes a large contribu- 
tion to profits. 

In fact, it was the development of 
Valium and its predecessor Librium 
in the early 1960's that made Roche a 
leading pharmaceutical company. 

Partly because of ever relentless 
competition—Roche claims that up 
to 700 Valium imitations and sub- 
stitutes are now marketed—the 
company’s drug sales have slipped 
for the past five years. 

Indeed, generics are starting to 
garner a slightly larger share of the 
tranquilizer market. Chlordiaze- 
poxide 10mg caps and meprobamate 
400mg tabs captured almost 4% of 
this drug class during the audit pe- 
riod.

Montgomery Ward’s recently opened prototype Family Profes- 
sional Service Center, located in a 150,000-sq.-ft. department store in 
Deerfield, Ill., is the general merchandiser’s most ambitious foray yet 
into health services. The center includes Ward’s first in-store leased 
dental and vital health testing centers, as well as such established 
leased departments as pharmacy, optical and health foods. In addi- 
tion, the center has a lawyer’s office. Ward’s expects to open more 
such unified Family Service Centers over the next couple of years, as 
well as continuing to add leased health-related departments to its 
stores on an individual basis. Plans call for 15 dental clinics to open 
in the next two to three years. New optical centers will be opening at 
the rate of about 20 per year.

Pay Less supports 
PLNW $24 offer 


NEW YORK—Based on the 
new tender offer of $24 a share 
from Pay Less Northwest, the 
Pay Less California board has 
recommended that its share- 
holders accept the new merger 
offer. 

On Feb. 1, Pay Less North- 
west announced it had ex- 
ecuted a definitive merger 
agreement to acquire Pay Less 
California by increasing its cash 
offer by $1.50, up from $22.50. 

Pay Less California said its 
shareholders of record on 
March 1 will meet on March 31 to 
vote on the merger. 

Pay Less California said ac- 
cording to a demand by the 
Jewel Cos., a special meeting 
will be held March 4 for share- 
holders of record Feb. 23 to vote 
ona previously announced mer- 
ger proposal by Jewel. 

Jewel, which signed a Nov. 9 
merger agreement with Pay 
Less California, is offering Pay 


Less California stockholders 
0.652 of Jewel common share 
for each Pay Less share they 
hold. Based on a Jewel stock 
price of $27.75 at presstime, 
Pay Less Caiifornia share- 
holders would receive the 
equivalent of $18.09 for each of 
their shares. 

In a prior move in the legal 
battle to acquire Pay Less Cal- 
ifornia, Pay Less Northwest has 
been requested by the Federal 
Trade Commission under an 
antitrust law to provide addi- 
tional information about its 
tender offer. Pay Less North- 
west was to have complied with 
the request on Feb. 1, and would 
therefore be eligible to buy addi- 
tional Pay Less California 
shares starting Feb. 11. 

On Jan. 18, a temporary re- 
straining order had been issued 
enjoining Jewel from acquiring 
additional Pay Less California 
shares pending a hearing. This 


action arises from a Jan. 4 
countersuit by Pay Less North- 
west seeking a preliminary in- 
junction against Jewel in U.S. 
Court for the Northern District of 
California. 

In his order, Federal Judge 
Charles Renfew stated in refer- 
ence to Jewel's plan to purchase 
Pay Less California shares both 
on the open market and pri- 
vately negotiated transactions 
that “there is a substantial ques- 
tion whether such purchases 
would constitute a violation of 
the Federal securities laws and 
the fiduciary duties of Jewel as a 
dominant shareholder of Pay 
Less California; that the pur- 
chases by [Jewel] of Pay Less 
California shares in the open 
market and in privately negoti- 
ated transaction threatens to 
cause [Pay Less Northwest] 
and other shareholders irre- 
parable injury.”

Armor to take reins as Thrift prexy 


“The primary thrust of my position 
will be to maintain the momentum 


of Lou Avner’s regime.” 


—James B. Armor 


executive vp of 357-unit Thrift Drug 
since 1976, has been named president 
of the chain, effective May 1. He suc- 
ceeds Louis L. Avner who will retire at 
age 65. 

“It's a little bit premature to discuss 
any future plans at this time,” the 53- 
year-old Armor said. “But | have been 
executive vp for four years, and Lou 
Avner and | have worked together 
closely on current programs. I'd say the 
primary thrust of my position will be to 
maintain the momentum of Lou Avner’s 
regime.” 

Armor started his career with Thrift's 
parent company, J. C. Penney, in 1948, 
as a shoe salesman in an Oklahoma 
City store. After a decade of service in 
Penney’s New York City-based offices, 
he was transferred to Thrift in 1971 as 
director of store operations, and was 
named executive vp five years later. 

Noting his strong operations back- 
ground, Armor said that three Thrift de- 


partments—the controller's office, real 
estate and loss prevention—would be 
reporting to him for the first time when 
he assumes the presidency. 

“I'd hope I'd be giving equal empha- 
sis to all aspects of the Thrift opera- 
tion,” he said. 

“lm an operations man,” he con- 
tinued, “and I'll have something to 
learn of nonoperations areas. But, 
above all, I’m a retail man.” 

Armor's retail philosophy is focused 
on performance at store level, and high 
customer service. 

“In our type of retail, there’s nothing 
that can beat Customer service,” he 
said. “Our retail stores are primary be- 
cause the central office doesn’t make 
any money at all. My aim is to get 110% 
out of everybody and have everybody 
have a bit of fun every day.” 

Thrifts 357 stores cover a trading 
area that includes 21 states—with 
stores operating under both the Thrift

LONGS DRUG STORES increased its annual per-store sales vol- 
ume to nearly $5.9 million in the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 1980, as 
compared to $5.4 million the year before. The 132-unit chain 
posted unaudited sales of $773 million for the year, a 17% improve- 
ment over $663 million the year before. Revenues for the fourth 
quarter alone amounted to $226 million, a 15% gain over $197 
million for the comparable period in the previous year.

unit drug and discount store chain. The Bismarck unit will in- 
clude a 6,000-sq.-ft. grocery box store operation and will carry a 
heavy concentration of promotional and seasonal items.

The Jewel Cos. has taken its furthest step yet toward integrating food and drug general 
merchandise in its combination stores in a just launched Jewel-Osco in St. Charles, Ill. Among the 
changes to promote integration of the two halves of the store, housewares (including plastics, 


bath accessories, kitchen utensils and cookware/glassware) are now located on the “food side”’ of 
the store, rather than in Osco Drug’s area. The store has also a cross aisle that runs the breadth of 
the store, rather than just on the Osco side (which is standard in most Jewel-Osco units) to 
increase customer flow between the drug store and the supermarket areas.

Orande Spansules (SmithKline 
& French).

COLUMBUS, Ohio—A 
Retail Performance Update 
by Management Horizons 
Inc., covering the last five 
fiscal years, shows the 63-

based in Pontiac, Mich., pac- 
ing 21 major chains with a 
sales growth rate of 27.94%. 

The 112-store Pay ’n Save 
Corp., headquartered in 
Seattle, follows closely be- 
hind with 27.87%. 

The median sales growth 
rate for the period by the 
chains reporting to the re- 
search-consulting firm was 
14.75%. 

In the category of return 
on net worth (profits divided 
by net worth in per cent), 
California’s Pay Less Drug

outlets, led the reporting 
chains with 19.6%.

for return on net worth was 
12.2%.

Price freeze fever 
grips more chains 


By Michael Friedman 

WASHINGTON—The 1,013-unit Eckerd Drug 
and Optel Corp.—which operates Mall Drug and 
Big L discount stores—have made the boldest 
moves to date in adding their names to the list of 
drug retailers voluntarily freezing prices, with 
Optel’s price-hike moratorium extending to 
“every item in the store.” 

At presstime, Cleveland-based Gray Drug had 
just announced a voluntary, 60-day price freeze 
on generic prescriptions and private label items, 
and the 680-unit Walgreen also had “a number of 
actions under study,” according to a spokesman. 
At least four other major chains were considering 
price ceilings on select categories, said an aide 
at the VWhite House Office of Consumer Affairs. 

Three Washington, D.C.-area chains—Peo- 
ples, Dart and Giant pharmacies—were the first 
to voluntarily adopt temporary moratoriums on 


retail-level price increases last month. 

In undertaking the self-imposed restraints, the 
chains will be bucking an estimated 600 manu- 
facturers price increases, in traditional drug cate- 
gories, in the month of April alone. Another 200 
to 300 increases are reportedly slated for May. 

Despite this, drug chains are gathering under 
the price-ceiling banner after White House Con- 
sumer Affairs Advisor Esther Peterson sent out a 
letter to the “top” 48 drug store operators, asking 
for a ceiling on consumer necessity prices for as 
long as possible. 

Although Optel never received the letter, sent 
only to chains with 25 or more Rx benches, the 
Holbrook, Mass.-based company instituted the 
most far-reaching program yet announced. 

“We're freezing prices for 90 days on every 
item in the store—some 10,000 sku's altogether, ”

Drugfair unloads its ailing 
Wrangler Wranch arm 


By Victoria Forgione 

ALEXANDRIA, Va.—Two 
short years after opening 
Wrangler Wranch Casual 
Clothing Shops, Drugfair is pull- 
ing up stakes and closing all 13 
Wranch locations. 

Although chain management 
Originally projected 40 Wranch 
units by 1982, they have already 
shuttered three this year, and 
are in the process of closing the 
remaining 10. 

Drugfair president Milton 
Elsberg attributed the dissolv- 
ing of the operation—which sold 
blue jeans and other casual at- 
tire—to a lackluster perfor- 
mance. “We decided to close 
the stores because they were 
unprofitabie,” said Elsberg, in 
an initial interview. “We got into 
the blue jean market after it 
peaked.” Elsberg further con- 
ceded that the advent in popu- 
larity of the designer jean might 
possibly have had something to 
do with the poor performance. 


In the chain's annual report 
for fiscal 1979, however, all 13 
Wranches were reported as 
meeting corporate goals. “Pub- 
lic acceptance of Wrangler 
Wranch has been excellent,” 
the report states, “and the sub- 
sidiary is meeting its profitability 
goals.” 

During Drugfair’s fiscal year 
ended Jan. 26, 1980, the 
Wrangler Wranch division lost 
$493,000 on operations, how- 
ever. The costs associated with 
the disposal of these units 
comes to $584,000, which 
makes the grand total charged 
against fiscal 1980 earnings 
equal to nearly $1.1 million. 
These losses helped knock 
Drugfair's fiscal 1980 earnings 
down by 53% to $754,000. 

_The chain's management in- 
dicates that blue jeans had 
peaked before the Wranches 
were opened. However, accord-

Drug store retailers brace 
for the Carter credit pinch 


By Clifford Feng 

NEW YORK—The Carter Ad- 
ministration’s plan to reduce in- 
flation by curbing excessive 
borrowing will be felt by the na- 
tion's drug retailers. In response 
to the plan, drug chain credit 
managers are re-evaluating 
their consumer credit opera- 
tions and are contemplating 
tighter lending restrictions. 

The Federal Reserve Board 
recently announced a series of 
measures to limit the growth of 
credit. One requirement is that 
certain lenders put 15% of con- 
sumer Credit increases that is in 
excess of the amount of credit 
outstanding on March 14 into a 
noninterest-bearing account 
with the Federal Reserve. The 
lenders affected include banks, 
retailers, gasoline and travel 
and entertainment card com- 
panies. It exempts lenders with 
less than $2 million of outstand- 
ing credit.

THE LOS ANGELES Regional Office of the National Labor Rela- 
tions Board is expected by mid-May to come up with a final ballot 
count on the battle between the Guild for Professional Pharma- 
cists and the Retail Clerks Union to represent some 400 pharma- 
cists of Sav-On Drugs. A count of early unchallenged ballots gave 


the Guild a lead. 


WITH GROWING numbers of drug store operators being preyed 
upon by drug abusers; the National Association of Retail Drug- 
gists (NARD) is pushing to make the theft of controlled sub- 


stances a Federal crime. 


REVCO IS all but certain to join the billionaire’s club of drug 
chains in fiscal 1980, as the 1,200-unit retailer posted a 15.6% 
increase in third-quarter sales to $271.9 million, bringing nine- 
month totals to $736.6 million, a 17.5% hike over last year. 


NEW YORK—Gains in net in- 
come those in sales 
for 16 major pharmaceutical 
manufacturers during 1979, in 
what for some was a record 
year, according to a survey con- 
ducted by Drug Store News. 

The 16 drug companies sur- 

amassed sales of $27.5 
billion during the year, an in- 
crease of 17%, and individual 
— that ranged from 8% to 
3%. Aggregate net income 
reached nearly $2.9 billion, re- 
flecting gains that ran from 1% 
to 43%, with one 41% drop, 
which was attributed to fiscal 
readjustments. 

The earnings-to-sales ratio 
for the 16 companies averaged 
a healthy 10.5%, with Smith- 
Kline taking the lead at 17%. 

The most spectacular gain in 
revenue among the companies 
was registered by Schering- 
Plough with $1.4 billion, an in- 
crease of 33%, with contribu- 
tions from such acquired com- 
panies as Scholl Inc. 

Among the giants, American 
Home Products scored a 15% 
jump in net income to $396 mil- 
lion, in contrast to an 11% gain in 
sales to $3.6 billion. 

Warner-Lambert ran No. 2 in 
revenues with $3.2 billion, a

Pharmacy 


Lower doses of estrogen 


NEW YORK—An increasing 
share of scripts for oral con- 
traceptives are continuing to 
move toward low dose estrogen 
formulations, according to data 
furnished by Decision Data, a 
division of Synergex Corpora- 
tion. 

Sources in the pharmaceuti- 
cal industry have indicated that 
these newer low dose formula- 
tions may “. . . give the pill anew 
lease on life.” 

“Physicians like the concept 
of a low estrogen formulation 
because these products cause 
fewer side effects and adverse 
reactions than their high es- 
trogen counterparts,” they said. 

It's generally conceded that 
fewer scripts are now being writ- 
ten for oral contraceptives be- 
cause women, especially those 
over 35 years of age, are con- 
cerned about these products 
damaging effects. 

These same sources within 
the industry report that “this 
trend is slackening because 
people are putting the products 
In proper perspective. Women 
are not discontinuing usage be- 
fore reaching 35 years of age, as 
they once did, because more 
positive reports about birth con- 
trol pills, especially low es- 
trogen tablets, are now avaii- 
able.” 

In order to capture a greater 
share of the market, firms are 


increasingly relying on products 
that compete in the 50mcg cate- 
gory. With a share of 53.7% and 
climbing, this market segment, 
along with the low dose es- 
trogen segment, represents 
prime candidates for new prod- 
uct entries. 

For example, Ortho Pharma- 
ceutical Co. recently launched a 
new entry in the low dose arena. 
Known as Ortho Novum 1/35, 
the new formulation joins the 
firm's companion low dose es- 
trogen product, Modicon, in 
competition against Lo/Ovral 
(Wyeth), Brevicon (Syntex), and 
Loestrin 1.5/30 (Parke Davis). 
Firms are increasingly seeking 
those eight out of 10 women in 
their child-bearing years who 
use birth control pills at some 
time or other, but may have dis- 
continued them because of ad- 
verse publicity. 

The research information pro- 
vided by Decision Data also 
points toward continued slip- 
page of retailer's already low 
margins for oral contraceptives. 
During August 1979, the top 19 
products accounted for 96.4% 
of the market, and registered an 
average retail margin of only 
4.6%. This continues a down- 
ward trend established pre- 
viously for these products. 

For example, Ovral carries an 
average price to the consumer 
of $7.75 per script, yet margin is 


give pill ‘new lease on life 


less than 15¢ to the pharmacy. 

Other findings reported in the 
analysis indicate that the mar- 
gin decline traces to increased 
cost of goods. Although the 
price of an average birth control 
script has increased 20%, it was 
not enough to offset retailers re- 
lentlessly rising cost of goods. 

The market is therefore char- 
acterized by shrinking margins, 
rising prices in the face of even 
higher cost increases, and a 
shifting toward low estrogen for- 
mulations.

Upjohn’s minoxidil approved for severe hypertension 


KALAMAZOO, Mich.—Up- 
john recently launched a power- 
ful direct-acting vasodilator that 
has been approved for severe 
hypertension in patients who 
have failed to respond to max- 
imum therapeutic doses of a di- 
uretic and two other antihyper- 
tensive agents. 

Called minoxidil (Loniten), the 
drug has been especially effec- 
tive for managing high blood 
pressure in patients with renal 
. failure, and has practically elimi- 
nated the need for bilateral 
nephrectomy among patients 
with life-threatening hyperten- 
sion resistant to conventional 
therapy. 

Minoxidil exerts a direct effect 


on arteriolar smooth muscle, 
similar to the effect observed 
with hydralazine and diazoxide. 
The dilation of constricted ar- 
terioles decreases peripheral 
vascular resistance and lowers 
blood pressure. 

The new drug has a half life of 
two to three hours, so following 
absorption, minoxidil rapidly 
disappears. The drug's anti- 
hypertensive action lasts for 
over 24 hours but does not cor- 
relate with plasma concentra- 
tions because minoxidil accu- 
mulates in the arterial wall. Over 
90% of an oral dose is elimi- 
nated in the urine primarily as 
metabolites. 

Usual daily dose of minoxidil 


is 10mg to 40mg, which can be 
administered in a single dose. It 
has been reported that some 
physicians start their patients 
on a dose of 1.25mg repeated 
over six hours. The dose is in- 
creased by 1.25mg at each rep- 
etition until blood pressure nor- 
malizes. Patients often get good 
results with as little as 10mg to 
20mg per day. 

Physicians also combine 
minoxidil with propranolol or 
clonidine, furosemide, and 
rigorous salt restriction in pa- 
tients with oliguric or anuric re- 
nal failure. Reports also indicate 
that many of these patients re- 
cover sufficient renal function to 
go off hemodialysis. 


Diuretic therapy 

Loniten must be used in con- 
junction with a diuretic in pa- 
tients relying on renal function 
for maintaining salt and water 
balance. Diuretics have been 
used at the following dosages 
when starting therapy with 
minoxidil: hydrochlorothiazide 
(50mg, b.i.d.) or other thiazides 
at equieffective dosage; chlor- 
thalidone (50mg to 100mg, 
ial furosemide 40mg, 

.i.d.). 

lf excessive salt and water re- 
tention results in a weight gain 
of more than five pounds, diuret- 
ic therapy should be changed to 
furosemide. 

Adverse effects of minoxidil 


therapy include reflex tachycar- 
dia, elevated plasma renin, and 
marked sodium and fluid reten- 
tion. For these reasons, the 
drug is administered under 
close medical supervision usu- 
ally with a beta blocker to pre- 
vent tachycardia and lower re- 
nin concentration, and with a 
potent diuretic to prevent mas- 
sive edema and congestive 
heart failure. 

The most alarming adverse 
effect is hirsuitism, which starts 
three to six weeks after begin- 
ning treatment and is almost 
universal. This unwanted hair is 
not permanent and disappears 
about one to six months after 
therapy is discontinued.

1980 Report of the Chain Drug Industry aan 


RIDING SUPERGROWTH INTO THE 80’S 


The chain drug industry has developed, over the last decade, into one of the most formidable 
arms of retailing. Propelled by the “supergrowth” trends of the 1970's, chain druggists 
are riding into the new decade armed with greater sales and profits records, 


more and bigger stores, broader merchandise mixes, and a health care orientation 
that has made them “recession- resistant? 


hains entered an 
era of super 
growth last year 
with a 15% gain 

in sales due in !arge part 
to their stores’ ability to 
attract increasingly 
higher levels of traffic. 


yf 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


Drug chains entered an era of 
super growth during 1979, complet- 
ing the year with a substantial sales 
gain, while moving even more 
rapidly into new, pioneering mer- 
chandising and service areas. 

Volume for the chain drug indus- 
try increased by an inflation-stoked 
14.8% last year as dollar sales for 
drug chains rose to $20.4 billion. In 
the process, the chain drug indus- 
try’s contribution to overal! drug 
store sales widened to 72.8% from 
70.2% in 1978. 

Chains (operations with two or 
more stores) have emerged at the 
start of the 1980’s as the super 
growth segment of the drug store 
business, and their mark on this in- 
dustry has become an indelible one. 
They dominate it; they set the pace, 
they are pioneering the trends, and 
they determine the drug store busi- 
ness future directions. 

The chain drug gains occurred last 
year against a backdrop of solid 
growth for the entire drug business. 
The total drug store volume in- 
creased 11% last year to $28.1 billion 
from $25.3 billion. Most of this 
growth obviously stems from the 
chain segment of the market. 

Independent segment 

The independent or single store 
segment of this market produced 
only a 1% increment in volume dur- 
ing 1979. Sales for this sector totaled 
$7.63 billion last year, up from $7.55 
billion the year before. 

Net profits were also up substan- 
tially for drug chains, with the gains 
being an estimated 15% to 18% in- 
dustrywide. Behind the increase 
were continued productivity gains 
at the store level and improved gross 
margins. Among the leading chains, 
Walgreen's profits climbed 26% for 
its fiscal year, while Thrifty’s surged 
29%. Rite Aid produced a 23% gain 
in profits for its fiscal year, and 
Kckerd’s net increased by 17%. 

Total industry profits were equal 
to $500 million to $600 million last 
year, the highest they have ever 
been. 

At this point in time, the chain 
business is characterized by a num- 
ber of trends including: 

@ rapid buildup of new units; 
® extension into new markets; 
®@ development of new store pro- 
totypes; 

@ launching of greater numbers of 
drug/food combo units; 

@ emphasis on health care lines; 

@ positioning of stores as conve- 


Sales in $ bils. 


nience units; 

® exceptionally fast-paced sales and 
earnings gains; 

@ high level of merger and acquisi- 
tion activity. 

It is true that much of last year’s 
super sales growth stemmed from 
the inflationary factor, but by no 
means all. From an inflationary 
standpoint for the overall economy, 
the rise in price levels last year was 
around 12%. However, much of this 
percentage of overall price rise is 
directly related to soaring energy 
costs (gasoline was up 60% last year) 
and rapidly climbing housing costs 
(also up around 60%). Specific sec- 
tors of the economy have lesser rates 
of inflation, including drug stores. 
Most chain merchandise managers 
estimate that inflation for the mer- 
chandise carried by drug stores 


came to around 7% to 8% last year. 
New stores 

The implication is that much of the 
remainder of the nearly 15% rate of 
sales growth developed by drug 
chains during 1979 stemmed from 
new stores and internal per-store 
gains. 

The chain drug industry has built 
a large number of new stores over 
the past several years, and much of 
the industry’s super growth has 
stemmed from the ongoing store 
programs of the major chains. The 
industry's net gain last year in num- 
bers of stores was equal to 474, one 
of the largest gains in years. The 
industry finished out the year with 
19,764 stores (a new record).

The industry’s growth has been 
sustained in large part by the large 
opening programs of the major 
chains. For example, Revco 
launched 118 stores, while Rite Aid 
added 86 units to its store count. 
Eckerd reached the 1,000 store 
mark (the second chain to do so) in 
the fall, and was able to launch 88 
stores during its fiscal 1979 year. 

At the same time, overall sales 
were bolstered by per-store sales 
gains. Average sales per chain drug 
store advanced 12% last year to $1.03 
million, the first time, incidentally, 
that this figure has exceeded a mil- 
lion dollars per year (on a weekly 
basis, the figure is around $19,000). 
Most major drug chains, however, 
expect that their stores ought to be 
doing $1.25 to $1.5 million just to be 
average, and larger units coming on 
stream now are expected by chain 
management teams to build up 


1979 


rapidly to figures well beyond this 
level. 

The average chain drug units 
weigh in at around 8,000 sq. ft. sell- 
ing including all units, both new, old 
and those coming on stream. New 
units, of course, tend to be larger, 
and according to Drug Store News’ 
survey, new stores last year aver- 
aged around 10,250 sq. ft., or nearly 
30% larger than the typical store 
overall. 

Productivity in sales per square 
foot totaled $130 last year, up some- 
what from the previous year’s vol- 
ume. Many major chains are aiming 
to produce $150 of sales per square 
foot of selling area, or better. 

High sales per square foot 

Chains such as Longs, operating 
super drug stores averaging $5 to $6 
million in volume annually, are capa- 
ble of producing sales per square 


foot of well over $200. More conven- 
tionally sized units can also produce 
over $150 per square foot in annual 
volume. 

The sharp increase in sales per 
store stems from a number of fac- 
tors. One is the increase in the size of 
the typical chain drug store, as just 
indicated by the large size of new 
stores opening currently. The trend 
toward larger units has been under 
way for some considerable time, and 
it is not just a question of all chains 
going to larger stores. Many opera- 
tions have found what they consider 
to be the ceiling for the size of their 
stores—a level that varies from 
chain to chain. However, few drug 
stores in excess of 30,000 sq. ft. (ex- 
cepting combination units) are 
opened, and many find the ceiling 
lower. The reasoning is that once a 
store gets larger, it begins to lose its 
drug image, and a strong drug store 
image is important to the way most 
chains want to be viewed by consum- 
ers. The concern is that if stores 
carry too much nondrug merchan- 
dise, they will lose that solid drug 
store image that is important to de- 
veloping a loyal customer following. 

However, even though there is a 
ceiling, much of the industry is oper- 
ating stores that are well below what 
individual chains consider the ceil- 
ing, so that as new larger stores 
come on stream (frequently consid- 
erably larger) and older units are 
shuttered, the average size of the 
store operated by drug chains has 
trended upward steadily. 

Expanded mix 

Another factor bolstering per- 
store volume has been the steady 
extension of the merchandise mix 
(aided by the existence of larger 
stores) into new and different areas, 
a trend that has supplemented 
ehains strong reinforcement of basic 
areas over the past several years. 

In fact, a number of merchandis- 
ing areas proved to be above-aver- 
age producers last year, and some of 
these were basic drug store mer- 
chandising areas. For example, toi- 
letries generated a 16% increment in 
volume in 1979, while cosmetics reg- 
istered a 17% gain in sales. 

Both these areas have been 
strongly emphasized by drug chains 
over the past several years, and cos- 
metics in fact, has undergone a com- 
plete overhaul in merchandising and 
presentation over the past two or 
three years. Many chains have be- 
gun opening up their cosmetics de-

partment to much more self-service, 
and have introduced the concept of 
assisted self-service to make the de- 
partment’s merchandise more ac- 
cessible to consumers. At the same 
time, visual impact of the depart- 
ment is being stressed with such ve-

Emphasis on toiletries 

Also, chains, recognizing the im- 
portance of toiletries to their con- 
sumer image, have paid a great deal 

of attention to the merchandising of 
the product area. Many programs 
exist for the purpose of ensuring 
that they do not experience outs in 
toiletries. 

There were some other facts, also, 
behind the cosmetics and toiletries 
sales gains last year. One was the 
fact that women, in an inflationary 
economy in which families are plac- 
ing tight controls on budgets, tend 
to begin downtrading. The implica- 
tion is that women are shifting their 
now limited purchasing power from 
more expensive dress and other arti- 
cles of clothing into cosmetics and 
toiletries, which now represent a 
more inexpensive way to make 
themselves beautiful. 

At the same time, a great deal of 
additional sales dollars flowed from 
the extension of the chain drug mix 
into areas outside of drug, toiletries 
and cosmetics. For example, Do-It- 
Yourself categories, including auto- 
motive and hardware, generated 
substantial sales growth last year, as 
more chains added these products or 
extended the footage devoted to 
them. In fact, in terms of automo- 
tive, this category has gotten a spe- 
cial boost from the gas crisis (as 
more people tinker with their cars to 
get better mileage) and soaring car 
prices (which place a premium on a 
family’s existing auto). 

Housewares growing 

Housewares also experienced a 
high rate of sales growth, along with 
toys, both of which categories chains 
have expended a great deal of mer- 
chanidising effort on over the past 

several years. 

All of these categories have been 
strongly supported over the past 
year and a half by extensive adver- 
tising and promotion. Most chains 
relied heavily on extra-heavy pro- 
motion to bolster sales growth dur- 
ing most of 1979 (and have continued 
to do this into 1980) in an effort to 
mitigate any ill effects of a possible 
recession. Moreover, most chain 
merchandisers sense that, due to in- 
flation, consumers are more than 
ever seeking value for their dollars, 


and promotion is one way to take 
that message to them effectively. 
Most chains are being far more care- 
ful about selecting items and have 
found that they must pick items for 
which the consumer will feel that he 
or she is receiving value. 

However, in terms of the chain 
drug industry extending its mix, 
two major, parallel trends are now 
apparently under way which may 
very well do much to significantly 
change the face of the chain drug

industry: One is the emergence of 
the drug store as a health care cen- 
ter and the other is the positioning of 
the drug store as a convenience out- 
let. 
Health care concept 
Probably the most important of 
the two trends is the very strong 
emphasis that drug chains are plac- 
ing on professional health care of all 
types in addition tc dispensing phar- 
maceuticals. This goes beyond 
merely stressing basic drug store 
product categories, such as health 
aids, from a merchandising point of 
view, although that trend is related. 
What is taking place is that drug 
chains are seeking to create for 
themselves the image of the drug 
store as a health care center. Using 
the pharmacy as a foundation, drug 
chains are adding on a variety of pro- 
fessional health care lines and ser- 
vices to provide consumers with 
extended offerings in the health care 
area. The aim is to attract the con- 
sumer with the message: “Come to 
the chain drug store for much of your 
health care needs, including those 
beyond prescription drugs and 
health aids.” The basis of this con- 


cept is the professional atmosphere 
projected by the store’s prescription 
department as well as the reptta- 
tion drug chains have earned in the 
marketplace for having tremendous 
selections of health aids at dis- 
counted prices. Physically these de- 
partments are normally grouped 
together to emphasize the existence 
of a health care package. 

The initial foray into this area was 
optics, and although some chains 
have backed away from this area, 
many have not. Optics is by no 
means dead in the chain drug indus- 
try, and at those chains where there 
is a strong commitment to make it 
go, it is becoming an integral part of 
a health care center concept. Over 
600 centers were in operation in the 
chain drug industry last year, and 
those chains that have decided to 
devote the resources and manage- 
ment time to do it successfully, have 
been able to benefit from the addi- 
tion of optical centers to their 
stores. 

Dental care 

The second major area that chains 
are moving into is dental care, and 
two chains (People and Revco) have 
already launched dental centers 
within their stores. Several more 
have active plans to do so. This pro- 
fessional health care area requires 
even more commitment than optics 
in that the store has to be modified 
to accept the plumbing and the den- 
tal chairs. Of course, due partly to 
legal restrictions, dental units are 
being handled. on a lease basis, in 
contrast to optics which in most 
cases is a company-owned opera- 
tion, so that the risk in dental is 
spread somewhat. Despite the diffi- 
culties, however, those chains going 
into dentistry are figuring that an 
expanded health care offerings con- 
cept based on the professional repu- 
tation built on Rx drugs will make 
dentistry go. Drug chains are also 
coming into this health care area 
much as they have in most others— 
they are providing goods and ser- 
vices at a highly competitive cost to 
the consumer. These chains are fig- 
uring that the rewards for providing 
dentistry as part of a health care 
package will be increased traffic, 
higher sales, and improved profits 
overall. 

What is perhaps most interesting 
about dental, is that this health area 
takes chains to a new level, in which, 
while optics was product selling 
with a very heavy overlay of service, 
dentistry is entirely service—no 
product is involved.

has a major optical operation and a 
strong commitment to convalescent

which emphasizes basic drug store 
merchandise and health care lines. 

Pharmacy vital 

Chains have also enhanced their 
health care image by emphasizing 
their pharmacy departments. A 
great many chains have launched ge- 
neric drug programs (where ap- 
plicable) and taken the message to 
consumers with extensive advertis- 
ing programs. The introduction of 
generic drug programs and the pro- 
motional efforts that supplement 
them are important factors in 
strengthening the professional im- 
age that drug chains have. 

Another factor also doing that has 
been the spread of computer phar- 
macy terminals. These machines 
have significantly widened the scope 


of chain pharmacy operations by al- 
lowing more efficient dispensing, 
cheaper third-party billing and pa- 
tient profiles. 

The other major thrust in the 
chain drug industry has been to 
position the chain drug store as a 
convenience outlet. Chains survived 
the 1973-74 stagflation era because 
they had neighborhood locations, 
discount prices, and a basically low- 
ticket mix of high demand necessity 
items. In a sense, chain drug stores 


have been convenience retailers for 


some time, especially since their 
mix has been extended beyond basic 
health aids and toiletries, into 
housewares, hardware, automotive 
and similar categories. 

Drug chains are now, however, 
consciously developing preduct lines 
that will make them convenience 
stores in consumers minds, and the 
most important among these prod- 
uct lines has been the rapid build-up 
of food sections. Most major chains 
now carry food in some form or an- 
other—be it promotional endcaps 
for ins-and-outs or a permanent sec- 
tion of a couple of thousand square 
feet to make the store a mini-drug/ 
food combo. 

For many chains food has proven 
to be an ideal reinforcement to a con- 
venience concept. The items are 
generally low ticket; they are high- 
demand items people regard as nec- 
essities, and they are promotable. 
The mix generally consists of juices, 
cereals, other dry and canned gro- 
ceries, condiments, sauces, ethnic 
foods and beer/soda. There are usu-

Gas crunch 

At this particular moment in his- 

tory, convenience shopping is ex- 


tremely important. The gas crunch 
has placed a premium on neighbor- 
hood locations, and no other retail 
sector is as well equipped as drug in 
this regard. At the same time, con- 
sumers are seeking one-stop shop- 
ping as never before to save on gas. 
Convenience food, for those who do 
not want to drive far or brave long 
supermarket lines, contributes 
strongly to this one-stop concept. 

Quite different from the mini- 
combo is the large 50,000-sq.-ft. 
plus full-scale drug/foud unit capa- 
ble of churning out $10 million and 
more in volume annually. This too 
follows a one-stop shopping philoso- 
phy. 

These large combination stores 
are becoming a major part of the 
chain drug business, and the con- 
cept received a shot in the arm last 
year with the completion of the

1980's with a variety of new concepts 
and a tremendous momentus in 
growth. Expectations are that they 
will significantly expand their busi- 
ness over the next several years.
