DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


AFFILIATED STORES PUSH ON 


Affiliated membership continued 
to grow faster than the increase in 
the overall market in 1979 as inde- 
pendents and small chains strength- 
ened their efforts to offset the 
growing dominance of the chain 
drug store. 

In 1979, affiliated membership in- 
creased 8.5% over the previous year. 
Almost 14,000 drug stores employed 
co-op or voluntary programs offered 
by wholesalers. Of the 13,975 affili- 
ated drug stores across the nation, 
approximately 86% or 12,025, were 
independents. The percentage of in- 
dependents that are affiliated with a 
wholesaler remained constant the 
last three years. On the other hand, 
chains comprise the remaining 14% 
or 1,830 affiliated members last year. 

Sales for the total affiliated mar- 
ket increased in 1979 by 16.6% to a 
record $4.98 billion compared to 
$4.27 billion the year earlier. Of the 
almost $5 billion in sales in 1979, in- 
dependents contributed the major 
share of volume, $4.11 billion. That is 
a 23.38% rise in sales by indepen- 
dents compared to a year ago. 

The number of chains involved in 
affiliated programs continues to 
rise, but not nearly at the same 
growth rate as the independents. 
Last year, chains contributed $0.87 
billion to the total affiliated market, 
a 14% increase over chain contribu- 
tion of $0.76 billion in 1978. In 1979, 
chain sales accounted for 17.5% of 
the almost $5 billion in sales re- 
ported by affiliated members. 

The average sales per store of af- 
filiated members climbed to a record 
$356,000, a 7.2% increase in 1979 
compared to $322,000 in 1978. Last 
year, the average independent’s 
sales per store was $342,000, up 
from $318,000 in 1978. Chains on the 
other hand, averaged $444,000 in 
sales per store compared to $415,000 
in sales the year before. 

The reason for the growth in the 
number of stores affiliated with co- 
ops or voluntary groups is because of 


the attractive programs wholesalers 
are using to lure nonmembers. In- 
ducements to retailers include elec- 
tronic order programs, planograms, 
and circulars for health and beauty 
aid and sundry promotions. 
Wholesaler services

Clearly, the past 12 months have 
been nothing short of dramatic for 
wholesale druggists.

chain operator the value of the 
wholesaler is the broad merchandise 
mix they can supply, products small 
operators need to order in order to 
survive among the growing chains.

needs of independents and small 
chains have broadened their mer- 
chandise mix in the last few years. 
Drug distributors are putting more 
emphasis on the front end of the 
pharmacy to get on board the trend 
of one source supplying. Nearly 88% 
of those questioned said they ex- 
panded their merchandise mix in the 
last five years. Frequently ex- 
panded lines include cosmetics, gift 
items, convalescent aids, house- 
wares and food. Almost one-third 
said they broadened their lines to 
include food. 

During the last decade, whole- 
salers have made a concerted effort 
to reach their customers through a 
stronger link with affiliated groups. 
The days when retailing cherry- 
picked suppliers are ending, most 
wholesalers believe, in order for 
both the retailer and the supplier to 
survive.

DRUG CHAINS ARE BUYING INTO 
NEW MAREETS, NEW DIRECTIONS 


Merger and acquisition activity 
moved to a new level in the chain 
drug industry last year, as, for the 
first time, a drug chain took over a 
major supermarket operation. 

The most important amalgama- 
tion last year: the merger of Skaggs 
and grocery chain American Stores, 
with Skaggs being the survivor cor- 
poration (although the company has 
assumed the American Stores 
name). The importance of this mer- 


ger lies not only in its magnitude (it 
created a $5 billion company) but 
rather in its potential impact on 
combination store retailing. It is 
also the first time that a major su- 
permarketer has been acquired by a 
drug chain. 

Acquisition fever was at such a 
pace in 1979 that retailers were even 
competing with one another in order 
to get what they considered the 
prize plum. Last year, for any small, 


prosperous chain, there always ap- 
peared to be a buyer. 

Consider the recent case'of Pay 
Less (Calif.) being courted by both 
Pay Less Northwest and Jewel 
Cos., a diversified supermarket 
chain in Chicago. While Pay Less 


(Calif.) was by no means in financial — 


difficulty, for the past few years the 
drug retailer had reported erratic 
earnings. 

In November, Jewel announced

By March 1980, it became clear, 
after Pay Less Northwest increased 
its tender offer to $24 a share, that it 
would be the winner in the competi- 
tion to acquire the 60-store drug 
chain. 

Actually, this year of acquisitions 
is an extension of the merger ac- 
tivity during the last 10 years. The 
growth of the super chain is no sur- 
prise as events at the beginning of 
the decade indicated when chains 
such as Skaggs acquired the 64- 
store Katz stores, when Eckerd pur- 
chased Madig-Dugan (40 stores) and 
when Revco bought Cole (28 stores). 


Key mergers 

Key mergers in 1979 included the 
Peoples acquisition of Haag Drugs of 
Indianapolis. The cash transaction 
gave the Alexandria, Va.-based Peo- 
ples chain 80 new stores, $80 million 
in sales and about $1 million in prof- 
its and stores in four previously un- 
penetrated states. Haag’s trading 
area is contiguous to Peoples’ mid- 
western markets. With the merger, 
Peoples owns about 480 stores. 

Just before the end of the year, 
Adams of Pawtucket, R.I., bought 
the 43-store Sun Drug chain of 
Butler, Pa. The move was made to 
bolster Adams’ position in Pennsy]l- 
vania. In the Keystone state, Adams 


already owned Eckerd of Pennsylva- 
nia and Quaker Drugs. Adams now 
operates 412 drug units in the north- 
east. 

A few months prior to the Sun 
transaction, Adams purchased Kent 
Drug stores, a six unit chain in cen- 
tral New York. 

One New York retailer that was 
buying last year was Fay’s. The firm 
acquired Key Drugs of Rochester, 
N.Y., and the 14 Craft Drug stores 
of Spartanburg, S.C. In 1978, Fay’s 
started its march into the South by 
buying Berkeley Drugs, a seven unit 
chain in Charlotte. Fay’s was unable 
to complete a merger with Mann 
Drugs of North Carolina in October. 
To strengthen its position in New 
York, Fay’s bought the 20 Key 
stores. The cash buy-out expanded 
Fay’s penetration into the Rochester 
area from four stores to 17 outlets. 

Walgreen secured a position in 
Wisconsin, particularly in the Mil- 
waukee area with the purchase of 16 
of the 19 Stein Drug stores. With the 
acquisition, Walgreen had 31 stores 
in the Milwaukee area and a total of 
47 outlets in Wisconsin. Walgreen's 
ended the year still wooing Ren- 
nebohm’s, a 17-chain store in Madi- 
son, Wis. If successful, the sale 
would give Walgreen a toehold in the 
south-central portion of the state, a 
virgin area for the firm. 

In June, Rite Aid bought eight of 
the nine bankrupt stores left in the 
Quality chain for $990,000. The units 
are in Delaware, New Jersey and 
Pennsylvania. In 1979, Rite Aid also 
bought nine Dixx Mart Inc. stores in 
central and lower New York State. 
Rite Aid now has nearly 800 stores. 

Cunningham Drug Stores bought 
16 Intercontinental Stores in Hawaii 
and Seattle, Wash. The purchase 
consisted of 12 Intercontinental 
stores on the island of Oahu, 11 of 
them in Honolulu, as well as two 
outlets on the island of Maui and two 
others in the Olympic Hotel in Seat- 
tle. This brings the number of Cun- 
ningham stores to about 180.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


NEW STORES: BIG GET BIGGER 


Drug chain sales and earnings in- 
creases have been partly fueled by 
the aggressive expansion programs 
adopted by retailers and by favor- 
able demographics. In 1979, it was 
no different. 

Last year the number of chains 
operating two or more stores in the 
United States was up 1.6% to 2,709 
compared to 2,666 in 1978. The num- 
ber of stores operated by these 
chains increased across the nation, 
up 2.6% to 19,764 stores compared to 
19,290 stores in 1978. 

While the number of corporations 
operating two stores (1,484), three 
stores (562) and four to nine stores 
(498) increased in 1979, the number 
of firms operating 10 or more stores 
dropped. Last year the number of 
medium-sized chains decreased 
from 172 companies in 1978 to 165 in 
1979. Most of the decrease in this 
size category is attributed to the ac- 
quisition of the medium-sized chains 
by larger chains. For the major 
chains, these purchases supplement 
their own construction plans and 
new store openings. 

In 1979 the drug chain with the 
largest number of retail outlets was 
once again Revco, which completed 
the year with 1,143 stores. Last year, 
Revco opened 113 new stores. Plac- 


ing second in quantity of stores is 
Jack Eckerd Corp. which completed 
ealendar 1979 with 1,006 stores. 
Eckerd now joins Revco in the elite 
club of drug chains with 1,000 or 
more stores. Eckerd opened a total 
of 88 stores in 1979. This retailer, 
headquartered in Clearwater, F'la., 
gets the award for opening the most 
stores in one week—22 units were 
opened in early November. 

Rite Aid Corp., on the East Coast, 
opened 86 new stores in 1979 and had 
a total of 800 by the end of its fiscal 
1980. The chain, based in Pennsylva- 
nia, is next in line to become a mem- 
ber of the 1,000+ store club. 

Other chains that opened more 
than 20 units last year include Ad- 
ams (65), Walgreen (47), CVS (89), 
Osco (27) and SupeRx (387). 

Reveo, which led chains with the 
greatest number of stores also led 
chains in the number of remodeled 
stores, with 73. In 1978, Revco re- 
modeled 60 old stores. Thrifty Corp. 
of Los Angeles renovated 50 of its 
older outlets and Drugfair of Alex- 
andria, Va., which remodeled 33 
stores in 1978, renovated 28 last 
year. Skillern’s of Dallas, which led 
chains in the number of remodelings 
in 1978 with 104, only remodeled 22 
in 1979.

CHAINS _— MARKET GRIP 


In the last decade the trend has 
been toward consolidation of chain 
ownership as the number of com- 
panies operating chains has de- 
creased from a high in 1975 of 3,008 
to 2,709 in 1979. This trend is ex- 
pected to continue as larger chains 
continue to buy out medium sized 
and small chains. 

While the number of firms operat- 
ing chains has been on the decline, 
chain share of market for the entire 
retail drug industry has been on the 
upswing. As a group, chains hada 
71% share of sales of a retail drug 
market of $28.050 billion. In com- 
parison, 10 years ago, the chain 
share of market was only 54.9% of an 
$11.9 billion retail drug market. Last 
year, the 10 chains with the largest 
annual sales volume accounted for 
more than one-third of the total dol- 
lars spent by consumers in drug 
stores. 

Further documentation that there 
is a trend toward consolidation is the 
fact that the number of chains oper- 
ating 10 units or more has dropped 
from 172 in 1978 to 165 in 1979. 

However, in total, in 1979 there 
were a record number of stores 
being operated by chains—19,764— 


an increase of 474 stores. 

The growth of the major chains 
has been at the expense of the small- 
and medium-sized firms. In the 
United States, corporations with 10 
or more stores control about 28% of 
all chain drug stores. 

Nevertheless, the number of com- 
panies operating chains under the 
10-or-more-units level did increase 
in 1979 over 1978. The number of 
companies operating two stores or 
more increased by 17 to 1,484 in 1979 
from 1,467 in 1978. The number of 
stores these companies operate rose 
from 2,934 in 1978 to 2,968 in 1979. 

The number of companies operat- 
ing three stores increased by 138 to 
562 up from 549 in 1978. The number 
of stores they operated grew by 39 
units to 1,686 compared to 1978. 

The number of companies operat- 
ing four to nine stores increased by 
21 to 498 in 1979. The number of 
stores they operated increased by 47 
to 2,596 compared to 1978. 

The trend of larger chains acquir- 
ing smaller operations will no doubt 

continue as large chains seek to 
boost sales and their number of 
stores quickly. And more impor- 
tantly, the advantage in acquiring

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


CHAIN STOCKS STILL GOOD BUY 


After strong and healthy growth 
in 1978, chain drug store stock prices 
continued to climb. But in 1979, the 
average growth rate of the 21 public 
chains tapered off slightly compared 
to the previous year. Nevertheless, 
Wall Street investment analysts 
continue to have high regard for the 
industry, citing good earnings po- 
tential for 1980. 

The average stock price of the 21 
public chains increased by slightly 
more than 15% in 1979 over the pre- 
vious year. In 1978, the average 
price per share increased 16% over 
the year before. 

In terms of the number of shares 
traded, drug chain issue volume was 
down 13% in 1979 compared to 1978. 

Last year there was a turnaround 
in the average price earnings ratio 
for the chains, increasing to 8.4 from 
8.0 in 1978. This ratio, however, is 
still down from the average price 
earnings ratio of 9 in 1977. 

In 1979, there was one less public 
chain. Skaggs Cos. is no longer 
listed because of its merger with 
American Stores Co. 

In 1979, 16 of the 21 public chains 
stocks closed the year above their 
closing price in 1978. Shares of two 
chains, Genovese and Sav-On, 
closed 1979 unchanged from the last 
price in 1978. In 1979, 11 of the 21 
chains reached new highs in stock 
values. 

Top gainers for 1979 

The chain industry’s top gainer 
last year was Pay Less (Calif.), the 
Oakland-based firm. The company’s 
stock climbed 105%, closing at the 
end of the year at $19.50 per share, 


up from $9.50 per share at the end of 


1978. 

Speculation about a proposed 
takeover by either Jewel Cos. or Pay 
Less Northwest pushed Pay Less 
(Calif.) stock up in the fourth quar- 
ter. The chain’s stock closed at its 
high for the year. 

Other top gainers in 1979 were 


Dart Drug, up 64% to $8.63 per 
share, Walgreen, up 34% to $33.25 
at year-end, Rite Aid, up 32.5% to 
$26.13 and Fay’s, up 30% to $11.38 
per share. 

Many securities analysts are bull- 
ish about future prospects of the 
chain drug industry and the related 
pharmaceuticals industry. They say 
that while other retail sales may 
slump in the event of a recession, the 
chain drug and pharmaceuticals in- 
dustries will be more resistant. 

Analysts’ recommendations 

According to Monroe H. Green- 
stein, an analyst for Bear Sterns & 
Co.: “Chain drug stock should do 
very well in the last three quarters 
of 1980. Generally, the companys’ 
earnings have a high degree of resis- 


McEvoy recommends three stocks 
in particular: Walgreen, Rite Aid 
and Longs. He cites Walgreen as at- 
tractive because it is undervalued 
and is in “a recovery situation.” He 
says Longs is a good conservative 
company and would therefore be at- 
tractive to a customer seeking long- 
term growth. McEvoy expects that 
most of the chains will report at least 
a 15% increase in earnings this year. 

McEvoy says Rite Aid’s sales and 
earnings have grown at a compound 
annual rate of 17% and 36% respec- 
tively, since 1975. He expects Rite 
Aid’s fiscal earnings to be about 
$2.90 per share in fiscal 1980, for 
fiscal 1981 about $3.45 per share.

stock should do better than average

A natural succession 

Approaching his retirement May 1 
as president of the 357-outlet, 21- 
state Thrift Drug Co., 65-year-old 
Louis L. Avner looked no further 
than his No. 2 man, James B. Ar- 
mor, executive vp since 1976, to suc- 
ceed him. 

Armor, 53, emphasized that he 
and Avner had “worked together 
closely for four years.” 

Armor’s own career momentum 
had been something to behold. Hav- 
ing started as a shoe salesman in 
1948 with Thrift’s parent, J. C. Pen- 
ney, he moved into Penney’s New 
York office, then over to Thrift in 
1971 as director of store operations 
and up to executive vp five years 
later. It was important te Armor, 
assuming his new role, that Thrift’s 
controller, real estate office and loss 
prevention unit would be reporting 
to him. 

“I'd hoped,” he said, “that I’d be 
giving equal emphasis to all aspects 
of the Thrift operation. I’m an oper- 
ations man and I'll have something 
to learn about nonoperations areas. 
But above all, I’m a retail man. 

“In our type of retail, there’s noth- 
ing that can beat customer service. 
... My aim is to get 110% out of 
everybody and have everybody have 
a bit of fun every day.” As he ap- 
proaches his new position, Thrift 
was enjoying the fruits of a iast fiscai 


year that marked an 18.1% increase 
in sales to $411 million. 
A family tradition 

In January, directors of the 52- 
store Begley Drug Co., based in 
Richmond, Ky., named Robert J. 
Begley board chairman to succeed 
his father, Robert B. Begley, 67, 
founder of the chain, who died of a 
heart attack Dec. 4. 

Merger leads to loss 

One of the key men in the acquisi- 
tion by the 382-unit Adams Drug 
Co., based in Pawtucket, R.I., of the 
well-run, 43-store Sun Drug, head- 
quartered in Butler, Pa., was the 
latter’s president Kenneth R. 
Chane. 

Following the November deal, 
Chane said he’d recommended the 
sale to Sun’s parent, Spang Stores 
Inc. 

“I recommended that Spang di- 
vest themselves of the retail opera- 
tion because it really wasn’t for 
them,” said Chane. With the dis- 
closure of the deal, Chane left office, 
saying he planned to do consulting 
duty with drug chains in the em- 
ployee training and marketing 
areas. The rest of Sun’s top manage- 
ment remained.

READY FOR A CHALLENGING YEAR 


What are drug chains’ chief execu- 
tives expecting for 1980? Here’s 
what several presidents and ceos

year.

that the drug

discount

For the first time in chain drug 
history, four retailers topped the $1 
billion mark in sales. The newest 
member of the billionaire’s club is 
Reveo D. 8S. Inc., which now joins 
Walgreen, Eckerd and Skaggs. 

The top 50 chains in the nation 
rang up more than 75% of total chain 
sales. In 1979, these chains ac- 
counted for more than $15 billion of 
total chain sales, which reached a 
record $20 billion. 

Asa group, chains had a 71% share 
of retail drug industry sales of 
$28,050 billion, according to a report 
by the U.S. Department of Com- 
merce. 

Truly, the 70’s was the decade of 
the super chain. Last year the top 10 
chains took in about one-third, or 
almost $10 billion, of the total dollars 
spent by consumers in drug stores. 

Setting the pace was American 
Stores Co. (formerly Skaggs Cos.)

Increase in chain stores 
The total number of chains operat- 
ang two or more stores increased 
0.6% in 1979 to 2,709 compared to 
2,666 in 1978. The number of stores 
operated by these chains grew 2.6% 
to 19,764 compared to 19,290 stores 
1978. Last year the growth rate of 
the number of stores under the chain 
bwnership tapered off as only 474 
istores were added. This compares to 
846 stores that were added in 1978 
and 728 stores added in 1977. 
In order to get an idea of the im- 
pact of major chains on the entire 
etail drug industry, compare the 
ollowing figures. In 1960, chains 
ad less than half (41%) of the $7.2 
illion retail drug market. In 1969, 
hains accounted for 54% of sales of 
an $11.9 billion retail drug market. 
Today chains control more than 70% 
of the $28 billion market. 
| In 1979, the number of drug retail- 
s operating four or more stores 
ew to 672 companies, up from 650 
he year earlier. The number of re- 
ilers operating more than 100 


ores dropped to 28, down from 30.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


BROADER MERCHANDISE LINES 
ADD TO SHOPPING CONVENIENCE 


The goal of one stop and conve- 
nience shopping came to fruition in 
the 1970's as several chains were able 
to broaden their merchandise mixes 
because of newly built larger stores. 

Some chains took the full-line 
store concept one step further and 
took a giant leap forward by opening 
40,000 sq. ft. or more combination 

food and drug stores. 

The major reason behind the de- 
velopment of the expanded product 
lines was to lure consumers to spend 
their dollars in drug stores. The one- 
stop shopping concept, that became 
a reality in the last decade, eould not 
have come at a more’ opportune 
time, an era when the retail cus- 
tomer was seeking to limit his driv- 
ing because of gasoline. shortages 
that reached record peaks. 

THE SUPER DRUG STORES. 
The development of the superstores 
took place on the West Coast, and 
Southwest. The first chains to ex- 

yeriment and develop them included 
Skaggs, Longs and: Pay ’n Save. 
‘hese stores can be identified by 
uheir size. They generally start at 

5,000 sq. ft. and up. 

The increased size of the super- 
stores has allowed chain drug store 
buyers to expand or even add new 
merchandise categories that they 
previously could not carry because 
of space limitations. The three de- 
partments most frequently broad- 
ened are the conyenience food sec- 
dion, auto and apparel. Some stores 
have taken advantage of the addi- 
tional footage by adding a greater 


amount of high-ticket items includ- 
ing televisions, microwave ovens and 
lawn and garden equipment. 

For example, Gray has used the 
expertise it has gained from its 
Rink’s discount store operation to 
add a wide variety of general mer- 
chandise to its drug stores. Gener- 
ally, the Gray Super stores range in 
size between 17,000 to 20,000 sq. ft. 

Genovese has a 24,000-sq.-ft. 
store in Wallington, N.J., that car- 
ries everything from automotive 
supplies, housewares and food to 
telephone equipment. 

Another example of the variety of 
products offered by superstores is 
seen in the northern units of the 
Fay’s chain. These outlets feature a 
good amount of high-ticket general 
merchandise including furniture, 
sporting goods, lawn supplies and a 
good assortment of radios and tele- 
visions. 

THE CONVENTIONAL 
STORES. In these retail outlets the 
emphasis is also on broad merchan- 
dise lines, often encompassing the 
same departments as the super- 
stores, but the difference is that it is 
on a smaller scale. The conventional 
chain stores range in size from about 
8,500 sq. ft. to 15,000 sq. ft. 

A good example of these mini-su- 
perstores is how Fay’s is setting up 
the merchandising programs of the 
Craft stores it acquired as a scaled 
down version of its northern super- 
stores. 

Others, during the last decade 
have introduced small convenience 


food sections of 1,000 sq. ft. or more. 
Both Medi Mart and Optel have done 
this. Another favorite area of expan- 
sion for the conventional stores has 
been in reading and magazine sec- 
tions. The chains have found them to 
be profitable areas. 

With the expansion of diversified 
health care services, several chains 
are sectioning off corners in conven- 
tional sized stores and turning them 
into either hearing aid, dental or op- 
tical centers. In September, Peoples 
Drug of Alexandria, Va., leased 
space in three of its stores to den- 
tists who opened clinics. Others, in- 
cluding Walgreen, Eckerd and Med- 
icare-Glaser have allocated space to 
optical centers. 

THE BANTAMS. Despite the 
trend toward a broadened merchan- 
dise mix to offer one-stop shopping, 
small bantam stores ranging from 
3,000 to 8,500 sq. ft. are also thriv- 
ing. Two chains, which can be re- 
garded as specialists in running 
several hundred bantam sized stores 
are Revco and Rite Aid. Rite Aid 
recently opened its 800th store in 
the northeast with the average pro- 
totype at about 6,700 sq. ft. 

Revco, which years ago started 
building its original stores at 2,000 
sq. ft. is now constructing stores in 
the 7,000- to 8,500-sq.-ft. range. 
This chain, known for its bantams 
has even experimented with the op- 
eration of a superstore with the 
opening of a 19,000-sq.-ft. unit in 
Lorain, Ohio. That store houses a

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


CENTRAL WAREHOUSING PAYS OFF | 


The benefits of centralized ware- 
housing have handsomely paid back 
drug chain retailers’ initial invest- 
ment in distribution centers. Total 
control of product flow and sales 
items, reduced inventories and mer- 
chandise buying deals are the major 
assets of large distribution centers, 
which offset their liabilities in plant 
space, warehouse staff and machin- 
ery costs. 

Maintaining a full and almost con- 
stant stock at store level, as well as 
increased inventory turns, central 
distribution systems are achieving 
greater productivity levels for drug 
chains, despite a money-tight en- 
vironment with current interest 
rates rising to as high as 20%. 

Central warehousing’s relatively 
short distance radius from the 
branch store networks enable com- 
pany-owned or leased trucks to 
make store deliveries in two to three 
days. Often, “piggybacking” mer- 
chandise between the warehouse 
and different stores, or backhauling 
merchandise directly from manufac- 
turers, also expedites deliveries. 

One shipment processed through 
a chain’s own distribution system 
may save as many as 250 separate 
shipments from a wholesaler, re- 
ported one Midwestern drug chain. 

Central computerization of pric- 
ing, billing and ordering has also 
dramatically cut costs for many 
drug chain retailers. A central buy- 
ing computer, for instance, may en- 
able one buyer to do the job of 50 
buyers in a nonautomated distribu- 
tion system. 

Automated conveyor belts, flow 
racks, merchandise diverters, sort- 
ing and picking machines are also 
conserving a considerable amount of 
manpower. 

Sav-On’s 505,000-sq.-ft. facility’s 
442 miles of conveyors, scanners, and 
its automatic sorting system can 
handle 400,000 merchandise cases in 
eight hours, according to Dale 
Short, district operations manager. 

“We invested in this distribution 
center for the sheer economics of 
central warehousing—better ser- 
vice, fuller shelves,” adds Short. 

Fifty top drug chains in warehous- 
ing surveyed by Drug Store News 


over the past two years have also 
cast a vote of confidence in the long- 
term economy of central distribu- 
tion centers. In two years time, 
these chains total warehouse square 
footage has grown from 13.5 million 
sq. ft. to roughly 17 million sq. ft. At 
least half of these warehouse pace- 
setters have enlarged their existing 
facilities anywhere from 1,000 sq. ft. 
to 100,000 sq. ft. 

Summing up the warehouse ex- 
pansion fever for the larger and mid- 
dle-sized drug store chains, Dave 
Schwartz, director of real estate for 
the 170-unit Optel Corporation 
based in Holbrook, Mass., com- 
mented: “A large warehouse backup 
stock which can quickly replenish 
branch stores enables these stores 
to carry more merchandise depart- 
ments and in greater depth in order 
to remain competitive in the drug 
store market.”

“We cannot afford to have back- 
rooms full of merchandise. Our 
stores only average 10,000 sq. ft. to 
14,000 sq. ft. Our central ware- 
houses, which store and can ship 
full-case quantities to our stores 
within two days, help build up our 
inventory astronomically and give 
us a fast turnaround,” added Peo- 


ples Robert Crichlow, vp distribu- 
tion. Peoples will consolidate its 
Richmond and Alexandria, Va., fa- 
cilities with the construction of a 
400,000-sq.-ft. unit to be complete 
by 1982. 

Rite Aid’s new Poca, W. Va.-based 
217,000-sq.-ft. warehouse will help 
achieve management's goal of a max- 
imum 250-mile radius between cen- 
tral warehouses and branch stores. 

Previously, Rite Aid designated 
one warehouse to serve 400 branch 
stores, but now, warehouses will 
supply 300 stores, as energy and 
transportation costs are making de- 
centralized warehouses more eco- 
nomical, according to Heinz Boldes, 
senior vp, distribution, who specu- 
lates that other drug chains with 
geographically widespread units 
may also adapt satellite distribution 
centers. 

Strengthening their distribution 
systems by expanding existing facil- 
ities, as well as building additional 
warehouses, drug chains are also 
aiming to increase productivity with 
optimal use of their present equip- 
ment, as well as with the acquisition 
of more refined machinery. 

Computerized order systems pro- 
grams, once afforded only by the 
larger drug chains in warehousing, 
are also being instituted by the me- 
dium-sized chains. 

Modern equipment and systema- 
tic planning are also becoming an 
integral part of trucking proce- 
dures. Rite Aid’s tractor wind de- 
flectors have proved fuel efficient, 
while Optel’s truck monitoring de- 
vices have helped safeguard against 
merchandise pilferage on delivery 
routes. 

Peoples continues to maximize de- 
livery time by “carving out trading 
zones for trucks and cutting down on 
mileage, frequently enabling vehi- 
cles to make only one trip with little 
or no backtracking,” said Crichlow. 

Training warehouse personnel to 
make better use of equipment and 
systems—“quality control through 
human involvement”—will also 
boost productivity to peak levels, 
notes drug chain management. 

An orderly training sequence, be- 
ginning with an entry level order 
picker’s job, further transfers to 
other merchandise departments 
and assignments to veteran ware- 


-house employees can build a cohe- 


sive and responsible warehouse 
team, 

Working closely with small groups 
of new employees, Rite Aid’s ware- 
house training supervisors can in- 
struct them in the company’s par- 
ticular pricing and order picking 
methods. 

Rix’s president Richard Weinberg 
is optimistic that raises in order 
pickers’ salaries will increase their 
on-the-job dedication and perfor- 
mance. 

Now more than ever, with “every- 
thing available and feasible in terms 
of machinery, programs, and train- 
able personnel,” according to Rite 
Aid’s Boldes, productivity gains will 
remain the most urgent priority for 
distribution centers.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


A decade ago, visionary retailers 
such as Sam Skaggs saw a way to 
increase per-store sales by putting 
food and drug products under one 
roof and behind a single bank of 
checkouts—without sacrificing the 
space assortment or presentation of 
one for another. This concept be- 
came reality during the last decade. 

What was once a dream for Sam 
Skaggs has become reality not only 
for his own American Stores Co. 
(the powerful new corporate com- 
bination of a major grocery retailer 
and Skaggs drug stores) but for the 
drug and supermarket industry in 
general. Following the Skaggs’ ex- 
periment—in which Skaggs’ drug 
store expertise was joined by the 
food merchandising know-how of Al- 
bertson’s—other drug chains (in- 
cluding Walgreen, Page and Osco) 
and food chains (including Kroger, 
A&P and Jewel) have followed suit. 

The impact of the combination 
store concept is nothing short of 
monumental in the world of retail- 
ing. Combos now transcend the 
basic food-drug marriage that 
started the ball rolling. New match- 
ups include home center-drug and 
automotive—drug centers have 
proved successful. 

The key to the success of combina- 
tion stores really harkens back to 
Skaggs early experiments in 1970. 
The drug retailer knew that a pros- 
perous food-drug store would be a 
new animal, one with two distinct, 
equal personalities but one entity 
nonetheless. When he joined forces 
with supermarketer Joe Albertson 
to open the first jointly owned com- 
bination food-drug unit, the founda- 
tion was set. 

The creation, a prototype that 
Skaggs has stuck to since the first 
grand opening in 1970, is a 55,000- 
sq.-ft. unit with a complete food and 
drug store, split down the middle 
but united by a common bank of 
checkstands. 

Frozen food 

A center-aisle row of frozen food 
coolers served as the line of demar- 
cation, and there was no overlap of 
merchandise. Skaggs-Albertson’s 
also offered depth of merchandise 


unparalleled by either food or drug 
retailers. For example, the food end 
of the combo included full meat 
coolers, produce bins, a hot-deli and 
in-store bakery. The drug end was 
equipped with a complete health aid 
and toiletries sections, cosmetics, a 
candy-tobacco front-end and a full 
pharmacy operation with at least 
two pharmacists on duty on key 
hours. 

In addition, Skaggs-Albertson’s 
devoted more space, and depth to 
sundries than some discounters. For 
example, the combo didn’t just offer 
the fast-moving, most popular prod- 
uct lines in the auto department. It 
carried complete DIY auto sections 
with high-end items like booster ca- 


bles, headlights and car floor mats, 
plus the usual waxes, oil, oil filters 
and cleansers. 

In January 1977, as the partner- 
ship was drawing to a close, the 
Skaggs-Albertson’s combination 
stores numbered 58 in the South- 
western states. Per-store combo vol- 
ume averaged $8.8 million. 

Today, Skaggs has a new combo 
partner in the Alpha Beta super- 
markets (a subsidiary of American 
Stores). The Skaggs organization 
has started opening combos in wide- 
spread markets under the Alpha 
Beta logo. Today Skaggs has 43 com- 
bos in six states. Per-store volume is 
approximately $15 million. 

Two sizes 

The newest combos come in two 
sizes: a small, 48,000-sq.-ft. unit 
with roughly 35,000 sq. ft. devoted 
to selling space and a large, 60,000- 


ag” ~~ _ ten 4 Uf 


% -_** 


sq.-ft. unit with 45,000 sq. ft. given 
to selling space. 

What came after the initial 
Skaggs experiments in combos can 
only be looked upon as an explosion 
in the retail industry, one that in- 
volves 450 units. 

Imitating the Skaggs-Albertson’s 
stores, the Walgreen drug chain of 
Deerfield, Ill., teamed up with the 
Schnucks supermarket chain of 
Bridgeton, Mo., in 1976. With Cape 
Girardeau, Mo., as the team’s first 
combo site, two other 50,000-sq.-ft. 
units were constructed in Evanville, 
Ind. 

The basic Schnucks- Walgreen 
closely resembles the Skaggs-Al- 
bertson’s combo. The chief dif- 
ference is size at 50,000 sq. ft., 
yielding a 40,000-sq.-ft. selling 
area. An identical fourth combo 
store was opened in Fort Smith, 
Ark. 

Supermarketer A&P took the 
plunge in 1977, setting up a combo 
subsidiary named Family Mart. To 
date, 18 Family Marts have sprung 
up in five states—the Carolinas, 
Georgia, Alabama and Florida. 
Eight or nine new units are on the 
drawing boards for 1980. 

The basic Family Mart is a 56,000- 
sq.-ft. unit closely related to the 
Skaggs-Albertson’s 50-50 food and 
drug format. 

Family Mart has been committed 
more strongly to sundries with the 
addition of two promotional mer- 
chandise aisles for year-round use, 
and stepped DIY sections, hard- 
ware, automotive and paint sup- 
plies. 

The combo concept was a natural 
for Dallas-based Cullum Cos., par- 
ent of Tom Thumb supermarkets 
and Page Drugs. Right after 
Skaggs-Albertson’s made its splash 
in the Texas market, Cullum de- 
cided to tear down the wal. separat- 
ing a Tom Thumb supermarket from 
a Page drug store. Soon after, the 
lure of combo volume had the re- 
tailer hooked, and in 1973 Cullum 
opened its first Tom Thumb/Page 
from scratch. 

At last count, Cullum operated 17 
combos in the Texas market, with

three to five more units projected for 
next year. Although they share 
many markets, there are few sim- 
ilarities between the Tom Thumb/ 
Page stores and the Skaggs combos. 
The most obvious difference is store 
size—Cullum’s combos are 43,200 
sq. ft. compared to Skaggs’ 55,000 
sq. ft. plus operations. 

Also, Tom Thumb/Page does a 
strong food business which out- 
strips general merchandise and 
drug sales. Consequently, per-store 
volume is approximately $12 million, 
compared to Skaggs’ $15 million per- 
store combo volume. 

Cullum does not subscribe to the 
Skaggs formula of success. Rather 
than divide the store into two sepa- 
rate retail areas, Cullum allows food 
and drug merchandise to naturally 
merge in the center aisles. For ex- 
ample, housewares from the drug 
side overlap with the frozen food cof- 
fins into a gourmet foods sections. 

“There is no distinct dividing line 
in our combos,” says Tom Hairston, 
executive vice president of Tom 
Thumb/Page. “It’s all under one roof. 
The middle third of the store sees 
most of the overlap. But there’s traf- 
fic flow from one side to the other, 
encouraged by this overlap.” 

Tom Thumb/Page is doing about 
20% of its business in the sundries 
categories, a share of store volume 
that management would very much 
like to improve by deepening gen- 
eral merchandise departments. 

Cullum also distinguishes itself 
from other combo operators by 
boosting its professional image in 
the food-drug outlets. To accomplish 
this, the retailer positions its combo 
store Rx near the front. 

Professional identity 

“It is important to maintain a 
strong professional identity, as well 
as the element of convenience,” says 
Hairston. “Placing the pharmacy up 
front serves these purposes.” 

The food and drug combination 
store is not the only marriage that 
can be found. With inflation fanning 
the flames of the DIY trend, the 
drug/home center outlet has become 
an increasingly popular modification 
of the combo theme. 

Just last fall Rea and Derick of 
Northumberland, Pa., threw its hat 
into the ring with a 7,000-sq.-ft. 
drug/home center operation. The 


\two-store combo, divided approx- 


ately 50-50 between drug and 

Y space, was called an experi- 
ment and not a prototype by a com- 
pany spokesman. 

Buk the fact that an essentially 
conservative chain would even con- 
sider a \rug/home center combo en- 
terprise is a sign of the times. In 
fact, the entire chain drug sector has 
been keeping a watchful eye on the 
hybrid units\that have been spring- 
ing up in various markets across the 
nation. 

Seattle-based Pay ’n Save was the 
West Coast pioneer in this merchan- 
dising area, having tested the con- 
cept a decade ago in Alaska. Of 
course, Pay ’n Save was able to take 
advantage of the expertise it devel- 
oped in operating its Ernst Home 
Center subsidiary, which includes 
some 50 or so freestanding DIY 
stores. 

Roughly 50,000 sq. ft., Pay ’n Save 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


combos split the mix down the mid- 
dle between drug related merchan- 
dise and home center goods. Chain 
management claims that these units 
bring in as much as three times the 
volume of a conventional drug store. 
While gross margin percentages 
are approximately the same, dollar 
margins on most home center items 
are higher and the traffic-building 
appeal of the combo increases turns 
overall. The hybrid requires about 
$1 million in inventory or about 
twice as much as the average free- 
standing Pay ’n Save drug store. 


Today, Pay ’n Save has expanded 
its stake in the drug/home center 
concept to six units with additional 
openings slated for Anchorage, 
Alaska, and Sacramento, Calif., 
later this year. The corporation also 
operates a combo under the Ernst 
logo, in Rock Springs, Wyo. 

Sav-On Drugs caught onto the 
combo trend some four years ago, 
and has built 10 drug/home center 
hybrids to date. Ranging in size 
from 40,000 to 50,000 sq. ft.; the 
Sav-On versions also feature a 
10,000-sq.-ft. outdoor lot to accom- 
modate nursery merchandise and 
expanded lumber departments. 

Pay Less, now part of Pay Less 
Northwest, entered the combo fray 
only two years ago with a couple of 
60,000-sq.-ft. units. Moving ag- 
gressively, however, the chain has 
parlayed its holdings into 11 drug/ 
home centers, with two more on the 
way. 

Pay Less’ mix includes builder's 
supplies, lumber, paneling, wrought 


iron railings, particle board cabi- 
nets, work benches, pull window 
shades, lighting fixtures and wall 
decor items. Hardware and plumb- 
ing supplies are the key DIY catego- 
ries, however, contributing to 5% of 
total sales. 

On the East Coast, the un- 
disputed drug/home center power is 
the Landover, Md.-based Dart 
Drug. Its 18 combos represent the 
largest group of such units in the 
country, but the drug and DIY ele- 
ments are less clearly defined than 
in other such operations.

Dart adopted the home center ap- 
proach to compete with other Wash- 
ington, D.C., chains, which have 
been active in molding the combina- 
tion concept to their own needs. 

White Drug of North Dakota has 
also experimented with the drug/ 
home center idea, having opened its 
second 45,000-sq.-ft. outlet last 
year. However, only 10,000 sq. ft. 
and some 30% of the merchandise 
mix is devoted to the home improve- 
ment categories, according to a 
White executive. 

What’s more, White management 
appears to have shelved the drug/ 
home center angle for the time 
being, in order to pay more attention 
to the chain’s drug/apparel combina- 
tions. 

Clearly, other changes will crop 
up in the combination store format 
as this newest retailing entity con- 
tinues to mature. But with or with- 
out changes, one thing is certain— 
the combo is going to remain a fact of 
retailing life for some time. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


SCOPE OF HEALTH CARE WIDENS 


Drug stores are recouping in- 
store traffic lost to supermarkets 
and discounters through a direction 
of diversified health care that in- 
volves dental clinics, convalescent 
aids, optical departments, and in- 
store screening tests, to name just a 
few freshly paved avenues of profes- 
sionalism. 

Two trends appear to be the force 
behind this movement: 

@ During the 1980's those over 65 
years of age will be one of the fast- 
est-growing segments of the United 
States population. 

®@ Government and private insurers 
are seeking ways to hold profes- 
sional services and hospital costs 
down. 

The result of these two trends 
means more emphasis will be placed 
on out-of-hospital patient care. 

DENTAL CARE. There is no 
doubt that dental centers can be mu- 
tually beneficial to chains and con- 
sumers. Chains obtain the benefit of 
a strong health care image. And con- 
sumers are offered walk-in conve- 
nience, extended office hours, lower 
fees, credit terms and acceptance of 
third-party plans. 

Peoples Drug ventured into den- 
tal centers by opening two units dur- 
ing 1979 and added another during 
1980. All three are located in the 
metro D.C. market and each one is 
open 72 hours per week. 

In-store, the chain has positioned 
the center adjacent to its pharmacy 
and optical centers, reinforcing the 
store’s professional health care im- 
age. Unlike the optical center and 
pharmacy, the dental center is not 
owned by Peoples, but by a private 
corporation called Family Dental 
Centers. 

Family Dental Centers is owned 
and operated by Dr. Mark Taff in 
conjunction with Peoples Drug. Taff 
leases the space from Peoples which 
designates the site as well as the in- 
store location of the centers. From 
that point, Taff takes over, outfitting 
the offices and hiring the dentists 
who are employees of Family Dental 
Centers, not Peoples. 

“There's a market to be tapped out 
there,” says Taff, “ .. 55% of the 
population does not regularly see a 
dentist.” 


Fees are structured on a sliding 
scale and are clearly posted in the 
waiting area. Taff says, “Our fee of 
$17 for an examination is not that 
much lower than the national aver- 
age. A more complicated procedure 
like root canal, however, is signifi- 
cantly lower priced than the average 
fee.” 

The 1,300-sq.-ft. center will even- 
tually accommodate up to five full- 
time dentists and two hygienists 
plus office personnel. At the present 
time, the six-room office is staffed 
by one full-time dentist and hygien- 
ist, areceptionist and the services of 
visiting dental specialists. 

Patient response has been very 
good, despite the fact that Peoples is 
going very slowly with advertising. 
In the first two weeks of operation 
the chain’s Maryland center doubled 
its patient load. 


Revco, the second drug chain to 
launch dental units, concurs with 
the need for better availability of 
dental services. Phillip Lopate, 
D.D.S., president of the Dental 
Care Clinic at Revco says, “The 
American public’s need for dental 


services has been well documented .” 


Lopate, along with Earl B. 
Legome, and Bruce D. Schwartz, 
both practicing dentists, own and 
operate the Dental Care Clinic, Rev- 
co’s first dental center. 

The center, which recently opened 
ina Lorain, Ohio Revco, is set up on 


a similar basis to the centers at Peo- 
ples. 

CONVALESCENT AIDS. The 
prevailing attitude among drug 
chain executives toward convales- 
cent aids as a growth area remains 
one of caution. No single chain has 
plunged into the business in a big 
way. 

Hook, with three freestanding 
units, is the leader. Walgreen, Peo- 
ples, Medicare-Glaser, and Begley 
are planning, or are about to open, 
their first freestanding convalescent 
aid and home health care centers. 
Other chains are content to expand 
their existing 4-ft. or 6-ft. in-store 
sections. 

Hook with three 6,000-sq.-ft. to 
7,000-sq.-ft. convalescent aids 
stores, is expanding its line of equip- 
ment. The Indianapolis-based chain 
is taking on exercise equipment, in 
addition to its broad line of convales- 
cent aids. 

HEALTH SCREENING. In- 
store screening for various medical 
problems is taking on added impor- 
tance as pharmacy departments 
strive to establish a broader position 
as community health care profes- 
sionals. 

“We’ve run in-store screenings for 
high blood pressure and diabetes on 
many occasions,” says Leonard Gen- 
ovese, president of Genovese. “It’s 
difficult to measure the effect of the 
programs on in-store traffic or sales, 
but we see benefits in the long run 
when it comes to our image in the 
community.” 

The recognized leader among re- 
tailers conducting mass screenings 


is St. Louis-based Medicine Shoppe 
International. Operating primarily 
as a franchiser in 44 states, the firm 
makes available no less than 13 
screening and information clinics, 


testing for such diverse problems as _- 


high blood pressure, oral cancer, 
glaucoma, poor vision and hearing, 
and sickle cell anemia. 


According to Susan Purvis, coor- — 


dinator of Medicine Shoppes’ pro- 
grams, “Every one of the outlets 
holds at least one of the clinics on a 
regular basis. And in new stores, we 
recommend a constant clinic sched- 


ule—from 12 to 20 screenings a year. — 


This establishes the pharmacist as a 
health care professional in the com- 
munity.” 

Ken Anderson, professional ser- 
vices director of Medicare-Glaser, 
says that he can’t gauge a sales in- 
crease but there is an upswing in 
store traffic. 

“Our registered nurse rotates 
from store to store, visiting each of 
15 stores every two weeks,” he says. 
“Patients often don’t wait for the 
nurse, they follow him around. 
When the nurse is in the store peo- 
ple gather there.” 

OPTICAL DEPARTMENTS. 
The past year saw mixed results 
among chains competing for a share 


of the optical market. Peoples, | 


Eckerd, Pay ’n Save, Walgreen and 
Medicare-Glaser enjoyed financial 
success and will make a greater com- 
mitment to optical care in the fu- 
ture. 

A number of drug chains, how- 
ever, bowed out of the optical mar- 
ket, among them, Perry, Gray and 
Sentry. And, last year, Cunningham 
closed six of its eight centers. 

Executives in the industry gener- 
ally concede that “optical centers are 
not nearly as profitable as they once 
were.” 

Osco discovered that customer ac- 
ceptance comes slowly, and the com- 
pany addressed this problem 
uniquely. Osco recently signed an 
agreement with House of Vision, a 
well-known optical retailer in Chi- 
cago, thereby lending instant con- 
sumer recognition to the drug 
chain's optical centers. 

Commitment, adequate capital- 
ization, patience and vertical inte- 
gration represent the ingredients in 
a winning formula for these centers. 

According to John Starr, manager 
of Walgreen optical centers, “Hav- 
ing your own lab allows you to con- 
trol the quality of the work that is 
going out.” 

Expense control also plays a ma- 
jor role in this area. Eckerd, Peo- 
ples, Walgreen, Medicare-Glaser 
and Pay ’n Save do a portion or all 
their own lab work. Lower operat- 
ing expenses result because there is 
no middleman. 

Walgreen and Peoples are also ex- 
panding into optometric centers 
where eye exams are conducted by 
on-site optometrists. 

Centers staffed with optometrists 
will also be in a position to.capitalize 
on contact lenses, an area estimated 
to account for 40% to 50% of the 
overall optical business. 


rug chains are 
taking advantage 
of the growing 
trend toward 
more out-of-hospital pa- 
tient care by offering a 
wide array of health care 
services. Success in these 
areas is often deter- 
mined by the extent of 
the chain’s commitment, 
sufficient capitalization 
and patience.

The year 1979 was marked by dra- 
natic acquisitions and surprising in- 
novations, by sudden management 
coups and penetration into new ter- 
ritories. The chain drug industry 
_ demonstrated once again the imag- 
ination and aggressiveness that has 
set it apart as one of the most vital 
retail sectors in our economy. 

Here, then, are the highlights of 
1979: 

In January, generic equivalency 
faced its first challenge in court 
when manufacturer Hoechs-Rous- 
sel filed a deceptive advertising suit 

‘against Generix, charging the latter 
with unfair competition through the 
promotion of its Goldline brand of 
furosemide as the “equivalent” of 
Hoechst’s Lasix—a patented oral di- 
uretic. 

February saw Fay’s Drug take its 
second step into the Southeast with 
its acquisition of the 14-store Craft’s 
Drug chain in South Carolina. The 
move gave Fay’s 21 units in the Sun- 
belt. 

Later that month, Skaggs Cos. 
, began merger talks with American 
Stores Co., and the formation of a 
28-state, $5-billion retailing empire 
loomed on the horizon. It later de- 
veloped that Skaggs was slated to be 
the survivor if a merger took place. 

In March, Schnucks-Walgreen 

ended a 16-month lull in new store 
openings with the launching of its 
fourth food/drug combination store 
in Fort Smith, Ark. The 56,000-sq.- 
ft. operation, stocking about 31,000 
»sku’s in all, was slated to be the pro- 
‘4otype for future expansion. At the 
same time, Walgreen opened its 
first full-fledged mini-combo in a 
“Chicago location, with some 12,000 
“q. ft. of selling space. 
,- March also saw Drugfair of Alex- 
‘ndria’s annual financial report, 
Which showed a 37.8% drop in earn- 
ings due to increased remodeling ex- 
penses and other overhead costs. 
The decrease was also due, in part, 
to an abbreviated fiscal year. 

In April, the floundering Cour- 
tesy Drug chain found a winning 
combination in the form of three 
Rock bottom limited assortment box 
stores, which the chain “opened” 
through conversions of existing 
units. The hush-hush experiment 
marked the introduction of the box 
store concept to the New York Met- 
ropolitan Area. 

Pay ’n Save 

Later in the month, Pay ’n Save 
announced plans to make its first 
venture into centralized distribution 
with a1 million-sq.-ft. facility, slated 


to open in the summer of 1980, in. 


Auburn, Wash. 

In May, Fay’s played on the ac- 
quisition theme again when it signed 
an agreement in principle to pur- 
chase the assets of the 20-store Key 
Drug chain in August. The deal was 
to reinforce Fay’s New York State 
holdings when it went through. 

That same month, Walgreen also 
arranged a takeover—that of 16 
Stein Drug outlets, thereby pushing 
its store count in Wisconsin up to 45. 
The Stein group represented annual 
sales of approximately $30 million, 
and the deal also included the chain's 


40,000-sq.-ft. Milwaukee ware- 
house. 

At about the same time, SupeRx 
Drug, based in Cincinnati, launched 
the chain’s first distribution center 
in Melbourne, Fla. The 220,000-sq.- 
ft. facility was targeted to even- 
tually supply 90% of the items 
stocked in SupeRx’s 85 Florida out- 
lets. 

Also in May, Skaggs Cos. all but 
secured its merger with American 


South with some 210,000 sq. ft. of 
storage capacity. The Charleston 
center was slated to serve 135 Rite 
Aid units in North Carolina, Ten- 
nessee, South Carolina, West Vir- 
ginia, Ohio, Kentucky and parts of 
western Pennsylvania. 

In August, Peoples became the 
first chain in the country to intro- 
duce dental centers into its stores. 
The 1,000-sq.-ft. pioneer centers 
opened in conventional Peoples out-

by July. The Aiken facility, Revco’s

expected to ease the pressure on the 
overburdened Knoxville, Tenn., and

Later in the month, the industry 
was jolted when Koffler Ltd., the 
giant Canadian drug store fran- 
chisor, lured top marketing strate- 
gist Al Towle away from his position 
as senior vp at Peoples Drug to

ing a big step toward vertical inte- 
gration. The manufacturer brought 
to the union $5 million in annual 
sales and the capacity to expand the 
4% to 5% that Peoples’ private label 
contributed to total revenues. 

By July, Walgreen had struck out 
after another Wisconsin drug store 
chain with thoughts of acquisition. 
The prospective prize was Ren- 
nebohm Drug Stores, a $10-million 
operation with 17 units around the 
state capitol of Madison. 

Rite Aid 

That same month, Rite Aid 
brought on-stream its Charleston,

facilitating further expansion in the

Drugfair’s loss

reported a $463,000 loss for its sec-

ment program, “Operation Excel- 
lence,” and cut its advertising costs 
substantially in an effort to lessen 
the burden.

chain’s warehousing capacity.

@ Total sales: Corporate sales have been used; 

drug store volume has not been broken out from 

the nondrug volume. 

© Net income: This is before special items. 

e Return on investment: The ROI has been 

computed on stockholders investment at the end 

of the year. 

@ Stores: Counts are generally for drug stores (or 
leased department) unless footnote indicates oth- 

erwise. 

@ Sales per store: This figure includes drug store 
volume only, except where noted. Sales per store is 
computed on stores open at year's end, and thus 
the figure tends to be an understatement. Where 
available, sales per store open the full year have 
been used and noted. 

e Gross margin: Those cases where the cost of 
goods sold includes other items (occupancy costs, 
warehousing expenses, buying costs, etc.) have 
been noted. The inclusion of such items in cost of 
goods sold reduces both gross margin and the 
expense ratio. Where possible, such costs have 
been removed and put in operating expenses. 

e Expense ratio: The expense ratio is for general 
costs of operation, such as selling, general, admin- 
istrative, occupancy and warehousing expenses, 
as percentage of sales to make it correspond as 
much as possible to cash outlays for operations, 
depreciation and amortization have been ex- 
cluded. 

© Begley: All data include the results of the dry 
cleaning operations, except “Gross margins,” 
“Stores,” and “Sales per store,” which are for the

inventory valuation.

counting was converted to LIFO in 1974.

goods sold includes store occupancy and ware- 
housing expenses.

1980.

Eckerd (Clearwater, Fla.) alone. Depreciation is 
included in expenses in 1976. All data is corporate 
except “Stores” and “Sales per store” which are for 
drug units only. Corporate data includes nondurg 
operations. During 1978, the company adopted 
LIFO method of determining the cost of substan- 
tially all inventories. The change reduced net earn- 
ings by approximately $3.5 million. 

@ Fay’s: Chain converted to LIFO in 1974. 


@ Genovese: Depreciation is included in ex- 
penses in 1975 and 1976. All years are as-re- 
ported.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


Chain drug retailers entered the 
1980’s with an increased emphasis on 
health care-oriented services, a 
stepped up merchandise mix, and a 
broader conceptual view of the in- 
dustry. 


In a recessionary period, drug 
chain sales for the year advanced 
14.8% to $20.4 billion as compared 
with 1978 sales of $17.8 billion. The 
basics of the merchandise mix re- 
main prescription, proprietary 
drugs and toiletries, which ac- 
counted for 43.2% of total store vol- 
ume, and generated $9 billion dur- 
ing 1979. 

All departments turned in a solid 
performance during 1979, and cer- 
tain trends in productivity and con- 
sumer preference emerged. 
® Prescriptions—Total sales 
reached a new high of $3.62 billion, 
as the Rx department captured 
17.7% of total drug store volume. 
The dollar gain stemmed almost en- 
tirely from the price hike of the aver- 
age prescription. And while depart- 
ment sales rose 14.6%, the number 
of scripts filled went down. However 
the increase in the prescription cost 
created a 12% rate of growth in daily 
per pharmacy dollar sales. 

@ Drugs/proprietaries—Account- 
ing for 15.4% of total drug store 
sales, drug/proprietaries generated 
a dollar volume of $3.1 billion during 
1979, 213.8% increase over 1978's fig- 
ure of $2.8 billion. 

@ Toiletries—After topping the $2 
billion mark during 1978, this cate- 
gory surpassed its performance in 
1978 and generated a 16.3% increase 
over last year’s figures. Sales rose to 
$2.4 billion as compared with 1978 
sales of $2 billion, and captured 
11.7% of total chain drug volume. 
@ Cosmetics—Generating a 17.3% 
sales increase during 1979, this cate- 
gory topped $1 billion for the first 
time. This category can do no wrong 
for chain drug retailers, and ac- 
counts for 5.7% of total chain drug 
sales. 

® Stationery—Stationery posted a 
healthy 13% sales gain over 1978, as 
dollar volume rose to $1 billion dur- 
ing 1979. Increased promotion by re- 
tailers and the increased use of 
organizational material and supplies 
by consumers have helped put spar- 


kle into the category. 

e Candy—Rising prices of cocoa 
and sugar during 1978 caused a less- 
than-favorable performance for this 
category last year. The downtrend 
seems to have reversed itself in 1979, 
as the candy category posted a 9% 
increase over 1978 figures and gen- 
erated $818 million in dollar volume. 
Best sellers remain single packs of 
gum and mints as well as single 
candy bars, while sales of seasonal 
candy were also on the increase. 
Consumers showed a marked pref- 
erence for brand name boxed candy, 
and a willingness to spend more dol- 
lars for what they perceived as 
value. 

@ Tobacco—Sales were up during 
1979, and posted an 11.1% increase 
over 1978 sales. Dollar volume rose 
to nearly $2 billion as the category 
accounted for 9.7% of total chain 
drug sales. Cigarette sales were on 
the upswing, as low-tar varieties 
took over the lead from other 
higher-tar brands. Cigar sales de- 
creased with a decline in manufac- 
turer promotion. 


e Housewares—Sales rose an 
above-average 15.7% during 1979, as 
consumer interest in their homes in- 
creased. Gourmet cookware and KD 
furniture as well as dish and glass- 
ware provided much of the excite- 
ment to this category, which cap- 
tured 7.5% of total drug store sales. 
© Toys—Always a category in a 
state of flux, toys turned in a solid 
sales performance during 1979. Gen- 
erating a 13.6% increase over 1978, 
dollar volume advanced to $678 mil- 
lion. Electronic toys, and plenty of 
them, were what consumers wanted 
from drug chains during 1979, and 
electronic toys and games were the 
reason for much of the sales activity 
in this category. 

@e Photo—Much of this category’s 
15.8% increase was due to the rising 
price of silver, used in the production 
of film. Dollar volume rose to $914 
million, and accounted for 4.5% of 
total store sales. Purchases trended 
away from the 126 cartridge film as 
more consumers discarded older 
cameras in favor of 110 models. 

@ General merchandise—Cate- 
gory sales topped $1 billion during 
1979, an increase of 15.8% over 1978 
figures. Sunglasses gave much of 
the excitement to the category as 
manufacturer winter lines extended 
the sunglasses selling period for re- 
tailers. Sporting goods also turned 
in an exceptional performance for 
most retailers as sales of sports 
equipment topped $124 million. 

@ DIY—This is a new category bro- 
ken out for 1979 sales for the first 
time. An increase in consumer inter- 
est in maintaining their own homes 
and cars has spurred sales of this 
category. Increasing 15.9% over 1978 
sales, DIY turned in a healthy sales 
performance generating a dollar vol- 
ume of $546 million. Hardware, auto 
accessories, batteries, and paint/ 
paint supplies make up this growing 
category. 

® Grocery/liquor—This category 
turned in the most dramatic sales 
performance during 1979, generat- 
ing a dollar volume of $1.1 billion and 
increasing a substantial 20.9% over 
1978 figures. Convenience foods and 
a change in format for drug chains 
carrying substantial food sections 
spurred sales, as did the availability 
of a one-stop shopping convenience 
outlet for working women. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


MERCHANDISERS SPEAK OUT 


How do drug chains chief merchan- 
disers see 1980 stacking up? Here’s 
what several of them predict will be 
the merchandising trends and diffi- 
culties during 1980. 


_ Vern A. Brunner, 
vice president, marketing 
Walgreen Co. 


“Walgreen 
is committed 
to building 
8,000-sq. -ft. 
to 9,000-sq.- 
ft. stores in 
the 1980’. A 
7,000-sq.-ft. 
to 10,000- -Sq.- 
ft. space is a ee 
viable size for a very important 1980 
store prototype, the convenience 
drug store, carrying general mer- 
chandise as well as the traditional 
pharmaceuticals, and health and 
beauty aids. 

“While drugs and pharmaceuticals 
will remain the heart of the busi- 
ness, and pharmacists must stay on 
top of Government regulations and 
new product offerings, they must 
also concentrate on finetuning their 
sundry convenience lines. Closely 
watching profits per square foot, 
buyers must cherry pick the 20% of 
items which account for 80% of a 
category sales. In highly profitable 
product areas, such as greeting 
cards and stationery is for Wal- 
green, druggists will of course offer 
a much wider range of merchandise. 

“Market sites and demographics 
will help determine the type of con- 
venience merchandise a store car- 
ries. Druggists must understand 
the needs of their customers. Of 
course, if the druggist offers quality 
merchandise he will also be success- 
ful with it.” 


David Eisenberg, 
vp, marketing 
Peoples Drug 


“Inflation 
will be a fact 
of life and it 
will not be 
under control 
at least until | 
the third » 
quarter. 

Drug stores 

will fare well 

in this kind of environment. Con- 
sumers will be trading down to drug 
stores from department stores in 
such areas as cosmetics and also 
toys. And while they are still looking 
for value, they are still buying with 
confidence. We must give them 
value. 

“I see a hurry-up on manufacturer 
intros to bring forth new products 
into the market, and a flurry of new 
H&BA products. Anything that is 
already in the pipeling will come on 
stream quickly; then there will be a 
hiatus of new product development. 
There will also be a lot of re-estab- 
lishing of old brands that have 


plateaued, and a re-emphasis of old 
products. 

“The high cost of money, at 20%, 
will mean a severe reduction in in- 
ventory. Shipping will be more diffi- 
cult because manufacturers will also 
be cutting back on inventory. There 
are already logistics problems—less 
than a carload is being pooled by 
shippers and is not delivered 
quickly. Dating is becoming impor- 
tant. 

“There will also be less selling 
days between Thanksgiving and 
Christmas. We will have to have 
more hard-hitting prices and grab 
the early sale. We think that Christ- 
mas will be good.” 


Harry Steck, 
director of merchandising, 
Thrift Drug 


“I am looking at the retailer buy- 
ing categories amd spending more 
time to establish a good price/value 
relationship for the consumer.” 

“There will be an end to the dis- 
posable era—not in paper prod- 
ucts—but in items like disposable 
lighters, cameras and other items 
which do not have to be disposable. 
Consumers will be looking more at 
price and value. They will be looking 
more closely at what they buy, in- 
order to garner the best value for 
their money and will be looking for 
longevity. With this, they will be 
trading up to quality.” 


Allan Klein,

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


FEWER SCRIPTS A GENERIC WOE 


Chain drug prescription business 
expanded hy 14.6% last year, as dol- 
lar volume climbed to $3.62 billion, a 
new record. 

The gain stemmed almost entirely 
from a substantial rise in the price of 
the average script (brought about by 
a soaring cost of goods sold factor), 
with added boosts coming from an 
increase in the number of chain-op- 
erated pharmacies and many new 
product introductions. 

The number of scripts filled by the 
average store, howevér, declined 
somewhat, following 1978’s only 
marginal gain. Moreover, the ratio of 
Rx dollar volume to overall chain 
drug sales slipped slightly to 17.7% 
in 1979 from 17.8% in the previous 
year. 

The average charge per prescrip- 
tion climbed by 12.5% last year to 
$7.20 from $6.40 in 1978, as inflation- 
ary pressures took hold in the pre- 
scription area. 

The rise in the average prescrip- 
tion charge helped chain pharmacies 
to develop a 12% rate of growth in 
dollar sales per day per pharmacy. 
This figure climbed to $965 from 
$864. 

The number of prescriptions dis- 
pensed per pharmacy per day 
dropped by one script to 134 in 1979 
from 135 in the year before. 

However, declining script volume 
was not the only obstacle to develop- 
ing rising dollar sales in chain phar- 
macy departments last year. Other 
factors include even more products 
being MACed, slightly increased 
demand for generics, and limited 
growth in third-party prescriptions. 

Although generic scripts are less 
costly to patients—averaging $5.03/ 
script—these drugs now account for 
only 12% of the entire prescription 
market. 

Generic scripts on upswing 

The number of generic scripts 
written grew 2% over the previous 
year and the leading 20 generic 
products, which account for nearly 
75% of all generic Rxs, captured al- 
most 9% of all scripts filled in the 
United States. 

It has been predicted by some 
analysts that generics would play a

significant role in the United States 
drug market. As even more prod- 
ucts come off patent, this would ap- 
pear to be a logical prediction. Other 
groups disagree, saying that large 
research-intense firms will continue 
to replace older products with new 
improved second and third genera- 
tion product variations. 

Nonetheless, the key factor is the 
decline in scripts. According to 
Thomas R. Weinberger of Roths- 
child Unterberg and Towbin, an in- 
vestment advisory firm in New 
York, “The decline in new and refill 
prescriptions . . . is consistent with 
a downtrend in the number of pa- 
tient visits to office-based physi- 
clans... . 

“Those who follow the drug indus- 
try believe that sales and earnings 
gains are coming more as a function 
of pricing strategies and new prod- 
uct introductions than as a result of 
unit sales increases of established 
products.” 

The average number of units in a 
typical prescription has increased. 
Chain professional directors indicate 
that this situation partly traces to 
third-party prescription plans. 
These plans, in an effort to reduce 
costs through less frequent dispens- 
ing fees, result in more medication 
being dispensed against a standard 
or flat fee. The result is more medi- 
cation for patients, reduced costs to 
the third-party insurance plan, and 
decreased margin for the pharmacy. 

Another aspect of the decline in 
the number of scripts is a trend to- 
ward self medication as the F.D.A. 
re-evaluates selected products, such 
as low strength hydrocortisone, and 
moves them to OTC status. Consum- 
ers can thus avoid the cost of going 
to a physician's office in order to ac- 
quire such medication. At the same 
time, from the other end of the spec- 
trum, selected products have been 
reclassified as controlled substances 
by F.D.A. As a result, prescription 
refills are limited, resulting in fewer 
scripts being dispensed. 

Third-party scripts gain 

Other factors impacting on drug 
stores during 1979 include the ever- 
growing presence of Federal and 
state governments. For example, 
the Federal Government’s Maximum 
Allowable Cost pricing program has 
been expanded and now includes 
more prescription products. This 
fact coupled with the repeals of state 
antisubstitution and the addition of 
state drug formularies has set the 
stage for even greater drug product 
selection by pharmacists with price, 


not quality, taking on prime impor- 
tance. 

The trend toward third-party 
scripts increased marginally during 
1979 and they now account for 
18%-20% of all scripts filled in the 
United States. Unilateral changes in 
contracts benefiting the third-party 
insurer, including slow payments by 
some state Medicaid plans (over 90 
days in some instances) and low dis- 
pensing fees, have all caused cash 
flow problems for chain pharmacy 
operations. 

Increasing availability of non- 
¥.D.A.-approved drugs in the na- 
tion’s hospital and retail pharmacies 
represents a continuing problem 
that will soon have broad implica- 
tions for drug product selection. 
State boards of pharmacy are advis- 
ing pharmacists who are in doubt 
about the status of a particular firm’s 
product to “find out.” As this prob- 
lem continues, F.D.A. will act to 
curb distribution of such products 
by keeping pharmacists better in- 
formed on whether a drug is ap- 
proved or nonapproved. 

“Nonapproved generic drugs 
aren’t in our program,” says a pro- 
fessional director for a large East 
Coast chain. “We do, however, use 
generics that we feel comfortable 
with. 

“Before it’s even considered for in- 
ventory, a generic supplier must 
provide proof of product quality and 
guarantee these standards in writ- 
ing,” says the executive. 

Computers come of age 

Pharmacy computers are also 

forcing changes in day-to-day man- 


agement of stores where they are 


installed. 

“I see computers taking over rou- 
tine tasks,” says a chain exec. “They 
will really become popular when 
they are cost justified.” 

Other chain executives indicate 
that computers offer pharmacy a 
better alternative than assistants or 
technicians. “A well-designed com- 
puter system can provide better pa- 
tient care than reliance on pharmacy 
support personnel,” say other indus- 
try executives. 

The whole justification for sup- 
port personnel is to provide pharma- 
cists the opportunity to counsel 
patients. This is a good concept, but 
some chain execs express caution. 
“Counseling can’t work, unless peo- 
ple are willing to pay for pharma- 
cists’ time,” they say. “Until this 
happens the whole situation: will re- 
main only a concept with little 
chance of full implementation.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


Pegged, gravity-fed, blister- 
packed, displayed on open-access 
cases, merchandised on etageres— 
chain drug retailers offered consum- 
ers cosmetics in a myriad of ways 
during 1979. 

And based on the brisk, above- 
the-overall-average sales pace that 
developed in cosmetics last year, 
consumers apparently responded 
strongly and positively to almost 
every merchandising strategem 
chain drug cosmeticians used 

In fact for chains, cosmetic sales 
for 1979 topped $1 billion for the first 
time, featured a 17.3% rate of 
growth, and widened their slice of 
the chain drug industry. 

Chain cosmetics buyers at- 
tributed the better-than-17% vol- 
ume gain to $1.16 billion to a highly 
inflationary economy in which reces- 
sion always seemed just around the 
corner. During this period, families 
placed controls on budgets, and 
women apparently cut back on pur- 
chases of dresses and other clothes 
and turned to a more inexpensive 
way to be beautiful—heavier usage 
of cosmetics. 

As women turned to cosmetics to 
a greater extent, a number of cate- 
gories showed sales strength. Fra- 
grances continue to command a 
great deal of attention from consum- 
ers, but this category, too often dis- 
regarded in the past, was claiming 
and will continue to claim a large 
segment of department sales. 

Traditional low-enders, pegged 
eye and lip colors, came on strong 
and attracted more attention than 
ever before. Lines which heretofore 
had been classified as budget are 
breaking out of the low-end mold 
and providing consumers with some 
of the color and sophistication they 
seek. And wnat’s more, these lines 
are delivering to consumers what 
they want at a price that is very 
attractive. 

Targeting a new consumer 

Manufacturers of these products 
are extending product lines with 
items that will appeal to the older as 
well as the younger consumer who 
had traditionally bought their prod- 


uct. Manufacturers have updated, 
upgraded and stepped-up produc- 
tion of their cosmetic lines to attract 
a new and growing market seg- 
ment—the working woman. 

Retailers have been quick to emu- 
late this kind of thinking, and the 
cosmetics departments of 1979 re- 
flected this move to capture this new 
consumer, who has more money to 
spend and more need for cosmetics. 
The year 1979 saw a refinement of 
the shift toward open cosmetics de- 
partments which started two years 
ago. More than before retailers 
opened up the cosmetics depart- 
ment, providing easy access to prod- 
ucts and thus encouraging quick 
selection and more multiple pur- 
chases. The woman consumer that 
emerged during 1979 had changed— 
she was most likely working outside 
of the home, had more money to 
spend and less time to shop, and in 
all likelihood had a greater demand 
for cosmetic products. 

As the sophistication of fashion 
was heightened during 1979, prices 
were inflated. Again the consumer 
of 1979 turned to cosmetics to pro- 
vide what her wardrobe could not— 
a new look for every occasion. 
Rather than spend $100 on a new 
dress, she spent $10 pampering her- 
self with a new eyeshadow or blush, 
and had a new look for a special ap-

pointment. Cosmetics represented 
more than an accompaniment to 
clothes during 1979—it represented 
a way to vary personal fashion while 
staying within the bounds of a 
shrinking budget. 

Of all the categories, eye color 
stood out ahead of its counterparts. 
Pencils have emerged as the up-and- 
coming cosmetic accessory for the 
80's. 

For the price of one eyeshadow, 
consumers receive a product that 
has a threefold use—shadow, liner, 
and accent. Pencils represent what 
consumers of the 80's will be looking 
for in all products, an adaptability 
that will make a product useful to 
them in a variety of ways. 

Nail has remained a strong cate- 
gory for most retailers, although it 
did not make the extraordinary 
gains during 1979 that it registered 
several years ago. Nonetheless, con- 
sumers are still spending a signifi- 
cant dollar amount on nail products. 
Significantly, the consumer of 1979 
spent a good deal of her nail care 
dollar on nail treatments . 

The move toward treatment lines 
in generai has begun to emerge as a 
trend within drug store cosmetic de- 
partments, although it has yet to 
pick up the steam in drug stores that 
it has in department stores. Still, 
facial treatments registered a strong 
18.9% sales increase—an indication 
of the increased interest in facial 
creams and lotions. 


While drug chains are relying 
more heavily on open-access depart- 
ments, they have by no means aban- 
doned the service aspects of cosmet- 
ics selling. Using an assisted self- 
service concept, chains feel that 
more sales can be achieved by hav- 
ing a cosmetician available for con- 
sultation than by having a totally 
unmanned department. Although 
consumers don’t have the time for a 
full makeup, according to chain drug 
buyers, there was a greater chance 
of making a sale when someone 
could show a consumer what to do 
with a certain product. 


Cosmetics departments in chain 
drug stores made tremendous gains 
during 1979, and with the prospect 
of continuing inflation and tighter 
credit, it is likely the reasons behind 
the increasingly heavy usage of cos- 
metics will continue.
