DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


One of the major chain drug de- 
partments, toiletries generated $2.4 
billion during 1979, an increase of 
16.3% over 1978 sales. Accounting 
for 11.7% of drug store sales, toilet- 
ries was distinguished by more than 
a few of its categories. 

Ethnic products (including cos- 
metics) stood out as the front-run- 
ner during 1979 as the total ethnic 
cosmetics market had an estimated 
growth rate of 17% through 1984. 
Drug store sales rose 18.5% during 
1979, accounting for 6% of the toilet- 
ries departments sales and generat- 
ing a volume of $136 million. 

There are more than 12 million 
black women customers in the 
United States and chain drug stores 
have become one of the major out- 
lets for black skin care, makeup and 
toiletry product lines. 

Honey & Spice, the popularly 
priced makeup, is a strong seller for 
most drug chains, which reported 
good sales increases for both the 
makeup and skin care line. Accord- 
ing to a recent Commerce Depart- 
ment report, black women spend 
well over $50 million a year on cos- 
metics presently. 

In light of the growing market, in 
1979 chain retailers started to pay 
more attention to, and broaden the 
line selection in, their ethnic depart- 
ments. Departments range in size 
from 3-ft. sections to 40-ft. runs as 
more retailers experiment with mix. 

Johnson Products, manufacturers 
of Afro-Sheen and M&M°’s Stay-Sof 
still dominate department shelves, 
but new products by Clairol, L’Oreal 
and Revlon have broken in to the 
growing market, bent on securing 
some of the high-dollar-volume po- 
tential. 

Hair care is still a hot issue for 
most consumers and a strong cate- 
gory for drug chains. During 1979, 
shampoos generated $249 million, 
an increase of 17.5% over 1978 sales. 


Rinses and conditioners also had a 
strong showing, increasing 16.8% 
over 1978 sales, and contributing 
$163 million to department reve- 
nues. 

Sassoon is still the hottest sham- 
poo, conditioner, rinse and spray 
line, consistently turning in a strong 
sales performance for drug chains. 
But a new category is coming up fast 
and starting to have a substantial 
sales impact. The category—profes- 
sional hair care products. The 
sales—phenomenal. 

More than ever before, profes- 
sional hair care products seem to 
have caught consumers’ imagina- 
tions during 1979. The cost of a salon 
visit has risen substantially during 
the year, therefore consumers have 
cut back on professional hair care 
attention. Professional products 
provide a way for consumers to have 
professional salon treatments at 
very affordable prices. 

The attraction of professional 
products is double-sided—retailers 
report margins of 40% to 50%, and 
six to 10 turns per year, and buyers 
are increasing professional sections 
to accommodate the increased de- 
mand for products. 


Razors and blades, including dis- 
posable varieties also generated 
hefty sales increases during 1979. 
Saies for the category rose 17.5%, to 
$111 million, compared to 1978 sales 
of $94 million. 

Much of the growth in the razor/ 
blades category was generated by 
bonded blades and the growing 


number of disposables. 
Bonded razor blades (primarily 


twin blade systems) had an esti- 
mated growth of 47% during 1979, 
while disposable growth was tar- 
geted at 25% for the same period. 
Moreover, statistics indicate that 
double edge, injector and band are 
on the decline. 

Sales of these categories, accord- 
ing to chain retailers, have been 
helped by increased manufacturer 
print and TV advertising as well as 
in-store promotion and display. 

Consumers in 1979 also took an 
increased interest in the care and 
treatment of their skin, as sales for 
hand, skin and body creams and lo- 
tions together totaled $425 million. 
Oil of Olay is far and away the best 
selling face lotion, although reports 
on the new Sassoon skin care line 
have been positive. 

Consumers are not confining their 
new found interest in skin care to 
body and face creams, however, but 
paying more attention to skin that is 
exposed to the sun. 

Suntan/sunburn preparations 
rose 17.3% over 1978 sales of $88 mil- 
lion, to $103 million, as increased 
concern and warnings about the 
damaging effects of the sun’s rays 
helped to spur sales of suntan, prod- 
ucts. 

Consumers looking for skin pro- 
tection have a wide array of products 
to choose from: Coppertone, Hawai- 
ian Tropic, Native Tan, Eclipse, 
Sundown, Pre-Sun, Pizbuin, Block 
Out, Sea and Ski and many others. 
A very large factor in sales of suntan 


products hinges on PABA content 


(paraaminobenzoic acid) and sun

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


STATIONERY WRITES A BILLION 


Stationery sales were on the rise 
during 1979, due to stronger mer- 
chandising plans for greeting card 
sections and the increased consumer 
use of home/office supplies. 

Category sales topped $1 billion 
during 1979, a 12.9% increase over 
1978. Greeting cards made up a full 
third of department sales, generat- 
ing $355 million, up 14.8% over last 
year’s $309 million. 

Traditionally a productive cate- 
gory that provides retailers with 
good margins and high cash flow, in 
1979 retailers strove to wring even 
better sales from this category— 
and succeeded. 

Departments were enlarged dur- 
ing 1979, and some chains reported 
carrying 50 running feet and more, 
as retailers endeavored to provide 
consumers with a greater depth and 
variety of selection. Manufacturer 
provided overhead signing and 
point-of-purchase material added an 
extra dimension to in-store promo- 
tion—and helped to spur sales. 

Chain drug retailers also took ad- 
vantage of various manufacturer 
programs to help create not merely 
greeting card sections, but greeting 
card centers. American Greetings 
and Gibson Greeting Cards are two 
of the manufacturers programs that 
chain retailers are using. 

Home office area expanding 

But although the real push for 
productivity is taking place in greet- 
ing card sections, school/home office 
supplies is a category few retailers 
could ignore during 1979. 

School and home/office supplies 
accounted for one quarter of depart- 
ment sales, generating $266 million, 
a 10.8% increase over 1978's figure of 
$207 million. 

The increased activity in this par- 
ticular subcategory indicates the 
growing consumer need to get orga- 
nized. More than ever before, con- 
sumers have to contend with an 
increasing amount of bills, budgets 
and receipts which are piling up on

Looseleaf binders, however lost

consumers showed a preference for

college ruling. Organizer folders by

Popular with the younger set were 
the character notebooks and sup- 
plies—Muppets, Snoopy or Peanuts

Retailers also tried to boost prof-

1979. Sales rose 12.2% to $190 million 
and captured 17% of department 
sales, as chains experimented with 
family reading centers. 

Previously, most chains had lim-

assortment of paperbacks and mag-

of paperback 3/$1 type promotions.

pand the small sections to 8 ft. or 
more to include popular first-run pa- 
perbacks as well as home, fashion, 
craft and hobby magazines. 

Writing instruments generated 
$77 million during 1979, an increase 
of 10.6%. Eraser Mate, Gillette's big 
news during 1978, continued to be a 
hot item. However, Gillette had a 
supply problem and Eraser Mates 
were hard to come by for retailers 
and consumers alike. 

Lower-priced BIC, in multipacks 
and assortment packs, continues to 
be a strong seller, and a popular pro- 
motional item.

the expanded greeting card sec-

tured 6.2% of the total department 
sales while generating some $65 mil- 
lion in category revenues. Coordi- 
nating ribbons, bows and rever- 
sawrap prints have helped to hype 
department sales, as well. 

Social stationery remains a staple 
category for the department. Notes,

of 7.8% over 1978.

and envelopes made profitable and 
popular in-store promotional items 
for most retailers.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


SMOKES SIGNALS STILL STRONG 


Despite Health, Education and 
Welfare’s continuing antismoking 
campaign, chain tobacco sales held 
steady during 1979. 

Chain consumers spent $1.9 billion 
in tobacco departments last year, an 
increase of 11.1% over 1978's sales. 

Cigarette sales still account for a 
majority—66.3%—of department 
sales, and generated during 1979 an 
11.2% increase to $1.3 billion. 

What made cigarettes a success 
story in a year that was rampant 
with antismoking pressures was the 
success of the low-tar, low-nicotine 
brands. 

Late in 1978, Dr. Gio Gori, a scien- 
tist working in association with 
H.E.W., implied that certain brands 
(Carlton specifically) were not as 
harmful, and a smoker could have 10 
or more of the low-tar to one of some 
other higher-tar smokes. 

Chain drug tobacco buyers at- 
tribute to Gori’s statement the 
strong sales surge in low-tar ciga- 
rettes that occurred during 1979. In 
addition, the introduction of Reyn- 
old’s Doral III, Lorillard’s Kent III 
and Triumph, also spurred sales ac- 
tion in those cigarettes claiming 5mg 
of tar and under classification. 

As chains look to 1980 operations, 
retailers feel confident that the bulk 
of their sales will go to low-tar 
brands. In fact, nationwide, well 
over 90% of cigarettes sold have leis 
than 20mg of tar. 

Cigar sales slump 

The news is not as good for cigar 
sales, however, as consumption con- 
tinued to drop. During 1979, dollar 
sales rose a meager 7.1%, generat- 
ing total industry volume of $338 
million. Per cent of department 
sales dropped from 1978's 17.8% to a 
new low, 17.2%. 

Buyers feel that one large factor in 
the declining sale and use of cigars is 
the lack of manufacturer advertising 
and promotion. Retailers contend 
that with the decline of cigar adver- 
tising and the incidence of stepped- 
up cigarette promotion, cigars will 
virtually be a flat category by 1980. 

Loose tobacco use growing 

In sharp contrast to the declining 
cigar sales, loose tobacco has be- 
come a fast-growing department 
category. 


GP ies Sie <g ” 


Toting up an increase of 18.7%, 
loose tobacco sales topped $141 mil- 
lion last year and captured 7.1% of 
total department sales, a figure that 
is up from a 6.7% share in 1978. 

Black tobaccos—Black Cavendish 
in particular—have enjoyed the 
most marked sales increases. 
Brands such as Borkum Riff, 
Amphora and Katz and Black are 
the acknowledged leaders. 

Part of the dramatic increase in 
the tobacco/tobacco products cate- 
gory is due to increased sales of 
chewing tobacco and snuff. Most re- 
tailers are reporting that during 
1979 chewing tobacco sales “have 
been outstanding.” Workhorse, 
Redman have been two dominant 
brands. 

Snuff sales are also up, albeit not 
as dramatically as chewing tobacco. 
Buyers attribute the growing sales 
in these two sub-categories to an in- 
creased use of these products by 
younger consumers, and those try- 
ing to quit the smoking habit. Buy- 
ers are looking for increased activity 
in these categories. 

Accessories spark sales 

While tobacco/tobacco products 
had a good sales showing, buyers 
were also pleased with lighter and 
smoking accessory sales. This cate- 
gory registered the second largest 
sales increase—up 12.8% in 1979 fol-

Disposable lighters sparked the

are going to specialty stores where 
consumers can find a greater vari-

o-it-yourself sales 
continue to in- 
crease as gas- 
oline-deprived 
consumers look for pro- 
jects to fill the additional 
hours now spent in their 
homes. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


Increased gasoline prices forced 
more consumers to stay at home 
during 1979, and their attention was 
focused on their homes, and home 
decorating and repair. At the same 
time, soaring home maintenance 
costs resulted in consumers spend- 
ing more time and money sprucing 
up their homes and backyards them- 
selves, rather than going to an out- 
side contractor. 

A recent consumer survey by ad- 
vertising agency Batten, Barten, 
Durstine & Osborn Inc., indicated 
that an “overwhelming 67% of con- 
sumers report that they are spend- 
ing more time at home as a direct 
result of the gas crunch.” 

The report went on to hypothesize 
that “.. marketers of at-home 
sports equipment, do-it-yourself 
tools and home-improvement mate- 
rials might also profit as consumers 
strive to keep active during their 
additional hours in the home.” 

As a direct result of inflationary 
pressures, what was once a mer- 
chandising stepchild became serious 
business during 1979. Do-it-yourself 
sections and products were sought 
after by consumers anxious to pare 
down the rising cost of day-to-day 
living, as well as fill their increased 
time at home productively. 

As prices on home and auto re- 
pairs rose, so did DIY sales, gener- 
ating a total $546 million during the 
past year. 

Hardware leads department 


Le 
“Ss 
erp. 
oe 


Hardware commanded the largest 
percentage of department sales, 
generating $203 million or 37.1% of 
department revenues. Most hard- 
ware sections remain jobbed as re- 
tailers continue to build the neces- 
sary expertise in this area. The 
limited mix of nails, switchplates 
and extension cords has been re- 
placed by a larger and more varied 
merchandise mix, as retailers ex- 
panded hardware department foot- 
age. 

Plumbing supplies and tools as 
well as electrical supplies and such 
items as tool boxes are being added 
to department mix. And as the price 
of home repair continues to rise, re- 
tailers indicated that they will con- 
tinue to add merchandise in order to 
supply the homeowner with the nec- 
essary products to do household re- 
pairs. 

According to the Consumer Price 
Index, the cost of maintenance and 
repairs rose 10.4% during the period 
from January ’79 to December ’79. 
In addition the cost of maintenance 
and repair services rose 10.6%. Add 
to that the increase in homeowner- 
ship for the same period—21.1%— 
and it becomes not only wise, but 
economically necessary for consum- 
ers to effect their own repairs in 
order to trim maintenance costs. 

Automotive accessories have tra- 
ditionally been used as traffic draws 
by most chains. However, during 
1979, automotive joined the long list

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


PICTURE'S BRIGHT FOR PHOTO 


An increased interest in amateur 
photography helped bolster photo 
department sales sharply during 
1979. Sales rose 15.8% for the year, 
generating almost $1 billion in de- 
partment revenues for the chain 
drug industry last year. 

Film and processing are the meat 
and potatoes of the photo depart- 
ment, providing a solid traffic base 
for the whole department. 

Capturing 38.2% of department 
sales, film is the largest single cate- 
gory within the department. During 
1979, film sales rose 19.8% and added 
some $350 million to department 
sales. 

Still color and instant color films 
stole the show from black & white 
film, which, with the exception of 
35mm, have been almost completely 
phased out of drug store photo de- 
partments. 

During 1979, 110 film came up 
strong, outdistancing former favor- 
ite 126, as more consumers turned in 
older 126 cameras in favor of 110’s. 

Instant film, specifically SX-70, 
has done well for chain drug retail- 
ers, generating good profit from 
high-dollar margins. Instant picture 
film sales were up a sharp 21% with 
sales figures topping $162 million. 
With its high retail prices ($6.25 to 
$7.49), instant film can yield up to 
three times the dollar profit of regu- 
lar still-color film. 

Increased silver prices also did 
more than their share in raising the 
price of film. For a while, retailers 
reported that consumers were buy- 
ing film in bulk, and storing it in 
refrigerators to avoid another sharp 
price increase. 

Looking for value 

More so than in the past, photo 
departments were categorized by a 
growing number of promotions, as 
consumers looked increasingly not 
merely for good value, but for extra 
value. 

Processing, which generated an 
exceptional $275 million and ac- 
counted for 30% of department 
sales, has been the springboard for 
retailer promotions. 

Two prints for the price of one, 24- 
hour or one-day service with a pro- 


cessing guarantee, dollar-off cou- 
poning, and free products with a 
processing order, have all helped to 
hype processing sales. And process- 
ing orders stimulate new film pur- 
chase, as well as sales of eameras 
and accessories. 

Most importantly of all, retailers 
found it wasn’t enough anymore to 
offer only a variety of film and pro- 
cessing. To capture sales, and keep 
consumers, chain merchandisers 
had to offer a full line of photo sup- 
plies—a complete service depart- 
ment. 

Expanding mix and services 

What this meant for some retail- 
ers was a rethinking of merchandise 
mix and floor space. Both high- and 
middle-priced cameras were added 
to the mix, as were flash attach- 
ments and other photographic ac- 
cessories. During 1979, retailers 
aimed at presenting a full circle of 
products and services to customers. 

This attention to a full-service 
concept seems to be benefiting 
photo department sales. During 
1979, cameras brought in $96 million

Candy sales in chain drug stores 
rose 9% last year to $818 million, 
contributing 4% of the industry’s 
overall volume in the process. The 
growth rate generated in 1979, 
moreover, was sharply ahead of the 
6.5% increase posted by chain drug 
candy departments in 1978 when re- 
tailers were beset with rising prices 
of both sugar and cocoa. 

However, the department share of 
the overall business was in fact down 
from last year’s ratio (4.2%), as 
candy sales gains continued to lag 
the overall increases of the chain 
drug industry. 

Part of the improved candy perfor- 
mance during 1979 was due in no 
small part to accelerated promo- 
tional activity by retailers, who 
broadened advertising bases. 

Candy bars turned in the strong- 
est performance as sales of this sub- 
category increased 11.9% to $207 
million, capturing 25% of total de- 
partment sales. 

Single bars and small packs of two 
to four have replaced the eight and 
10 multipacks in popularity with the 
majority of purchases now being sin- 
gle bars. | 

The trend toward health-food ori- 
ented candy bars that had seemed to 
be growing during 1978, has not con- 
tinued. Chewy and nut-filled bars, 
bolstered by many new entries, did, 
however, spur 1979 sales. 

Retailers feel that this surge in 
candy bar purchases is the consum- 
ers way of pampering himself in an 
era of ever-rising inflation. Most 
consumers regard candy as a luxury 
item. 

Chewing gum 

Single-pack gum sales were also 
strong performers for chain drug 
candy departments during 1979. 
Generating 11% of total department 
sales, chewing gum sales rose 11.2% 
to $86 million. New sugarless gums 
and bubblegums as well as a gum for 
denture wearers helped speed sales. 

Although bagged candy ac- 
counted for a full 28% of department 
sales, the category increased only 
6.8% to $225 million. Many retailers 
feel that this slowdown of bagged 


* sees on Antti zi if , Ag Fad 


candy sales was due in part to the 
reluctance of consumers to spend 
much more than $1 for bagged vari- 
eties. Smaller bags, which retailed 
for under $1 and were promoted un- 
der that price, had almost complete 
sell-through as the sales of the 
over-$1 items tended to tail off. 

But despite consumer reluctance 
to spend more than $1 on an every- 
day basis, retailers reported sea- 
sonal sales better than ever, with 
increased volume occurring for vir- 
tually every item. 

Generating more than $211 million 
during 1979, seasonal candy made a 
strong showing, accounting for 26% 
of department sales and toting up a 
9% sales increase for the year. 

Attractive packaging by manufac- 
turers and strong promotion by re- 
tailers did much to strengthen the 
category and boost sales. Name 
brands as well as off-brands sold 
equally well for seasonal candy, un- 
like boxed candy where brand 
names sold the product. 

Boxed candy turned in a meager 
6.1% increase during 1979, due to 
increased prices. Nevertheless, the 
category generated $83 million in 
sales, capturing 10% of total depart- 
ment sales. Name brand boxed lines 


4 


—Whitman’s and Russell Stover— 
were in some cases the only boxed 
lines which moved out of season. 

Although prices of these brands 
are consistently higher than off or 
lesser known brands, consumers 
showed a consistent preference for 
the quality-assured image that these 
manufacturers present. Most retail- 
ers feel that this trend toward a 
brand name preference on non- 
necessity items will become more 
and more apparent as inflation con- 
tinues. 

Breath mints and other single-

mentioned by buyers as contribut-

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


HOUSEWARES SITTING PRETTY 


Despite rising inflation and con- 
sumer household budgetry cut- 
backs, housewares continued to 
flourish during 1979. 

Sales for the category topped $1.5 
billion, indicating an overall gain of 
=" over 1978's figure of $1.3 bil- 

on. 

Plastics and rubber housewares 
remained a strong category in spite 
of the rising cost of petrochemicals, 
which sent prices skyrocketing. 
Sales rose 17.2% to $342 million and 
captured 22.2% of the total depart- 
ment sales. | 

Rubbermaid remains the consum- 
ers favorite brand of plastic product, 
and retailers respond in kind—some 
stocking 40 ft. and up of Rubber- 
maid household plastics. Manufac- 
turer-supplied displays and POP 
material help stimulate sales for the 
participating retailer and foster con- 
sumer identification. Almond, last 
year’s new color, is still the current 
favorite. 

Rising paper-products prices also 
helped stimulate sales in the house- 
wares department. Sales rose to 
$128 million, an 18.1% increase over 
1978 sales of $107 million. More than 
before, private label and off-brands 
are infiltrating the paper-goods 
market as consumers look for a bet- 
ter deal on disposables. 

Furniture sales boom 

Houseware sales were further en- 
hanced by the big boom in furniture 
sales. Generating $47 million in de- 
partment sales, the furniture cate- 
gory rose 17.9% from the 1978 figure 
of $39 million. 

More and more chains are adding 
to the basic selection to give the con- 
sumer a greater variety of items. 
Bookcases, desks, entertainment 
centers and etageres were all best- 
sellers. Bentwood coatracks and 
bentwood and wicker rocking chairs 
were the favored promotional items. 
Wicker furniture was also men- 


tioned as a top furniture category, 
although space for display and stock 
are still the major problems. How- 
ever, most retailers reported that 
wicker and knockdown furniture 
could bring in margins of 40% to 50% 
and sometimes higher, and with 
those margin figures, many retail- 
ers are creating separate furniture 
centers within their stores. 

The rising price of gasoline pre- 
cipitated an increase in sales of out- 
door furniture during 1979. Since 
more and more families vacationed 
at home, patio furniture and bar- 
becue sales went up while people 
focused more attention on pamper- 
ing themselves at home. The most 
popular items were canvas “direc- 
tor” lawn chairs, which buyers re- 
ported consumers also used as in- 
door furniture. Leisure loungers 
were also strong at most chains and 
good promotables. 

Dining and entertaining at home 
was yet another trend precipitated 
by inflation during 1979. And buyers 
noted that sales of glassware, cook- 
ware and dishware reflected this 
trend. During 1979, sales for the cat- 
egory rose 16.9% to $171 million, as 
consumers concentrated on their 
culinary efforts. 

Pyrex, Corningware and Corelle 
were all strong items during 1979, as 
consumers indicated a stronger 
preference for items that could per- 
form in a variety of cooking facilities, 
from microwave oven to conven- 
tional oven to freezer. 

House and kitchen gadgets and 
gourmet cookware were also favor- 
ite consumer picks during 1979. 
Sales rose 15.7% to $101 million for 
the accessory category, as compared 
to $87 million generated during 
1978. 

Consumer fascination with gour- 
met cookware and gadgetry, more 
than anything else, helped spur this 
category's growth. Those products

strong for most chains, as are coffee-

are also experiencing good sales

also helped stimulate multiple sales.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


TOY SALES AREN'T 


Toys turned in a strong perfor- 
mance during 1979 as department 
sales rose 13.6% producing sales of 
$678 million. 

Games, including the electronics 
variety, walked away with the lead, 
generating 16.9% of $114 million to- 
tal department sales, and increasing 
a hefty 17.3% over 1978 sales of $97 
million. 

Plush toys, which have made 
rather modest showings the past 
several years, produced a strong 
comeback during 1979, generating a 
sales increase of 16.3% and a dollar 
volume of $53 million. Pre-school 
toys (including Fisher-Price) re- 
mained steady earners and posted a 
15.3% increase on sales of $64 mil- 
lion, while cars and staple boxed 
toys together brought in $178 mil- 
lion, emphasizing consumer demand 
for tried-and-true basic merchan- 
dise. 

There is no question that the con- 
tinued popularity of electronic 
games and calculators helped spur 
the uptrend in a department which 
is almost always in a state of flux. 

Retailers reported full sell- 
through on the “big name” elec- 
tronics—Merlin, Simon—despite 
high tickets, Excellent promotional 
items, buyers reported that when 
name electronics were advertised, 
sales “went through the roof.” De- 
mand for all types of electronics held 
fast throughout the year and be- 
came so great during the Christmas 
period that some retailers were 
caught short when manufacturers 
became unable to fill orders. 

But if electronics provided much 
of the sales pizzazz during 1979, it 
was to the low-end staples—pegged 
toys and games—that retailers 
looked for bread and butter sales. 

Low-end toy sales stable 

Capturing 14.3% of department 
sales, pegged toys contributed $96 
million to chain drug revenues dur- 
ing 1979. 

Lower-priced articles like Slinky, 
pocket and card games as well as 


‘small cars and other pegged toys, 


accounted for the majority of im-

their youngsters, without laying out 
a substantial amount of dollars. 
Movie merchandise moves 
Retailer interest was further pi- 
qued by TV and movie tie-in mer- 
chandise, which feature such popu- 
lar characters as The Hulk, Super- 
man, and Spiderman, as well as 
characters from “Star Trek” and 
“Star Wars.” These characters are 
reproduced on everything from 
lunch boxes, pencil cases, puzzles 
and coloring books to plastic action 
figures, and can be a source of added 
sales revenue, if, and only if, the TV 
Series or movie is well-received. 
And while some retailers are plan- 
ning increased sales for movie mer- 
chandise from “Star Wars’ its se- 
quel, “The Empire Strikes Back,” 
and “Superman II,” other retailers 
are eschewing this tie-in merchan- 
dise altogether. For these buyers 
there is an all-too-clear memory of a 
movie that didn’t work and the large 
amounts of closeouts that followed. 
But if buyers are bullish about 


movie and TV merchandise sales, 
they seem somewhat reluctant to 
predict sales of inflatables—a strong 
summer promotional item. 

Prices for the inflatable rafts, 
Swim rings and small pools have 
risen as much as 33% over the past 
year, due to the worsening oil short- 
age. And buyers don’t see those in- 
creases reversing themselves. Key 
to these sales, according to most 
buyers, is keeping the price points 
under $10, something which could 
well become impossible. 

Dolls and board games—favorites 
like Monopoly and Scrabble—have 
shown good increases as consumers 
continue a trend toward buying 
basics as prices continue to rise. 

Hobbies and crafts, up 12.3% with 
sales of $42 million during 1979, have 
decreased in store footage, as retail- 
ers feel specialty craft stores be- 
cause of the variety they can offer 
consumers, cutting into chain sales. 

But looking forward into the 
1980's, retailers are ready to make a 
commitment to electronics and 
basics which they feel will beeome 
the foundation of department busi- 
ness during the coming decade. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


A STRONG YEAR FOR SUNDRIES 


General merchandise racked up 
some substantial gains during 1979, 
as what was once an amorphous col- 
lection of category selections, began 
to take definition. Sales rose 15.8% 
to $1.1 billion, as compared to 1978 
figures of $987 million. 

Sunglasses came on strong during 
1979, as manufacturers broadened 
line selection to include winter sport 
lines. Retailers welcomed the longer 
selling season for this high-mar- 
gined category, which stretched the 
00%-60% gross margins to their 
maximum potential. 

Sales rose to $162.2 million, a 
17.3% increase over 1978's perfor- 
mance. Furthermore, the extended 
selling season increased the cate- 
gory’s share of department sales to 
14% as compared to last years 9.5%. 

Manufacturers and retailers alike 
have stressed the fashion accessory 
image for the sunglasses lines, as 
style plays an increasingly impor- 
tant role in eyewear purchases. 

Most popular for the winter sales 
are the apres-ski types of frames, 
which feature elastic bands, and 
multicolored frames. While the in- 
flux of designer lines has also helped 
to bolster sunglass sales. 

Bonneau, Foster Grant, Corning 
Glassworks Sun Sensor line are all 
selling well for drug retailers. 

Changing styles and fashions also 
had an impact on personal care ap- 
pliances during 1979. Generating an 
increase of 17.1%, personal care dol- 
lar volume rose to $212 million and 
captured 18.5% of total department 
sales. 

Gone are yesterday’s natural 
grooming styles, replaced in fashion 
by a more sophisticated, groomed 
look. And consumers are respond- 
ing by styling, curling, setting and 
pampering themselves to achieve to- 
day’s look. Hair care items, espe- 
cially, increased their market share, 
according to a Frost and Sullivan 
report, from 41% to 48% between 


1970 and 1978, while oral hygiene 
product sales plummeted from $46 
million to $26 million. 

Pet supplies 

Pet needs turned in a strong per- 
formance during 1979, as the pet 
care market continued to grow. 
Sales rose 17.3% to garner $135 mil- 
lion for the general merchandise de- 
partment. 

As the number of households car- 
ing for dogs or cats grew to 80 mil- 
lion during the past decade, retail- 
ers began to rethink the space 
devoted to the high-margin pet need 
category. To accommodate the rising 
demand for pet needs and food prod- 
ucts, retailers have increased pet 
sections, to 12 ft. and oftimes 24 ft. 
Furthermore, retailers are optimis- 
tic about the growth of this category 
as the dog/cat population is esti- 
mated to grow to 78 million by the 
end of the 1980's. 

Flea and Tick collars are far and 
away the No. 1 item for chain retail- 
ers. Miller-Morton and Hartz Moun- 
tain, set the pace for collar sales. As 
favored promotional items, retailers

Sporting goods 

As American consumers tighten 
the belt on luxuries, vacations have 
been one of the extras most have 
been forced to forego. Increased lei- 
sure time at home, plus an increased 
national interest in sports and phys- 
ical fitness have combined to make 
sporting goods a $17.9 billion indus- 
try. 

Chain drug retailers are vying for 
their piece of the sporting goods pie, 
as they increased footage and beefed 
up merchandise during 1979, captur- 
ing their fair share of sporting goods 
sales. | 

Sporting goods generated a dollar 
volume of $124 million during 1979, 
increasing 16.9% over 1978 sales. 
Chain retailers feel that key to good 
sales are brand name equipment and 
increased promotional activity. Rac- 
quetball racquets, running shoes, 
and equipment for games which can 
be played at home such as ping-pong 
or basketball have all shown marked 
increases during 1979. 

Brand-name products 

Retailers are also heavily into ad- 
vertising, contending that the con- 
sumer must be aware that the chain 
carries sports equipment. However, 
other retailers use advertisemenis 
mainly for traffic pull, but all retail- 
ers agree on one thing—consumers 
want brand name merchandise. 

Branded items have an increased 
importance to consumers in tennis 
equipment sales, where even the be- 
ginner can easily recognize the 
brand names. 


Retailers are even more optimistic 
about, the sporting goods category 
for the coming year and are expand- 
ing and stepping up the mix. In the 
coming year, they will include bad- 
minton sets, croquet sets, and 
higher priced baseball mitts, in ad- 
dition to stocking a limited assort- 
ment of hiking and camping gear.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


Chain drug stores began to use 
their food/liquor departments to 
build profits rather than traffic dur- 
ing 1979. Some chains expanded sec- 
tions to include a greater variety of 
foods, others relocated the sections 
to better accommodate the conve- 
nience-minded shopper. All re- 
ported that food sections were top 
performers. 

Sales rose a record 20.9% during 
1979, showing the greatest rate of 
growth among all the categories, as 
sales rose to $1.1 billion. 

Liquor/wine continues to contrib- 
ute the greatest percentage of sales 
to this department. During 1979, li- 
quor/wine generated $549 million, a 
16.9% increase over 1978, and cap- 
tured 47.8% of department sales. 
Chains have found liquor/wine to 
provide them with good multiple 
sales and tremendous turnover, 
while affording the consumer an 
easy, convenient access to a variety 
of spirits. When beer is added, the 
total sales topped $625 million—a 
16.7% increase over 1978. 

Soft drinks also provided a good 
percentage of department sales, 
generating $166 million and account- 
ing for 14.4% of department sales. A 
popular promotional item for many 
chains, soft drink sales increased 
15.2% during 1979. 

But the largest gains in this de- 
partment occurred with staple, ba- 
sic food products. Canned goods and 
condiments recorded a 21.4% sales 
increase, generating $46 million. 
Dry groceries, another basic item 
category, generated a 22.3% sales 
gain on $40 million. Together these 
categories accounted for 7.6% of de- 
partment sales. 

Stocking basics 

The increased sales in these two 
categories is due in part to the chain 
drug retailers’ concentration on 
stocking the basics that consumers 
need. During 1979, retailers found 
that part and parcel of the food sec- 
tion’s attraction to the consumer is 
the easy availability of staple gro- 
cery items. 


And as gas and time become more 
expensive, the consumer looks for a 
nearby outlet where milk, or bread 
or cereal can be picked up quickly 
and without a long drive. 

For many consumers during 1979, 
the chain drug food outlet took on 
the convenience aspects of the long- 
gone Mom and Pop grocery opera- 
tion, and provided merchandise at 
supermarket prices as well. 

Convenience is the word that 
could categorize chain drug food op- 
erations during 1979. Retailers 
stocked more basics, and more con- 
venience foods for the two paycheck 
family. Retailers have added frozen 
foods, diet foods, and cold meats to 
the drug store mix. Working moth- 
ers can easily provide a dinner for 
their families from chain drug 
shelves. 

Determining location 

Retailers no longer adhere to a 
standard format or prototype layout 
for food sections. Store location is 
determined with easy outside access 
the uppermost consideration. 

When selecting sites for a grocery 
department, chains favored large 
population centers in or near cities.

Peanuts, cashews and pistachios

helped the sale of these items.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


AMERICAN STORES A 
PIONEERING LEGEND 


RESULTS. Pioneering the era of 
the giant combination chain, the 
new American Stores Co. now em- 
braces a thriving 28-state empire of 
nearly 1,200 retail enterprises that 
some observers expect to give birth 
to a food/drug chain of 100 units. 

On a pro forma basis, American 
Stores Co. reported a 19% sales in- 
crease to $6.121 billion for the 53 
weeks ended Feb. 2, 1980 compared 
to $5.138 billion for the 52 weeks 
ended Dec. 28, 1978. Pro forma net 
earnings were up 24.5% to $62.8 mil- 
lion for the 53 weeks ended Feb. 2, 
1980, compared to $50.5 million for 
the 52 weeks ended Dec. 28, 1978. 
Pro forma earnings per common 
share were up 31% to $5.29 from 
$4.03 for the two periods. 

The company’s drug operations, 
which include the Skaggs Drug Cen- 
ters, the drug and food combination 
stores and the Rea and Derick drug 
chain, are estimated to have gener- 
ated $1.5 billion in sales in 1979. 

Masterminded by L. S. Skaggs, 
board chairman and president of 
American, the family of enterprises 
is nothing if not diverse, consisting 
as it does of 758 supermarkets, 336 
drug stores, 42 drug/food combo 
outlets, 53 restaurants and three 
discount stores. 

COMBINATION STORES. As 
the merchandising personality of 
the sprawling new complex takes 
form, interest is focusing on Ameri- 
can’s Alpha Beta combo stores, with 
their private label and distinctive 
style. 

“Sam Skaggs was after Alpha 
Beta and that operation is undoubt- 

edly the prime prize of the merger,” 
observes one security analyst. “The 
other operations can be useful, but 
that is the one that provides Skaggs 
with the food expertise that he feels 


diss 


he needs to push forward the com- 
bination concept.” 

Skaggs, of course, has been in the 
vanguard of combo store develop- 
ment, since joining forces in 1970 
with supermarketer Albertson's in 
putting together a chain of full-line, 
food/drug stores that flourished 
through the seven years of their 
partnership—and still do under di- 
vided command. 

It may be, as some contend, that 
the highly centralized Alpha Beta 
operation and the decentralized 
Skaggs have a lot to learn from each 
other. 

The Alpha Betas enjoy an attrac- 
tive pricing policy with their exten- 
sive merchandise mix, energetic 
advertising and promotional style, 
all supported by strong distribution 
facilities. 

Alpha Beta store managers, un- 
like their gold-coated Skaggs coun- 
terparts, make few buying, pricing 
or other merchandising decisions in 
their operations. 

Already, what is now the Skaggs- 
Alpha Beta supercenter is develop- 
ing its own personality. The shopper 
is confronted by two distinctly iden- 
tifiable entities—the promotional 
drug store and the full-line super- 
market. The impression: two stores 
under one roof. 

In the near future, the Skaggs- 
Alpha Betas will be multiplying in 
Idaho, Nevada, Utah and Arizona. 


The Skaggs Supercenters had sim- 


ilarly been scheduled for growth in 
New Mexico, Texas, Oklahoma and 
Arkansas. 

The value of the Alpha Beta logo 
and the probability of its extended 
use by Skaggs is enhanced by its 
array of respected private-label 
items.

mains to be seen, despite the fact 
that they are credited with outper- 
forming most other chain drug store 
operations in the nation. 

It’s considered most likely that the 
new American Stores will put the 
brakes on drug center development 
and channel investment into com- 
bination stores. 

How the Acme supermarkets will 
fit into the overall scheme of the new 
American is not yet clear, but not to 
be discounted, considering their fa- 
vorable market performance. 

Acme, prior to the Skaggs take- 
over, had been refining its opera- 
tions by dropping less profitable, 
smaller units, including 30 stores in 
western Pennsylvania and 40 more 
in New York. 

The supermarket chain has been 
operating 361 outlets in seven East- 
ern states, deriving 34% of its vol- 
ume from its home market in Phila- 
delphia. Store growth is now being 
channeled into the Delaware Valley 
market, where 14 new outlets are 
planned by midyear. Leases for 10 
former Food Fair/Pantry Pride units 
were acquired last year and are 
being reopened one by one, after re- 
styling. 

The subject of much speculation is 
the place of the Rea & Derick drug 
chain in the new corporate fold, con- 
sidering the Skaggs dedication to 
the drug/food combo concept. 

On its own, Rea & Derick stacks 
up as a Solid 134-store enterprise, 
with outlets in Pennsylvania, Mary- 
land and New York, delivering $7 
million in net earnings, while draw- 
ing 30% of sales from pharmacy de- 
partments. It has taken one step 
toward combo merchandising with 
the opening of a drug/home center.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


WALGREEN CONTINUES TO GROW 


RESULTS. Walgreen Co. sales 
and earnings growth continued to 
accelerate through the first half of 
fiscal 1980, extending an upward 


trend which started in 1977. 

Sales for the six months ended 
Feb. 29, 1980, increased 15% to $784 
million over a year earlier, while net 
profits increased 22% to $18.2 mil- 
lion for the same period. This com- 
pares to a sales growth rate in fiscal 
1979 of 12.7%, during which time 
Walgreen volume reached $1.345 bil- 
lion, and earnings on continuing op- 
erations grew 17.4% to $30.3 million. 

March sales figures, however, sug- 


gest that rough economic weather 


may be ahead. Sales for the month 
increased only 10%, which trans- 
lates into little or no real per-store 
sales growth considering the impact 


of inflation and the fact that part of 


that increase was generated by 21

earlier. 

Despite slowing sales growth in 
March, Walgreen appears headed 
for another excellent year. The 746- 
store chain has shown a consistent 
ability in recent years to keep earn- 
ings from continuing operations 
growing at a faster rate than sales. 
(Net income in 1977 grew only 5.7% 
when losses for the discontinued 
Globe discount department store 
operation are considered, but it 
grew 35.4% when only continuing 
operations are considered. ) 

Walgreen’s net margin has im- 
proved steadily since 1977, rising to 
2.3% on a LIFO basis in 1979, up 
from 2.0% in 1978 and only 1.4% in 
1977. The chain’s pretax margin last 
year stood at 3.9%, virtually un- 
changed from the previous year, 
while the return-on-assets measure 
increased from 4.6% in 1978 to 7.5%, 

EXPANSION. While new con- 
struction starts have tailed off na- 
tionally, Walgreen continues to open 
new stores at a rapid pace. The chain 
expects to open 50 new drug stores 
and 12 new restaurants, compared to 
38 new drug stores and three new 
restaurants opened last year. (This 
total does not include the 16-store 
Stein chain bought in fiscal 1979.) 

One reason why Walgreen has 
been able to expand rapidly and still 
maintain high earnings growth is 
that the chain has concentrated on 
developing existing markets. Be- 
cause the Walgreen name is well- 
known, the additional costs of adver- 
tising, distribution and supervision 
normally associated with opening 


new stores are kept to a minimum. 


Moreover, Walgreen has enviable 
geographic distribution, with 
strength not only in Midwestern 
markets such as Chicago, Mil- 
waukee and St. Louis, but in nine 
expanding metro areas in the South 


and Southwest. 


In addition, Walgreen last year 
dramatically strengthened its Wis- 
consin presence with the purchase of 
the Stein chain, and with the pend- 
ing acquisition of the 30-unit Ren- 


nebohm chain located in Madison. 
OPERATIONS. Walgreen has 
shown a willingness to experiment, 
reflected most recently in the deci- 
sion to open the chain’s first free- 
standing convalescent aids center 
this spring. Most attention, how- 
ever, remains focused on improving 
productivity in the company’s basic 
business of running drug stores. 
Store remodelings continue to get 
major emphasis, with 65 major proj- 
ects planned for 1980, compared to 
45 last year. The goal of this program 
is to boost existing store sales witha 
relatively small investment. 


DIVERSIFICATION. Food-ser- 
vice sales increased only 4% in 1979 
to $90.5 million, while operating 
profits declined. Offsetting a soft 
year in the food-service business 
last year were sizable increases in 
interest income (up from $1.7 million 
in 1978 to $4.4 million in 1979) and 
equity income from Walgreen’s Mex- 
ican affiliate and the four Schnucks- 
Walgreen combination food/drug 
stores Walgreen operates in part- 
nership with Schnucks Markets of 
St. Louis. 


LONGS STILL AHEAD 


RESULTS. Longs maintained its 
position at the forefront of the chain 
drug industry in a number of statis- 
tical categories in fiscal 1980, ended 
Jan. 31. Based on annual sales of 
$773 million, the chain pulled in ap- 
proximately $240 per square foot of 
selling space, or nearly $5.9 million 
per store. Revenues for the year 
past also represented a gain of 16.5% 
over $664 million in fiseal 1979. 

Net income improved 13.1% to 
$26.7 million from $23.6 million the 
previous year. Per-share earnings 
climbed to $2.53, as compared to 
$2.23 at this time last year. The 
chain’s net-to-sales ratio slipped 
slightly to 3.5%, however, after hav- 
ing hovered at 3.6% for a number of 
years, due to increased expenses. 

Most of the slippage was seen in 
the fourth quarter, when net profits 
came to $8.2 million—only a 6% in- 
crease over $7.8 million the year be- 
fore. As aresult, Longs’ net-to-sales 
ratio for the quarter fell from 3.9% 
in fiscal 1979 to 3.6% in the period 
just ended. 

EXPANSION. In fiscal 1980, 
Longs built 18 new stores (two of 
them replacements for older, small- 
er locations) and shuttered a single 
unit. This gave the chain a net gain 
of 12 outlets, for a total of 180 at 
year’s end. 


But more importantly, Longs en- 
tered its fifth state—Nevada—and 
expanded its trading area to include 
six states. The roster breaks down 
this way: 111 units in California, 12 in 
Hawaii, 4 in Arizona and 1 apiece in 
Oregon, Alaska and Nevada. 

Until 1977, Longs had operated on 
a much more concentrated market- 
ing basis, restricting its expansion 
to California and Hawaii. In 1977, 
however, the chain launched a single 
store in Anchorage, followed a vear 
later with Arizona and Oregon out- 
posts, and debuted just last year in 
Carson City, Nev. 

The far-flung pioneer store strat- 
egy is made possible by Longs’ ad- 
herence to direct shipments for all 
its merchandise. The chain departs 
from that approach only in Hawaii, 
where a small, 19,000-sq.-ft. dis- 
tribution center is maintained due to 
the 2,000-mile supply line. 

DECENTRALIZATION. In a 
Longs operation, it is the store man- 
ager and the district manager who 
make the day-to-day business deci- 
sions. The store manager hires and 
fires, buys 100% of his needs, sets 
his own markdown schedule and es- 
tablishes price on every item. 

This highly decentralized ap- 
proach has worked well for Longs. 

REMODELING. Longs com- 


Longs has boosted its per-store 
volume to nearly $5.9 million

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


ECKERD TOPS 1,000-UNIT MARK 


GROWTH. The 15-state Eckerd 
Drug chain—subsidiary of Clearwa- 
ter, Fla.-based Jack Eckerd Corp.— 
shot past the 1,000-store mark in 
November 1979, with the record 
opening of 22 new outlets in one 
week. Eckerd Drug, thus, joins 
Revco at the 1,000-store-plus 
plateau. 

Since the close of the chain’s fiscal 
year—July 28, 1979—Eckerd has 
opened 56 units to date. Fiscal 1979 
saw the addition of 88 units, in keep- 
ing with Eckerd’s 10% growth rate 
per year policy. A devotee of the 
Sunbelt states, Eckerd’s growth has 
taken place primarily in that region, 
with the marketplaces of three 
states—Texas, North Carolina, and 
the retailer’s home turf of Florida— 
leading the way. 

RESULTS. For the six-month pe- 
riod ended Jan. 26, 1980, J.E.C. 
rolled up earnings of $36 million on 
sales of $760 million, scoring in- 
creases of 15.1% and 16.1% respec- 
tively, over comparable figures for 
the same period last year. 

Earnings per share reached $1.52, 
from $1.33 last year. 

Second quarter net earnings for 
J.E.C., meanwhile, were reported 
at $25.8 million, an increase of 15.7% 
over last year, while sales were 
listed at $442.8 million, up 14.8%. 

The retailer’s 38-unit J Byrons de- 
partment store division increased 
its net earnings 39.9% and its sales 
17.3% in the second quarter. For the 


six months, its net earnings in- 
creased 35.1% and sales 19.3%. 

For fiscal 1979, J.E.C.’s sales to- 
taled $1.325 billion, a 17.1% increase 
over $1.131 billion, the year-ago fig- 
ure. On a LIFO basis, net earnings 
reached $59.3 million over 1978’s 
$50.6 million, also a 17.1% increase. 
Per share LIFO earnings were 
$2.53, as compared to $2.17 in 1978. 

LIFO earnings as a per cent of 
sales remained stable at 4.5%. 

On a FIFO basis, net earnings 
would have been $64.4 million, up 
18.9% from 1978's $54.1 million. Per 
share FIFO earnings were $2.75, as 
compared to $2.32. The 1979 FIFO 
net-to-sales ratio would have been 
4.9%, up from the previous year’s 
4.8%. 

J.E.C.’s drug division, the corpo- 
ration’s largest subsidiary, amassed 
sales of $1.21 billion in 1979, an in- 
crease of 16.7% over year-ago fig-

GRAY DRUG DIVISION SALES UP 


RESULTS. For the first time in 
several years, sales growth in Gray’s 
discount department store division 
dropped below that for the drug 
store division. 

Rink’s sales for the first nine 
months of fiscal 1980 totaled $198.1 
million, up 8.6% from $182.4 million 
a year earlier. This contrasts with a 
16% increase in sales for fiscal 1979 
which helped Rink’s offset a decline 
that year in operating profits in the 
drug store division. As aresult Gray 
was able to post an overall increase 
in net income of 6.3% on a FIFO 
basis to $6.6 million. 

Gray switched to LIFO account- 
ing last year, which had the effect of 
reducing net earnings by $2.2 mil- 
lion to $4.4 million. Because of this 
accounting change, which lowered 
Gray taxes by reducing reported in- 
come, Gray actually reported a net 
earnings decline in 1979. 

Sales in the drug store division 
through Jan. 26, 1980, the end of the 
third quarter, totaled $138.9 million. 
This represented a 9.3% increase 
from a year earlier. Although sales 
growth in the division slowed from 
the 12% pace of 1979, operating prof- 
its showed positive growth. 

Net income for the first three 
quarters for both the drug and dlis- 
count store operations totaled $4.4 
million, excluding an $840,000 gain 
on the sale of 14 Florida drug stores. 
Net income for the three quarters 
represents a 3.6% increase over the 


same period last year. When the 
gain on the Florida sale is included, 
net earnings for the three quarters 
totaled $5.2 million, and increased 
to 23.5% over last year. 

Gray’s net margin excluding the 
Florida sale equaled 1.3% for the 
first nine months. 

Rink’s lower sales growth in 1980 
can only be described as a disap- 
pointment, considering the fact that 
two new Rink’s stores opened dur- 
ing the reporting period. 

Although not exactly spectacular, 
the 9.3% sales gain in Gray drug 
stores through the first three quar- 
ters of 1980 understates actual 
growth because during that time 
Gray sold 14 Florida stores. As a 
result, as of Jan. 26, Gray operated 
four fewer drug stores than at the 
start of the fiscal year. 

STORES. So far this year, Gray 
has opened 10 new drug stores, in- 
cluding six in Ohio and four in Flor- 
ida, bringing the chain’s total to 
about 190. Forty-one of those stores 
are located in Florida. 

The relatively strong sales and 
earnings gains in 1980 for the drug 
store division indicate that Gray’s re- 
modeling program is working. So 
far, 11 stores have been remodeled, 
with many of them involving en- 
largement and conversion to Gray's 
“superstore format.” Superstores 
are generally over 12,000 sq. ft. in 
size and carry expanded general 
merchandise departments. 


DIVERSIFICATION. Despite 
the drug division’s reported higher 
sales for the first three quarters of 
fiscal 1980, the Rink’s division will 
report greater sales than the drug 
stores due to a new sales breakout 
system. 

The new reporting system is that 
the leased drug departments in dis- 
count stores have been transferred 
to Rink’s, and are no longer being 
reported as Gray drug store sales. 
Last year, these leased drug depart- 
ments produced sales of $27.3 mil- 
lion.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


REVCO'S BILLION-DOLLAR YEAR 


RESULTS. For powerhouse Rev- 
co D.S., which hit the 1,000-store 
mark in early 1978, a second achieve- 
ment—the chain’s first billion-dollar 
sales year—is a mere fiscal quarter 
away. 

For the third quarter of fiscal 
1980, Reveo posted a 15.6% sales 
gain, making it all but certain that 
the company will well-exceed the $1 
billion mark during the remaining 16 
weeks of the fiscal year. Sales for the 
period, ended Feb. 9, 1980, which 
included the Christmas selling sea- 
son, totaled $271.9 million, up from 
$234.8 million for the same quarter 
last year. 

Earnings for the quarter totaled 
$10.3 million, up 13.5% from a year 
earlier. 

Thirty-six week totals show sales 
increased 17.5% to $739.5 million. 
Net earnings for the same period 
totaled $26.1 million, an increase of 
16.5% from 1978. 

Revco’ sales and earnings growth 
performance so far this year is run- 
ning slightly ahead of last fiscal year, 
when the chain posted 17.1% growth 
in sales and 14.5% growth in profits. 

For fiscal 1979, ended June 2, Rev- 
co's net sales were $928 million, as 
compared to $792 million in fiscal 
1978. Net earnings were $33.6 mil- 
lion, or $2.51 per common share, as 
compared with $29.4 million, or 
$2.21 per common share in 1978. 

EXPANSION. At the close of fis- 
cal 1979, Reveo opened 115 units and 
shuttered three, for a net growth of 
113 units, bringing total outlets at 


year-end to 1,030 and maintaining 
growth goals of at least 10% per year. 
Also in fiseal 1979, Reveo entered its 
24th state—Arkansas—with four 
new units. The chain also remodeled 
73 older units during the fiscal year. 

STORES. Chiefly a bantam store 
chain (Revco’s 1970 prototype was 
4,500 sq. ft.), the drug retailer has 
pumped up the size of its stores over 
the course of the decade. Today, new 
stores weigh in at roughly 8,450 sq. 
ft. and carry some 8,000 sku’s, as 
compared to 2,800 sku’s per store in 
1970. 

Though Reveco’s prescription vol- 
ume was 25.3% of total drug store 
sales in 1979, the larger stores have 
given way to expanded sales in other 
drug store categories. For example, 
categories like vitamins, drugs and 
patent medicines, beauty aids, ciga- 
rettes, toiletries and sundries, 
spawned 69.2% of total drug store 
sales in fiscal 1979, a 0.2% increase 
over the year-ago figure. 


Reveo also merchandises more 


than 380 private label products, 


which accounted for sales of more 


than $47 million last year.

pharmacy computer system. 

More recently, Revco walked an- 
other health care path with the 
opening of the first “Dental Care 
Clinie at Revco,” in a Lorain, Ohio 
store.

Dart Drug as net income for the

fiscal 1979. 

Net margins widened to 1.5% of 
1980 sales, up from 1.2% during 
1979, a direct result of the decrease 
in cost of sales, store occupancy and 
warehousing expenses as a percent- 
age of sales.

OPERATIONS. Dart operates 75 
retail drug stores throughout the 
metropolitan Washington, D.C., 
area, as well as in the neighboring 
states of Virginia and Maryland. 

Highly promotional, Dart units 
average 15,000 sq. ft., although 
store sizes vary greatly. Most of the 
discount drug stores carry a broad 
range of nationally advertised and 
private label merchandise, including 
in its broad mix, prescription and 
proprietary drugs, toiletries, cos- 
metics, automobile accessories, 
eandy and tobacco, photographic 
supplies, sporting goods, garden 
and lawn supplies, hardware, small 
appliances, paints and household 
items, as well as greeting cards and 
stationery, school supplies, maga- 
zines, baby needs, toys and a small 
assortment of soft goods. In addi- 
tion, the company operates eight 
leased optical centers which were 
opened during fiscal 1977. 

The chain also operates a 480,000- 
sq.-ft. warehouse situated at its 
Landover headquarters. 


DIVERSIFICATION. In addi- 
tion to drug stores, Dart operates a 
number of highly profitable subsid- 
iary retail operations. 

During fiscal 1976 the retail inno- 
vator developed a drug/home center 
concept in Washington, D.C., and at 
the close of fiscal 1980, operated 18 
units. Averaging 50,000 sq. ft., the 
combination stores carry lumber, 
building supplies and a broad range 
of hardware and DIY materials, as 
well as a full line of drug store prod- 
ucts. 

In early 1978, the chain opened 
two Crown Book stores in D.C., and 
today operates 14 throughout Vir- 
ginia, Maryland and the metro D.C. 
area. Averaging 4,000 sq. ft., the 
stores stock a broad range of books 
and magazines, offering in excess of 
20,000 titles and discounts up to 
50%. 

The chain’s newest diversification, 
however, emerged late in fiscal 1980, 
when Dart popped three Trak Auto- 
motive units. 

Freestanding units, Trak Auto 
carries 8,000 sq. ft. of full line auto 
parts and accessories, offering con- 
sumers more than 10,000 sku’. 

Currently, Dart operates seven 
units, with plans to add eight to 12 
more by next September. The close 
of fiscal 1980 had Dart unveiling 
plans for a 60,000-sq.-ft. automotive 
warehouse in home city, Landover. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


SUPERX HAS ITS UPS AND DOWNS 


RESULTS. Despite the sharp 
drop in SupeRx’s operating profits 
in 1979, Kroger Co. management re- 
mains committed to rapid expansion 
and renovation of the drug store 
chain. 

Sales for calendar year 1979 in- 
creased from $522 million in 1978 to 
$567 million, an increase of 8.6%. 
This compares to an actual decline in 
sales in 1978 of 0.1%. Boosting sales 
last year was the first net increase in 
SupeRx’s store count since 1976. At 
the end of last year, SupeRx oper- 
ated 504 drug stores compared to 
487 a year earlier, a net gain of 17. 

Operating profits, on the other 
hand, declined 43.3% from $22.6 
million in 1978 to $12.8 million last 
year. In contrast, operating profits 
in 1978 increased 29% at a time when 
SupeRx opened only seven new 
stores and closed 48. Company offi- 
cials attribute the drop in operating 
profits to rising costs which were not 
compensated for by sales. Sharply 
higher operating costs in 1979 can be 
attributed in large part to start up 
expenses for the chain’s 38 new and 
acquired stores. 

OPERATIONS. A continuing 
problem for SupeR.x is low sales pro- 
ductivity in its stores, a problem

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


PERRY NOW A MAJOR CHAIN 


GROWTH. Three developments 
at Perry Drug Stores Inc. in 1980 
emphasize what has, in fact, been a 
reality for a couple of years—Perry 
is now a major drug store chain. 

By the end of Perry’s fiscal year on 
Oct. 31, 1980, the chain will have 72 
stores opened, most likely giving it 
the top position in the state. 

Secondly, Perry is likely to open 
its first drug store outside of Michi- 
gan either late this fiscal year or 
early next. Acquisitions either in 
the drug store field or in related 
businesses also remain a top man- 
agement priority. 

Thirdly, the chain recently was ac- 
cepted for listing on the American 
Stock Exchange. 

RESULTS. What remains to be 
seen in the coming years is if the 
chain can continue to grow at the 
rate it has over the last six years. 
From 1974-79, for example, the 
chain doubled its store count from 36 
to 67, tripled sales from $36.9 to 
$109.3 million and almost quintupled 
net earnings from $433,000 to $2.5 
million. 

Simple mathematics suggests a 
slower growth rate because as the 
sales and earnings base expands, 
annual growth rates in the high 20% 
to 30% range become increasingly 
difficult to maintain. Chairman and 
president Jack A. Robinson recog- 
nizes this, and is projecting an an- 
nual sales advance of about 17% 
through fiscal 1988, and an annual 
profit growth of about the same per- 
centage, give or take a point or two. 
If this growth pace is maintained, 
Perry will pass the $200 million 
mark in sales and the 100-store mark 
in stores by the end of fiscal 1983. 


Last year sales increased 23%, 
while before-tax profits increased 
13% to $4.1 million and net profits 
increased 19%. For the second year 
in a row, sales growth outpaced 
earnings growth, suggesting that 
Perry’s high rate of store openings in 
recent years is beginning to have a 
significant drag effect on earnings. 

Still, Perry’s pretax margin, 
which slipped in fiscal 1979 from 
4.1% to 3.8%, is above the chain drug 
industry average. Last year the 
company’s net margin was 2.3%, 
compared to 2.4% for the two pre- 
vious years. Perry’s return on assets 
ratio also continued a steady decline 
from a high of 8.2% in 1977 to 6.3% 
last year. 

After a strong sales and earnings 
performance through fiscal 1979, 
made all the more remarkable be- 
cause Perry achieved it despite poor 
economic conditions in the Greater 
Detroit area, first quarter sales and 
profits growth has slowed. 

OPERATIONS. Key to Perry’s 
ability in recent years to expand 
rapidly and still maintain a high rate 
of profitability have been the success 
of the chain’s auto/home center com- 
bination stores, and also its ability to 
bring its 9,000-sq.-ft. to 10,0C0-sq.- 
ft. Perry drug stores to profitability 
within as little as six month’s time. 

Perry has one of the highest sales 
per square foot levels for the indus- 
try, averaging $230 for the retail 
selling area last year. Per square 
foot sales in auto/home centers 
which have been open at least two 
years are significantly higher. It is 
the profit potential of these drug 
stores, which range up to 15,000 sq. 
ft. and have large automotive de-

which have allowed Perry to mini-

These small combos, which no one 
else in the drug store industry has 
really tried to copy, have also had a 
good impact on gross margins. The 
large automotives, sporting goods, 
hardware and pet supplies depart-

drug store business. In fiscal 1979, 
for example, Perry’s LIFO-based 
gross margin was 30.5%.

chain’s expected 72 stores, will be 
combos. 


HOOK GROWS, DIVERSIFIES 


EXPANSION. For Hook Drugs 
Inc., 1979 was a year of rapid growth 
and diversification, resulting in the 
opening of 24 new stores. 

During the calendar year, the 258- 
store chain opened 18 new drug 
stores, including three in Illinois, 
the first ever to be operated by Hook 
outside Indiana. Three stores closed 
during the year. 

Hook diversified last year with 


the opening of the chain's first four 
Quik-Way convenience food marts 
and the purchase of the H. Lieber 
photofinishing company, 

In addition, Hook opened two 
more Hook convalescent aids and 
sickroom supply stores next to Hook 
drug stores, bringing the chain’s 
total to three and giving it leader- 
ship among drug chains in that field. 

Management has not said how 
many new stores are planned for 
1980, but based on recent precedent 
Hook should open about 10 or more. 
The chain has opened at least nine 
new stores in each of the last five 
years. 

RESULTS. Hook sales topped 
$200 million for the first time last 
year, increasing 12.5% to $207.2 mil- 
lion. This compared to $184.2 million 
in sales in 1978. Much of that per-

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


PEOPLES PIONEERS PROFITABLY 


RESULTS. For Peoples Drug 
Stores, the payoff is now in full 
swing from the revitalization pro- 
grams initiated four years ago when 
Lane and Peoples merged and new 
management took the reins at Peo- 
ples. 

Sales for the fiscal year ended 
Sept. 29, 1979 rose by 9% to $441.1 
million, as profits climbed 17% to 
$6.5 million. The Alexandria, Va.- 
based chain’s net margins (on a 
LIFO basis) expanded to 1.5% from 
1.4% and the return on shareholders’ 
equity widened to 13.8% from 
13.5%. 

Trends continued in the opening 
quarter of the current fiscal year, as 
sales rose 18%, year to year, while 
net income expanded by 26%. Sales 
for the 16 weeks ended Jan. 19 were 
reported at $169.4 million, while net 
income was $3.5 million. 

DIVERSIFICATION. In the last 
several years, Peoples has emerged 
as one of the more innovative com- 
panies in the chain drug business. 
For example, it has been one of sev- 
eral chains that not only pioneered 
the optical center business but also 
made a commitment to it so that 
Peoples now has one of the strongest 
optical operations in the chain drug 
industry. It now consists of 43 cen- 
ters in the Peoples, Lane and Reed 
divisions, plus two cutting and edg- 


ing labs, one in Alexandria and the 
other in Atlanta. 

Peoples has also become very ag- 
gressive in developing a strong 
health care image for its drug stores 
by adding new health care products 
and services into a drug store en- 
vironment. These operations sup- 
plement Peoples’ basic pharmacy 
business, which accounts for about 
20% of overall volume, or around $90 
million annually. 

In addition to optical, Peoples was 
the first chain to launch in-store 
dental centers, and the chain now 
has three in operation. 

In addition to its health care im-

ACQUISITIONS. Peoples made a 
number of acquisitions during 1979. 
The first, made during the Septem- 
ber 1979 fiscal year, was that of 
B. H. Krueger, a contract manufac- 
turer of private label toiletries. 

After the close of the fiscal year, 
Peoples acquired a controlling inter- 
est in Haag Drug in Indianapolis, 
which is being extended to full own- 
ership. Haag, with annual sales of 
roughly $80 million, operates 80 
stores in Indiana, Illinois and Iowa.

units. Following the close of the fis-

and last year, 19 stores got the treat- 
ment. 


SIGNALS MIXED AT CUNNINGHAM 


RESULTS. Cunningham has put 
together two successive years of 
profit growth on moderate sales 
gains, but the outlook for continued 
improvement in fiscal 1980 is 
clouded. 

The first half results indicate that 
while sales continue to grow at 
about the same rate as last year— 
8.5% —sharply rising operating 
costs have sent profits into a plunge. 
During the six months ended Feb. 
29, earnings dropped 22.3% to 
$733,000, compared to $943,000 a 
year earlier. 

Cunningham’s strategy over the 
last 10 years has been to shrink the 
size of the chain by closing marginal 
stores and replacing some of them 
with larger, better-located units. 
Between 1969 and 1979 the chain 
shrunk by more than a fourth in 
store numbers, decreasing from 213 
to 156 as of Aug. 31, 1979. 

During fiscal 1978 and 1977 that 
strategy, coupled with the chain’s 
expansion of its resort, office and 
hotel small store division, showed 
signs of paying off. In both those 
years profits increased faster than 
sales. In 1979, for example, sales in- 
creased a modest 8.8% to $182.9 mil- 
lion, while pretax profits increased 
13.2% to $2.9 million (net profits in- 
creased 17.7% to $1.7 million). In fis- 
cal 1978 the growth gap was even 
greater: 55.8% for pretax profits vs. 
8.1% for sales. 

Although the sales increases in 
both 1979 and 1978 were modest, 
they were accomplished in each case 
with fewer stores than the preced- 


Cunningham Drugs: 
Number of units shrink 


1979 


ing year, the result being that store 
sales productivity grew faster than 
overall sales gains. In 1979 average 
sales in all Cunningham stores 
amounted to $1.165 million, up 9.8% 
over a year earlier. 

The problem for the future is that 
although 1978 and 1979 represent an 
improvement, sales gains have not 
been strong enough to give the chain 
a “cushion” against rising operating 
costs, a trend which seems certain 
to accelerate even more during 1980. 

EXPANSION. Cunningham has 
been hampered in its goal of sharply 
increasing sales by a sometimes er- 
ratic merchandise policy in its full- 
line drug stores and by the fact that 
the company is stuck with a large 
number of aging stores in less desir- 
able locations. 

In 1979 one new Cunningham 
store was opened, but this year 


three to four new full-line stores are 
slated to open. In addition, the chain 
continues to expand and remodel ex- 
isting stores, with six slated for 
work in 1980 compared to 10 last 
year. 

OPERATIONS. Whether Cun- 
ningham’s twin policy of improving 
store productivity in its full-line 
drug stores and expanding into 
growing population centers through 
its small store division will give the 
chain the sales growth to cover ris- 
ing operating costs still remains to 
be seen. But from a financial point of 
view, Cunningham is a much strong- 
er chain today than it was four or 
five years ago. 

Long-term debt, which in 1973 to- 
taled $4 million; or 14.5% of total 
capitalization, has been drastically 
reduced so that last year it totaled 
only $620,000, or only 2.1% of cap- 
italization. Interest charges, conse- 
quently, have also been sharply 
reduced. Last year they totaled only 
$140,000. 

The company’s improved financial 
position is reflected in the fact that 
capital spending in 1979 was in- 
creased over 52% from a year ear- 
lier, to $2.9 million, and virtually all 
of that came from internally gener- 
ated funds. 

The chain has also improved its 
pretax and net margins steadily dur- 
ing the last two years, although both 
remain low by chain standards. In 
1979 Cunningham’s net margin was 
0.9% and its pretax margin, 1.6%. 
Return on shareholders equity was 
5.9%, up from 5.3% a year earlier.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


THRIFTY IMPROVEMENTS PAY OFF 


RESULTS. Improvements in op- 
erations, store design and merchan- 
dising continued to make their mark 
on the bottom line at Thrifty Drug in 
the fiscal year ended Aug. 31, 1979. 

Net income expanded 32.9%, from 
$10.7 million in 1978 to $14.2 million. 
Sales increased 13.1% to $858.4 mil- 
lion from $759.2 million, and the 
company’s net-to-sales ratio of 1.65% 
was its best performance in six 
years. 

Both sales and earnings leveled off 
somewhat in the first quarter of fis- 
eal 1980, ended Nov. 30, due to un- 
usual conditions. Revenues ex- 
panded only 9.6% to $208.1 million 
from $189.9 million the year before, 
while net income increased only 
7.0% to $1.9 million from $1.8 mil- 
lion. 

This development, however, is di- 
rectly related to the rain and snow 
storms that plagued Thrifty loca- 
tions throughout northern Califor- 
nia and the Pacific Northwest in the 
month of November, when the 
Christmas buying season was just 
getting under way. 

Approximately 80% of revenues in 
fiscal 1979 were rung up by 517 
Thrifty drug stores. The balance of 
sales were generated by 53 sporting 
goods outlets, 33 food service units, 
four discount department stores and 
an imports business, Newman Im- 
porting.

stores and shuttered 11 during the

plans call for the opening of 25 new 
drug stores. 

What’s more, Thrifty has moved to 
improve its consumer franchise by 
upping its TV and radio advertising 
budget by 50%. 


RITE AID GETS HIGH MARKS 


RESULTS. Despite a switch to 
the LIFO accounting method of in- 
ventory valuation, Rite Aid posted 
large increases in both sales and 
earnings for the fiscal year ended 
March 1, 1980. Sales for the year 
amounted to $811 million, a gain of 
26.7% over $640 million the year be- 
fore, while net profits from continu- 
ing operations expanded 23.5% to 
$30.2 million from $24.5 million. 

Meanwhile, per-share earnings 
from continuing operations in- 
creased to $2.88 from $2.34 (not in- 
cluding a $0.20-per-share profit 
from Rite Aid’s discontinued nurs- 
ing home business in fiscal 1979), and 
though the chain’s net-to-sales ratio 
slipped to 3.7% from 3.8%, it re- 
mained among the best marks in the 
industry. 

In the fourth quarter alone, Rite 
Aid amassed sales of $227 million, a 
gain of 28.9% over $176 million in the 
comparable period the year before. 
Net income from operations im- 
proved as well, showing a 28.7% in- 
crease to $10.3 million from $8 
million a year ago. 


The corporation’s changeover to 
the LIFO approach for “a significant 
portion” of its inventory was 
brought about, according to man- 
agement, in order to “more closely 
match current costs with current 
revenues’ in a rapidly inflating econ- 
omy. The effect of the maneuver is to 
reduce net income in the final quar- 
ter of fiscal 1980 by $839,000, or 


about $0.08 per share, and to dimin- 
ish net income for the entire year by 
$2.1 million, or approximately $0.20 
per share. 

EXPANSION. At year’s end, Rite 
Aid boasted an even 800 outlets, 
representing a net gain of 9.9%, or 
72 stores, over last year’s count of 
728. This was the result of some 86 
outlets added to the chain through 
either construction or acquisition, 
minus a total of 14 closings. 

A significant portion of this 
growth is attributable to Rite Aid’s 
takeover of two small strings of 
stores. In May, the company bought 
eight Delaware-area Quality Drug 
units for nearly $1 million, and fol- 
lowed up in November with the pur- 
chase of the nine-store Dixx chain in 
New York State’s Hudson Valley. 

Since the start of fiscal 1981, the 
corporation has launched eight new 
outposts, and is proceeding toward 
management's plan of expanding at a 
rate of 10% each year. At this rate, 
Rite Aid will become the third chain 
to break the 1,000-store mark, after 
Reveo and Eckerd. 

DISTRIBUTION. In July 1979, 
Rite Aid opened its Charleston, 
W.Va., distribution center, thereby 
facilitating further Southern expan- 
sion with 210,000 sq. ft. of storage 
capacity. 

REMODELING. The company 
has accelerated its ambitious remod- 
eling campaign, which encompassed 
50 stores in fiscal 1979, 60 stores in

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


DRUGFAIR STILL HOLDS ITS OWN 


RESULTS. Drugfair’s ability to 
bring sales dollars down to the bot- 
tom line was seriously hampered 
during fiscal 1980 by a variety of fac-

OPERATIONS. Drugfair oper- 
ates 170 promotional drug stores in 
five states (Maryland, Virginia, Del- 
aware, West Virginia and Pennsy]l-

Columbia. The typical size of a unit 
hovers around 17,000 sq. ft. (al- 
though sizes actually vary widely) 
and the average unit generates 
around $1.5 million in volume an- 
nually. 

Drugfair’s sales have grown stead- 
ily over the past five years, reaching 
$266 million last year from $200 mil- 
lion a year ago. Profits however, 


have been erratic and trended down- 
ward from 1976 through 1978, until 
the fiscal 1980 increment. The 
chain’s net-to-sales ratio was thin, 
ranging from 1.9% to 0.7% in fiscal 
1980. 

PROGRAMS. Drugfair operates 
in a highly competitive market 
which has been the scene of many 


costly discount battles over the past 
several decades. The chain com- 
petes with several aggressive drug 
chains which routinely introduce 
new advertising and promotional 
programs. 

In response to the pressures of the 
marketplace and the fact that the 
chain has not been a big profit pro- 
ducer, Drugfair in May of 1978 intro- 
duced its “Operation Excellence.” 
This program is designed to improve 
the chain’s image in the market- 
place, while at the same time tighten 
its internal operations and boost 
productivity. 

The component parts of “Opera- 
tion Excellence” feature an adver- 
tising program stressing service, 
efficiency and availability of prod- 
uct, a general drug program backed 
by consumer commercials and 
chainwide store remodelings. To 
date, some 85 stores (50% of the 
total in operation) have been re- 
modeled. Twenty-eight of the stores 
were completed during fiscal 1980. 

SUBSIDIARY OPERATIONS. 
Drugfair operates a number of sub- 
sidiary operations, although at the 
close of fiscal 1980, they were re- 
ported in a state of flux. Three of the 
chain’s Wrangler Wranch units were 
shuttered while the remaining are 
slated for closure in the near future, 
due to unprofitability. 


The chain’s other subsidiary oper- 
ations, Scoops—an ice cream parlor 
chain, and Soup’r Scoops—a string 
of ice cream and sandwich shops are 
slated to follow the Wrangler 
Wranch operations in the coming 
months. 


BEGLEY PROFITS FROM GROWTH 


RESULTS. A growth drive in- 
volving new store openings, store 
acquisitions, and a remodeling pro- 
gram has done its work on Begley 
Drug Co.’s overall volume. 

Begley’s nine-month results for 
fiscal 1980 reveal a 16.8% sales ad- 
vance, to $32 million, over the year- 
ago figure of $27.4 million. Net earn- 
ings for the period grew 11.7%, to 
reach $1.1 million. Significantly, 
Begley’s net-to-sales ratio for the 
first nine months showed a substan- 
tial increase to 3.5%, over 2.6% for 
the same period last year. 

For fiscal 1979, ended March 31, 
1979, Begley’s sales of $36.3 million 
showed an 11.3% increase over the 
year-ago figure, $32.6 million. Net 
income for 1979 advanced 22.1% to 
$1.3 million.

now claims 77 units.

business pickup warrants additional 
space, store leases also provide for 
store expansion. Current per store

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


PAY LESS NW SECURES MERGER 


RESULTS. Pay Less Northwest 
recorded a 25.3% increase in net 
earnings for the fiscal year ended 
Jan. 31, 1980, on the strength of a 
stellar fourth quarter. 

Sales for the year amounted to 
$380.5 million, a 10.1% improvement 
over $345.6 million the year before. 
Net profits reached a record $12.4 
million, after $9.9 million in fiscal 
1979. 

Meanwhile, the chain’s per-share 
earnings climbed to $2.82 from $2.25 
a year ago, and its net-to-sales ratio 
expanded from 2.9% to 3.3%—its 
finest performance in at least a dec- 
ade. 

In the final quarter alone, sales 
grew 14.2% to $123.7 million from 
$108.3 million in the comparable pe- 
riod of fiscal 1979. Net earnings 
amounted to $6.3 million, an in- 
crease of 37% over $4.6 million the 
year before. Thus, Pay Less gar- 
nered more than half its annual prof- 
its in the Christmas quarter. 

ACQUISITION. Shortly after 
the end of the 1980 fiscal year, Pay 
Less Northwest purchased the 
shares it needed to secure a merger 
with its southern namesake, the Pay 
Less (Calif.) chain. At stake in the 
effort was the Oakland, Calif. chain’s 
60 stores, annual sales of $300 mil- 
lion and net earnings of $3.1 million 
in the last complete fiscal year. 

Only a shareholders’ vote stands 
between Pay Less Northwest and 
the completion of the acquisition, at 
this point, but since the Oregon-

OTHER EXPANSION. In the 
fiscal year ended January, Pay Less 
opened 11 new stores and shuttered 
two downtown locations for a net 
gain of seven and a total of 89. Since 
then, the chain has launched three 
units and closed one, and now counts 
91 locations to its credit. 

No less than 37 of these sites are in 
Pay Less’ home state of Oregon, 29 
are in Washington State, 18 are in 
California and the remaining seven 
do business in Idaho. The bulk of the 
chain’s Californian outlets operate 
under the Value Giant logo, having 
been acquired by Pay Less in the 
mid-70’s and allowed to keep their 
original names in order to avoid con- 
fusion with neighboring Pay Less 


(Calif.) stores. Two Washington 
units also trade under the House of 
Values banner, originally to remain 
distinct from the old Skaggs-Pay 
Less chain.
