opened in unfamiliar territory, such 
as Boise, Idaho, where Pay Less 
planted four new units in the fiscal 
year past. Out of the 11 outlets intro- 
duced last year, only two were tar- 
geted for existing markets, and 
about half of the eight new sites 
slated for the current fiscal year will 
also be located in new trading areas. 

DISTRIBUTION. Pay Less’ new 
distribution center in Wilsonville, 
Ore.—about 15 miles south of its for- 
mer Beaverton headquarters— 
came onstream in October 1979, 
with some 500,000 sq. ft. of ware- 
housing capacity. This increases the 
chain’s storage and supply capacity. 

STORES. Although all new units 
have been set to include 30,000 sq. 
ft. to 32,000 sq. ft. of selling space, 
the chain average stands at 29,000 
sq. ft. with older locations weighing 
in as low as 9,900 sq. ft. and as high 
as 48,000 sq. ft. The merchandise 
presentation is heavily committed to 
sundries and general merchandise, 
thanks to the size of most units. 

Nevertheless, the entire roster, 
with the exception of a couple of 
Value Giants, feature pharmacies. 
Pay Less has managed to maintain 
its professional image, while provid- 
ing the shopper with a wide array of 
nontraditional merchandise. 


PAY LESS (CAL.) GETS ‘HOOKED’ 


RESULTS. A $346,000 nonrecur- 
ring loss in comparison with last 
year’s 53-week fiscal year mitigated 
healthy percentage increases in 
both sales and profits for Pay Less 
(Calif.) in the fiscal year ended Jan. 
31, 1980. 

Sales for the year amounted to 
$300 million, an increase of 8.5% 
over $276 million accumulated last 
year. Net profits improved 6.5% to 
$3.1 million from $2.9 million on the 
same basis. 

At the same time, per-share earn- 
ings climbed slightly to $1.38 from 
$1.31, and the chain’s net-to-sales 
ratio slid to 1.038% from 1.05%. 

However, these results reflect a 
loss of $346,000, or approximately 
12% of net profits, due to costs asso- 
ciated with merger negotiations and 
litigation arising from the Pay Less 
(Calif.)-Pay Less Northwest-Jewel 
Cos. triangle. Also, fiscal 1980 re- 
sults suffer by nearly 2% in a com- 
parison with 53-week results the 
year before. 

Thus, Pay Less (Calif.) gains in 
profits from operations were actu- 
ally much higher than reported to- 
tals suggest. 

MARKETS. Pay Less closed the 
ledger on fiscal 1980 with 60 outlets, 
and has since added a single unit for 
a total of 61. This represents a net 
gain of only two stores over last 
year’s mark, but the chain's strategy

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


A LANDMARK YEAR FOR SAV-ON 


RESULTS. A changeover to the 
LIFO accounting method obscured 
another landmark year in both sales 
and earnings for the thriving Sav-On 
chain. While revenues climbed to 
$527 million, a healthy 15.5% in- 
crease over $456 million the year be- 
fore, profits dropped 9.6% to $8.8 
million from $9.7 million. At the 
same time, the company’s net-to- 
sale ratio declined to 1.7% from 
2.1%, and earnings per share fell to 
$1.18 from $1.32. 

According to Sav-On estimates, 
however, the chain made substantial 
advances in earnings for the year 
ended Dec. 31, 1979, if annual results 
are compared on the same basis. 
From a FIFO perspective, Sav-On 
amassed net profits of $11.5 mil- 
lion—a gain of 18.6% over fiscal 
1978—and per-share earnings of 
$1.55. Discounting the switch in ac- 
counting methods, the chain closed 
out the year with a 2.2% net profits- 
to-sales ratio. 

These improvements are partly 
attributable to the expansion of Sav- 
On’s roster, from 132 stores to 140 
stores, in the course of the fiscal 
year. The total reflects nine open- 
ings and one closing 

Another important factor is the 
increased productivity Sav-On has 
managed to squeeze out of the Pay 
Less (Calif.) units it acquired in 
March 1978, for $11 million. In 1978, 
these stores averaged only about $2 
million per store, as opposed to a

DIVERSIFICATION. Seven of 
the Pay Less locations, however, 
have formed the nucleus of Sav-On’s

Sav-On drug store.

slated for May. In the second case, 
an adjacent supermarket is being

a remodeling job. 

The chain also operates 19 in-store 
optical centers, a gain of 10 over nine 
units at this time last year. However, 
headquarters has postponed further 
expansion of the optical concept un- 
til there has been time for an ap- 
praisal of existing operations. 

DISTRIBUTION. The fiscal year 
past also saw the opening of the com- 
pany’s new distribution center, a 
570,000-sq.-ft. building on 20 acres 
in Anaheim. Before the Anaheim 
property was purchased in August 
1978, Sav-On had claimed a total of 
98,000 ft. in two separate distribu- 
tion centers in El Segundo, Calif., 
south of its former Marina Del Rey 
headquarters. Now, with approx- 
imately 500,000 sq. ft. of warehous- 
ing space, the chain has added some 
5,000 sku’s to its distribution list. 
The center is expected to reach full 
capacity by the end of this year. 

In the current fiscal year, Sav-On 
has made plans to launch 10 to 12 new 
stores. Two have already opened 
their doors and three or four more 
will be ready by mid-year, while the 
chain has closed just one older unit 
since Christmas. 


RIX IS PLAGUED BY SHRINKAGE 


RESULTS. Just when it looked as 
though Rix Corp. was back on track, 
severe shrinkage problems and ris- 
ing interest rates have worked to 
stall the chain’s progress. 

Sales in fiscal 1979, ended Sept. 1, 
increased 6.6% to $26.2 million from 
$24.6 million the year before. But 
for the same period, net income 
dropped to $163,532 from $436,348 
—a difference of more than 62%. 

At the same time, per-share prof- 
its fell from 70¢ to 26¢, and the com- 
pany’s net-to-sales ratio dipped be- 
low the 1% mark for the first quarter 
of fiscal 1980, ended Dec. 1, 1979, 
when sales expanded 7% to $6.8 mil- 
lion from $6.4 million. Net income 
for the period dropped only 0.2% to

shrinkage takes its toll 
on bottom line 


Profits in $ thousands 
s $ 8 & 


Fiscal years ended Aug.-Sept. 
Source: Company annual reports 


$94,600 from $94,800, and earnings 
per share remained stable at 15¢. 

Rix management has taken a 
number of steps to combat its severe 
shrinkage plague, which in 1979 
claimed $286,000 worth of inventory 
over and above 1978 levels. To im- 
prove store-level supervision, the 
company has appointed two regional 
sales managers, to whom local dis- 
trict managers report, and to com- 
bat internal shrink, management 
has named a new warehouse man- 
ager as well as a new director of loss 
prevention. 

“If inventory shrinkage ratios and 
interest costs had maintained last 
year’s levels,” says Rix president 
Richard L. Weinberg, “company 
profit for 1979 would have exceeded 
the prior year.” 

MARKETS. But those factors did 
not maintain prior levels, and the 
company felt the crunch in its ex- 
pansion plans. While three free- 
standing drug stores and six leased 
H&BA departments were sched- 
uled to open in fiscal 1979, for a total 
of 116 units, Rix managed only a net 
gain of five units. 

The company closed out the fiscal 
year with 37 freestanders and 75 
leased departments, but in the pro- 
cess shuttered several unprofitable 
outlets. 

Since the end of its fiscal year, Rix 
has become more ambitious in terms 
of expansion. A store in Natick, 
Mass., has been moved to a larger 


location, to allow room for a 500-sq.- 
ft. pharmacy. Also, three new free- 
standers have been launched. 

The remainder of the calendar 
year, according to Weinberg, should 
see the opening of five new locations, 
including three leased departments 
and two drug stores. 

Rix’s drug store operations are 
limited to five New England states 
—Maine, Massachusetts, New 
Hampshire, Rhode Island and Ver- 
mont. Average store size ranges 
from 2,500 sq. ft. in downtown loca- 
tions to 10,000 sq. ft. in regional 
malls and neighborhood shopping 
strips. 

STORES. While housewares, 
hardware, candy, greeting cards, 
live plants, toys and other sundries 
are becoming increasingly impor- 
tant in larger units, H&BA catego- 
ries still account for some 75% of net 
sales. 

The other major element in Rix’s 
business is a chain of leased H&BA 
departments in discount depart- 
ment stores, located for the most 
part in the South and Midwest. 

Rix management is optimistic 
about the company’s future, al- 
though it recognizes an uphill battle. 

“Business is continuing strong in 
the second quarter,” says Weinberg. 
“Since the beginning of the new fis- 
cal year, we appear to be making 
headway against our shrinkage 
problems. We foresee a greatly im- 
proved situation.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


THRIFT : STEADY AS SHE GROWS 


GROWTH. In fiscal 1980, ended 
Jan. 28, Pittsburgh-based Thrift 
Drug continued the deliberate, 
steady rate of expansion that has be- 
come its trademark. The J. C. Pen- 
ney division wrapped up the year 
with 357 retail drug outlets, includ- 
ing six leased departments. 

This marks a net gain of 15 units 
for Thrift, based on 19 openings and 
four closings in the course of the 
year. Also, the chain built its first 
from-the-ground-up unit in Dallas, 
adding it to the base of some 20 
stores it had gained in the Dallas 
area through acquisition. 

All in all, Thrift operates in about 
half the states in the Union, al- 
though its greatest strength lies in 
its home state, Pennsylvania (162 
freestanders). Also, some 30% of the 
chain does business under the Trea- 
sury Drug logo, which dates back to 
the days before J. C. Penney’s ac- 
quisition of the Thrift Drug com- 
pany more than a decade ago. 

RESULTS. Thrift reported total 
sales of $412 million in fiscal 1980, an 
increase of 15.7% over $356 million 
the year before. Even on a same- 
store basis (discounting the contri- 
bution of newly added units), the 
chain saw an 11.5% improvement in 
revenues. 

Earnings expanded as well, after 
having fallen off in fiscal 1979. The 
difference, it seems, was brought 
about through increased attention

STORES. At present, the chain 
has three basic prototypes: 12,000 
sq. ft., 14,000 sq. ft. and 17,600 sq. 
ft. All feature a mix that includes 
soft goods, giftware, glassware, 
promotional hardware, electrical 
items, baby goods and lawn and

first PHS—Personalized Health

fiscal 1979.

160 units equipped with PHS, and 
plans at headquarters call for an-

recently. Now, management re-

edged over into the black. 

FUTURE PLANS. Some 20 new 
stores are slated to be launched this 
year, although that number may 
change in accordance with the cost 
of borrowed money and construction 
schedules. Of these, three will be 
built in Fort Worth—a new market, 
although the chain is already repre- 
sented in the vicinity of Dallas. 

In addition, 24 stores are to be 
remodeled, according to the ongo- 
ing, five-year management plan. 


ADAMS TARING OVER 


EXPANSION. In fiscal 1979, ac- 
quisition was once again the name of 
the game for Adams. The Rhode Is- 
land-based chain finished the year 
with a record 412 drug stores, after 
adding 65 outlets and closing 14 for a 
net gain of 51 over last year’s total. 

While 16 new stores were started 
from scratch in the year past, no less 
than 49 came by way of two key take- 
overs. In August, Adams acquired 
six Kent Drug outlets in New York 
State’s southern tier, marking its 
first entry into the Binghamton 
market. More importantly, the Kent 
deal represented Adams’ largest ac- 
quisition in five years. 

Then, before the end of Novem- 
ber, the Rhode Islander purchased 
the Sun Drug Co. and its 43 Pitts- 
burgh-area stores. The year before, 
Sun had registered sales of some $20 
million, or nearly $500,000 per store 
on the basis of a bantam prototype. 

This aggressive stance brought to 
mind the chain’s expansion policies 
of the early 1970’s, which dictated 
the purchases of the Whelan, 
Nescott and Eckerd of Erie, Pa., 
operations, among others. 

RESULTS. Costs associated with 
acquisitions and new store open- 
ings, as well as stepped-up promo- 
tional activity at the store level, cut 
into Adams bottom line in the fiscal 
year ended Dec. 31, 1979. While 
sales for the year increased 13.9% to 
$176 million, from $154 million the 
year before, net earnings fell off 
14.3% to $2.5 million from $2.9 mil- 
lion. 


At the same time, per-share prof- 
its diminished from 71¢ to 61¢, and 
the chain’s net earnings-to-sales 
ratio decreased to 1.4% from last 
year’s mark of 1.9%. 

More than one-half of the com- 
pany’s net profits were garnered in 
the final quarter of fiscal 1979, which 
included sales of $53.2 million and 
earnings of $1.3 million. However, a 
much-increased commitment to con- 
sumer advertising and decreased 
gross margins, especially during the 
Christmas season, depressed the 
net-to-sales ratio for the quarter to 
2.5% from 3.5% the year before. 

Nevertheless, management re- 
ports that Adams’ discount image 
has benefited from the chain’s new 
commitment to lower prices and 
heavier advertising schedules. Sales 
results in the first few months of 
fiscal 1980 show increases which 
tend to offset a lower gross, accord- 
ing to headquarters, and this bodes 
well for the future of the chain.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


PAY ‘N SAVE STAKES OUT MONT. 


GROWTH. Pay ’n Save will be 
staking its claim to Montana this 
year. The company announced plans 
to build two Pay ’n Save drug stores 
and two Ernst Home Centers in 


Butte and in Great Falls—a total of 


four stores altogether—as part of an 
aggressive expansion plan that calls 
for some 27 new outlets and one re- 
placement unit by early 1981. 

This represents an accelerated 
rate of growth for the diversified re- 
tailer, following a net gain of 16 
stores, for a total of 199, in the fiscal 
year ended Feb. 2, 1980. 

RESULTS. Sales for the year 
were clocked at $709.1 million, a 
14.6% increase over $618.7 million 
the year before. Net income 
amounted to $19.3 million, a gain of

10.9% over $17.2 million in the pre-

The greatest contributor to corpo- 
rate revenues continued to be the 
drug store division, comprised of 89 
Pay ’n Saves and 23 Bi-Marts, with 
$433.8 million or 61% of the total. 
The drug division also generated 
49% of pretax profits on the basis of a 
$17.3 million effort. 

Pay ’n Save outlets follow a basic 
prototype of 22,000 sq. ft., include a 
wide variety of merchandise and 
average $3.5 million in annual sales. 
The Bi-Marts, with more room for 
promotional merchandise at 30,000 
sq. ft., are weighted more heavily 
toward sporting goods, housewares 
and hardware and carry less depth 
in the traditional drug store lines. 

To facilitate further expansion, 
Pay ’n Save last year divided its drug 
store holdings into three subdivi- 
sions. The company now includes 35 
units in its Seattle/Alaska grouping, 
22 in California/Hawaii, and 32 un- 
der the Northwest heading. In cal- 
endar 1980, the chain plans to add 
six Pay ’n Saves in Washington 
State, one in Hawaii and two in Mon- 
tana, as well as areplacement in An- 
chorage, Ala. 


MARKETS. With no plans for 


new store openings in California, 
and only one Pay ’n Save launched 
there last year, the corporation ap- 
pears to be de-emphasizing that re- 


gion as an area for development. In 
fact, the chain sold two stores in 
northern California to Lafayette- 
based Bill’s Drugs in 1978, and two 
more in 1979. 

Company spokesmen, however, 
deny that management has given up 
on the Golden State. Pay ’n Save’s 
explanation hinges on the simple 
question of profitability: Where 
stores were not making money, 
whether for reasons pertaining to 
overhead, competition or adminis- 
tration, they were placed on the 
block. 

DIVERSIFICATION. Pay ’n 
Save’s other retail operations, out- 
side the drug store category, have 
mostly been built upon acquisitions. 
Ernst Home Centers, for instance, 
now number 53, having been taken 
over by the corporation two decades 
ago. The 10 highly successful 
Sportswest units, contributing an 
average of $1.1 million annually, only 
saw the addition of sportswear into 


their mix after they were purchased. 


Pay ’n Save also owns two Yard 
Birds general merchandise units, 
two Von Tobel’s home improvement 
centers, and 20 Lamonts depart- 
ment stores. The department stores 
were again the result of an acquisi- 
tion, where an image change and an 
adherence to nationally advertised 
brands revitalized a marginal opera- 
tion. 


ACQUISITIONS BOOST 
FAY'S STORE COUNT 


RESULTS. Fay’s Drug saw huge 
increases in both sales and net prof- 
its for the fiscal year ended January 
1980, thanks to acquisitions that 
contributed a total of 34 outlets to 
the chain’s cause. 

Revenues for the year increased 
36.7% to $194 million, as opposed to 
$142 million the year before. Net 
earnings improved 21.5%, to $3 mil- 
lion from $2.5 million in fiseal 1979. 

Nearly one-third of sales and more 
than one-half of net earnings were 
garnered in the last quarter, which 
encompassed Christmas business. 
Revenues for that period alone to- 
taled $62 million, a gain of 41.2% 
over $44 million in the comparable 
quarter last year, while net profits 
expanded 14.4% to $1.7 million from 
$1.5 million. 

These fourth-quarter results are 
all the more impressive when one 
takes this into account: It was not 
until fiscal 1975 that Fay’s sales for 
the entire year surpassed $62 mil- 
lion, and the company passed the 
$1.6-million mark in annual profits 
as recently as fiscal 1978. 

Fay’s net-to-sales ratio, however, 
slipped in fiscal 1980 to 1.55% from 
1.75%, partly due to an interest ex- 
pense load of more than $1 million, 
which caused earnings to lag behind 
revenues. The other major expense 
in the year past, according to man- 
agement, was the cost of new store 
openings. 

EXPANSION. Despite the chain’s 


failure in its bid to acquire the 28- 
unit Mann Drug operation in North 
Carolina, Fay’s growth in fiscal 1980 
can only be described as meteoric. 
The Liverpool, N.Y.-based retailer 
finished the year with 104 stores, 
including 73 outlets in New York 
State, 1in Pennsylvania, 29 in South 
Carolina and 1 in North Carolina— 
for a net gain of 42 units over last 
year’s total, which translates into a 
growth rate of 68%. 

Of those stores added last year, 
only eight were built from the 
ground up. The remaining 34 arrived 
in the form of two important acquisi- 
tions—that of the 14-store Craft 
Drug chain on Feb. 1, 1979, and that 
of Key Drug’s 20 outlets exactly six 
months later. 

The Craft takeover was an exten- 
sion of Fay’s Sunbelt strategy, which 
saw the Northerner establish its 
first foothold in the Carolinas with 
the acquisition of seven-store 
Berkeley Drug in 1978. The pur- 
chase of Craft netted Fay’s a 21,000- 
sq.-ft. distribution center in Spar- 
tanburg, S.C., to which the chain 
has since added another 14,000 sq. 
ft. of storage space. 

The Key deal took place much 
closer to home, as Fay’s reinforced 
its upstate New York holdings with 
20 Rochester-area drug stores. 
Along with Key’s retail units, Fay’s 
took over the firm’s 65,000-sq.-ft. 
distribution center, easing the bur- 
den on the chain’s 250,000-sq.-ft. fa-

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 28, 1980 


GENOVESE: IN THE PINK AGAIN 


RESULTS. Genovese Drug re- 
bounded in fiscal 1980, ended Feb. 1, 
with record sales and profits, after 
fiscal 1979 saw an uncharacteristic 
drop in the company’s bottom line. 

Sales for the year amounted to 
$97.4 million, a 13.2% gain over $86.1 
million the year before, and a 22.9% 
gain over $79.3 million in fiscal 1978. 
At the same time, net profits ex- 
panded 65.1% to $1.6 million from a 
disappointing $900,000 in the pre- 
vious year, and showed a 10.0% in- 
crease over $1.4 million two years 
ago. 

The chain’s net-to-sales ratio, as a 
result, has climbed back to 1.6% 
after sagging to 1.1% in fiscal 1979. 
The prognosis: Genovese is back on 
track. 

Management attributes the turn- 
around to a strategy which empha- 
sized expense containment, inven- 
tory control, an increased invest- 
ment in store-level operations by 
way of an enlarged supervisory staff 
and a mix designed for greater gross 
profits. 

In fiscal 1979, operating costs (ad- 
ministrative and warehouse) hit 
nearly $23 million, or more than one- 
fourth of sales. Interest expenses 
came to $475,000, marking a 42% 
increase over interest expenses the 
year before, and advertising costs 
expanded 10% as well. 

But in fiscal 1980, a little belt- 
tightening and more attention to 
store-level functions has broadened 
Genovese’s profit picture. In fact, 


the chain now enjoys enough inter- 
nally generated funds to completely 
avoid short-term debt for the first 
time in many years. 

EXPANSION. Genovese has 
been adding new stores at the rate of 
two or three per year for the last few 
years, bringing the roster up to 53 at 
the end of fiscal 1980. A dozen of 
these outlets are situated in Con- 
necticut, with two in Massachu- 
setts, four in New Jersey and the 
remainder in New York State. The 
chain’s greatest concentration, how- 
ever, lies in New York City and Long 
Island. 

In fiseal 1981, Genovese will be 
stepping up its expansion program, 
with plans to build as many as five 
new units in existing trading areas. 
Although the chain broke into Mas- 
sachusetts for the first time as re- 
cently as calendar 1978, manage- 
ment is pursuing a backfilling policy 
when it comes to new store openings 
now. 

STORES. The chain’s current pro- 
totype for new units weighs in at 
12,000 sq. ft., which is considerably 
smaller than its Wallington, N.J., 
superstore (24,000 sq. ft.), and only 
slightly larger than the 10,000-sq.- 
ft. mold for older stores. However, 
with overhead costs soaring in the 
New York Metropolitan Area, a 
more compact prototype looks bet- 
ter to the management team in Mel- 
ville, N.Y. 

ALTERATIONS. In the fiscal 


year past, Genovese renovated two

OPTEL INVESTS IN REMODELING 


STORES. Optel Corp. continued 
to pare down its store count in fiscal 
1979, ended Dec. 31. The company 
operated 163 units at year’s end, in- 
cluding 121 H&BA outlets, 22 Mall 
Drug pharmacies and 20 leased de- 
partments. Overall, the chain expe- 
rienced a net loss of five units as 
compared to the year before, the 
shift lying in the closing of eight 
Big L H&BA units and the opening 
of three Mall locations. 

The prevailing philosophy these 
days in Optel’s Holbrook, Mass., 
headquarters is directed toward re- 
modelings rather than openings, 
however. In fact, some 45 Big L 
stores were converied to the logo 
MD this year, to give the H&BA 
outlets a common link with their sis- 
ter division, Mall Drug. In addition 
to a new decor package, the phar- 
macy-less MD locations have been 
equipped with Optel’s MD private 
label line of drug store merchandise. 

STRATEGIES. Optel’s merchan- 
dising team also came up with an- 
other variation on the Big L theme 
last year with the advent of the first 
Sav-A-Lot “true discount” store, 
launched in November. Boasting the 
low overhead and discount image of 
a limited-item box store, the Sav-A- 
Lot outlet in Fall River, Mass., nev- 
ertheless carries off-sizes in single 
facings, stocks a large selection of 
convenience foods and features a de- 
partment store-type treatment for 


its fragrances and cosmetics. 
RESULTS. Despite these costly 
remodeling programs, Optel re- 
corded sales and earnings gains for 
the fiscal year. Sales in 1979 totaled 
$104.1 million, an increase of 112% 
over $49 million in fiscal 1978. Net 
income improved 22.7% to $2.3 mil- 
lion from $1.9 million, and earnings 
per share increased to 26¢ from 24¢.

CHAIN STORE AGE Drug Magazine 


Published by Lebhar-Friedman Inc./June 9, 1980 


| Rampage in Miami 


Slams doors shut 
on retail business 


MIAMI—The drug store com- 
munity was one of the many vic- 
tims of three days of rioting, 
arson and looting that ravaged 
the northwestern precinct of this 
city, after black elements re- 
sponded violently to the acquit- 
tal of four white police officers in 
the murder of a black man here. 

While stores of the Eckerd, 
Walgreen, Gray and SupeRx 
chains lost thousands of dollars 
of business due to shortened 
hours and an isolated hold-up, 
lone operators such as Jet 
Drug, Stone Rexall Drug and 
Jays Drug—situated in the 
heart of the troubled area— 
were looted and thoroughly gut- 
ted by vandals. A Grand Union 
in-store pharmacy on 54th 
Street was also ransacked, as 
first rioters and then roving 
bands of looters tore up entire 
blocks of small and large busi- 
nesses. 

A local wholesaler—Hatton 
Drug on N.W. 2nd Avenue—was 
burglarized in the course of the 
rampage, which lasted from 
early Saturday, May 17, until the 
morning of Tuesday, May 20. 
Looters made off with an un- 
known quantity of class 3, 4 and 
exempt narcotics, according to 
company president Joseph Hat- 
ton, but no property damage 


was sustained. 

‘A number of stores in the 
area have been burned down by 
vandals,” Hatton told Drug 
Stores News. “But we have se- 
curity guards on the premises at 
night, and we're still in busi- 
ness.” 

On the night of Monday, May 
19, the Eckerd Drug unit at 4878 
Biscayne Blvd. was robbed, al- 
though neither customers nor 
store personnel were injured. 
The exact amount taken by the 
thieves was not disclosed, but it 
is known that they emptied two 
cash registers of the day's pro- 
ceeds. 

Seven other Eckerd outlets 
were also “hurt” to varying de- 
grees by limited hours in what 
has been calied the worst racial 
disturbance ever to hit an Amer- 
ican city. Two 24-hour stores 
were forced to cut their hours in 
half, and a third store was 
closed aitogether for the dura- 
tion of the disturbance. 

No property damage was re- 
ported by Eckerd management. 
However, the chain lost thou- 
sands of dollars in potential 
business as a result of precau- 
tionary early closings. 

One SupeRx store manager, 
operating near the most heavily

Detroit area.

more often reflected in a slowed 
rate of sales growth compared 
to last year, not in an actual de-

tailing segments have reported.

WALGREEN WILL OPEN anew 200,000-sq.-ft. distribution cen- 
ter in Orlando, Fla., to service stores in the Southeast and Puerto 
Rico. In addition, the chain will spend $4 million for sophisticated 
materials handling equipment in the new center. At present, Wal- 
green operates a 44,000-sq.-ft. warehouse in Tampa, Fla. 


THE JACK ECKERD Corp. has posted a 12.5% gain in sales anda 
14.9% climb in earnings for the third quarter, ended April 26. Sales 
were $377 million, as compared to $335 million, the year-go figure. 
Net earnings amounted to $16.1 million, as compared to $14 mil- 
lion. For the first nine months of fiscal 1980, J.E.C.’s sales in- 
creased 14.9% and earnings increased 15%. 


ALBERTSON’S IS no longer seeking to acquire a drug chain and

DRUG CHAINS SEEK RIGHT EQUATION 
FOR DISTRIBUTION EFFICIENCY 


For drug chains, methods of mov- 
ing product from supplier to store 
are as varied and distinctive as the 
chains themselves. In fact, the best 
reflection of a chain’s distribution 
system can be found in the merchan- 
dising and operations personality of 
its stores. 

For example, Eckerd Drug, which 
utilizes small store stockrooms but 
maintains a merchandising con- 
tinuity throughout its 1,000-plus 
units, sports one of the most sophis- 
ticated centralized distribution sys- 
tems in the industry. Longs Drug, 
on the other hand, operates each 
store as a separate entrepreneur- 
ship, with heavy emphasis on store 
manager control. Asa result, Longs 
owns only a small warehouse (each 
unit has a sizable stockroom), and 
merchandise is often considerably 


different from one store to the next. 

But just as methods of distribu- 
tion differ from drug chain to drug 
chain, each retailer is in constant 
pursuit cf that distribution formula 
which makes the flow of goods thor- 
oughly efficient and cost-effective. 

In recent years, druggists—with 
internal costs spiraling beyond their 
control—have examined their busi- 
nesses in an attempt to trim operat- 
ing expenses. And distribution is 
one of those operations variables 
that chain cost-cutters have focused 
on. 

In addition, drug buyers today are 
re-evaluating the methods in which 
they purchase merchandise to make 
sure that when they order, they 
qualify for manufacturers’ minimum 
order requirements and thus take 
advantage of volume discounts. 


Buyers are more than ever on the 
lookout for deal merchandise. 

They are also weighing the vari- 
ances in costs and efficiency of pur- 
chasing merchandise through the 
three major sources of supply: the 
manufacturer, the drug wholesaler 
and the service merchandiser. 

They are re-evaluating the bene- 
fits of shipments from the manufac- 
turer or drug wholesaler to the 
chain’s distribution center rather 
than have shipments go directly to 
the individual store. 

In some cases such as Longs in 
California, where individual stores 
qualify for manufacturers’ discounts 
and where the type and quantities of 
merchandise carried is somewhat 
determined by the store manager, it 
pays to have the manufacturer ship 
directly to the store. 


However, more likely is the situa- 
tion of a chain with regional bantam 
or conventional stores, all located 
within a few hundred miles of its 
trading area. In such a case it is 
frequently more economical to have 
the manufacturer or drug whole- 
saler ship the merchandise through 
the chain’s distribution center to 
capitalize on manufacturers’ dis- 
counts, and to control inventory. 

Therefore, in the last two years 
one trend has emerged: The number 
of chains using centralized ware- 
housing to control inventory and re- 
duce costs has grown. In the last two 
years, total warehousing space in 
the chain drug industry has grown 
from 13.5 million sq. ft. in 1978 to 
more than 17 million sq. ft. In 1980, 
among the top 10 leaders in ware- 
housing space, total square footage 


n the last two 
years, the number 
of chains using 
centralized ware- 
housing has increased 
substantially. Behind the 
trend: Drug chains have 
found that it is often 
more economical in 
terms of inventory con- 
trol and volume dis- 
counts. 


has increased 25% to 9.987 million 
sq. ft. up from 7,441 million sq. ft. 

Also impressive is the number of 
major West Coast drug chains who 
today are relying more heavily on 
distribution centers as a means of 
controlling costs and inventory. For 
example, both Pay Less N.W. and 
Sav-On, two chains which used to 
have small- to medium-sized ware- 
houses, each recently began using 
505,000-sq.-ft. distribution com- 
plexes. 

For several chains (both that do 
and don’t have distribution centers) 
buying is also supplemented 
through service merchandisers. 
Use of the service merchandiser is 
especially effective for stores in 
product categories in which they 
have little expertise. The service 
merchandiser may provide the least 
expensive means to get the fastest- 
selling products on the shelf on a 
regular basis. 

At other times it may be more eco- 
nomical to purchase through the 
drug wholesaler, a market segment 
that has been increasing its share of 
chain business. A number of whole- 
salers like McKesson Drug Co., 
Bergen Brunswig and South- 
western Drug, have improved their 
programs considerably in order to 
attract chain druggists. 

According to a survey by Drug 
Store News of drug wholesalers, 
69% of the respondents said their 
customer base is growing and many 
attributed the increase to greater 
chain sales. An upswing of chain 
customers was reported by 52% of 
the respondents, and 34% said they 
view small chains and independents 
as their chief market in the coming 
years. A 1% to 10% jump in chain 
business was reported by nearly half 
of those queried. 

“As the cost of manufacturer calls 
on retailers increases, vendors are 
going to wholesalers in increasing 
numbers,” says Jack Fenstermaker, 
a San Francisco consultant to drug 
wholesalers and manufacturers. 

In a Drug Store News poll of chain 
retailers examining the degree to 
which they used the three suppliers, 
it was fourd that chains which did 
not own a warehouse or distribution 
center depended more heavily on 
drug wholesalers. In the average 
chain without a warehouse, respon- 
dents said almost half (49%) of the 
merchandise they purchased is from 
wholesalers. Approximately one- 
third (31%) of the merchandise is 
purchased from manufacturers and 
one-fifth of the products are sup- 
plied by service merchandisers. 

In contrast, chains that do have 
warehouses rely to a greater extent 
on shipments from manufacturers 
for their stock. In chains with dis- 
tribution centers, nearly three- 
quarters (74%) of the products are 
bought from manufacturers, 19% is 


from drug wholsalers and about 7% 
of the items are stocked by rack job- 
bers. 

In a survey of chains with ware- 
houses, the percentage of merchan- 
dise that travels through the dis- 
tribution centers, regardless of 
source, varies anywhere from 50% 
and up. . 

At Drug Fair, Alexandria, Va., 
about 65% of the merchandise sold in 
its stores has traveled through its 
500,000-sq.-ft. distribution com- 
plex, according to Morris Friedson, 
senior vp. The remaining 35% of 
merchandise for the 170-unit chain is 
shipped directly to stores by drug 
wholesalers or supplied by service 
merchandisers. 

Hook Drug, Indianapolis, Ind., on 
the other hand, runs a highly cen- 
tralized operation through its 
507,000-sq.-ft. distribution center. 

“Almost all merchandise in the 
stores comes through the warehouse 
so we can control inventory. Less 
than 5% is directly shipped to the 
stores,” says a spokesman. The 


Hook warehouse acts as a holding 
area for Hook stores that have vir-

Distribution networks emerge 


The critical operational change in 
the last decade has been the devel- 
opment of large efficient networks 
consisting of warehouses, satellite 
distribution centers for the larger 
drug retailers and trucking fleets. 
In the last two years the total square 
footage of warehousing in the indus- 
try has increased from 13:5 million 
sq. ft. in 1978 to more than 17 million 
sq. ft. in 1980. 

A variety of factors have governed 
the emergence and growth of this 
network, among them the rising 
cost of maintaining store level inven- 
tories which may not be used for 
several weeks, and the rising cost of 
shopping center rentals, which have 
made large backrooms economically 
unattractive. 

The control of product flow offered 
by acentral warehouse and distribu- 
tion center has offset the expenses of 
building and maintaining a struc- 
ture and the labor costs in staffing 
it. The warehouse aids management 
on monitoring sales by item, in re- 
ducing the inventory size and in buy- 
ing deal merchandise. 

Other warehousing recent ac- 
tivity includes the following: 

@ Sommers Drug of San Antonio, 
Tex., last month moved into a 
130,000-sq.-ft. distribution center 
giving the chain a warehousing ca- 
pacity four times greater than its old 
complex. 

@ This month, Walgreen will an- 
nounce plans for a new distribution 
center. 

@ Harco, Northport, Ala., will soon 
complete a 71,000-sq.-ft warehouse 
and office complex of which 60,000 
sq. ft. will be used for warehousing. 
Jim Harrison, president, says it 
should be finished by the end of the 
year. 

@ Kerr Drugs, Raleigh, N.C., will 
complete an 80,000-sq.-ft. ware- 
house this fall. 

@ Ribordy Drugs, Highland, Ind., 
is expected to break ground on anew 
distribution center sometime this 
summer. 

Store to warehouse distance 

Where possible, drug chains have 
located their distribution complexes 
so that no store is more than a half 
day’s drive away to eliminate the 
costs of layover for the driver and 
tying up the tractor-trailer for an 
extended period. With the costs of 
diesel fuel continually escalating, 
distribution executives are experi- 
menting with different truck routes 
to minimize the distance a truck has 
to travel and at the same time ade- 
quately service the stores. Most 
chains call on their stores an average 
of once a week, while some chains 
which have outlets with above-aver-

In the distribution centers of 
many chains, computerized order 
systems, once afforded only by the 
larger chains, are becoming more 
frequent in medium sized and 
smaller chains. Central comput- 
erized ordering, pricing and billing 
has dramatically cut the cost of dis- 
tribution for many retailers. Auto- 
mated conveyer belts, gravity flow 
racks, merchandise divertors, sort- 
ing and picking machines are also 
conserving and saving labor ex- 
penses. 

Sav-On'’s new warehouse boasts 
4.5 miles of conveyer belts, scanners 
and an automated storing system 
that can handle 400,000 cases in 
eignt hours, according to Dale 
Short, district operations manager. 
“We invested in this distribution 
center for the sheer economics of 
warehousing—better service, fuller 
shelves,” he adds.

its seven warehouses (the firm also 
uses five public warehouses). The 
program calls for a much greater use 
of the computer by 1985. According 
to John Brown, vice president of dis- 
tribution, “the computer will give us 
better control of receiving through 
an ontical scanning machine, deter- 
mine the best location of where to 
store the merchandise and support 
the SItematic system and give us 
better billing ability.” 

Walgreen also uses what it calls 
the field Domicile Plan in order to 
keep its trucks rolling. The system, 
a variation of the Pony Express mail

distances using several drivers 
along the way.

because you avoid the double sleeper

Cutting fuel costs 

Another method of saving costs 
related to freight is the purchasing 
of diesel fyel in bulk, according to Al 
Fair, distribution manager for Cun- 
ningham Drugs. This firm owns 138 
tractors and has about 48 trailers, 
one-third of which are leased. “We 
supply our fleet from several 10,000- 
gallon diesel tanks that we have,” he 
says. 

Another means of cutting costs is 
by getting more use out of tractors 
while trailers are being loaded and 
unloaded. For many chains this 
means owning twice as many trail- 
ers as they have tractors. Thus they 
avoid the need to buy extra tractors. 

Fair says that since the Cun- 
ningham fleet added air foils, trucks 
have been getting “up to a mile more 
per gallon.” 

“We have also been slowly switch- 
ing to radial tires on our trucks as 
they need changing,” he says. 

Chains, which are only permitted 
to do a limited amount of backhaul- 
ing, hope that a bill before Congress 
would ease some of the restrictions. 
The bill which was approved by the 
House and is now before the Senate, 
would further open up the tightly 
controlled trucking industry to in- 
creased competition. 

Backhauling has been another 
way chains have been able to make 
more effective use of their delivery 
trucks. Mos chains queried say they 
try to do it as often as they can, 
however, it is far from being a regu- 
lar practice. 

Typical was the explanation of Jim 
Harrison, president of Harco 
Drugs, Northport, Ala. “We do 
some backhauling to the extent the 
law will permit us and it has helped 
offset some costs.” 

Tom Weisert of Taylor Drugs says 
the company backhauls Christmas 
and promotional items, “but it is 
very difficult to time the backhaul if 
you have a limited fleet. If the trailer 
can’t be at the supplier at the time 
the supplier’s loading dock is free, 
then you can get into a scheduling 
hassle if our truck also has to deliver 
to three or four stores.”

: Rampage in Miami 


slams doors shut 
on retail business 


MIAMI—The drug store com- 
munity was one of the many vic- 
tims of three days of rioting, 
arson and looting that ravaged 
the northwestern precinctof this 
city, after black elements re- 
sponded violently to the acquit- 
tal of four white police officers in 
the murder of a black man here. 

While stores of the Eckerd, 
Walgreen, Gray and SupeRx 
chains lost thousands of dollars 
of business due to shortened 
hours and an isolated hold-up, 
lone operators such as Jet 
Drug, Stone Rexall Drug and 
Jay's Drug—situated_in the 
heart of the troubléd area— 
were looted and thoroughly gut- 
ted by vandals. A Grand Union 
in-store pharmacy on 54th 
Street was also ransacked, as 
first rioters and then roving 
bands of looters tore up entire 
blocks of small and large busi- 
nesses. — 

A local wholesaler—Hatton 
Drug on N.W. 2nd Avenue—was 
burglarized in the course of the 
rampage, which lasted from 
early Saturday, May 17, until the 
morning of Tuesday, May 20. 
Looters made off with an un- 
known quantity of class 3, 4 and 
exempt narcotics, according to 
company president Joseph Hat- 
ton, but no property damage 


was sustained. 

‘A number of stores in the 
area have been burned down by 
vandals,” Hatton told Drug 
Stores News. “But we have se- 
curity guards on the premises at 
night, and we're still in busi- 
ness. 

On the night of Monday, May 
19, the Eckerd Drug unit at 4878 
Biscayne Bivd. was robbed, al- 
though neither customers nor 
store personnel were injured. 
The exact amount taken by the 
thieves was not disclosed, but it 
is known that they emptied two 
cash registers of the day's pro- 
ceeds. 

Seven other Eckerd outlets 
were also “hurt” to varying de- 
grees by limited hours in what 
has been calied the worst racial 
disturbance ever to hit an Amer- 
ican city. Two 24-hour stores 
were forced to cut their hours in 
half, and a third store was 
closed altogether for the dura- 
tion of the disturbance. 

No property damage was re- 
ported by Eckerd management. 
However, the chain lost thou- 
sands of dollars in potential 
business as a result of precau- 
tionary early closings.

operating near the most heavily

DRUG CHAINS SEEK RIGHT EQUATION 
FOR DISTRIBUTION EFFICIENCY 


For drug chains, methods of mov- 
ing product from supplier to store 
are as varied and distinctive as the 
chains themselves. In fact,, the best 
reflection of a chain’s distribution 
system can be found in the merchan- 
dising and operations personality of 
its stores. 

For example, Eckerd Drug, which 
utilizes small store stockrooms but 
maintains a merchandising con- 
tinuity throughout its 1,000-plus 
units, sports one of the most sophis- 
ticated centralized distribution sys- 
tems in the industry. Longs Drug, 
on the other hand, operates each 
store as a separate entrepreneur- 
ship, with heavy emphasis on store 
manager control. As a result, Longs 
owns only a small warehouse (each 
unit has a sizable stockroom), and 
merchandise is often considerably 


different from one store to the next. 
But just as methods of distribu- 
tion differ from drug chain to drug 
chain, each retailer is in constant 
pursuit of that distribution formula 
which makes the flow of goods thor- 
oughly efficient and cost-effective. 
In recent years, druggists—with 
internal costs spiraling beyond their 
control—have examined their busi- 
nesses in an attempt to trim operat- 
ing expenses. And distribution is 
one of those operations variables 
that chain cost-cutters have focused 
on. a 
In addition, drug buyers today are 
re-evaluating the methods in which 
they purchase merchandise to make 
sure that when they order, they 
qualify for manufacturers’ minimum 
order requirements and thus take 
advantage of volume discounts. 


Buyers are more than ever on the 
lookout for deal merchandise. 

They are‘glso weighing the vari- 
ances in costsvand efficiency of pur- 
chasing merchandise through the 
three major sources of supply: the 
manufacturer, the drug wholesaler 
and the service merchandiser. 

They are re-evaluating the bene- 
fits of shipments from the manufac- 
turer or drug wholesaler to the 
chain’s distribution center rather 
than have shipments go directly to 
the individual store. 

In some cases such as Longs in 
California, where individual stores 
qualify for manufacturers’ discounts 
and where the type and quantities of 
merchandise carried is somewhat 
determined by the store manager, it 
pays to have the manufacturer ship 
directly to the store. 


However, more likely is the situa- 
tion of a chain with regional bantam 
or conventional stores, all located 
within a few hundred miles of its 
trading area. In such a case it is 
frequently more economical to have: 
the manufacturer or drug whole- 
saler ship the merchandise through 
the chain’s distribution center to 
capitalize on manufactiirers’ dis- 
counts, and to control inventory. 

Therefore, in the last two years 
one trend has emerged: The number 
of chains using centralized ware- 
housing to control inventory and re- 
duce costs has grown. In the last two 
years, total warehousing space in 
the chain drug industry has grown 
from 13.5 million sq. ft. in 1978 to 
more than 17 million sq. ft. In 1980, 
among the top 10 leaders in ware- 
housing space, total square footage

Distribution networks emerge 

The critical operational change in 
the last decade has been the devel- 
opment of large efficient networks 
consisting of warehouses, satellite 
distribution centers for the larger 
drug retailers and trucking fleets. 
In the last two years the total square 
footage of warehousing in the indus- 
try has increased from 13:5 million 
sq. ft. in 1978 to more than 17 million 
sq. ft. in 1980. 

A variety of factors have governed 
the emergence and growth of this 
network, among them the rising 
cost of maintaining store level inven- 
tories which may not be used for 
several weeks, and the rising cost of 
shopping center rentals, which have 
made large backrooms economically 
unattractive. | 

The control of product flow offered 
by acentral warehouse and distribu- 
tion center has offset the expenses of 
building and maintaining a struc- 
ture and the labor costs in staffing 
it. The warehouse aids management 
on monitoring sales by item, in re- 
ducing the inventory size and in buy- 
ing deal merchandise.

Store to warehouse distance

located their distribution complexes 
so that no store is more than a half 
day’s drive away to eliminate the 
costs of layover for the driver and 
tying up the tractor-trailer for an 
extended period. With the costs of 
diesel fuel continually escalating, 
distribution executives are experi- 
menting with different truck routes 
to minimize the distance a truck has 
to travel and at the same time ade- 
quately service the stores. Most 
chains call on their stores an average 
of once a week, while some chains 
which have outlets with above-aver-

In the distribution centers of 
many chains, computerized order 
systems, once afforded only by the 
larger chains, are becoming more 
frequent in medium sized and 
smaller chains. Central comput- 
erized ordering, pricing and billing 
has dramatically cut the cost of dis- 
tribution for many retailers. Auto- 
mated conveyer belts, gravity flow 
racks, merchandise divertors, sort- 
ing and picking machines are also 
conserving and saving labor ex- 
penses. 

Sav-On’s new warehouse boasts 
4.5 miles of conveyer belts, scanners 
and an automated storing system 
that can handle 400,000 cases in 
eight hours, according to Dale 
Short, district operations manager. 
“We invested in this distribution 
center for the sheer economics of 
warehousing—better service, fuller 
shelves,” he adds.

uses five public warehouses). The 
program calls for a much greater use 
of the computer by 1985. According 
to John Brown, vice president of dis- 
tribution, “the computer will give us 
better control of receivingthrough 
an optical scanning machine, deter- 
mine the best location off where to 
store the merchandise-anhd support 
the SItematic system and give us 
better billing ability.” 

Walgreen also uses what it calls 
the field Domicile Plan in order to 
keep its trucks rolling. The system, 
a variation of the Pony i:xpress mail 
service, has trucks traveling long 
distances using several drivers 
along the way.

because you avoid the double sleeper

Cutting fuel costs 

Another method of saving costs 
related to freight is the purchasing 
of diesel fyel in bulk, according to Al 
Fair, distribution manager for Cun- 
ningham Drugs. This firm owns 13 
tractors and has about 48 trailers, 
one-third of which are leased. “We 
supply our fleet from several 10,000- 
gallon diesel tanks that we have,” he 
says. 

Another means of cutting costs is 
by getting more use out. of tractors 
while trailers are being loaded and 
unloaded. For many chains this 
means owning twice as many trail- 
ers as they have tractors. Thus they 
avoid the need to buy extra tractors. 

Fair says that since the Cun- 
ningham fleet added air foils, trucks 
have been getting “up tea mile more 
per gallon.” 

“We have also been slowly switch- 
ing to radial tires on our trucks as 
they need changing,” he says. 

Chains, which are only permitted 
to do a limited amount of backhaul- 
ing, hope that a bill before Congress 
would ease some of the restrictions. 
The bill which was approved by the 
House and is now before the Senate, 


would further open up the tightly 


controlled trucking industry to in- 
creased competition. 

Backhauling has been another 
way chains have been able to make 
more effective tuse of their delivery 
trucks. Mos chains queried say they 
try to do it as often as they can, 
however, it is far from being a regu- 
lar practice. 

Typical was the explanation of Jim 
Harrison, president of Harco 
Drugs, Norinport, Ala. “We do 
some backhauling to the extent the 
law will permit us and it has helped 
offset some costs.” 

Tom Weisert of Taylor Drugs says 
the company backhauls Christmas 
and promotional items, “but it is 
very difficult to time the backhaul if 
you have a limited fleet. If the trailer 
can’t be at the supplier at the time 
the supplier’s loading dock is free, 
then you can get into a scheduling 
hassle if our truck also has to deliver 
to three or four stores.”

Stores fight recession 
with promos, coupons 


DSNews Roundup 

Drug stores are stepping up advertis- 
ing and promotion in a move to head off 
the impact of recession. 

The step-up comes despite fears that 
aggressive price promotion will put a 
damper on profits and spark regional 
price wars. 

In anticipation of slowing sales growth 
rates, executives say that new advertis- 
ing and promotion efforts, ranging from 
double-couponing, more frequent use of 
circulars and heavier TV advertising, are 
now a requisite for continued growth this 
year. 

To a considerable extent, the promo- 
tional step-up is being accompanied by 
a shift in advertising media, from news- 
paper to television, and in product cate- 
gory emphasis, from “big-ticket” items to 
basic goods, as the chains try to prevent 
the current soft sales trend from flatten- 
ing and then turning downward. 

“We're looking for traffic,” says one 
sales promotion executive. And a grow- 
ing number of chains are pulling out the 
~~ to get it: -~

12% decline in income for the year 
ended May 3, now plans to beef up its 
advertising with new TV commercials.

dium before, a spokesman says Gray 
wants to “strengthen our consumer im- 
age.” Also in the works is a new corpo- 
rate logo. 

@ Begley, couponing heavily this year, 
plans a further step-up and is soon likely 
to move into TV for the first time. 

@ Standard hit the tube this past spring 
with a television compaign and is likely

275 items.

G STORE NEWS, July 21, 1980 


- Top-Moving Build Volume 


Drug store retailers are mapping 
massive promotional efforts for the 
last half of 1980 as the spectre of a 
major recession looms ever larger. 

Even though inflation has slowed 
somewhat, the factors of rising un- 
employment, declining purchasing 
power and a generally gloomy busi- 
ness atmosphere have prompted 
consumers to tighten their belts. 
More than ever before, drug store 
customers are demanding value for 
their money as they attempt to 
stretch their disposable income as 


far as possible. 

As a result, even though drug 
store sales have remained much 
stronger through June than in many 
other retail sectors, many drug re- 
tailers feel it is extremely important 
to project a strong discount image to 
consumers—an image that can only 
be effectively developed with pro- 
motion of top-moving health and 
beauty aid items. 

In 1980 Drug Store News Product 
Performance Report delivers the 
most up-to-date information on 


these leading products that retailers 
can use as a merchandising and pro- 
motional aid. A perusal of the follow- 
ing pages will show: 

@ Top 100 items listed by both unit 
and dollar volume. 

e@ The breakdown of those products 
which return the highest number of 
profit dollars, divided into six 
groups and numbered in decreasing 
order of item productivity. 

e A listing of Triple A products 
within 16 different merchandise cat- 
egories. The items in this break- 


down are those which experienced 
heavy movement and continuous 
promotional activity. Products are 
alphabetically listed within each cat- 
egory, and each has both an every- 
day and promotional price range 
listed. 

The report also gives an indication 
of which products will warrant addi- 
tional promotional activity in the up- 
coming year, as well as provides an 
overview of the merchandising year 
past. 


It is often said that drug stores are 


he top 100 best 
selling items are 
the basis of the 
promotion mix of 
drug stores. These are 
the items that are used to 
create the strong price 
image that drug retailers 
are seeking to create in 
the marketplace, and 
drug retailers feature 
— items regularly in 
S. 


recession-resistant by the nature of 
the mix they carry: low-ticket, high- 
demand items. The statement, how- 
ever, does not go far enough: While 
it’s certainly true that the bulk of the 
drug store sales mix is in health and 
beauty aids, one aspect of drug 
stores ability to resist recession lies 
in the willingness and capability of 


drug store retailers to promote their 
products. 

As a consequence of this thinking, 
major chains, as well as leading in- 
dependents and small chain opera- 
tions, are seeking to build store 
traffic in an effort to ward off any 
downtrading by consumers. In put- 
ting these promotions together, 


DRUG STORE NEWS, July 21, 1980 


drug store retailers have rightly se- 
lected a high proportion of health 
and beauty aid items. One reason for 
this is that these items are excellent 
promotionals—heavily demanded, 
price-sensitive and easily identifi- 


inforce the drug store image.

RAZOR ADS SHARPEN CATEGORY | 


Bonded, double-edged, dispos- 
able or swivel system—the con- 
sumer in the market for a good shave 
won't be disappointed. 

Heavy media advertising coupled 
with strong in-store promotion 
made this a $111 million category and 
indications are it is and will continue 
to grow at a strong and steady rate. 

Bonded blades, usually twin blade 
systems, have taken a lion’s share of 
the market lately, while other shav- 
ing blades seem to have slacked off a 
bit. Swivel systems are doing quite 
well against the proliferation of 
blades. 

Disposables are still big news. 
More multipacks—a consumer fa- 
vorite—are showing up and the 
amount of promotion done in this 
category is helping to boost its 
growth on to bigger and better 
things. 

No longer an exclusive male do- 
main, manufacturers added some 
zest to the market with a shaving 
system for the ladies. 

Shaving creams remain a steady 
product category. There is con- 
tinued promotional activity in this 
category, although there have been 
increased in-store displays and pro- 
motional materials of late which are 
designed to stir things up a little.

NEW IMAGE POLISHING DENTAL 


Despite the deep-cutting that 
characterizes toothpaste sales in 
particular, the dental and oral 
hygiene category continues to de- 
liver an average gross margin of ap- 
proximately 25%, with the most 
profitable items reaching 30%. 

Sales of oral hygiene products in 
chain drug stores were clocked at 
some $288 million in 1979, after a 
14.7% increase over volume levels 
the year before. As a result, the cat- 
egory contributed a better-than-9% 
share of total proprietaries depart- 
ment volume. 

What’s more, the emphasis on the 
health care image as a means of set- 
ting the discount drug store apart 
from the discount variety store has 
prompted such chains as Peoples to 
beef up its dental care presenta- 
tions. In the long run, this should 
increase chain drug stores’ share of 
the market—although buyers agree 
that the more promotable items in 
the dental mix have been irretriev- 
ably lost to supermarkets.

While competition among national 
brands and from the private label 
quarter have sharply reduced gross 
margins on nationally advertised 
pain relievers, this product group 
remains a highly effective promo- 
tional area. 

With limited shelf space, and a 
need to churn out profit dollars from 
every foot of shelf area, retailers are 
becoming increasingly selective in 
this category, and new products will 
have a tough time breaking into the 
line-up.

FEMININE HYGIENE SALES UP __ 


Feminine hygiene products, and 
more specifically the success of a rel- 
atively new product, helped bolster 
the bottom line for the entire pro- 
prietary department. 

Sales for feminine hygiene prod- 
ucts and pregnancy tests in 1979 
rose 17.3% over 1978 figures. The 
category accounted for 7.1% of sales 
of the proprietary department and 
generated $227 million in sales. 

A shot in the arm has been given 
by sales of in-home pregnancy test 
kits. Since their introduction three 
years ago, the kits have created a 
new $25 million a year market.

HEALTHY 
IS ‘IN’ FOR 
HAIR CARE 


No one can argue that hair care is 
still big H&BA business, although 
shampoo has not shown the growth 
it has in the recent past. Long time 
staples continue to be steady sell- 
ers, while a variety of new products 
are adding further promotional 
punch to the category. 

On the hot sheet for 1980—care 
and conditioning. | 

The newest entries into the hair 
care category, are shampoos which 
combine the cleansing features of a 
shampoo with the conditioning ben- 
efits of a rinse, all without leaving a 
film on the hair. Emphasis will be on 
hair health as well as cleanliness. 

Hair color is another hair care cat- 
egory which has shown good 
growth. Ever-spiraling inflation has 
coerced consumers to rethink their 
attitude toward home hair coloring 
preparations and more women are 
coloring their own hair at home. 

The return of aerosol-formula hair 
spray to the retail shelves has taken 
some of the wind out of nonaerosol 
sales, although pump sprays still 
have 45% of the dollars in the drug 
category. And although consumers 
are not willing to return to the old 
rigidly structured coifs of years gone 
by, they are looking to the lighter 
formulas, Rave Clairmist, Final Net 
for the degree of control they need.

NATURAL VITAMINS A BOOS 


Natural vitamins are making a ||... psec ewer eee ry 7 
name for themselves in chain drug «°° * pM NE 4 ‘ow 
stores and boosting sales for the en- . beg So ORS Me GO Ee A wy 
tire vitamin category, as peopleseek 
to take better care of themselves. se 
Thus, drug retailers are regaining 
some of the ground they lost to 
health food stores. 

The category as a whole kicked 
nearly $290 million into the chain 
drug coffers iast year, or more than 
9% of total department volume in 
proprietaries. This represented a 
16.6% increase over sales totals the 
year before, showing merchandisers 
that nutrition was good business, 
more than ever before. 

Private label vitamins are a big 
factor in this growth, with a twofold 
value to the chain that offers them. 
First, they link to a health care im- 
age that the consumer can easily 
recognize—and second, they pro- 
vide margins substantially better 
than those supplied by outside ven- 
dors. 

What’s more, as chains give vi- 
tamins a bigger play—as in nutri- 
tion centers and expanded depart- 
ments—the category is likely to 
attain more prominence as a key de- 
partment. Most buyers say that vi- 
tamins have a long way to go before 
they reach their potential.

MILLION 


A BOOM 
IN BABY 


Disposable diapers contributed 
more than 8% to the total $264 mil- 
lion that baby needs grossed last 
year, as retailers find out that babies 
are still big business. 

Faced with the post-war babies 
who have come of age and are start- 
ing their own families, retailers are 
experiencing an increased demand 
for disposable diapers, formula, and 
various toiletry items. 

Despite formidable competition 
from other disposable diaper manu- 
facturers, Pampers is maintaining 
its position as category leader. 

Disposable diapers in general are 
being used heavily for promotion 
purposes and are fast-moving items. 

Toiletries is another strong area 
for the baby needs category, as large 
sizes continue to dominate the sales. 
Baby formula is selling almost ex- 
clusively in ready-to-use and ready- 
to-feed liquids, as more and more 
women continue to trade price for 
convenience. 


ANTACIDS 
HIT $227 


Chain drug industry sales in ethi- 
cal laxatives and antacids topped the 
$428 million mark in 1979, and more 
importantly drug stores maintained 
their share of sales with about three- 
fourths of the national market. 

By product category, antacids ac- 
counted for 7.2% of the average pro- 
prietary department sales. These 
products registered sales of $227 
million in 1979, a 12.5% increase in 
sales over the year before. 

In comparison, laxatives ac- 
counted for a smaller percentage of 
department sales, 6.3%, of the aver- 
age proprietary department. Last 
year laxatives sales increased 13.7% 
to $201 million in chain drug stores. 

Antacids are still a highly com- 
petitive business as gross margins 
range from near zero for traffic 
builders such as Maalox to nearly 
30% for less popular brands. 


SUN PREPS 
BRIGHTEN 


SKIN CARE 


In 1979, sales for hand, skin and 
body creams, taken as a group, to- 
taled some $425 million—or 17.8% of 
all chain drug toiletries volume. But 
the greatest growth in skin care has 
been generated by an increasing 
awareness of the need to protect 
sensitive skin from the harmful rays 
of the sun. 

In fact, sales of suntan and sun- 
burn preparations expanded more 
than 17% in 1979, to a record $103 
million for the category. Consumers 
have a wide range of products to 
choose from, ranging from all-but- 
opaque protective creams to “profes-

DRUG STORE NEWS, July 21, 1980 


EULESS, Tex.—Eli Lilly con- 
tinues to strengthen its already 
dominant hold on the drug store 
market for penicillin and 
cephalosporin-based antibio- 
tics with a 51.9% share of retail 
scripts, up nearly 3.5 share 
points over year-ago levels. 

The firm's increase comes on 
the heels of a three-point gain 
chalked up last year. 

Eight Lilly products are 
among the top 25 ranked by De- 
cision Data in its November 
1979 survey. These drugs in- 
clude Keflex 250mg, V-Cillin K 
250mg, Keflex 500mg, V-Cillin 
K 500mg, V-Cillin K sol. 250mq/- 
5ml, Keflex susp 250mg/5ml, 
Keflex susp 125mg/5ml, and V- 
Cillin K sol 125mg/5mI. 

The market could even be 
more skewed toward Lilly be- 
cause data generated in the sur- 
vey do not take into account 
hospital sales, a major user of 
injectable and oral medications. 
Also, the incidence of flu—with 
its direct correlation to antibiotic 
sales—was late in arriving last 
winter: It finally did show up, but 
at the beginning of 1980, after 
data for this survey were col- 
lected. 

But most importantly, the full 
impact of Lilly's Ceclor launched 
in October 1979 isn't reflected in 
these data. 


Eli Lilly captures 
more than 52% of 
antibiotic market 


According to the New York- 
based investment research firm 
of Wertheim & Co., “Lilly’s 
Ceclor is potentially the most 
significant new antibiotic 
launched, and worldwide reve- 
nues from the drug may exceed 
$200 million within the fore- 
seeable future.” 

David Saks, an analyst at 


‘Wertheim, indicates that in the 


area of hospital-oriented inject- 
ables, Merck’s Mefoxin (a 
cephalosporin) may outstrip 
Lilly's Mandol since the former 
has some advantages in treat- 
ing gram negative infections. “It 
now appears that Mefoxin is ac- 
celerating in usage,” says Saks, 
“whereas Mandol is flattening. 

“Among all antibiotic fami- 
lies,” he says, “cephalosporins 
will continue to expand the fast- 
est and increase market share 
because of their unique 
therapeutic advantages, i.e., 
range of effectiveness, safety, 
and potency.” 

The future also appears 
promising since Lilly has li- 
censed a third generation 
cephalosporin (oxacephalo- 
sporin LY127935) from a Jap- 
anese firm, Shinogi. 

Pfizer is also the licensee for 
a cephalosporin, cefaperazone 
(T1551), a product developed by 
Toyama.

F.D.A. evaluates SK’s chlorpromazine hydrochloride 


ROCKVILLE, Md.—After re- 
viewing the results of a series of 
SmithKline efficacy studies for 
chlorpromazine hydrochloride, 
Officials at F.D.A.’s Bureau of 
Drugs have determined that the 
tranquilizer/antiemetic is effec- 
tive for most, but not all of its 
label indications. 

Specifically, the bureau found 
the studies lacking in substan- 
tial evidence of the drug's effec- 
tiveness for relief from mild 
alcoholic withdrawal symptoms, 
neurotic anxiety, or “apprehen- 


sion and suffering” in cancer pa- 
tients. 

In contrast, F.D.A. drug reg- 
ulators found SmithKline’s Thor- 
azine and other chloropro- 
mazine HCI versions to be 
effective for the following label 
indications: 

@ the management of man- 
ifestations of psychotic disor- 
ders; 

@ to control nausea and vomit- 
ing; 

“ty for relief of restlessness and 
apprehension before surgery; 


@ for acute intermittent por- 
phyria; 

® as an adjunct in the treatment 
of tetanus; 

@ to control manifestations of 
the manic type of manic depres- 
sive illness; and 

@ for relief of intractable hic- 


cups. 

In addition, F.D.A. drug reg- 
ulators acted on the recommen- 
dation of the agency's Psycho- 
pharmacological Agents Ad- 
visory Panel and reworded an- 
other label indication. 


Although the studies did not 
provide substantial evidence 
that the drug is effective in deal- 
ing with “moderate to severe ag- 
itation, hyperactivity, or ag- 
gressiveness in disturbed chii- 
dren,” that panel found that “if 
certain language modifications 
were made to the indication, 
sufficient well-controlled stud- 
ies exist that provide substantial 
evidence of effectiveness.” 

Accordingly, F.D.A. officials 
are proposing to reword the in- 
dication as follows: 


“For the treatment of severe 
behavior problems in children 
marked by combativeness and/ 
or explosive hyperexcitable be- 
havior [out of to im- 


following symptoms: impulsi- 
vity, difficulty s atten- 
tion, agg mood 

and poor 


tolerance.

“Lo 


on F.D.A. regulators 


WASHINGTON—U.S. Gen- 
eral Accounting Office (G.A.O.) 
researchers have issued a ma- 
jor new report confirming indus- 
try suspicions that overly cau- 
tious Food and Drug Adminis- 
tration regulators have contrib- 
uted to a national Bg » a 

Despite recent F.D.A. efforts 
to expedite approval of new 
“breakthrough” drugs, the 
United States continues to lag 
far behind other industrialized 
countries in approving “impor- 
tant” new pharmaceutical prod- 
ucts, the study indicated. 

Specifically, the report found 
that the average F.D.A. approval 
time for 14 important new drugs 
introduced since 1975 amount- 
ed to 23 months. In contrast, the 
approval process in Switzerland 
averaged only about half as 
long, while in Britain those 
same 14 important new phar- 
maceuticals were available to 
British patients within an aver- 


ORAL-B HAS PROVEN IT! 


age of five months after intro- 
duction. 

But while G.A.O. laid most of 
the blame for this “drug lag” on 
F.D.A. regulators, the agency in- 
dicated that Congress, con- 
sumer activists and the phar- 
maceutical manufacturing in- 
dustry itself have also contrib- 
uted to the delays. 

lronically, the G.A.O. study it- 
self has come under criticism for 
taking nearly three years to 
reach the conclusion that 
F.D.A.’s “lengthy approval pro- 
cess delays the benefits impor- 
tant drugs can provide to the 
public.” 

Although the Federal Food 
Drug and Cosmetic Act calls on 
F.D.A. to review and reach a de- 
cision on new drug applications 
within 180 days, hardly any new 
pharmaceuticals are actually 
cleared within that six month pe- 
riod. 

After studying each of the 132 
new drugs submitted to the 
agency for approval during 
1975, G.A.O. found that only 
one of these drugs was cleared 
in less than 180 days. 

By May of 1979 only 52% of 
the 1975 NDAs had been ap- 
proved by F.D.A., and it took the 
agency an average of..20 
months each to reach a decision 
on these drugs, the report 
noted. : 

G.A.O. then undertook a re- 
view of all 14 “important” new 
drugs submitted for marketing 
approval between July 1975 and 
February 1978, only to come up 
with an even more disturbing 
finding: all but one of these 14 
products became available to 
patients in one of five foreign 
countries surveyed well before 
they were approved for market- 
ing in the United States. 

Examples : 

Among the specific examples 
cited in the report: 
® somatotropin, a drug used to 
promote growth in hormone-de- 
ficient children, became _avail- 
able in Sweden in 1971, but was 
not approved by F.D.A. until 
1976; 
® propranolol, an important ad- 
vancement in treating high 
blood pressure, was marketed 
seven years earlier in Britain; 
® disopyramide, a drug to cor- 
rect abnormal heart rhythm, 
was Offered to British patients 
for five years before gaining ap- 
proval from F.D.A.; and 
®@ bromocryptine, an anti-Par- 
kinson agent, was approved by 
the Swiss almost three years 
before it became available to 
Americans. 

_ Among the factors contribut- 
ing to F.D.A.’s lengthy new drug 
approval process, according to 
G.A.O., are the agency's time- 
consuming “chemistry and 
manufacturing control review,” 
an “uneven workload” on 


Federal org reviewers, and 
“imprecise F.D.A. guidelines” 
which are “subject to varying in- 
terpretations.” 

_ Other causes of the drug lag 
“include intense Congressional 
and consumer scrutiny of the 
drug approval process, adver- 
sary relationships between 
F.D.A. and the drug industry, 
and F.D.A.’s conservative ap- 
proach to drug regulation,” the 
investigators conciuded. 

But G.A.O. also maintained 
that pharmaceutical manufac- 
turers themselves contributed 
to the delays, concluding that 
the “industry submits in- 
complete NDAs and is slow to 
resolve deficiencies.”

DRUG ST@RE NEWS 


1980 REFERENCE FOR 
PHARMACY PRACTICE 


This year Drug Store News has updated last year's issue of the Pharmacist's Reference. It has been 
determined through interviews with numerous pharmacists that a need exists for business-oriented informa- 
tion, especially in view of ever greater competition. Accordingly, information in this year's reference is divided 
into a business section, a clinical section and a continuing education quiz on the clinical material. This 
material is designed to help pharmacists function more efficiently and knowledgeably in the performance of 
their professional duties. 


Section 1 is a commercial section that contains a myriad of business data useful to practicing pharmacists. 
Included in the section are the top 200 drugs, profiles of leading acute care drugs, a bulk buying guide, pricing 
strategies, inventory control systems, selected manufacturers trade terms and many more features. Numer- 
ous sources have been used to compile the business section, however, a sizable portion was obtained from 
Arlington, Tex.-based Decision Data. 


Section 2, the clinical section, contains background on vitamin deficiencies, drug/drug and food/drug 
interactions and sugar free liquids. Also found in the section, is background material on soft contact lens 
solutions and a drug consultation guide of leading products. 


Section 3 is a 100 question continuing education quiz. This comprehensive test is based entirely upon the 
editorial material contained in the clinical and generic sections of the Reference. Following successful 
completion of the test, pharmacists will be better prepared to instruct their patients and advise physicians on 
such matters as unwanted side effects of leading prescription drugs.

REFERENCE FOR PHARMACY PRACTICE/AUGUST 1980 


The relative importance of the 
top 200 pharmaceutical products 
can't be over emphasized: They 
play an important role in an aver- 
age pharmacy's sales and inven- 
tory control. A leading pharmaceu- 
tical marketing research supplier 
claims the top 200 Rx products ac- 
count for 70 per cent of all new 
scripts filled in the United States; 
the top 50 products, nearly 41 per 
cent of all new prescriptions. 

Information in this section can 
be used for planning and control 


. Mt 


Top 200 Products Ranked 


ling inventory, estimating dollar 
sales volume, and budgeting gross 
profit. Three criteria are used to 
rank the top 200 products: 

@ Total number of scripts 

@ Dollar volume 

@ Dollar margin 

Analysis of these three criteria 
reveals that the number of pre- 
scriptions and retai!. dollar volume 
should not be the sole measures of 
a pharmacy's volume. For exam- 
ple, data presented here indicate 
that Tylenol with Codeine 30mg, 


Darvocet-N 100mg, Dalmane 
30mg and Lanoxin 0.25mg each 
rank higher in terms of dollar mar- 
gin generated than in terms of dol- 
lar sales. Other products, such as 
birth control pills, rank higher in 
terms of dollar volume, yet are 
lower in terms of dollar margin con- 
tributed. 

The importance of new products 
is reflectea by Tagamet, which in 
the span of a few short years, is 
now the leading dollar volume 
product on pharmacists shelves.

Dispensing Profiles 


Selecting a method for pricing competitive prod- 
department remains a major 


ucts in the 


Drug Usage Report (see section titled Planning Dif- 
ferent Pricing Strategies), which can be computer 
generated. The most frequently dispensed drugs are 
listed in the Report in descending order. Pharmacists 
can compare the leading drugs dispensed from the 
list of Top 200 Products in this Reference. 

The example presented below represents a hypo- 
thetical list of what a pharmacy's selection of leading 
products might look like. 


Number of 
Description Per Month 
Valium 5mg 42 


Dyazide 38 
i 31 


In this example, the list begins with Valium S5mg 
and ends with Hydrodiuril 50mg. 

After the list is compiled, it must be updated from 
time to time as competitive conditions dictate. Drugs 
toward the bottom of the list should be examined 
Critically. Every drug that can no longer justify its 
position on the list should be removed. For the sake 
of completeness and consistency pharmacists 
should consider adding alternative product strengths 
to the list, i.e., Valium 2mg and Lasix 20mg. 

The end result is a list of 20 to 30 discounted prod- 
ucts which significantly influence consumers image 
of a pharmacy.

result, products used in the treatment of nonchronic 
conditions make significant contributions to a phar- 
macy's overall gross margin. 

Maintenance care products such as Lasix, 
Dyazide, and Tagamet are another matter. These 
products typically have above average refill rates that 
represent significant numbers of repeat purchases. 
Often times retailers per cent margins for such prod- 
ucts are low (see Dyazide chart below). 

For example, competitive maintenance drugs typ- 
ically yield gross margins from 27% to 37%, whereas 
pharmaceuticals used to treat nonchronic conditions 
generate margins of 40% to 60%. Products such as 
E.E.S. 400, Synalgos DC, and Phenaphen with Co- 
deine #3 don’t offer sizable refill rates; they do, how- 
ever, offer above average margins of 44%, 53% and 
61% respectively.

Selected quantities dispensed (0-12, 13-16, 17-18, 
19-20, 21-24, 25-30, 31-36, 37-50, and 51-100) are 
shown relative to the per cent of prescriptions dis- 
pensed at that quantity, the per cent of scripts refilled 
at each quantity, the average gross margin per cent 
obtained for each quantity, and the contribution each 
quantity produces toward the brand's overall per cent 
gross margin (see table below). 

The percentage of Rxs dispensed and the average 
gross margin per cent reflect how these values may 
vary depending on the amount of drug dispensed. 

The row labeled per cent refill indicates refills as a 
percentage of all scripts relative to the various quan- 
tities of drug dispensed. 

The amount that each prescription quantity con- 
tributes to a brand's total gross margin is calculated 
by multiplying the per cent of scripts dispensed by the 
average gross margin per cent and dividing the prod- 
uct by 100. When the contributions for each quantity 
are summed, they total slightly more than the brand's 
per cent gross margin due to rounding. 

Information presented here should key pharma- 
cists to the importance of pricing prescriptions on a 
sliding scale, which is dependent on the quantities of 
drug dispensed. Analysis of this material reveals that 
per cent margins are frequently lower as the quantity 
dispensed becomes larger. As a result, greatest con- 
sumer savings (lower store margins) trace to prod- 
ucts dispensed in the 51-100 group. 

Rationale behind this pricing structure centers on 
elimination of container cost and fast turnover, i.e., 
there is no inventory carrying charge (for an unsold 
quantity) after the bottle is dispensed. Opening a 
container, therefore, necessitates an added fee be- 
cause the undispensed portion has not been sold 
and represents an added cost to the retailer. 

The patterns that prevail for maintenance drugs are 
not the same as patterns noted for drugs used in the 
treatment of nonchronic illnesses. Products such as 
Vibramycin, Tylenol with Codeine 30mg, and Drixoral 
each have a markedly different pattern than mainte- 
nance pharmaceuticals. 


Acute Care Products 

In last year's Reference for Pharmacy Practice, 
dispensing profiles wefe analyzed for 24 leading Rx 
products used to treat a variety of conditions that 
required maintenance drug therapy. The products 
chosen each had refill rates greater than 50%. Valium 
was an exception, since it is a controlled substance,

13-16, 19-20, 25-30, or 31-36 is quite typical. More 
importantly, smaller quantities frequently carry siza- 
ble per cent gross margins. Since quantities of 
51-100, are not dispensed very often, these larger 
quantities usually do not make a sizable contribution 
to the retailers average per cent margin for the brand. 


Maintenance Products 

Patterns observed for maintenance products such 
as Lanoxin are somewhat different than those noted 
for products used to treat nonchronic conditions. 
Maintenance drugs are frequently dispensed in large 
quantities of 51-100, usually 100. Even though per 
cent margin is lowest for 100's, this quantity is still the 
single most important contributor to gross margin
