owing primarily to the sizable percentage of scripts 
dispensed in this group. In many cases (Dilantin, 
Dyazide, Loniten) the contribution made by the 
51-100 group accounts for more than half of the 
brand's total gross margin, all other categories (1-50) 
account for the balance. 

Drugs used to treat nonchronic conditions make 
their greatest contribution to overall per cent gross 
margin in the 25-30 group of units dispensed. 

This represents an opportunity to increase margin 
by revising pricing schedules of products dispensed 
in an assortment of quantities. If for example 50% of 
the contribution to gross margin is derived from 
groups of 50 or less, then for every price increase of 
2%, margin will increase by 1%. Indeed, this repre- 
sents a prime area where many pharmacies should 
first consider adjustments in their pricing schedules. 

Ornade Spansules represents a typical example of 
a drug where greater margins could be obtained. 
Over 70% of all prescriptions filled fall in the 1-30 
group, and per cent gross margin ranges from 63% to 
43% for the (1-30) group. This group also contributes 
35 of the brand's 42 gross margin points or approx- 
imately 83% of the brand's entire margin. This means 
that all other quantities (31-100) contribute only 17 
points to the brands margin. 

As a result, if prices are increased 10% for all 
scripts in the 1-30 category, then gross margin for the 
brand would advance 8.3 points. This represents a 
quick effective method to advance prescription de- 
partment margin without tarnishing the pharmacy’'s 
price image.

Bulk Buying Guide For Leading Products 


Products are ranked in order starting with those 
having the largest numbers of capsules or tablets 
dispensed from an average store during a typical 
month, i.e., February. 

As a rule of thumb, pharmacies should never 
order more than a month's supply of a fast-mov- 
ing item unless an additional per cent discount per 
month can be obtained for every month that the 
item remains on the shelf. In other words, if suffi- 
cient savings from bulk purchases are not ob- 
tained or demand doesn’t warrant purchasing 
large quantities, pharmacists should buy smaller 
quantities. This is especially true when products 
can be acquired in packaging that can be dis- 
pensed directly to patients, thereby saving the 
pharmacy container costs. Remember, the goal is 
to have an inventory turn of at least 4.5X per year. 
The optimum is between 6 and 7 turns per annum. 

This guide is based on products average de- 
mand, which varies from pharmacy to pharmacy. 
Birth control pills, nonbranded products, liquids, 
creams and ointments have been omitted. In addi- 
tion, products with high usage rates during winter 
months, such as antibiotics, may be overstated be- 
cause these data are compiled for February. 

Pricing data are taken from the Prescription Pric- 


Rank Product Manufacturer 


Size 


ing Guide of April 1980. In order to maintain sim- 
plicity and consistency from company to company, 
only average wholesale prices (AWP) are used. 

Ithough some AWP costs have no doubt changed 
since April, the relationships established among 
these brands small and bulk sizes have for the most 
part remained consistent. 

Product rank for this section is obtained from Deci- 
sion Data. If you turn to the summary table in the 
section of the reference titled “Planning Different 
Pricing Strategies,” you'll note the column of figures 
on the left are headed “average number of capsules 
or tablets sold per pharmacy. 

These figures represent the cornerstone around 
which a bulk — chart for your prescription de- 
partment can be built. First, however, you must deter- 
mine the average prescription volume for the leading 
brands in your pharmacy department. 

This information can be obtained rapidly through 
the use of electronic data processing. Although a 
manual inspection of the Rx files will also accomplish 
the same purpose, the procedure is quite time con- 
suming to attempt in a busy department. 

Once the products are ranked relative to one an- 
other, it is possible to compare small and bulk quan- 
tities among the leaders that will lower cost of goods.

Planning Different Pricing Strategies 


In many pharmacies there is a multi-tiered pricing 
policy. In the examples that follow four different pric- 
ing levels are utilized. One level recognizes products 
that are a necessity; however, due to competition, 
margins are low or nonexistant, i.e., birth control pills. 
Another level might include the top 25 products, 
which are usually also very competitive. The third 
level may include the leading 100 drugs exclusive of 
the top 25. The final group could include all other 
drugs carried in the inventory.

In practice this information can be obtained 
through the use of electronic data processing sys- 
tems. It can also be obtained by adding additional 
data to the daily prescription report. The prescription 
number and selling price plus the number of new and 
refill scripts are already recorded. Additional informa- 
tion that should be recorded at the same time in- 
cludes the name of the drug and its cost per quantity 
dispensed. Then it is possible to have a daily summ- 
ary sheet with margins available. 

Data by brand are totaled, then compiled and 
placed in a table similar to the one provided in this 
section (see One-Month Averages). 

It is not necessary to sum information on every 
product dispensed. Once the top 100 products have 
been identified and the percent of total scripts deter- 
mined, you can obtain the percentage of business for 


the “all other” category. Simply subtract the contribu- 
tion of the first 3 categories from 100%, the difference 
represents percent of all volume contributed by the 
“all others” category. 

This exercise will allow pharmacists to plan various 
pricing alternatives. For example, if in the interest of 
becoming more competitive, 25 more drugs are 
priced like the top 25 drugs, margin becomes 35.3%.

Top 20 Generic Products 


In order to provide readers with a full picture of the 
— market, a section on generic products is 
included as part of this year's Reference. Since physi- 
cians may prescribe multisource drugs by their 

name or common generic name, it's 
imperative that pharmacists identify those products 
playing the most important roles in generic prescrib- 
ing. 


Accordingly in this section of the Reference, an 
overview comparison of trends between new and 
refill scripts—utilizing branded or generic drugs—is 


Branded products clearly dominate the market in 
terms of new and refill scripts written by physicians in 
private practice, but these prescriptions declined 
Close to 3% during 1979. 

Generics on the other hand, advanced almost 2% 
during this time. No doubt this trend traces directly to 

ated drug product selection laws now on the 
books in over 40 states. 

The top 20 drugs prescribed by their generic 
names reflect the availability of multisource products, 
especially antibiotics. Indeed, the top 5 generic prod- 
ucts prescribed are ampicillin, gat penicillin 
VK, erythromycin, and amoxicillin. These drugs also 


rank high on the list of top 200 products — the 
most pa Sg For example, 18 of the drugs 
prescribed generically place on this list. 

Physician prescribing habits change from phar- 
macy to pharmacy and area to area, however, by 
recognizing those drugs most likely to be prescribed 
generically, pharmacists can keep their inventories 
more evenly balanced. 

The importance of these 20 products can’t be over- 
emphasized. Scripts written generically now account 
for 14.1% of all the new prescriptions. By stocking the 
20 most frequently prescribed generic products, 
pharmacists will have on hand those products that 
fulfill almost 78% of new prescriptions written for 
generic products. 

The top 20 products also account for 73% of all 
generic products prescribed, i.e., new and refill 
scripts combined. 

in terms of average prescription prices, generics 
are less expensive than branded drugs. During 1979, 
patients paid an average prescription price of $7.03, 
an advance of 9.2% over the previous year's level. 

The average price of a generic script advanced 
_— to $5.03, while branded drugs increased 9.9% 
to $7.35.

Box-store concept 
gaining momentum 


SupeRx converts 
conventional unit 
to a Super-X-tra 


Drug Emporium 
franchise 
bows in Dallas 


COLUMBUS, Ohio— 
SupeRx recently converted a 
store here to Super-X-tra 
Drug World, the chain’s first 
venture into low-margin 
drug store operations. 

The chain’s executives will 
not say what their plans are 
for operation, or if any more 
are planned, except to say 
that the store is an experi- 
ment. 

The 12,000-sq.-ft. unit is 
open 24 hours a day, includ- 
ing the pharmacy, and is lo- 
cated just a few blocks away 
from the second Drug Em- 
porium to open in Columbus. 
The first Drug Emporium, 
which opened two years ago 
here, produced over $4 mil- 
lion in sales in its second 
year, and because of that 
store’s extraordinary suc- 
cess, the owners have since 
franchised the format to oth- 
ers. 

The Super-X-tra store ad- 
vertises extra low every day 
prices. Health and beauty 
aids make up the bulk of the 
store offering. Cosmetics 
and greeting cards are dis- 
counted, as is the policy in 
the nearby Drug Emporium, 
and Rx prescriptions are 
priced lower than in conven- 
tional drug stores. 

Low-margin stores tend to 
be cluttered in appearance, 
although SupeRx manage- 
ment is reportedly interested 
in keeping the look of a regu- 
lar drug store and in keeping 
case displays in aisles to a 
minimum. 

SupeRx executives say the 
new outlet is an experiment, 
and they decline to discuss 
their plans for the store.

The operator of the first

uary. No site has been se-

in 1977 by Philip Wilber, a

the stores shortly thereafter. 
There are now franchised 
stores in Cincinnati and 
Phoenix. This month, a fran- 
chised stere will open in 
Kansas City.

ROCKVILLE, Md.—Food 
and Drug Administration regula- 
tors released the names of more 
than 30 generic products which 
Federal officials claim are being 
marketed illegally to the nation's 
pharmacists without approved 
New Drug Applications (NDAs). 

The action marks the latest 
offensive in F.D.A.’s running 
legal battle with Premo, Phar- 
madyne and a handful of other 
generic drug manufacturers 
who have been distributing un- 
approved products even though 
agency regulators contend 
there is “no assurance” that 
their versions “are bioequivalent 
or therapeutically equivalent” to 
the approved brand name coun- 
terparts. 

In addition to Premo and 
Pharmadyne—the two New 
Jersey-based generic pro- 
ducers which have been in the 
forefront of the legal battle over 
unapproved drugs—the new 
F.D.A. list als@ includes several 


other manufacturers charged by 
Government regulators with dis- 
tributing drugs illegally: 
Chelsea Laboratories (Inwood, 
N.Y.); Camall (Detroit); Clay 
Park Laboratories (Bronx, N.Y.); 
Superpharm (Central Islip, 
N.Y.); and Zenith Laboratories 
(Northvale, N.J.).

InSearch Of New Solutions 


Many independent druggists rec- 
ognize the need for new, bold ap- 
proaches in the conduct of their 
business, but do not seek such ap- 
proaches in their traditional 
strengths. 

Asa result, many are still groping 
for solutions to their ever-multiply- 
ing economic and competitive prob- 
lems, and do not have a highly pos- 
itive attitude about their niche in the 
marketplace. 

But, by the same token, many in- 
dependents do recognize the bastion 
of their business—the ability to de- 
velop strong relationships with pa- 
tients and to function as community 
drug stores, even though they have 


not yet found a means of translating 
this strength into an aggressive, 
competitive strategem. 

So indicates a survey recently con- 
ducted for Drug Store News of 500 
independent pharmacists across the 
nation. The survey was handled by 
Lebhar-Friedman Research and 
queried independent drug store 
owners as to how their operations 
performed now, what their pros- 
pects are for the future and what 
~aga competitive strengths might 

The picture by the survey is that of 
an industry segment seeking a new 
role in the marketplace, but as yet 
still strongly bonded to what can be 


termed traditional strengths, some 
of which remain extremely impor- 
tant and others of which indepen- 
dents would do well to put aside. 
For example, one of the clearest 
messages to come out of the statis- 
tics is that 92.5% of the independent 
pharmacists interviewed felt that 
they had very strong relationships 
with their customers and that this 
was an extremely important aspect 
of how they conducted their busi- 
ness. This, in fact, is a key statistic 
in this study because it represents 
one of the strongest .and most uni- 
versal feelings expressed by inde- 
pendent drug store owners. No oth- 
er statistic in the DRSN survey pro-

“What can we offer that a chain

ings and early openings. The ability 
to recognize a customer and call her 
by name—to ask how her child is— 
to develop a personal relationship.” 
So says Lester Eisenberg of Cen-

remarks appear to be representa- 
tive of the independents all across 
the country. Dick Burgess, of Re-

Wash., says that, in his opinion, per- 
sonal service is one of the three con- 
ditions on which the survival of the 
independent ultimately rests.

very little deviation, held true for all 
independents regardless of dollar 
volume, size of store, number of 
pharmacists employed and number 
of scripts filled per day. A percent- 
age of 89.5% (for stores less than 
1,000 sq. ft.) was the lowest figure 
and 95.2% was the highest (for 
stores doing over a half million in 
sales annually). 

In many ways, this ratio is the 
strength and weakness of the inde- 
pendent drug store market. The 
strength lies in the fact that this 
kind of hold on consumers is ex- 
tremely difficult for others to dupli- 
cate, provides on-going sales of a 
very substantial amount, and bonds 
the consumer to the store like noth- 
ing else. Chain execs frequently say 
that a good independent is the 
toughest competition to meet—and 
this is the reason why. 

At the same time, dependence on 
this form of competition—or mes- 
merization with it—has frequently 
prevented independents from devel- 
oping some other policies that may 
help them function in the market- 
place. 

Other important factors 

The importance of strong relation- 
ships with patients in the minds of 
independents cannot be overesti- 
mated. However, there are several 
other statistics that also reveal 
what’s important to the independent 
drug store owner: 

e A total of 52.9% of the respon- 
dents felt that the characteristic 
“highly professional, clinical image” 
applied greatly to independent drug 
stores. 

@ Some 54.6% felt that operating 
with a drug/health-oriented mix was 
a very good description of an inde- 
pendent drug store. 

@ Some 54.2% thought that inde- 
pendent drug stores featured com- 
munity involvement due to their 
neighborhood locations. 

All of these characteristics, which 
are elements of the traditional way 
of thinking about an independent 
store, do not project nearly as 
strong an image to the owners of 
those independents as do strong re- 
lationships with patients. This even 
includes the “professional, clinical” 
image, which many consider to be 
the hallmark of the independent. 

But quite rightly, independents 
themselves recognize the suprem- 


DRUG STORE NEWS, August 4, 1980 


acy of strong relationships with pa- 
tients, and while. emphasizing a 
professional image in their opera- 
tions, place it second to the other. 

By the same token, several! other 
characteristics, which detract from 
the traditional view of the typical 
independent pharmacy, are not in 
fact considered very important by 
the majority of independent store 
owners. For example, only 41.2% 
considered the phrase “merchandise 
flexibility” to be appropriate to the 
independent store. 

Of course, there is a degree of vari- 
ability here in that the larger inde- 
pendent (those operating over 5,000 
sq. ft. of space or doing over a half 
million dollars in volume annually) 
saw some validity to this descrip- 
tion. 

Those with more footage, some 
52.3%, said that it applied greatly 
and to those with $500,000 or more 
in sales, 51.8% indicated that it ap- 
plied greatly. But, for the majority 
of independent store owners, mer- 
chandising flexibility is not a charac- 
teristic they feel they have a great 
deal of. 

Pricing flexibility 

In addition, pricing flexibility is 
not considered an important charac- 
teristic of independent drug store 
operations. A total of 36.3%—only a 
little better than a third—thought 
that this characteristic was a good 
description of an independent drug 
store. 

Finally, only 23.7% of those inde- 
pendent owners interviewed felt 
that operating with a promotional 
general merchandise-type mix was a 
highly accurate description of an in- 


dependent drug store. In this case 
also, however, those independents 
with larger stores and higher sales 
were more prone to see themselves 
in a promotional mold. 

As a generalization, few indepen- 
dents have much penetration into 
the general merchandise area, 
which limits their ability to create a 
really promotional image for their 
stores. 

When asked by interviewers, how 
they saw themselves, by far the sin- 
gle most important response was as 
“a community/neighborhood phar- 
macy”—the percentage was 55.2%. 
Only 9.3% viewed themselves as an 
apothecary type of operation, and 
only 14.4% saw themselves, accord- 
ing to the survey, as a traditional 
drug store with gift/boutique items. 

At the same time, only 9.1% con- 
sidered themselves scaled-down 
versions of a major chain drug oper- 
ation, and only 3.4% said their im- 
age was that of a highly promotional 
drug store. 

Personal quality 

Independents, thus, viewed 
themselves primarily and most im- 
portant as community outlets, 
drawing their marketing strength 
from their closeness to the neighbor- 
hood they serve. Only secondarily— 
but still importantly—do they see 
themselves as a purely professional 
or professionally oriented type of op- 
eration. Of course, this does not 
mean they consider themselves pro- 
motional, because the survey specif- 
ically indicates that such is not the 
case. 

Given their own view of them- 
selves, independents assess the 
marketplace in which they function 
in a somewhat defensive manner. 
According to the DRSN survey, in- 
dependent store owners see the 
market much as any other type of 
retailer does, and the three major 
competitors are the obvious ones— 
supermarkets, discount stores and 
drug chains. In terms of overall com- 
petition, independents, like many at 
the chains, see the supermarkets as 
the biggest competitor of the inde- 
pendent drug store. : 

However, what is surprising is the 
intensity of this feeling. A total of 
34.1% of the respondents to the 
Drug Store News survey felt that 
supermarkets were the most effec- 
tive competitor of independent drug 
stores. In comparison, 24.3% felt 
that discount stores were the major 
competition, and 24.1% felt that the 
major competitor was the chain 
drug sector. Only 1.2% felt that oth- 
er independents were the major 
competitor—independents assess- 
ment of their own segment as a ma- 
jor competitive factor. 

Another surprise is in fact that in 
the area of prescriptions, indepen- 
dents view the drug: chains as their 
major competition, despite the in-

As stores get larger, and develop a

The percentages in the H&BA area 
are much more tightly grouped, 
with the supermarkets becoming 
less and less the most important

Vulnerable position 

The independent sees his own role 
in the marketplace more or less as 
the chains see him: the vulnerable 
end of the market trying to survive 
battles with larger, frequently 
tougher competition. For example, 
only 6.1% of the independents inter- 


viewed consider other independents 
to be major competitors. 


At the same time, only 5.9% of the 
independents responding to the sur- 
vey indicated that they felt that their 
stores were extremely effectively 
merchandised, and only 35.3% felt 
they had done a very effective job in 
merchandise. The largest group of 
respondents (47.3%) only felt that 
they had been “somewhat” effective 
in their merchandising efforts. 

Moreover, 58.8% of independents 
interviewed felt that they had diffi- 
culty in generating sales growth, 
and 52.7% of that total felt it was due 
to their being an independent drug 
store, while only 38.3% thought it 
was a universal drug store problem. 

And, when asked what the rea- 
sons were for independents going 
out of business, a total of 43% indi- 


cated that it was due to too much 
competition. The responses to na- 
ture of the competition included 
“price-cutting by chains,” “pres- 
sures from discounters,” “inability 
to cope with competitive prices,” 
“competition from the chains,” and 
“discounting.” 

The message is that the indepen- 
dent drug store owners do not pic- 
ture themselves as major competi- 
tive factors in the marketplace and 
feel themselves vulnerable to other 
competitors in the market. 

But independent owners indicated 
other reasons for going out of busi- 
ness, which also relate to their lack 
of marketing power. For example, 
31% of the respondents stated that 


financial problems caused the de- 
mise of many independent drug 
stores. About a third of these were 
due to underfinancing, and another 
third to slow (or lack of) payment on 
third-party claims. However, about 
15% indicated that low sales volume 
and resulting poor profitability 
caused the business failures. 
Lack of expertise 

Another 22% of the total number 
of respondents to the Drug Store 
News survey mentioned that busi- 
ness failures of independents related 
back to a lack of merchandising and 
management expertise. About 68% 
of this 22% noted that poor business 
management was the cause of the 
bankruptcies. 

Other reasons mentioned included 
“lack of knowledge of promotions,” 
“poor inventory control,” and “bad, 
inadequate merchandise—didn’t 
know what to do with the products.” 
Once again, the message here is that 
the independent drug store owners 
do not see their end of the drug store 
market as having the necessary 
qualifications at the present time for 
surviving, much less prospering, in 
a very competitive market. 

Why else did independents feel 
other independents go out of busi- 
ness? There was a broadly based 
feeling that many independents 
were unwilling to change with the 
times or unable to “adapt to com- 
petitive pricing.” Of course, all the 
other business difficulties that affect 
every retailer were included such as 
changes in neighborhood, shopping 
patterns, and so forth. 

But if independents feel that they 
are participating in the drug store 
market as the weaker and more vul- 
nerable factor, they all agree that 
they must change their way of doing 
business. In fact, according to the 
survey, 75% of the independents in-

What are some of the activities

One of the most important re-

tant method of combatting competi-

method was advertising, according 
to the survey, and some 44% of the 
independents interviewed indicated 
that this was a major effort to fight 
competition. 

Displays and promotions 

Other major responses to the com- 
petitive threat included greater use 
of displays and promotional mate- 
rials, and surprisingly, joining a vol- 
untary or cooperative group to have 
access to a wide variety of competi- 
tive and operational services. 

All of these techniques are part of 
the chain arsenal in competing in the 
marketplace, and they presuppose 
that the drug store deploying them 
will take on a more vromotional, 


general merchandise image than 


was the case before. 

What the independents do not em- 
phasize in developing competitive 
methods are their own basic 
strengths—mainly the strong com- 
munity link, the tight patient rela- 
tionships, the more professional as- 
pect of their stores (as they them- 
selves see it). For example, in the 
survey, only 2% of the respondents 
included greater or improved per- 
sonal contact as an effort to combat 
competition. Only 2% stressed im- 
proving customer relations. Only 3% 
emphasized the promotion of a 
strong professional or clinical image 
to their customers. 

Ideal mix 

Again, 68% of the sample indi- 
cated that the ideal drug store mix 
would be prescription drugs, pro- 
prietaries, toiletries, plus general 
merchandise. Only 30% stated that 
the ideal mix would be just prescrip- 
tions, over-the-counter drugs and 
toiletries, without general merchan- 
dise. (About 2% of the sample had no 
opinion on this question. ) 

Independent drug store owners 
see their salvation outside of their 
traditional areas of expertise or 
their traditional strengths, but rec- 
ognize when asked that these tradi- 
tional strengths are tremendously 
important to them. 

When queried on why they would 
prefer a general merchandise mix, 
the independents surveyed most of- 
ten cited the need to satisfy a range 
of consumer demands, provide one- 
stop shopping convenience and at- 
tract customer traffic. Only 7% 
mentioned sales and 5% mentioned 
profits as factors in their responses. 

Yet when asked in what ways the 


vt 


Source: Lebhar-Friedman Research 


© 1 Promote integrity/professionalism/image 3% 


independent drug store operation 
will have to change in the future, 
there was no clearcut commitment 
to increased service on the part of 
the independent. Rather, responses 
varied all across the board. 

The largest group—49% of those 
who feel that there must be some 
kind of change—are looking toward 
improved operational practices, in- 
cluding “more efficient business 
management” and becoming “more 
competitive,” as the way to go. No 
less than 23% of those who say that a 
change is needed expect that the 
change will come in cost structure, 
with competitive pricing high on the 
list. 

Foreseeable changes 

Moreover, 18% are seeking altera- 
tions in the drug store mix, and 14% 
in order systems. But only 34% 
talked about such factors as profes- 
sional image, community involve- 
ment, personal service and cus- 
tomer interaction, when asked what 
changes will be necessary for the 


independent operation. 

“We want to get involved in the 
community more in the future,” says 
Lester Eisenberg. “We already have 
a senior citizen discount program on 
OTC merchandise as well as on pre- 
scriptions. And we brought in a 
blood pressure machine for people 
on maintenance programs. In gen- 
eral, the way for the independent 
pharmacist to go is to become more 
community-minded.” 

But Eisenberg is in the minority, 
and this points to a dichotomy in the 
mind of the independent pharma- 
cist. While he sees personal service, 
professional image, community in- 
volvement and convenience as his 
greatest strengths today, he is look- 
ing to price, selection and more so- 
phisticated business practices in the 
future. 

And for the independent, at a 
crossroads in his history, the wis- 
dom of this decision could mean the 
difference between survival and ex- 
tinction.

son Drug Co. is going national 
on costume jewelry, expanding 
its home health care selection, 
and testing five other product 
categories it has designated as 
prime expansion targets. 

The other five include fra- 
grances, stationery, kitchen- 
ware, hardware and automotive. 
If test results warrant, McKes- 
son will distribute nationally 
within a year. ~, 

Home health care, marketed 
under McKesson’'s Sun Mark la- 
bel for many years, primarily 
focuses on convalescent aids 
and health-related personal 
care appliances such as mas- 
sagers, vaporizers, humidifiers, 
etc. Three years ago it added 
home blood pressure kits. In 
November 1979, it introduced 
elastic supports nationally. On 


Aug. 1, 1980, McKesson rolled 
out emergency oxygen units, 
and in the fall of 1980 it will go 
national with digital fever ther- 
mometers.

seven categories may duplicate 
the inventory of subsidiary

WASHINGTON—The “high- 
er markups rg J chains enjoy 
on their generic business is the 
engine that has begun to sub- 
stantially reduce consumer 
[prescription drug] prices,” two 
top Federal Trade Commission 
economists told critics of drug 
product selection laws. 

Moreover, while pharmacy 
margins for generic drugs are 
“currently high,” FTC econo- 
mists Robert L. Steiner and J. 
Howard Beales predicted that 
“competition among pharma- 
cists will drive them down sub- 
stantially, to the level of, say, 
private label! aspirin.” 

The strongly worded FTC de- 
fense of drug store generic pric- 
ing practices was issued in 
response to a recent front-page 
Washington Post article alleg- 
ing that D.C.-area drug chains 
and independents were price- 
gouging patients on low-cost 


generic drug versions. 

That article called “generic 
drug laws a boon—but not to 
consumers,” and suggested 
that the rash of new state prod- 
uct selection laws enacted dur- 
ing the 1970's “has provided 
only marginal savings for con- 
sumers and major profits for 
drug stores.”

recent Post survey of prescrip- 
tion pricing policies at three 
Washington-based drug 
chains—Peoples, Drugfair and 
Dart—as well as 15 indepen- 
dent pharmacies in the D.C. 
area.

VANCOUVER, Wash.—It's 
back-to-business-as-usual in 
the post-ash world of Mt. St. 
Helens, but drug stcre opera- 
tors—and consumers—are still 
casting a wary eye on the moun- 
tain 30 miles from here. 

After three eruptions in two 
months, the still-simmering vol- 
Cano is very much in everyone's 
mind. In the case of drug stores 
in the path of the first two shoot- 
ups (Vancouver, Portland, 
Idaho, Montana, and Eastern 
Washington), its been a mixed 
verdict, with long-range posi- 
tives overriding short-term 
negatives. 

The positives: zooming sales 
of surgical masks, eyedrops, air 
filters, oil filters, St. Helens-im- 
printed shirts and other sou- 
venirs. 

Negatives: store volume the 
week following each eruption 
dropped sharply. The sale of 
camping goods nose-dived. Ag- 
riculture—especially strawberry 
and raspberry fields—was hurt 
badly. And tourist business— 
front lined by convention can- 
cellations—dipped and still has 
not totally recovered.” 

“We are happy business is 
back to normal,” said Jack Phe- 
lan, president of Bi-Mart Co., a 
division of Pay 'n Save Drugs. 
Bi-Mart had two of its stores in 
Yakima, Wash. (100 miles away 
from the volcano) and 
Ellensburg (90 miles away) af- 
fected by the downpour of ash 
from the initial eruption. 

Phelan said his stores were 
closed the Sunday after the first 
explosion and operated short- 
ened hours the following day, 
but since then the two 30,000- 
sq.-ft. stores have been operat- 
ing regularly. 

He said during the week after 
the initial eruption, sales fell off 
30% compared to a norma! 
week. “There was a run on 
emergency supplies such as 
push brooms, masks, auto ac- 
cessories and wiper blades,” 
said Phelan. He said auto- 
mobile air filters were the tough- 
est items to keep in supply 
because of the numerous sku’s. 
“We carry about a total of 360 
Car filters in each store, or about 
three filters in each size. We 
sent a truck to replenish the 
stores, but some sizes of air fil-

Thrift expansion tied 
to smaller prototype 


PITTSBURGH—A new, 
scaled-down prototype and the 
decision to concentrate on ex- 
isting markets are the major ele- 
ments in Thrift Drug’s expan- 
sion drive for the near future, 
Drug Store News has learned. 

In designating key markets in 
its 21-state trading range as pri- 
ority areas for new store open- 
ings, Thrift management has 
adopted a backfilling stance, 
according to chain president 
Jim Armor. 

“Previously, we were looking 
anywhere there was a good lo- 
cation,” said vp, administration 
Bob Hannan. “But now, it is 
more practical from supervisory, 
advertising and distribution 
standpoints to fill out existing 
markets. This is our expansion 
strategy for the near term.” 

The vehicle for new stores, 
said Armor, will be the 9,400- 
sq.-ft. prototype that the chain 
launched recently in a Pitts- 
burgh suburb. Prior to the open- 
ing of this outlet, Thrift had been 
committed to two basic proto- 
types—12,000 ft. and 17,600 
ft—although the larger of the 
two had been discontinued

Fox-Vliet widens corporate structure 


OKLAHOMA CITY—Fox- 
Vliet has added two new mer- 
chandising positions to its cor- 
porate lineup and terminated its 
longstanding relationship with 
the Associated ts (AD) 
ad program in favor of its own as 
the wholesaler moves closer to 
what it terms a “total source” 
concept. 

The wholesaler’s organiza- 
tional structure now features a 
corporate general merchandise 
and sundry buyer and a corpo- 
rate health and beauty aid buy- 
er. 

Fox-Vliet, according to Wil- 
liam Tauscher, chairman and 
ceo, is seeking to position itself 
as the provider of most of the 
services and products that its 
retail accounts will need to com- 
pete with in the 1980's. This in- 
cludes a wide range of prod- 
ucts, especially general and 
sundry merchandise which in- 
dependents frequently find diffi- 
Cult to buy. 

To this end, the wholesaler 
has installed Jim Wilson, 32, as 
corporate general merchandise 
and sundry manager. He will be 
responsible for buying all gen- 
eral merchandise and sundry 
products, as well as being in 
charge of completing Fox-Vliet's 
planned product line expansion 
into the general merchandise 
area. 

In addition to Buying general 
merchandise, Wilson will be de- 
veloping promotional circulars 
for the additional lines. In the 
fall, Fox-Vliet expects to offer an 


optional four- or eight-page cir- 
cular featuring general mer- 
chandise and sundries. 

Wilson has 12 years of experi- 
ence with Shawnee Evans and 
Central States Distributors. 

Another addition to the pur- 
chasing staff is Bob Silberg who 
has joined Fox-Vliet as corpo- 
rate H&BA buyer. Silberg, 49, 

joins corporate purchasing 
manager Charlie Cruthird, and 
corporate pharmaceutical buy-

Cruthird, who until recently 
had a major role in purchasing 
H&BA, will now concentrate his 
efforts on deal and promotional 


buying and screening of items 
for Fox-Vliet'’s advertising pro- 
grams. Silberg, who will be lo- 
cated in Wichita, will be in 
charge of buying H&BA’s for all 
three of the company’s divi- 
sions. 

Silberg’s background in- 
cludes 11 years of H&BA buying 
with Milgram Food Stores Inc., a 
grocery chain in Kansas City. 

As of June 1980, Fox-Vliet ter- 
minated its agreement with 
monthly cooperative advertising 
program Associated Druggist 
and replaced AD with its own 
program designed internally 
and managed by Grant Parrott.

jand money leads to greater efficiency 


As more and more consumers take 
advantage of third-party benefits 
from Government agencies and in- 
surance companies, and as drug 
store net profit continues to shrink, 
pharmacists are being forced to find 
more efficient methods to reduce op- 
erating costs. Faced with the propo- 
sition of being buried by paperwork 
as the result of third-party benefit 
fj programs, and stricter Government 
rules on the record-keeping of pre- 
Scription medicines, some 2,000 to 
2,000 druggists may have found a 
remedy to their problem: the phar- 
macy computer system. 

Following the principles adopted 
by other retailers, modern phar- 


macy managers are seeking to keep 
a tighter control of inventories, to 
reduce the amount of time the phar- 
macist spends on clerical functions 
and are trying to increase productiv- 
ity. In the front of the drug store, 
the merchandising function has 
been streamlined with order-entry 
systems, computerized velocity re- 
ports and with electronic registers. 
For the first time, store managers 
and pharmacists are looking behind 
the pharmacy counter. 

According to one industry consul- 
tant, Judith L. King, RPH., by the 
year 1985, some 25,000 of the esti- 
mated 46,000 pharmacies in the na- 
tion will have a computer system. Of 


those that have installed systems to- 
day, most are in independent drug 
stores or small chains. For these op- 


erations, the computer is a piece of 


survival equipment as large chains 
continue to make inroads on their 
markets. 

While the major chains generally 
set the trend for the drug industry, 
in this case they haven’t, but at the 
same time they shouldn’t be consid- 
ered sleeping giants. A handful of 
major chains including Medicare- 
Glaser, Thrift, Walgreen and Pay 
Less Northwest have developed and 
installed their own in-house phar- 
macy computer systems. Revco, the 
chain with the greatest number of 


stores, has announced it will install 
Honeywell’s COMPASS system in 10 
of its units as a pilot program. Other 
major chains including Osco, Jack 
Eckerd and Rite Aid are testing 
various systems in their stores in 
preparation for chainwide systems. 

“Independents have adopted the 
systems faster because they are 
threatened by the chains and they 
recognize it as a tool of remaining 
competitive,” said Rich Turpin of 
McPike, a drug wholesaler in Kan- 
sas City, a firm that supplies a com- 
puter system. According to John 
Kocourek, national marketing man- 
ager for pharmacy systems at Hon- 
eywell, “Independents have been

about 2,000 to 2,500 
pharmacy comput- 
ers in operation in the 
nation, and the number 
is growing. Independent 
drug stores far outnum- 
ber the drug chains with 
working systems. 


more aggressive in this area because 
there is generally one man that 
makes the decision on whether to

the investment is much less.” He 
said most large chains have steering 
committees that will make the deci- 
sion that will cost the chain millions 


and test them in their stores and 
compare them. This process can 


take years.

computerization in drug stores is the 
introduction of third-party benefit 
programs, of which there are more 
than 350 in the nation. According to

MAGAZINE: 


he impetus for 
the expansion of 
pharmacy com- 
puter systems 
came in the early 70’s 
when Federal and state 
governments and insur- 
ance companies offered 
third-party reimburse- 
ment for prescription 
medicine. Up till then, 
the druggist was able to 
cope with the paper flow 
that passed before him. 


T 


’ 


@ finding the appropriate claim 

form 

® completing the claim form 

® correcting and completing re- 

jected claims 

© researching rejected claims 

® reconciling vouchers against 

claims 

® maintaining accounts receivables 
Almost all of these clerical tasks 

can be performed by a computer. In 

addition, on the routine dispensing 

of prescriptions, the computer has 

shown it is capable of printing la- 

bels, doing drug/drug interactions, 

maintaining patient profiles, alert- 

ing pharmacists to allergies or dis- 

eases a patient might have, keeping 

price updates, and it can give the 

pharmacist an instant list of suitable 


generic substitutions and prices. 


By relieving the pharmacist of 
many of the time-consuming tasks, 
the Rx terminai system allows him 
more time to manage his business, 
fill a greater number of prescrip- 
tions and allows him to spend more 
time consulting with his customers 
or to perform clinical functions. 

Over the years as demand of the 
pharmacist’s time has increased, the 
industry has turned to support per- 
sonnel to relieve him of some of the 
pressures. To help the pharmacists, 
the industry has added bookkeep- 
ers, clerks, typists and pushed hard 


DRUG STORE NEWS, September 1, 1980 


A nationwide study revealed that pharmacists were performing 16 clerical tasks, all of which can be performed by a computer today. 


for pharmacy technicians. 

Even more important is the fact 
that by going tape-to-tape with 
third-party carriers, a retailer can 
increase the accuracy of his submis- 
sions, reduce rejections, and save 
himself a great deal of time and 
money in the process. 

One chain pharmacy director 
noted that after his system went 
tape-to-tape with a major carrier, 
that the pharmacy terminal system 
“had very nearly paid for itself.” 

Thrift Drug, for example, with its 
PHS system, is tape-to-tape with 
New Jersey Medicaid, Pennsylva- 
niaS Pharmacy Assistance for the 
Aged, and PAID. 

But the problem is that these were 
only interim measures, because 
while they were saving the pharma- 
cist time, it was still costing him a lot 
of money in additional pay roll. 
These remedies over the last 20 
years only temporarily arrested the 
problem, but did not provide the 
cure. 

However, today with the avail- 
ability of a variety of computers both 
stand-alone and on-line, the phar- 
macist has the ability to act once 
again as a true professional. Com- 
puters are now available from more 
than two dozen suppliers at dif- 
ferent prices. 

A number of individuals, recog- 


nizing a need in the industry, have 
jumped on the bandwagon and have 
created the overnight emergence of 
several pharmacy computer system 
companies. And almost equally as 
rapid is the disappearance of some of 
these systems’ providers. 

Large chains that have the finan- 
cial ability to develop their own in- 
house programs have been able to 
bypass the packaged systems on the 
market. The cost of developing and 
implementing an in-house system 
runs about $5 million, according to 
industry sources. “We couldn’t find 
any system suited to our needs,” 
said Gary Praderelli, director of 
management information systems 
at Walgreen, a chain that developed 
its Intercom system. 

“We believe we have the Cadillac 
system of the industry,” explained 
Janice Meikle, manager of Personal 
Health Service, the Thrift Drug in- 
house system. 

But, if you don’t have an extra $5 
million to start and develop your 
own system and you still want a 
pharmacy computer system, one 
can be installed for as low as about 
$500 per month. While you won’t 
have the luxury of doing everything 
the way you have been in a pre- 
packaged system, the time and 
money saved should offset the cost of 
doing things a little differently.

The following is a list of drug 
chains that have developed their 
own pharmacy computer systems

the next few months so that by the 
end of 1981 each of the nearly 100

hooked up to the on-line system. 
Medicom, started in 1975, is also 
being marketed to outsiders, but so 
far none have been sold. 

@ Pay Less Northwest. This drug 
chain has completed the hooking up 
of all of its newly acquired Pay Less 
California stores. There are 150 
stores linked to the on-line system. 


The in-house system, which has no 
name, is also being used by two in- 
dependents. While the chain is not 
actively soliciting outside subscri- 
bers, it will accommodate those in- 
terested in joining the chain’s com- 
puter system. 

@ Revco D.S. Inc. This is the latest 
chain to announce the introduction 
of a pilot pharmacy computer pro- 
gram. The plan calls for the installa- 
tion of 10 COMPASS units by the 
end of the year. The first unit is 
being put in this month. 

Revco is using the COMPASS sys- 
tem that is from Honeywell, and 
General Computer Corp., a Revco 
subsidiary since early 1979. General 


Computer has spent 10 years devel- 
oping the software for the program. 
Since May ’79, General Computer 
has teamed up with Honeywell 
which is building the hardware and 
marketing and servicing the system 
nationally. 

Revco plans to install systems in 
most of its stores in the next few 
years as part of its program to 1m- 
prove productivity and customer 
service. “We’re ready to move ahead 
with this as soon as we can thor- 
oughly document the profit contri- 
butions that we believe can be rea- 
lized,” said H. Scott Leeseberg,

program for this system can be customized to meet the specific needs 
of the retailer. In some cases, depending on the capacity of the com- 
puter memory, a stand-alone can be modified using remote terminals in 
close proximity to the CPU to create a mini-network. 

The only drawback to this system is the slightly higher cost than an 
on-line system. But prices for stand-alone systems have been dropping 
as computer technology and manufacturing improve. Most vendors 
emphasize full ownership rather than leased agreements. 


Unlike the independent system, some functions for this system must be 
handled through a central processing unit after store hours, although it 


can be programmed for a wider variety of functions. Again, expense is a 
factor with the stand-alone dependent system. 


A large group of on-line stores can communicate with one central 
processing unit through CRT of printer terminals, on a time-shared or 
wait-your-turn basis. Costs on this system are low, as the vendor 
generally leases terminals and CPU costs are shared by all users. All 
functions are handled at one source. Time sharing though can some- 
times mean slow response time, especially during peak usage hours. 


A popular system among large chains, in-store terminals are linked to a 
central computer that is in communication with a regional mainframe 
computer operated by the vendor. Any number of stores can go on-line, 
and costs, again, are low through leased arrangements. All services, as 
with a time-shared system, are performed at one source. 

Programs on this system are pretty much fixed, and there are few

MAJOR COMPUTER DISTRIBUTORS 


The following is a list and descrip- 
tion of the 14 major pharmacy com- 
puter distributors and the systems 
they offer (each has more than 30

1. ApotheTech. This pharmacy 
Systems company currently only 
services California. As an alterna-

ApotheTech units may be purchased 
for $26,540 plus a monthly service 
fee of $240. 

Special features include a three 
section printer that prints the pre- 
scription label, Medicaid form and 
also a receipt all at the same time, 
eliminating the time and labor in- 
volved in “batching” the forms at the 
end of the day to check for accuracy. 
Files are alphabetized with this sys- 
tem. 

2. AutoScript. This system, avail-

configuration, is available in all 50 
states. The computer unit (CPU) is 
capable of supporting up to six ter- 
minals at the same time. There are 
systems installed in Massachusetts, 
New York, Connecticut, New 
Jersey, West Virginia and Kentucky.

LATE NEWS 


GRAY DRUG STORES INC. reported a net loss of $911,000 for the 
first quarter, ended Aug. 2. In the comparable quarter last year, 
net income totaled $648,000 on a LIFO basis. Sales in the first 
quarter of fiscal 1981, for the drug and discount store operations 
combined, rose 6.7% to $109.6 million, while sales at this time last 
year amounted to $102.7 million. 


MALL DRUGS, based in Holbrook, Mass., is about to launch its 
first drug/food mini-combination outlet in Springfield, Mass., 
under the Sav-A-Lot banner. The convenience food mix, according 
to Mall president Ed Sussman, will be granted approximately 
one-third of 9,000 sq. ft. of selling space, while the “drug” portion 
will resemble the three Sav-A-Lot box stores already in operation.

macy, more may be added to other Byerly outlets in the future.

Chains rev up remodeling 


DRSN ROUNDUP 

Drug chains, faced witin grow- 
ing demands to maintain sales 
and earnings growth with a re- 
duced number of new store 
openings, are currently acceler- 
ating the rate of store remodel- 
ings and redecorations. 

In the words of one executive, 
the question boils down to the 
fact that “paint is cheaper than 
property.” 

A survey of leading chains by 
Drug Store News found the 
range of such remodelings and 
redecorations is as broad as the 
stores involved, from a low of 
$8,500 for Walgreen Co.'s basic 
“decor package” to $200,000 
for Pay 'n Save Corp.'s major 
overhaul, which includes adding 
square footage. 

According to Sheldon W. 
Fantle, president and chief ex- 


ecutive officer at Peoples Drug 
Stores of Alexandria, Va., the 
“one reason why Peoples and 
others are remodeling is that 
new stores aren't coming on as 
fast because developers have 
been holding back due to the 
high cost of [real estate] financ- 
ing.” 

Since Peoples grew by ac- 
quisition, Fantle pointed out, its 
store size varies greatly, but on 
the average it spends about 
$50,000 per store on remodel- 
ing. The results also vary in 
magnitude, but not direction. 
“There is an immediate in- 
crease in volume and bottom- 
line profit, even though you have 
increased depreciation,” Fantle 
stated. Although it's “difficult to 
quantify, in volume, some stores 
increase by 10%, and some as

Drugfair is 
evaluating 
dental care 


ALEXANDRIA, Va.—Top 
Drugfair officials are watching 
Peoples in-store dental clinics 
closely with an eye toward 
launching a competing opera- 
tion in the Washington, D.C. 
area. 

In a statement acknowledg- 
ing the chain's interest in dental 
care facilities, Drugfair presi- 
dent Milton Ellsberg stressed 
that no final decision has been 
reached on the plan. But at the 
same time, he confirmed spec- 
ulation that the Virginia-based 
drug chain was indeed “evaluat- 
ing’ dental clinics. 

Peoples, Drugfair's chief rival 
in the hotly competitive Wash- 
ington Rx market, uncorked its 
string of in-store dental care op- 
erations over a year ago, and 
Currently operates three such 
units: one in southwest D.C. 
and two in Maryland. 

Each of the three Peoples 
units, which charge rates signif- 
icantly below those of private, 
office-based dentists in the 
area, are reportedly drawing an 
average of more than 600 pa- 
tients daily. 

lf Drugfair follows Peoples 
into the dentistry field, the chain 
may find itself in no better than 
third place in its own hometown 
market. National general mer- 
chandise giant Montgomery 
Ward has already announced 
plans to expand its dentistry op- 
erations to the Washington-Bal- 
timore market with four clinics 
later this year. 

Ward currently operates eight 
such units in other parts of the 
country. 

Several discount store 
chains—including Korvettes 
and Times Square Stores—are 
operating dentistry clinics in the 
New York City area, while a 
number of similar facilities have 
already gained a foothold on the 
West Coast.

WORCESTER, Mass.—Lin-

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 15, 1980 


Skaggs Drug stores in southern 
California vary in layout and 
scope. Most, however, follow 
this pattern: 

There is a regular gondola 
home (minimum 15 ft.) for un- 
sold ad items. Ad items start on 
endcaps—two to five per store. 

Ad items are first given a full 
end. After the ad period is over, 
the unsold merchandise is 
grouped with other carryover 
items on the same end. After 
another week or two, unsold 
end merchandise is transferred 
to its regular gondola home. 

Depending on consumer ac- 
ceptibility, the item can be 
priced two ways on the end: (1) 
at the ad price until it sells down; 
(2) or it can go back to the regu- 
lar price after the ad period.

REGS PUT THE SQUEEZE 
ON PHARMACY PROFITS 


hain and community 

pharmacies have been 

inundated with new laws 

and regulations over the 

years and, although the 
pace shows signs of slowing, this 
past year was no exception. 

States have mandated practice 
areas as diverse as drug product se- 
lection and patient consultation In an 
effort to contain costs, yet guaran- 
tee the delivery of quality profes- 
sional services. 

Despite these twin goals, a se- 
rious question remains unanswered: 
Can retail pharmacy continue to 


prosper in light of the added costs 
associated with increased Govern- 
ment and private third-party in- 
volvement, especially when coupled 
with a sputtering economy? 

To answer this question Drug 
Store News has examined trends in 
retail pharmacy and summarized 
state legislation affecting the profes- 
sion. 

Retail trends 

Pharmacy departments in both 
chain and independent drug stores 
generated $7.8 billion in Rx sales 
during 1979, an increase of 9% over 
1978, according to data released by 


S Ltd., an Ambler, Pa.-based 
> et research supplier. 

Growth at the retail level traces to 
increases in the price of an average 
prescription which stem from hikes 
in the Rx department’ cost of goods 
sold. 

Chain and independent phar- 
macies each recorded marginal 
gains in the number of scripts filled, 
yet prescription prices are increas- 
ing at a rate of 6.5% per annum ac- 
cording to the latest Firestone drug 
price index. 

Chains 
Chain drug prescription depart- 


ment performance trends for the 
first half of 1980 reveal that scripts 
have increased to 136 per day per 
outlet and average daily Rx receipts 
now tot .1 $993 for this area. 

Executives in the chain industry 
state the reasons for limited growth 
in the numbers of scripts trace to 
multiple causes: a deep recession, 
fewer patient visits to physicians  of- 
fices, greater consumer reliance on 
self-medication, and more units 
(tabs/caps, ete.) being dispensed per 
script. 

“Indeed, the jump in average Rx 
prices to consumers is misleading,” 


o far, 1980 repre- 


year for Federal 
as well as state 
programs affecting phar- 
macy,’ says Robert 
Bolger, president of 
NACDS.

say Firestone researchers. “It fails 
to take into account the trend to- 
ward larger prescription sizes being 
dispensed through the nation’s phar- 
macies.” 

Twenty years ago the average pre- 
scription retailed for $3.22—exactly 
half the $6.44 average Rx price in 
1978, and well under 50% of last 
year’s record $7.03 average, accord- 
ing to the study. 

Since 1960, however, Rx sizes have 
been increasing steadily, and when 
this factor is taken into account, 
average retail prescription prices 
(on a tablet-by-tablet basis) have in- 
creased less than 30% over the past 
two decades, according to Fire- 
stone’ figures. 

The Pharmaceutical Manufactur- 
ers Association, which sponsors the 
annual Firestone drug price study, 
put it slightly differently: “Adjusting 
for size,” PMA said, “it now costs 
$4.18 to buy the same amount of 
medication that was dispensed: for 
$3.22 in 1960.” | 

The new Firestone figures also 
contradict earlier Government fig- 
ures from the Labor Department's 
Bureau of Labor Statistics indicat- 
ing that the rate of inflation for pre- 
scription drugs at the retail level 
softened somewhat last vear. 

In contrast to the B.L.S. num- 
bers, which indicate that consumer 
Rx prices rose 7.3% last year (vs. 
8.2% in 1978), Firestone maintains 
that retail prescription charges 
climbed 6.5% during 1979 (vs. only 
2.6% the year before). 

Firestone uses a different “mar- 
ket basket” of Rx products than the 
Government to measure price 
changes, and typically his figures 
show smaller year-to-year fluctua- 
tions than the corresponding Gov- 
ernment numbers. 

On the other hand, the new Fire- 
stone index shows that manufac- 


_ turer drug prices rose at a slower 


rate than retail prices, and less 


| quickly than in 1978. 


Trends 

Specifically, the latest PMA-Fire- 
stone figures indicate that prices 
charged by drug manufacturers 
climbed only 5.2% last year, vs. 5.4% 
in 1978. Curiously, the B.L.S. re- 
ports show exactly the opposite 
trend with pharmaceutical manufac- 
turer prices rising 7.1% in 1979, vs. 
5.2% the year before. 

Both sets of figures, however, are 
sharply lower than the Govern- 
ment’s reported changes for all prod- 
ucts in the producer and consumer 
price increases last year. 

Overall, consumer prices climbed 
12.9%. 

Not all prescription products 
posted price increases last year, 
however, the PMA figures indicate. 
The average price of a penicillin pre- 
scription, for example, dropped 
2.8% during 1979, while average 
manufacturer prices charged for all 
analgesics, anti-infectives and 
cough and cold remedies also de- 
clined last year.

Oral contraceptives experienced 
the largest price run up during 1979, 
primarily as a result of stiff manu- 
facturer price hikes. Producer 
prices for these products jumped 
23.7% last year, according to Fire- 
stone, while the average pharmacy 
charge for an OC prescription 
climbed 21.1%. 

The accompanying table repre- 
sents Firestone’s projected manu- 
facturer and retailer price shifts 
from key drug categories during 
1979. 

According to the report, since 
1960 diuretics, anti-infectives, and 
hormones have experienced the 
greatest increases in Rx size (more 
than 90%), while antiarthritics, vi- 
tamins, and antiobesity drugs have 
had the smallest increase (40% or 
less) in Rx size. 

Quantity dispensed is related to 
the price of an average prescription, 
which in chains climbed slightly over 
1% to $7.30 during the first half of 
1980 compared to $7.20 during 1979, 
and $6.40 in 1978 as inflationary 
pressures continue to impact on the 

tX area. 

Per cent share of new and refill 
scripts remain relatively unchanged 


with new scripts accounting for 53% 

of the total and refills accounting for 

the balance in a typical chain outlet. 
Third-party plans 

Another factor of major concern to 
chain professional directors and in- 
dependent pharmacy owners alike is 
the growth of third-party Rx plans. 

According to Decision Data, a 
market research supplier, third- 
party plans now account for 19% of 
all seripts filled in retail pharmacies. 
Commercial third-party plans ac- 
count for 15% and Medicaid scripts 
account for 4%. 

“The figures vary from state to 
state, but on the average almost one 
seript in five is paid for by a third 
party,” say Decision Data analysts. 

Pointing toward the future, a 
chain exee from Michigan says, “I 
suspect we will reach a point where 
most prescriptions will be dispensed 
via a third-party arrangement.” 

Another chain vice president of 
professional affairs claims there are 
new third-party plans coming on 
stream every day in California. 
While a director of pharmacy from 
an Ohio-based chain indicates that 
the chain’s third-party Rx volume is 
growing at the rate of 15% per an- 
num. 

This can create problems because 
third-party programs tend to create 
cash flow problems when they make 
up a significant portion of a phar- 
macy’ overall script volume. 

Execs from the Midwest predict 
1980-81 will be the “year of the 
Health Maintenance Organization.” 
Although HMOs aren’t a major fac- 
tor now, he predicts they will be in 
the future. 

Apparently existing HMOs are 
now considering adding prescription 
drug benefits to their programs. 
Chains are being asked to provide 
Rx service through existing outlets

Cost justification 

Pharmacy computers for an Rx 
department are generally cost-justi- 
fied when the outlet is doing at least 
100 scripts a day. “But this figure can 
be misleading,” says an administra- 
tor. “When third-party scripts com- 
prise a large portion of a pharmacy’ 


total Rx volume, this figure can drop 


10% to 15%.” 

Volume purchase plans (VPP), a 
system whereby a state owns some 
Rx inventory and places it ina Medi- 
caid pharmacy, also has chain and 
independent pharmacists con- 
cerned. The pharmacy would use 
the state’s inventory when dispens- 
ing selected Medicaid scripts and 
the store would be reimbursed with 
a dispensing fee. 

A VPP was originally proposed in 
California, but was killed in 1977 by 
state legislators because the plan 
was tied to a 30¢ incentive fee to 
pharmacists. The fee was supposed 
to encourage pharmacists to sub- 
stitute VPP drugs on Rxs written 
for drugs from a state list. 

The plan is now up for recon- 
sideration in California. Apparently

the dominant sales position among 
nonchain retail drug outlets.

volume of $391,000 per outlet, up

Three main factors have contrib-

According to Car! H. Deiner, edi-

are 10t implementing price in- 
creases as rapidly as possible.” 

Indeed, the results of a survey of 
community pharmacists conducted 
by Drug Store News indicates that 
pharmacists are reluctant to pass on 
price increases to consumers 
quickly and Rxmen often prefer to 
wait a month or two to do so. 

A second factor traces to a pricing 
schedule that reduces per cent gross 
margin on high-ticket maintenance 
drugs in order to stay competitive. 

Another factor centers on third- 
party scripts. In order to reduce 
costs through less frequent dispens- 
ing fees, third-party administrators 
push for greater Rx quantities. Asa 
result more medication is dispensed 
against a flat fee resulting in more 
medication for patients, reduced 
costs to the third-party insurance 
plan, and decreases in margin for 
the pharmacy. 

Says Alan J. Vogenberg, owner of 
Windsor pharmacy in Levittown, 
Pa., “Another problem created by 
third-party programs is a waiting 
period of six to seven weeks before 
payment is received.” 

Independent pharmacists also in- 
dicate that generic pharmaceuticals 
will continue to play a role in phar- 
macy practice. 

“In many states,” says a pharmacy 
owner, “MAC and a formulary are 
forcing the generic issue.”

BURTON C. PERFIT 


CLEARWATER, Fla.—Bur- 
ton C. (Bud) Perfit has been 
named president of the Eckerd 
Drug Co.—a newly created 
post—in a move to strengthen 
management within the Jack 
Eckerd Corporation's drug divi- 
sion, its largest retail subsidiary. 

Perfit, 51, had served as se- 
nior vp-marketing for the 1,068- 
unit chain for the past five years. 

In a related management 
shift, Leslie D. Reagin Ill, 36, 
formerly senior vp-store opera- 
tions, has been appointed ex- 
ecutive vp of the drug division, 
another new post. 

Perfit and Reagin will be re- 
sponsible for all drug store oper- 
ations, reporting to Stewart 
Turley, JEC's cnairman and 
pres:dejiii. 

In explaining the new man- 


LESLIE D. REAGIN 


Perfit named pres. 
of Eckerd Drug 


agement structure, Perfit said 
that JEC’s drug division had 
been “lean in top manage- 
ment.” 

JByrons department stores 
and Eckerd’s Apparel, the two 
other major retailing arms of the 
corporation, are both managed 
by chief executives reporting to 
Turley. 

“This move further estab- 
lishes the drug store business 
as an independent entity vis-a- 
vis the corporation,” Perfit said. 

Perfit also noted that the new, 
well-defined management sys- 
tem within each JEC subsidiary 
would “position the company to 
acquire other specialty retailers 
over the next five years,” a strat- 
egy that JEC has been following 
over the past few years.

K mart enters dental area 
with 3 units in Denver 


DENVER—Low-cost family 
dental centers have been 
opened in three K mart stores 
here in the past few months. 

The new clinics, located 
alongside the pharmacy depart- 
ments in each of the three 
K mart outlets, offer general 
dental services at prices about 
10% to 20% lower than those 
normally charged by private 
dentists in the area. 

Business has grown rapidly at 
the clinics since the first one, in 
the suburb of Arvada, opened 
on July 25, according to a den- 
tist who is an associate at one of 
the centers. 

“We're seeing an average of 
100 patients a week,” the dentist 
said. “We used to take walk-in 
patients. Now they have to 
make appointments at least two 
weeks in advance.” 

Each of the clinics is staffed 
by three dentists who work on a 
part-time basis. The staff of

“operatories,” where the den-

the practice of each center 
grows, the space will be ex-

in size at each store. 

The clinics have been getting 
referrals from some area spe- 
Cialists, according to the dentist. 
They, in turn, refer patients with

to the same specialists. These

50.

NEW YORK—Initial reports 
from drug chains indicate there 
has been no drop in tampon

Drug Administration's warning 
that use of tampons may be 
linked to toxic shock syndrome.

agreement with the F.D.A. 
launched an unprecedented 
media blitz outlining the prob- 
lems of toxic shock syndrome 
and details of how consumers 
can get a refund for Rely tam- 
pons. The four-week national 
consumer education campaign 
started Oct. 6 and is being car- 
ried in newspapers and on tele- 
vision and radio stations. 

Chain drug retailers said 
Procter & Gamble’s voluntary 
withdrawal of its Rely tampon 
has resulted in women switch- 
ing to other brands of tampons, 
rather than to sanitary napkins. 

Tampon products such as 
Tampax, Playtex, Johnson & 
Johnson's 0.b. and Kimberly- 
Clark's Kotex have picked up 
sales by oe the void left by 
the removal of Rely. 

The Center for Disease Con- 
trol stated women can reduce 
the risk of developing toxic 
shock syndrome, a sometimes 
fatal form of blood poisoning, by 
avoiding the use of tampons. 
The Center said the disease is 
rare when tampons are not 
used. A high percentage of the 
approximately 299 cases and 
25 deaths reported have been 
associated with a single brand, 
Rely The Center has also cau- 
tioned that toxic shock syn- 
drome has occurred among 
users of all brands of tampens.

NACDS speakers 
give high marks 
to health care 


DENVER—The expanding 
role that drug stores are playing 
in health care was the focus of 
several talks at the recent phar- 
maceutical conference spon- 


sored by the National Associa- 
tion of Chain Drug Stores. 
“Diversified health care can 
help chain pharmacy depart- 
ments preserve their profes- 


sional image by projecting a 


very strong, very visible health 
care image,” Roy White, editor 
of Drug Store News, told phar- 
macists gathered at the five-day 
conference here. 

Increasingly, White said, drug 
stores are venturing into such 
areas as dental and optical 
care, hearing aid centers anc 
convalescent and sickroom 
supplies. 

By doing so, he said? they re- 
inforce “the positive health care 
image already created by pre- 
scriptions.” 

White noted another impor- 
tant reason for widening the 
health care image: “Other 
health care areas beyond phar- 
macy can be a pathway,” he 
said, “to the enhancement and 
enlargement of [the pharmacy 
department's] traffic, sales and 
profits.” 


But White emphasized three 
important points that chains 
must consider before undertak- 
ing an expansion into diversified 
areas of health care: 

e Acommitment must be made 
to the concept 

e Service and quality have to 
be emphasized. 

@ Management must be devel- 
oped to handle the new depart- 
ments. 

Picking up on the theme of 


expanding health care roles for 


pharmacists and drug stores 


were Beatrice Adreon, R.Ph., of 


Pharmacy Counseling Services 
Inc., and Berkeley V. Bennett, 


partner of Washington Counsel/ 


Medicine and Health. 

Adreon, whose Arlington, 
Va.-based service provides 
ongoing medication monitoring 
and counseling, gave several 
pointers to drug stores consid- 
ering the addition of such a ser- 
vice. 

Less austere setting 

For one thing, she said, “pa- 
tients have clearly demon- 
strated that they are more com- 
fortable, relaxed and receptive 
inaless austere setting.” There- 
fore, she added, the office 
should somewhat resemble a 


BGs 


Roy White 


family living room or den. 

Adreon suggested that the 
dispensary and counseling 
areas should be “separated but 
not totally isolated. This sepa- 
rate delineation would help 
create the proper atmosphere 
for effective counseling.” 

She also talked about the im- 
portance of a library to her 
counseling service. “It has be- 
come indispensible,” she said, 
“both as an aid and a byproduct; 
that is, my library is my data 
collector for both immediate use 
and future research.” 

Adreon also had a cautionary 
note for pharmacists whose 
chains have computer networks 
linking stores. In starting a 
counseling service, she said,

Revco acquires eight 


stores in Kentucky 


CLEVELAN®&—Revco DS 
Inc. has expanded its Kentucky 
operations with the acquisition 
of eight Sav-Rite drug stores op- 
erated by Dale Sales Inc., a ser- 
vice merchandiser located in 
Evansville, Ind. 

The expansion of the drug 
store giant ties in with a projec- 
tion made by its president, 
Sidney Dworkin, that company 
sales would double within the 
next five years. 

Dworkin told shareholders at 
Revco’s annual meeting last 
month that by 1985 the chain 
would surpass $2 billion in 
sales. It has taken Revco 24 
years to reach the $1 billion 
mark. | 

The eight new Kentucky 
stores fit in well with Revco's op- 
erations, according to vp Marvin 
Solganik. They average 8,000- 
9,000 sq. ft., and are thus equiv- 
alent in size to the newest drug 
stores the chain is building to- 
day. 

The newly acquired stores 
are located in Hopkinsville (two 
outlets), Georgetown, Hender- 
son, Madisonville, Murray and 
Somerset. 

At the chain's annual meet- 
ing, Dworkin reported a 17.8% 
sales increase to $1.09 billion 
for the year ending May 31, 
1980.

AD unveils 3 major new programs 


DURANGO, Colo.—Associ- 
ated Druggists, a voluntary 
group of 2,000 drug retailers, 
has unveiled a new multimedia 
advertising campaign, its first 
line of private label products, 
and a merchandising-manage- 
ment training program—each 
designed primarily to give the 
group more national exposure. 

The new programs were pre- 
sented for the first time at Asso- 
ciated Druggists recent annual 
meeting, held here before a 
gathering of 150 AD whole- 
salers, manufacturers and 
guests. 

Like other AD programs, 
these new packages represent 
an attempt to close the gap be- 
tween independent and chain 
operator, by supplying the sin- 
gle-unit druggist with the buying 
power, advertising strength and 
consumer recognition that 
chains enjoy. 

The foundation of AD’s latest 
offerings is a group in-store and 
external advertising plan called 
AD/ID, in which clusters of inde- 
pendents in the same market 
areas group together for a con- 
tinuous chain-type media cam- 
paign under the Associated 
Druggists logo. 

Independents who join AD/ID 
receive lighted outdoor signs 
featuring the AD logo, with a 


blank panel for individual store 
names. They also take part in 
group print, radio and TV adver- 
tising under the Associated 
Druggists umbrella, and mer- 
chandise their stores with an 
every day low-price concept, 
using AD’s Circle of Savings in- 
store materials. 
20-store test area 

Associated Druggists first 
launched the program as a test 
last March in 20 Birmingham, 
Ala., stores, all serviced by 
wholesaler Walker Drug. 

Robert Blackshear, an AD co- 
ordinator, worked with the Bir- 
mingham stores and Walker to 
help set up TV and radio ad 
schedules, in addition to select- 
ing special sale items with re- 
gional appeal. 

The Birmingham group runs 
two print ads each month—the 
first being the traditional Associ- 
ated Druggists monthly ad, the 
second featuring the select, 
special merchandise, including 
several food items like potato 
chips and soda. | 

In addition, the group uses 
25-40 TV and radio ‘spots per 
month. AD produced both video 
and radio commercials and 
each spot features three to five 
different store names and ad- 
dresses. 

To furthur enhance their 


chain image, the Birmingham 
stores were encouraged to shop 
competing chain druggists and 
set up their own discount pricing 
structures. The stores also took 
a group ad in the local Yellow 
Pages—complete with the AD 
logo—that lists each unit as an 
AD store. 

“The group even ran one ad 
that billed it as the biggest chain 
in Birmingham,” said Barry 
Downing, AD board chairman. 

Each AD/ID retailer in Bir- 
mingham paid a one-time fee of 
$1,000, which included the out- 
door sign installation, plus 
$450/month for the ongoing me- 


dia programs. 

But Downing emphasized 
that costs for the package in 
other markets would vary. 

“Stores getting into the pro- 
gram now would simply have to 
buy the lighted sign for $500 
with installation,” he said. “The 
monthly costs would probably 
vary from as low as $100 to 
$700.” 

independents sign up 

Since the Birmingham experi- 
ment, eight independents in the 
Texarkana, Tex., area—via 
wholesaler Walsh-Lumpkin— 
have also signed on the pro-

ALEXANDRIA, Va.—In a 
move to further standardize the 
distribution of ey aretrsing J for 
its retail divisions, Peoples Drug 
has named Nicholas Simon and 
Richard Schuman regional 
group vice presidents at a 
shareholders meeting here. 

Both men will report to Peo- 
ples’ president and ceo, 
Sheldon W. Fantle. 

Simon, formerly group vp of 
the Reed Division, headquar- 
tered in Atlanta, now heads up 
the Reed, Lane and Haag divi- 
sions, which encompass more 
than 200 retail drug outlets. 

Simon came to ples eight 
years ago as director of opera- 
tions. He was appointed group 
vp for the Reed division in 1977.

Reed Division's operations, until 
his appointment to group vp. 

Stephen Schuman, former 
group vp of the Lane Division, 
has also been promoted. He 
now serves as corporate vp in

senior officer's responsibility for 
new programs and future inno-

for corporate marketing strat-

cant by the departure of Al

been named vp, secretary and

appointments completes a ma-

and Arnold Bussey, group vp for 
the Haag Division, will now re-

NUMBERS, BUT IT HASN'T BEEN EASY 


A slowdown in the rate of shop- 
ping center development, due to the 
high cost of construction capital, has 
dented but not daunted the pace of 
new-store expansion in the chain 
drug store sector. Plans for the cur- 
rent fiscal year, in fact, are even 
more aggressive than those ex- 
ecuted last year. 

These are the conclusions of a 
Drug Store News survey of the top 
25 drug chains, presently operating 
some 9,256 retail outlets, or nearly 
half of the entire ‘industry. 

In the last complete fiscal year, 
these chains launched no fewer than 
628 new units, for a growth rate of 
7.4%. In the current fiscal year, thev 
are slated to throw out the welcome 


mat in 731 locations—an increase of 
8.0%. 


The top four chains by number of 
stores—-Reveo, Eckerd, Rite Aid 
and Walgreen—alone spawned 312 
new units, for a gain of nearly 9.0%. 

But it hasn’t been easy, chain 
execs agree. 

Developers out of funds 

“Developers have really shut 
down, as a result of the high interest 
rates on construction money,” says 
Dave Eisenberg, vp/marketing for 
the Virginia-headquartered Peoples 
Drug operation. “We have even seen 
delaying tactics on projects already 
under way. And because of this foot- 
dragging, we were limited to 25 new 
store openings in the last year. 

“We wanted to open 15 stores last 
year,” says Milton Elsberg, presi- 
dent and ceo of the Washington, 
D.C.-area Drugfair chain. “We were 


only able to open eight. With build- 
ing costs and méaey costs, loca- 
tions—I mean good locations—are 
not turning up as they have in the 
past.” 

“We have been unable to line up 
new store sites for 1981,” reports Bill 
Harrison Sr., chairman of the Ken- 
tucky-based Taylor Drug company. 
“We’re not dragging our heels, ei- 
ther. It’s the developers. With con- 
struction capital costing them as 
much as 3% above the prime rate, 
they’re having their problems.” 

“It seems more difficult than ever 
to find viable, new sites,” observes 
Edward Habegger, vp/properties 
and real estate for Gray Drug in 
Cleveland, Ohio. “We have not seen 
the ready flow of traditional strip 
center development.” 


Nevertheless, says Habegger, 
Gray has been able to keep its ex- 
pansion plans on track. 

“You have to develop more sites on 
your own,” he points out, “and you 
have to work a little harder. It’s 
times like these that invite the inge- 
nuity of the entrepreneur.” 

Slower openings 

At Rite Aid, the entrepreneurial 
plan of attack has included the con- 
struction of “a few more freestand- 
ing units, in densely populated 
areas,” according to chairman Alex 
Grass. “We have had to be more ag- 
gressive, but we are getting the 
numbers we are looking for. We 
planned to open 80 stores this year,” 
says Grass, “and at the midway 
point, we have opened 38.” 

Jim Armor, president of Thrift

Drug, is also looking out for down- 
town locations as part of his expan- 
sion scheme. “I would strongly 
consider urban locations in Pitts- 
burgh and Philadelphia,” says Ar- 
mor. “I think that urban locations 
are feasible for us at this time.” 

In some areas, though, the cost of 
going downtown can be prohibitive. 

“Rates in the D.C. area are astro- 
nomical,” reports Eisenberg of Peo- 
ples. “To develop a store now, you 
would have to pay $20 to $25 per 
square foot—thank goodness we 
have been in those sites awhile now.” 

By contrast, says Eisenberg, loca- 
tions in the D.C. suburbs can be ob- 
tained for less than $10 per foot, and 
in Peoples’ rural trading areas, costs 
can go as low as $4.50. 

Mall costs staggering 

“In New England, I would say 
that mall locations are the best loca- 
tions,” maintains Rick Weinberg, 
president of Rix Corp., a Massachu- 
setts-based operator of drug stores 
and leased departments. “But those 
locations start at $10 and go up— 
way up. With a store of any size, the 
cost is staggering.” 

in neighborhood strip centers, 
however, costs can drop to only $4a 
square foot, says Weinberg. 

In Texas, Dean Groussman, presi- 
dent of Skillern’s, also feels the heat 
of competition for prime sites. 
“Texas is a growth area, and there 
are more people looking for loca- 
tions,” he observes. “In addition, 
the retailer is getting more sophisti- 
cated about site selection, because of 
rising prices. He can’t take a chance 
on waiting too long for a return on 
his investment. As a result, the best 
locations are more difficult than ever 
to get.” 

The new Skillern’s marketing 
team aims to continue searching for 
sites in “bedroom communities,” 
where the chain has traditionally 
been strong. Although costs usually 
fall into the neighborhood of $8 to 
$10 a square foot in these areas, the 
Skillern’s operation reports that it is 
finding and signing leases in the 
$5.50 to $6 range. 

Malone & Hyde, headquartered in 
Memphis, Tenn., finds that even 
when the sites are available, the 
costs can be too high. 

“We are having our share of prob- 
lems with developers,” attests Ben 
Walton, director of market research 
for the 160-store retail operation. 
“They are definitely slowing down, 
and they are also getting a little out 
of line in terms of the volume per- 
centages they’re asking. In some 
cases, they have just encroached too 
far on potential profitability, and 
we’ve told them to forget it.” 

However, says Walton, the com- 
pany’s needs for internal growth are 
not as demanding as those of larger 
operations. 

“We have a smaller base than an 
Eckerd or a Revco,” he points out, 


New store construction has been delayed by shopping center developers.
