a Bh. 


“so we don’t have to come up with as 
many new locations—although 
we're planning at least 20 new stores 
in the coming year. One factor that 
has worked in our favor, is that with 
the slowdown among developers has 
come a slowdown among local retail- 
ers looking for sites.” 
No slack in remodeling 

The slowdown on the retail level 
has been less pronounced than at the 
construction level because retailers 
have been able to juggle their finan- 
cial commitments in order to main- 
tain internal expansion. At Gray 
Drug, for instance, this has meant a 
reordering of remodeling priorities. 

“We’re not cutting down on the 
number of remodelings,” explains 
Habegger. “We’re just taking the 
less comprehensive—and less ex- 
pensive—ones first, and leaving the 


bigger jobs for later on.” 

At Peoples Drug, management 
opted for the opposite direction. 

“In order to maintain volume and 
profit growth, without the benefit of 
as many store openings as we would 
have liked, we stepped up our re- 
modeling program,” says Eisen- 
berg. “Generally, we can make a real 
difference in store productivity 
through remodeling—and you have 
to keep expanding on your capital, 
one way or the other.” 

But when acquisitions are not fea- 
sible, chains are seeking to contain 
the costs of doing business by limit- 
ing their internal expansion to tradi- 
tional trading areas. This is the case 
at Thrift Drug, for instance, where 
president Jim Armor has decided on 
a “backfilling” policy and at Gen- 
ovese Drug, in Melville, N.Y., 
where management is presently 
concentrating on launching stores 
on Long Island. 

In general, the feeling among 
chain drug store executives is one of 
aggressiveness. But there is also the 
expectation that today’s lag in new 
shopping center development will be 
felt for a couple of years, at least. 

“Right now, it’s just a question of 
pushing and tugging a little harder 
to get good shopping center loca- 
tions,” says Eisenberg. “The loca- 
tions are there if you want to look for 
them. But when it could really hurt 
us is a couple of years down the 
pike”—when demand could catch up 
with supply.

er 


ucts. Some states do, however, make 
it difficult for physicians to forbid 
substitution. For example, these 
states forbid the use of preprinted or 
stamped instructions to “dispense as 
written” or that the branded prod- 
uct is “medically necessary.” Rather, 
such mentions must be written in a 
physician’s own handwriting. 

Physicians permitting substitu- 
tion generally leave the option of 
drug product selection to the phar- 
macist. 

Formularies are another incentive 
toward substitution, but they do re- 
strict drug usage to the products 
listed. 

Studies verify that formularies 
encourage substitution, perhaps be. 
cause pharmacists feel more confi- 
dent with a listed drug’s safety and 
efficacy. On the other hand, formu- 
laries sometimes discourage sub- 
stitution because they restrict the 
number of products available for 
substitution. 

Pharmacists indicate their big- 
gest problem is finding reliable 
sources to supply quality generic 
products. 

In addition to positive formularies 
listing products which may be sub- 
stituted, there are also negative for- 
mularies that list nonbioequivalent 
drugs for which substitution is for- 
bidden. 

In fact two states, Florida and 
Louisiana require both a positive 
and negative formulary. For exam- 
ple, Louisiana’s negative formulary 
lists some 15 noninterchangeable 
drug products for which substitu- 
tion is prohibited. 

Liability 

Many states have also recognized 
the added liability incurred by phy- 
sicians and pharmacists when drug 
product selection is implemented. In 
these states practitioners are ex- 
empt from liability incurred when a 
generic drug is dispensed under the 
state’s drug product selection law. 

Apparently these extra efforts at 
promoting substitution are paying 


DRUG STORE NEWS, September 15, 1980 


Many pharmacists still process scripts by 
hand. 


off, conclusions reached in many 
studies indicate some consumer sav- 
ings, 1.e., In Florida savings aver- 
aged $1.92 per Rx, while in Michigan 
and Wisconsin savings averaged 
$1.23 and 84¢ respectively. 

Other surveys indicate that phar- 
macists have an opportunity, but 
they are not taking full advantage of 
it, yet. 

Physician opposition to generic 
prescribing varies from state to 
state. In New York State the refusal 
rate among physicians to write ge- 
neric scripts ran up to 75%. In Mich- 
igan and Wisconsin, physicians are 
refusing to permit substitution on 
multisource prescriptions about 4% 
of the time. 

Evidence also indicates that phar- 
macists are somewhat hesitant to 
substitute unless a financial incen- 
tive is available. In many states ge- 
neri¢c substitution yields no extra 
profit for pharmacists but creates 
extra work. 

When additional savings must be 
passed on to consumers, it means 
pharmacists must carry duplicate 
inventory without receiving any ex- 
tra incentive. 

The absolute dollar gross profit 
stays the same, but the $2.00 reduc- 
tion in price must be passed on to the 
consumer. 


Extra work is required of the 
pharmacist, primarily in the form of 
additional labeling and record keep- 
ing whenever substitution occurs. 
In addition, nearly all states man- 
date that the pharmacist inform the 
consumer of substitution or obtain 
the patient’s consent. 

Although pharmacists originally 
supported substitution laws, a few 
did recognize the inherent problems 
associated with the change. 

These opponents indicate that in 
addition to creating extra work, 
these laws would increase pharma- 
cists’ liability, bewilder physicians, 
and lead consumers to expect unre- 
alistic savings. 

Despite all the pros and cons sur- 
rounding substitution, it now ap- 
pears to be gaining favor as more 
pharmacists and physicians become 
familiar with their state’s law. 

More important, many states have 
a second generation of legislation in 
the offing that could make generic 
substitution evolve more favorably 
toward pharmacists. 

Many states are finding that their 
laws need revision to make them 
work better. 

Released in January 1979, the 
FTC/F.D.A. draft of a model sub- 
stitution act may be helpful to states 
that consider revising their sub- 
stitution laws. 

At the same time the F.D.A. dis- 
tributed its list of all the drugs it had 
approved along with their generic 
equivalents. 

With states updating their sub- 
stitution laws and others rewriting 
their pharmacy practice acts, there 
is little doubt that regulatory legis- 
lation will continue to change the 
practice of pharmacy. 

Unfortunately it appears the pro- 
fession no longer has the extra 
cushion of cash to absorb future 
costly measures without further 
consolidation of outlets, thereby 
making it more difficult for patients 
to obtain professional pharmaceuti- 
cal services.

WASHINGTON—Final new 
patient package insert regula- 
tions unveiled by Health and 
Human Resources Secretary 
Patricia Harris will require the 
nation's drug stores to begin dis- 
pensing PPIs for nearly 20% of 
all new prescriptions filled an- 
nually beginning next summer. 

The final PPI requirements, 
issued in a surprise move by 
Harris and Food and Drug Ad- 
ministration Commissioner Jere 
Goyan earlier this month, will 
mandate the distribution of 
some 360 million patient inserts 
over the next three years and 
add tens of millions of dollars to 
retail pharmacy operating costs. 

All told, 10 drugs or classes of 
drugs will be subject to the man- 
datory PP! dispensing require- 
ments slated te take effect next 
May, June and July (down from 
50 to 75 individual products and 
drug classes originally pro- 
posed for the F.D.A. patient la- 
beling “pilot study.”) 

In a statement released the 
same day Harris announced the 
final rules, National Association 
of Chain Drug Stores (NACDS) 
president Robert Bolger at- 
tacked F.D.A. for engaging in 
“the classic bureaucratic power 
play of rushing into another ex- 
pensive regulatory program

Sav-A-Lot adds 
convenience food 


By Michael Friedman 

SPRINGFIELD, Mass.— 
Here on the site of a former su- 
permarket, Mall Drug has boldly 
poured a 3,000-sq.-ft. conve- 
nience food department into its 
Sav-A-Lot box store mold, 
thereby creating what can only 
be described as the industry's 
first box-store-style food-drug 
mini-combo. 

“It's not an approach we 
would use everywhere, said 
Mall Drug president Ed Suss- 
man in a recent phone interview 
with Drug Store News. “We had 
the space, and we warted to try 
something different. It’s not 
everywhere that we can move in 
and take over a 14,000-sq.-ft. 
store.” 


In fact, when Mall launches its 
fifth Sav-A-Lot in Tarrington, 
Conn., next month, it will look 
much like the Sav-A-Lot pro- 
totype outlet in Fall River, 
Mass.—about 7,000 sq. ft. of 
selling space, with high-velocity 
H&BA, obtained on deal, domi- 
nating the mix. 

But Sussman is one of the 
more innovative executives in 
the chain drug business, and in 
the case of the Springfield mini- 
combo he broke with all conven- 
tion. 

“Who is to say that a box store 
must contain some depart- 
ments and not others?” he said 
recently.

Dart tries 


‘box store’ 
experiment 


RICHMOND—Dart Drug 
broke in on the box store boom 
with a 10,000-sq.-ft. suburban 
Richmond unit that top chain of- 
ficials are cautiously calling a 
“one shot experiment.” 

The new non-Rx “drug store,” 
tagged “Total +,” is not a pure 
box store operation at all, but a 
hybrid unit combining several 
existing Dart merchandising 
and promotional concepts with 
a heavy dose of deal-oriented 
cut-case specials. 

The result: a juiced up mini 
version of Dart’s standard super 
drug stores offering “every item, 
every day, just above whole- 
sale.” 

Although the Landover, Md.- 
based chain has four such 
Super stores circling the Rich- 
mond market area now, com- 
pany Officials have made no 
attempt to piggyback Total + 
onto these units. 

In fact, there's no Dart identi- 
fication at ail, either in the new 
store's advertising or in the unit 
itself. 

To observers familiar with the 
chain's other retail offshoots, 
however, Total +'s parentage is 
obvious.

2.1 million Sav-On shares of the

The tender offer is the initial 
step in the merger of the Jewel 
Development Corp., a Jewel 
Cos. subsidiary, and Sav-On 
Drugs Inc. The Jewel offer is not 
conditioned upon any minimum 
shares being tendered. 

The second step is the meet-

additional sales from existing

which last year had sales of 
$197 million, expects to have 
close to 250 Sears stores under 


contract. Sav-A-Stop merchan- 
disers will set up, reorder, stock

ments.

DRUGFAIR HAS apparently climbed out of its financial dol- 
drums, posting substantial gains in sales and earnings for the 
second quarter, ended July 31. Sales increased 10.9% to $72.2 
million. Earnings amounted to $268,880, an improvement of 
$681,923 over a $413,043 loss in last year’s second quarter. The 
chain’s net-to-sales ratio climbed to 4.1%.

AUGUST SALES for Walgreen Co. increased 14.4% to $133.7: 
million, as compared to $116.8 million for the same month last! 
year. Except for March and June, Walgreen’s monthly sales have 
shown at least a 10% gain over previous year figures.

NEW YORK—When Associ- 
ated Chain Drug Stores 
launches its annual merchan- 
dising program on Sept. 30, two 
new chains will be among the 
members in attendance, ac- 
cording to the group's president, 
lra Shain. 

Participating for the first time 
in the event, which includes an 
opening day of seminars fol- 
lowed by two-and-a-half days of 
vendor exhibitions at the Grand 
Hyatt Hotel, wil! be the Pitts- 
burgh-based Thrift Drug opera- 
tions and the rapidly growing 
Shoppers Drug Mart string in 
Florida and Georgia. 

Thrift has long been recog- 
nized as a chain drug power, but 
this is the J. C. Penney subsid- 
iary's first association with other 
chains in a buying organization. 
While Shoppers Drug Mart is 
made up of individually fran- 
chised outlets under its unique 
“associate” system, wherein 
every store has its own mer- 
chandise manager, the chain 
will be represented by president 
Al Towle and at least one other 
corporate executive. 

“We're attending the show in 
New York, basically, to ap- 
proach suppliers on a one-to- 
one basis, and go over indi- 


Hyatt 


vidual probiems and oppor- 
tunities. We'll also be gathering 
information for our stores,” says 
Towle, “and making recommen- 
dations when we come back.” 

A bonus for those who have 
come to see the various vendor- 
exhibitors lies in the round of 15 
after-lunch presentations on 
Tuesday, Sept. 30. 

“Topics for these presenta- 
tions include various aspects of 
merchandising, advertising, op- 
erations, compensation—any- 
thing that chain executives are 
involved in on a day-to-day 
basis,” says Shain. “These pre- 
sentations will be made mostly 
by members, but also by invited 
guests.”

Ribordy set 
for central 
distribution 


PORTAGE, Ind.—With cen- 
tral distribution in the cards for 
next year, Ribordy Drugs Inc. 
has already adjusted store plan- 
ning to that future. 

At 12,000 sq. ft. in size, the 
chain's 21st store, located in 
Portage, is smaller and more 
tightly merchandised than oth- 
ers which have opened in recent 
years and which range up to 
17,500 sq. ft. in total area. 

“We're definitely getting 
smaller,” explains Jim Cline, di- 
rector of store operations for 
Ribordy. He hastens to add that 
the shrinkage has not resulted 
in any loss of display area. 
Rather, the coming of central 
distribution has allowed the 
chain to make more efficient 
use of the space available. 

For example, the Portage 
store has only 1,600 sq. ft. in 
backroom, or just 13% of total 
Store area. This contrasts with 
most other Ribordy stores 
which operate with large back- 
rooms to handle the many direct 
shipments from manufacturers. 
(Besides these large back- 
rooms, the chain has also 
leased some warehouse 
space.) 

Secondly, the coming of cen- 
tral distribution will allow for 
more efficient use of selling 
area. “We've tightened up on

BATTLE CREEK, Mich.— 
The new Muir drug store which 
opened here last month is the 
second in the chain to order 
merchandise through Ben 
Frankiin, the variety store chain, 
and the first to include a large 
(2,500-sq.-ft.) Hallmark card 
section. 

The 11,500-sq.-ft. store also 
has the distinction of being the 
largest in the 26-unit chain and 
the company’s third in Battle 
Creek, a western Michigan city 
of about 40,000 population. 

One reason Muir turned to 
Ben Franklin is the size of the 
new store. “We're set up to fill up 
a store of 7,000-8,000 sa. ft., 
but one not so big,” explains De- 
nnis Klenk, president of the 
chain. 

Muir orders what it wants from 
the Ben Franklin distribution 
center in Chicago (there are no 
minimum purchase require- 
ments). The advantage, accord- 
ing to James Muir, vice-presi- 
dent of merchandising, is that 
the Muir chain is able to tap the 
experience of Ben Franklin as it 
expands into new merchandis- 
ing areas. (Ben Franklin mer- 
chandisers helped set up the 
departments it supplies in the 
Battle Creek store.) 

For example, instead of a 60- 
ft. toy department, which is typi- 
cal of other Muir stores, the Bat- 
tle Creek unit has a 120-ft. toy

To Our Friends In The Retail Drug Industry 


By means of this annual publication, we are 
taking the opportunity for the 44th time to say

fered us cooperation during past years.

of the economic factors most likely to influ- 
ence drug store sales at the present time as 
weil as a review of sales trends both nationally 
and by area.

aids, we have added a section on the growing 
importance of cosmetics in retail drug outlets 


We have included also a presentation by H. R. 


Janes, Nielsen Vice President and Manager of 
HBA/Drug Industry Services entitled “The Re- 
tail Drug Market Today... . The Likely Future.” 


We hope you find this Review both interesting 
and helpful for an overall! view of your growing 
industry

Confidence and Buying Plans Strengthen 


Consumer confidence, which has been on a 
declining curve since last fall and plunged 
abruptly this spring, moved up In June. Al- 
though the six point gain was of modest 


proportions, it was the first upturn in eight 
months (Chart 2). Compared with last month, 
a somewhat nigher proportion of respondents 
believe that business conditions will improve 
Six months ahead and more jobs will be 
available. Consumers, however, are still ap- 
prehensive about present business condi- 
tions. 


Intentions to buy also took an optimistic turn. 
Plans to buy improved for all of the series 
included in the survey. Intentions to buy a new 
or used Car increased to 6.6%, up from a prior 
0.U%. Interest in homes reflected a significant 
increase—up from 2.0% to 2.9%. Intentions to 
buy a major appliance also showed a modest 
gain, increasing just over a point to 22.7%. 
The largest gains were recorded for refrigera- 
tors and washing machines.

Also weighing heavily on the consumer 
psyche Is the still climbing cost of living. All 
items were up an average of 27 points,

In spite of the weak trend in the retail 
inventories of the 25 major product groups for 
all drug stores (Chart 17), chain drug stores 
increased average space allocations for 12 
out of 15 categories in this group. This is an 
exact reversal from last year when shelf space 
was reduced for 12 of these same product 
groups. The net gain amounted to an adadi- 
tional 29 linear feet, as only face creams and 
lotions lost space and there was no change In 
the average space allocated to oral antisep- 
tics and laxatives. 


Charts 18, 19, 20, and 21 provide an oppor- 
tunity to examine the average dollar sales 
achieved by dentifrices, disposable diapers. 
deodorants, & headache remedies in eacn 
type of outlet. | 


The average dollar sales rate per linear foot of 
shelf soace increased in 1979 relative to 1978 


in every example in grocery chains and mass 
merchandisers, and for all but one instance In 
drug Chains. By outlet, chain grocery outlets 
achieved higher dollar sales rates per linear 
shelf foot than either mass merchandisers 
(Second) or drug chains (third) again in 1979. 


A different picture emerged when examined 
relative to average dollar sales per store 
(Number of linear feet x average dollar sales). 
Mass merchandisers /ed in three categories 
and chain drug in the fourth—headache rem- 
edies. In fact, chain drug stores topped 
grocery chains In three of four product 
groups. The exception was disposable di- 
apers.

Question— 
What are the key trends that impact the future of drug 
retailing? 


Mr. Janes: 

The first forecast we will show positions the drug 
retail business as a substantial growth market. We 
see the 1985 retail drug market size being about $47 
billion which is about two-and-a-half times bigger 
than the 1975 market size. These numbers include 
inflation rates similar to what we have gone through 
over the past several years 


On a retail dollar basis the growth of the chain seg- 
ment of the drug business is even more dramatic 
Our forecasts assume that chains will continue their 
increased turnover rate per store. By 1985. we antic: 


pate the chain segment of the business being about 
the size of the total drug business in 1980 (Chart 22). 
We should note at this point that the definition of 
“chain to Nielsen is 4 or more stores under a Corpo- 
rate structure. So, some of your customers would be 
included .in our chain classification. We should also 
point out that some industry statistics use an ‘11 or 
more’ chain definition 


We also anticipate that independent retailers over 
$300,000 annual volume will Continue their strong 
trends through 1980 and on into 1985—-a doubling of 
volume in 10 years! With the developments of some 
of the programs being discussed at this convention 
| feel fairly secure that this forecast will be proven 
wrong—strong, large independents can probably 
see more improvement than Nave been built in these 
mathematical extrapolations 


AS previous presentations by us to the NWDA 
nave predicted, the total number of drug stores inthe 
United States continues to diminish. Our current 
forecast for the future sees this reduction CONTINUING 
Dut at a Somewhat reduced rate. The overall growth 
we just Saw, tnen, will be done by fewer and fewer 
stores 


However, the growth in number of chain stores con 
tinues to increase and by 1985 we anticipate 14,500 
so-classified drug stores (Chart 23)

creased to a 45% share while drug had not moved family (Chart 29) 


Any retailer or any organization supporting retailers 
Must recognize in their marketing efforts the needs 
of these very important family groups 


No analysis of demographic information would be 
complete without the very visible development of 
working women 


Again, using Census Bureau estimates, we can see 
that in 1975 about 39.9% of the total work force was 
accounted for by women. We estimate by 1980 that 
almost 41% will be women and that fully 42% will be 
by 1985 (Chart 30) 


Also important in this chart is the middle number in 
each set, the 25 to 34 age group, the prime years for 
purchasing decisions. By 1985. it is estimated that 
61% of all of the women of this age in the country wil 
be a part of the work force Thats a substantia! 
development from the 54% in 1975 


The implications to this development are substantia! 
While these people and their families will still be 
making substantial purchase decisions, they will be 
very busy and hard to reach. Any large-scale mar- 
keting strategy would have to include some method 
of communicating with these working women. Addi- 
tionally, their needs as consumers can be different 
from their non-outside-the-nome-working counter- 
Dart. 


Question— 
Does Nielsen note any shift in the geographic loca- 
tion of purchasing? 


Mr. Janes: 

I'm sure everyone's aware of the well-noted trends 
toward the Sun Belt and away from some of the more 
densely populated areas of the country 


Our own estimates. on possibly a more subtle basis 
_ Show business slowly drifting from the larger A coun- 
ties—those that are the most gensely populated ur- 
Dan areas of the country—to the more rura! counties 
that we described as B.C. and D 


You will note (Chart 31) that in 1972. 42 9% of the 
drug and proprietary sales in the US. traced to 
those very urban counties 

By 1978 that had shifted downward to 405%. al- 
though the dollars obviously increased 


The B counties, the less urban but stil! fairly dense 
areas, accounted for 28.6% of the drug store sales in 
/2 and that has slightly increased now to about 
29% 


Similarly, you will see share Improvements for the 
C & D county portions of the United States 


The implication to a wholesaler here iS the fact that in 
many locations of the country, where business had 
been less developed, we will probably continue to 
see improved business conditions in excess of na- 
tional averages 


Question— 
Is there anything else that YOU might like to point out 
IN painting this picture of the future? 


SSCS CT OTT OE OO OT CR TT TO TT TD TS OER, SAN Te ET, SS Eee eR Ne ee aN RT eT en es ee 


Mr. Janes: 

One thing that obviously comes to mind ts that the 
drug retailing environment appears to continue to 
expand what we might call their product assort 
ments 


Various special studies have been conducted and 
these individual developments are well noted. but 
we might Summarize a few of them. We know that 
optical centers have been an aggressive area for 
some retailers. Many retailers have developed sub- 
Stantial Cosmetic businesses through cosmeticians 
We've known of several developing hearing aid cen- 
ters. Of course, HMO's and home health care and 
nursing homes will certainly be issues in the future in 
the health care environment in general and drug 
Stores In particular (Chart 32) 


We've also seen recent evidence where retailers 
Nave flipped the coin so to speak and taken on the 
promotion of traffic builders that have historically 
been the area of the supermarket grocery store 


i think its only fair to surmise that this expansion of 
activity and product assortment will continue 


Question— 

You ve made several points regarding the interrela- 
tionship of the various classes of trade. Are there any 
otner developments in describing this future retail 
agrug environment that are evolving from this mixture 
of trade classes? 


Mr. Janes: 

One that comes to mind is the development | might 
describe as combo. Just the listings of the names on 
Chart 33 probably define the issue Clearly enough. 


A dual purpose seems to be served by this retailing 
concept. On one hand. Orug stores tend to have 
higher margin |tems but slower turn rates and. there- 
fore, they would like to Improve the turn on their 
Capital invested in inventory 


On the other hand. grocery stores have high volume, 
regularly recurring traffic that gives them very fast 
turning merchandise but usually at low Margin lev- 
els. They would certainly like to have some higher 
Margin items in their product mix 


The combo store development seems to be a natural 
merger of the need for traffic on one hand vs. the 
need for margin on the other hand 


While there's been some Shaking out of this develop- 
ment, | feel it fairly safe to predict a future retailing 
environment that includes substantial amounts of 
combo store development 


We are doing some research at this time trying to put 
together some numbers associated with this devel 
opment, and you will probably see results in various 
trade releases in the not-too-distant future

wide brand availability of numer-

increased and are reported at 
50.4% for this category, accord- 
ing to information supplied by 
Decision Data. 

Significant margin contribu- 
tions were noted for the follow- 
ing tetracyclines—Achromycin 
V 250mg, 61.3%; tetracycline 
(P-D) 250mg, 72.7%; Sumycin 
250mg, 62.5%; tetracycline (ge- 
neric) 74.2%—and, erythromy- 
cins by P-D, 53.1% and generic 
versions, 56.5%.

of ari acne condition or some

F.D.A. concern prompts new tranquilizer regs 


ROCKVILLE, Md.—The 
Food and Drug Administration 
has popped new bioequiv- 
alence requirements for nearly 
a score of key phenothiazines— 
a move that could spark whole- 
sale reformulations of many of 
the country’s most heavily pre- 
scribed tranquilizers and anti- 
emetics. 

The proposed new regula- 
tions, which include batch-by- 
batch in vitro dissolution testing 
requirements, were prompted 
by mounting concern at F.D.A. 
over studies showing marked 
bioinequivalence and “very er- 
ratic absorption” rates among 
various phenothiazine versions. 

In announcing the planned 
requirements, which will apply 


to all manufacturers of the 19 
affected drugs, F.D.A. regula- 
tors cited “well-documented ev- 
idence of actual bioequivalence 
differences among currently 
marketed brands of both oral 
and suppository formulations of 
phenothiazine products pro- 
duced by various manufactur- 
ers. 

As proposed by the agency, 
the bioequivalence require- 
ments will involve both in vivo 
testing in humans as well as in 
vitro dissolution tests for the fol- 
lowing phenothiazines: 
® acetophenazine maleate 
® butaperazine maleate 
® carphenazine maleate 
@ chlorpromazine 
® chlorpromazine hydro- 


chloride 

@ fluphenazine hydrochloride 
@ mesoridazine besylate 
perphenazine 
piperacetazine 
prochlorperazine 
prochlorperazine maleate 
promazine hydrocnioride 
promethazine hydrochloride 
thioridazine 

thioridazine hydrochloride 
trifluoperazine hydrochloride 
triflupromazine 
triflupromazine hydrochloride 
and 

® trimeprazine tartrate. 

The agency decided to pro- 
pose the new testing require- 
ments for all 19 phenothiazines 
as a group “because they are 
members of a class of drug 


products that have close struc- 
tural similarity and similar phar- 
macological, physiochemical, 
and pharmacokenic proper- 
ties,” F.D.A. drug regulators ex- 
plained. 

After citing various studies 
showing evidence of bioequiv- 
alence problems among various 
brands of these drugs, Federal 
Officials added that their con- 
cern was heightened by a “com- 
petent medical determination 
that a lack of bioequivalence 
would have a serious adverse 
effect in the treatment or pre- 
vention of a serious disease or 
condition.” 

Specifically, F.D.A. officials 
expressed fear that psychiatric 
patients, for whom pheno- 


thiazine products are frequently 
prescribed, may be unreliable 
sources of information concern- 
ing the equivalence of differing 
drug brands. 

“Because of the nature of 
these disorders, toxic effects or 
lack of efficacy that may be as- 
sociated with the use of bioin- 
equivalent phenothiazine drug 
products may go unrecognized 
by the physician,” they said. 

Quoting from a 1979 Final 
Task Force Report of the Ameri- 
can College of Neuropsycho- 
pharmacology, agency officials 
Said that “often any aberration 
in clinical symptoms is ascribed 
to the idiosyncracies of the pa- 
tient and rareiy ascribed to dif- 
ferences in drug products.”

CLEARWATER, Fla.—Bur- 
ton C. (Bud) Perfit has been 
named president of the Eckerd 
Drug Co.—a newly created 
post—in a move io strengthen 
management within the Jack 
Eckerd Corporation's drug divi- 
sion, its largest retail subsidiary. 

Perfit, 51, had served as se- 
nior vp-marketing for the 1,068- 
unit chain for the past five years. 

In a related management 
shift, Leslie D. Reagin Ill, 36, 
formerly senior vp-store opera- 
tions, has been appointed ex- 
ecutive vp of the drug division, 
another new post. 

Perfit and Reagin will be re- 
sponsible for all drug store oper- 
ations, reporting to Stewart 
Turley, JEC’s chairman and 
president.

nonunion employees and management.

Dental centers, next to pharmacy save customers up to 20% on bills. 


K mart enters dental area 
with 3 units in Denver 


DENVER—Low-cost family 
dental centers have been 
opened in three K mart stores 
here in the past few months. 

The new clinics, located 
alongside the pharmacy depart- 
menis in each of the three 
K mart outlets, offer general 
denta! services at prices about 
10% to 20% lower than those 
normally charged by private 
dentists in the area. 

Business has grown rapidly at 
the clinics since the first one, in 
the suburb of Arvada, opened 
on July 25, according to a Gen- 
tist who is an associate at one of 
the centers. 

“We're seeing an average of 
100 patients a week, the dentist 
said. “We used to take walk-in 
patients. Now they have to 
make appointments at least two 
weeks in advance.” 

Each of the clinics is staffed 
by three dentists who work on a 
part-time basis. The staff of 


each also has a dental hygien- 
ist, assistant and receptionist. 
All three centers are owned and 
operated by Stewart A. Moss, 
D.D.S., who leases the space 
from K mart. 

The dental center in each 
store contains three rooms, or 
“operatories,” where the den- 
tists do routine dental care. As 
the practice of each center 
grows, the space will be ex- 
panded, according to the den- 
tist. He said it could be doubled 
in size at each store. 

The clinics have been getting 
referrals from some area spe- 
cialists, according to the dentist. 
They, in turn, refer patients with 
more complicated dental needs 
to the same specialists. These 
include dental surgeons and 
orthodontists. 

Hours at the three clinics are 
9:30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. Monday 
through Friday and 10 a.m. to 6 


aturday.

350 new units in 1981 


By Michael Friedman

of a wave of new-store expan- 
sion, the top four drug chains by 
number of stores will be boost- 
ing their combined rosters by at 
least 350 units in the current fis- 
cal year, according to the results 
of a Drug Store News survey. 
This constitutes a growth rate 
of 9.1% for Revco, Eckerd, Rite 
Aid and Walgreen, as compared 
with a rate of slightly less than 
9.0% in the last fiscal year. 
Revco wiil once again ‘ead 
the expansion onslaught with 


120 new stores this year. Eckerd 
is not far behind, with plans for 
100 outlets, while Rite Aid has 
slated 80 and Walgreen at least 
50. 

In addition, other industry gi- 
ants—Thrifty, SupeRx and 
ples—will all be stepping up 
their new-store growth in com- 
parison to last year’s results. 
Thrifty, based in California, 
plans to launch 25 units this 
year, as opposed to 11; Peoples 
will be opening about 40, up 
from 25 the year before, and Su-

DENVER—The expanding 
role that drug stores are playing 
in health care was the focus of 
several talks at the recent phar- 
maceutical conference spon- 
the National Associa- 


sored b 


tion of Chain Drug Stores. 


“Diversified health care can 


help chain pharmacy depart- 
ments preserve their profes- 


sional image by projecting a 


very strong, very visible health 
care image,” Roy White, editor 
of Drug Store News, told phar- 
macists gathered at the five-day 
conference here. 

Increasingly, White said, drug 
stores are venturing into such 
areas as dental and optical 
care, hearing aid centers and 
convalescent and sickroom 
supplies. 

By doing so, he said? they re- 
inforce “the positive health care 
image already created by pre- 
scriptions.” 

White noted another impor- 
tant reason for widening the 
health care image: “Other 
health care areas beyond phar- 
macy can be a pathway,” he 
said, “to the enhancement and 
enlargement of [the pharmacy 
departments] traffic, sales and 
profits.” 


DURANGO, Colo.—Associ- 
ated Druggists, a voluntary 
group of 2,000 drug retailers, 
has unveiled a new multimedia 
advertising campaign, its first 
line of private label products, 
and a merchandising-manage- 
ment training program—each 
designed primarily to give the 
group more national exposure. 

The new programs were pre- 
sented for the first time at Asso- 
ciated Druggists recent annual 
meeting, held here before a 
gathering of 150 AD whole- 
salers, manufacturers and 
guests. 

Like other AD programs, 
these new packages represent 
an attempt to close the gap be- 
tween independent and chain 
operator, by supplying the sin- 
gle-unit druggist with the buying 
power, advertising strength and 
consumer recognition that 
chains enjoy. 

The foundation of AD’s latest 
offerings is a group in-store and 
external advertising pian called 
AD/ID, in which clusters of inde- 
pendents in the same market 
areas group together for a con- 
tinuous chain-type media cam- 
paign under the Associated 
Druggists logo. 

Independents who join AD/ID 
receive lighted outdoor signs 
featuring the AD logo, with a 


But White emphasized three 
important points that chains 


must consider before undertak- 
ing an expansion into diversified 
areas of health care: 
e Acommitment must be made 
to the concept 
e Service and quality have to 
be emphasized. 
@ Management must be devel- 
oped to handle the new depart- 
ments. 

Picking up on the theme of 


expanding health care roles for 


pharmacists and aig | stores 
were Beatrice Adreon, R. 


Inc., and Berkeley V. Bennett, 
partner of Washington Counsel/ 
Medicine and Health. 

Adreon, whose Arlington, 


Va.-based service provides 


ongoing medication monitoring 
and counseling, gave several 
pointers to drug stores consid- 
ering the addition of such a ser- 
vice. 
Less austere setting 

For one thing, she said, “pa- 
tients have clearly demon- 
strated that they are more com- 
fortable, relaxed and receptive 
in aless austere setting.” There- 
fore, she added, the office 
should somewhat resemble a 


blank panel for individual store 
names. They also take part in 
group print, radio and TV adver- 
tising under the Associated 
Druggists umbrella, and mer- 
chandise their stores with an 
every day low-price concept, 
using AD’s Circle of Savings in- 
store materials. 
20-store test area 

Associated Druggists first 
launched the program as a test 
last March in 20 Birmingham, 
Ala., stores, all serviced by 
wholesaler Walker Drug. 

Robert Blackshear, an AD co- 
ordinator, worked with the Bir- 
mingham stores and Walker to 
help set up TV and radio ad 
schedules, in addition to select- 
ing special sale items with re- 
gional appeal. 

The Birmingham group runs 
two print ads each month—the 
first being the traditional Associ- 
ated Druggists monthly ad, the 
second featuring the select,

CLEVELANM-Reveo DS

The expansion of the drug

sales would double within the 
next five years.

would surpass $2 billion in 
sales. It has taken Revco 24 
years to reach the $1 billion 
mark.

erations, according to vp Marvin

9,000 sq. ft., and are thus equiv- 
alent in size to the newest drug 
stores the chain is buildine ‘o- 
day. 

The newly acquired stores 
are located in Hopkinsville (two 
outlets), Georgetown, Hender- 
son, Madisonville, Murray and 
Somerset. 

At the chain's annual meet- 
ing, Dworkin reported a 17.8% 
sales increase to $1.09 billion 
for the year ending May 31, 
1980.

Peoples names new group vps 


ALEXANDRIA, Va.—In a 
move to further standardize the 
distribution of ig cater for 
its retail divisions, Peoples Drug 
has named Nicholas Simon and 
Richard Schuman regional 
group vice presidents at a 
shareholders meeting here. 

Both men will report to Peo- 
ples’ president and ceo, 
Sheldon W. Fantle. 

Simon, formerly group vp of 
the Reed Division, headquar- 
tered in Atlanta, now heads up 
the Reed, Lane and Haag divi- 
sions, which encompass more 
than 200 retail drug outlets. 

Simon came to les eight 
years ago as director of opera- 
tions. He was appointed group 
vp for the Reed division in 1977.

CHAIN STORE EXPANSION ‘80- RECORD 


NUMBERS, BUT IT HASN'T BEEN EASY 


A slowdown in the rate of shop- 
ping center development, due to the 
high cost of construction capital, has 
dented but not daunted the pace of 
new-store expansion in the chain 
drug store sector. Plans for the cur- 
rent fiscal year, in fact, are even 
more aggressive than those ex- 
ecuted last year. 

These are the conclusions of a 
Drug Store News survey of the top 
25 drug chains, presently operating 
some 9,256 retail outlets, or nearly 
half of the entire industry. 

In the last complete fiscal year, 
these chains launched no fewer than 
628 new units, for a growth rate of 
7.4%. In the current fiscal year, they 
are slated to throw out the welcome 
mat in 731 locations—an increase of 
8.0%. 


The top four chains by number of 
stores—Reveo, Eckerd, Rite Aid 
and Walgreen—alone spawned 312 
new units, for a gain of nearly 9.0%. 

But it hasn’t been easy, chain 
execs agree. 

Developers out of funds 

“Developers have really shut 
down, as a result of the high interest 
rates on construction money,” says 
Dave Eisenberg, vp/marketing for 
the Virginia-headquartered Peoples 
Drug operation. “We have even seen 
delaying tactics on projects already 
under way. And because of this foot- 
dragging, we were limited to 25 new 
store openings in the last year. 

“We wanted to open 15 stores last 
year,” says Milton Elsberg, presi- 
dent and ceo of the Washington, 
D.C.-area Drugfair chain. “We were 


only able to open eight. With build- 
ing costs and money costs, loca- 
tions—I mean good locations—are 
not turning up as they have in the 
past.” 

“We have been unable to line up 
new store sites for 1981,” reports Bill 
Harrison Sr., chairman of the Ken- 
tucky-based Taylor Drug company. 
“We’re not dragging our heels, e! 
ther. It’s the developers. With con- 
struction capital costing them as 
much as 3% above the prime rate, 
they’re having their problems.” 

“It seems more difficult than ever 
to find viable, new sites,” observes 
Kdward Habegger, vp/properties 
and real estate for Gray Drug in 
Cleveland, Ohio. “We have not seen 
the ready flow of traditional strip 
center development.” 


Nevertheless, says Habegger, 
Gray has been able to keep its ex- 
pansion plans on track. 

“You have to develop more sites on 
your own,” he points out, “and you 
have to work a little harder. It’s 
times like these that invite the inge- 
nuity of the entrepreneur.” 

Slower openings 

At Rite Aid, the entrepreneurial 
plan of attack has included the con- 
struction of “a few more freestand- 
ing units, in densely populated 
areas,” according to chairman Alex 
Grass. “We have had to be more ag- 
gressive, but we are getting the 
numbers we are looking for. We 
planned to open 80 stores this year,” 
says Grass, “and at the midway 
point, we have opened 38.” 

Jim Armor, president of Thrift 


=

in areas where a chain’s

REVCO DISCOUNT DRUGSI 


New store construction has been delayed by shopping center developers. 


Drug, is also looking out for down- 
town locations as part of his expan- 
sion scheme. “I would strongly 
consider urban locations in Pitts- 
burgh and Philadelphia,” says Ar- 
mor. “I think that urban locations 
are feasible for us at this time.” 

In some areas, though, the cost of 
going downtown can be prohibitive. 

“Rates in the D.C. area are astro- 
nomical,” reports Eisenberg of Peo- 
ples. “To develop a store now, you 
would have to pay $20 to $25 per 
square foot—thank goodness we 
have been in those sites awhile now.” 

By contrast, says Eisenberg, loca- 
tions in the D.C. suburbs can be ob- 
tained for less than $10 per foot, and 
in Peoples’ rural trading areas, costs 
can go as low as $4.50. 

Mall costs staggering 

“In New England, I would say 
that mall locations are the best loca- 
tions,” maintains Rick Weinberg, 
president of Rix Corp., a Massachu- 
setts-based operator of drug stores 
and leased departments. “But those 
locations start at $10 and go up— 
way up. With a store of any size, the 
cost is staggering .” 

In neighborhood strip centers, 
however, costs can drop to only $4a 
square foot, says Weinberg. 

In Texas, Dean Groussman, presi- 
dent of Skillern’s, also feels the heat 
of competition for prime sites. 
“Texas is a growth area, and there 
are more people looking for loca- 
tions,” he observes. “In addition, 
the retailer is getting more sophisti- 
cated about site selection, because of 
rising prices. He can’t take a chance 
on waiting too long for a return on 
his investment. As a result, the best 
locations are more difficult than ever 
to get.” 

The new Skillern’s marketing 
team aims to continue searching for 
sites in “bedroom communities,” 
where the chain has traditionally 
been strong. Although costs usually 
fall into the neighborhood of $8 to 
$10 a square foot in these areas, the 
Skillera’s operation reports that it is 
finding and signing leases in the 
$5.50 to $6 range. 

Malone & Hyde, headquartered in 
Memphis, Tenn., finds that even 
when the sites are available, the 
costs can be too high. 

“We.are having our share of prob- 
lems with developers,” attests Ben 
Walton, director of market research 
for the 160-store retail operation. 
“They are definitely slowing down, 
and they are also getting a little out 
of line in terms of the volume per- 
centages they’re asking. In some 
cases, they have just encroached too 
far on potential profitability, and 
we’ve told them to forget it.” 

However, says Walton, the com- 
pany’s needs for internal growth are 
not as demanding as those of larger 
operations. 

“We have a smaller base than an 
Eckerd or a Revco,” he points out,

“so we don’t have to come up with as 
many new locations—although 
we’re planning at least 20 new stores 
in the coming year. One factor that 
has worked in our favor, is that with 
the slowdown among developers has 
come a slowdown among local retail- 
ers looking for sites.” 
No slack in remodeling 

The slowdown on the retail level 
has been less pronounced than at the 
construction level because retailers 
have been able to juggle their finan- 
cial commitments in order to main- 
tain internal expansion. At Gray 
Drug, for instance, this has meant a 
reordering of remodeling priorities. 

“We’re not cutting down on the 
number of remodeiings,” explains 
Habegger. “We’re just taking the 
less comprehensive—and less ex- 
pensive—ones first, and leaving the 


bigger jobs for later on.” 

At Peoples Drug, management 
opted for the opposite direction. 

“In order to maintain volume and 
profit growth, without the benefit of 
as many store openings as we would 
have liked, we stepped up our re- 
modeling program,” says Eisen- 
berg. “Generally, we can make a real 
difference in store productivity 
through remodeling—and you have 
to keep expanding on your capital, 
one way or the other.” 

But when acquisitions are not fea- 
sible, chains are seeking to contain 
the costs of doing business by limit- 
ing their internal expansion to tradi- 
tional trading areas. This is the case 
at Thrift Drug, for instance, where 
president Jim Armor has decided on 
a “backfilling” policy and at Gen- 
ovese Drug, in Melville, N.Y., 
where management is presently 
concentrating on launching stores 
on Long Island. 

In general, the feeling among 
chain drug store executives is one of 
aggressiveness. But there is also the 
expectation that todays lag in new 
shopping center development will be 
felt for a couple of years, at least. 

“Right now, it’s just a question of 
pushing and tugging a little harder 
to get good shopping center loca- 
tions,” says Eisenberg. “The loca- 
tions are there if you want to look for 
them. But when it could really hurt 
us is a couple of years down the 
pike”—when demand could catch up 
with supply.
